PREFACE 

AT NO TIME in the history of the world has it been more important for Americans to know the story of modern Europe. Most of us have known already that our ancestors, and many of our ideas came from Europe, and that our civilization is European in origin. Thanks to great economic changes in the nineteenth century, our continent was brought nearer to Europe; and so close had become our contacts with the Old World that the First World War, a European struggle in its origins, came almost to our doors, and finally, indeed, engulfed us against our will. But now, even more truly, the Second World 

War has come upon us, with all the force of a tempest, from the Old World. 

How greatly that upheaval will affect us no one can yet know. But, whether we like it or not, we are part of a world order, and we should know something of the history of that continent across the ocean with which our fortunes are so closely linked

To the Teacher 

The story of modern Europe is too long to present with anything like completeness in a single volume; consequently, for lack of space, the period before the French and Industrial Revolutions has been made rather brief and some of the many aspects of Europe's varied civilization have also had to be condensed. It is hoped, however, that the pupils will glean from these pages a fuller acquaintance with the background of the Europe of today. 

Matters of form are often the subject of diverse opinions. In order to conform to a standard pattern, the publishers have felt it desirable that in the matter of capitalization this book should follow the usage prescribed by Webster's International Dictionary. Similarly, in the spelling of geographical names, the preferences given in the List of Geographic Names, compiled by the National Geographic Board, Washington, D.C., have been followed. 

To the Pupil 

In this book,

History is often enjoyed more fully if it is read as a story. therefore, headings and sub-headings have been reduced to a minimum. 

In order, however, to understand the connection between events and realize the significance of many seemingly unimportant characters, you often need guideposts and directions. For this reason previews and questions have been provided to indicate clearly the important topics treated in each division and chapter.

If you read and follow carefully the directions given on page 32 under Gaining Skill, which explain how to use the tools that this book provides, you will not only enjoy this course more fully but you will understand better the events taking place in the world you live in. There are other special helps given you

DIVISION ONE The Age of National Upbuilding 

WE WHO LIVE TODAY are heirs of the past. 

Let us therefore view our inheritance, the contribution made to human progress by some of our ancestors.

In the confused Middle Ages man was chiefly concerned about getting protection and developed a peculiar arrangement, feudalism, to this end. He also secured both physical and spiritual comfort from the Universal Church. 

Gradually, as commerce revived and towns grew, the wealth and influence of the middle class, merchants, master craftsmen, and lawyers, increased. Favoring an orderly government, this class helped the king increase his power at the expense of the feudal nobles.

Not only did modern governments begin to develop but great explorations increased the sphere of European influence. There was a revival of interest in the writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Quite naturally people became more interested in things of this world, and wanted to find out things for themselves rather than to take them on authority.

Meanwhile the Church was split by the Protestant Revolt. The causes of this revolt, as well as of the religious wars which followed, were economic and political quite as much as religious. During the course of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries most Continental countries followed the lead of France in centralizing the government, strengthening the army, and fighting to extend the national frontiers. Generally speaking, France, Prussia, Austria, and Russia increased in power or at least maintained their strength. Spain, Sweden, Poland, and Turkey had declined markedly by the end of this period.

It should be noted also that in England the kings failed to establish absolute power. By its control over the purse, and because of strong democratic traditions, Parliament was able not only to resist the tyranny of the 

Stuarts, but to oust them from the throne, and to establish definitely parliamentary supremacy over the Crown. Of course the triumph of Parliament was a victory for democracy only in a limited sense, since the landed aristocracy controlled both houses of the legislative body.

The passing of time marked a great increase in the comfort and luxury of living among the privileged classes. In England the nobility continued to exert great influence in governmental affairs, but in France members of the middle class increasingly came to hold important positions in the government, and to rival the nobles in comfortable living. The lower classes, on the other hand, continued to live a hand-to-mouth existence, whether in country or town.

A. Ancient Times 

Before the Greeks

HISTORY, AS THE RECORD of man's thoughts Times, and we are concerned more especially and doings, is a story of successive changes and developments until at last we come to man as he is today. In general, it is a story of human progress, though there are times, it is true, when man appears to go backward, and often he seems to advance much more in some ways than in others. Excluding from our attention the so-called prehistoric period when our knowledge of man is obtained from scanty relics, such as weapons, tools, and tombs, we are accustomed to divide history into three principal epochs: Ancient Times, the Middle

Ages, and Modern Times. In this particular study we are going to pass rapidly to Modern The progress of man from his first appearance on earth is, of course, too long a story to relate here, and indeed comparatively little is known about him until we find some written records. When, ceasing to wander about in search of pasture for his flocks, he settles down in more or less permanent habitations, even permitting himself to live under certain laws, then we feel that he has at last begun to be

civilized. Civilization, however, did not begin everywhere in the world at the same time. 

We find it first in Mesopotamia and Egypt somewhere between 5000 and 3000 B.C.¹

Then later we find it on the island of Crete in the Mediterranean, and still later in Syria and Palestine. There was even a civilization in China, which, because of its remoteness, had little influence in the West. Finally, about 1500 B.C., we come to a very famous people, the Greeks, who not only borrowed much knowledge from some of these more ancient peoples but contributed much themselves. 

The Greeks

The Greeks founded a number of states, each formed about a city; and as Athens was the most progressive of these states, it is from Athens that we derive our principal knowledge of Greek ways.

Let us mention a few of the things that made this ancient people famous. 

The Greeks were accustomed to assemble in one body to deliberate on public questions, and since a voice in the government was given to all natives except slaves, they applied what we understand by democracy in a somewhat limited form. Many of the Greeks were traders, and in order to make business easier they used money, and even lent it out for interest. They were also famous for their schools; they produced a number of scientists and men of letters; and they had a real love of beauty, which was illustrated by marvelous works of sculpture. But most Greeks were very independent in their feelings and inclined to be impulsive and even changeable. Hence, instead of standing together, they often quarreled with one another, and consequently became a prey to less civilized peoples who lived beyond their borders. In course of time, after many misfortunes, the Greeks came under the sway of a famous people from the West, I called the Romans. 

The Romans

We first hear of the Romans when the city of Rome was founded about 750 B.C. They were not as original a people as the Greeks, I B.C. stands for "before Christ"; A.D. for the Latin Anno 

Domini, "in the year of our Lord," or after the reputed birth year of Christ. and in fact they copied the Greeks in a good many things, as, for instance, in their government and literature. But they were a more practical people than the Greeks, and they were able in course of time to found a great empire, taking in much of the continent of Europe as well as the northern coast of Africa and part of western Asia. Every man within this empire, whatever might be his origin, was regarded as a Roman citizen; what culture he may have possessed came from Rome, and he lived under the laws of Rome. It would take too long to recall here why this great, unwieldy empire went to pieces. A large portion, with its capital at Constantinople or Byzantium, on the Bosporus, lasted down to A.D. 1453, but the western portion was gradually swamped by barbarians from the north of Europe; and the city of Rome itself finally fell in A.D. 476.

Broken as she was, however, Rome left her influence behind. Fine roads, aqueducts, and other public works afforded examples of what an intelligent people could achieve. 

Moreover, Roman law gave later rulers the conception of a system based on justice; while the centralized system of government shaped by the Romans became the pattern of later states. For centuries, too, the Roman language, Latin, was the language of all educated people, and wherever Rome's influence penetrated, that language greatly affected the native speech. Thus much of the English language is derived from Latin. Finally, the idea of world unity, which Rome had been supposed to represent, came to be carried on by the Universal Church, which had managed to save what was left of civilization after the destruction wrought by barbarous invaders. This brings us to a period commonly known as the Middle Ages. 

B. The Middle Ages 

The Middle Ages are the middle period falling between Ancient and Modern Times. 

It was a period when the world declined in civilization for a time. Yet it had something on which to build in the shape of the scraps of learning handed down by the Ancients, and its generations plodded their way upward until at last the world reached Modern Times.

In the more than six hundred years between the third map on page 4 and this one, Rome was conquered by the barbarians. 

The eastern part of what had been the Roman Empire was now known as the Byzantine Empire and remained independent until the middle of the fifteenth century. Charlemagne attempted to re-establish the Roman Empire in the West, but was only partially successful. He ruled an empire approximately twice the size of the British Isles or somewhat smaller than the State of Texas.

The Universal Church 

The central institution of the Middle Ages was the Church.

And by this we mean the Roman or Catholic Church, as distinguished from the Greek or Orthodox Church, which flourished at Constantinople and furnished the religion of the peoples of eastern Europe. 

While there were certain minor differences between the two, and each had its separate organization, they had a common source in the teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. Little by little the old paganism of the ancient civilized world had died out; so that, aside from the 

Jews, who believed in one god but did not subscribe to Christian teachings, the Christian religion had no rival of any importance until the Moors, in the eighth century, brought the ideas of the prophet, Mohammed, from northern 

Africa into Spain. But Mohammedanism was eventually suppressed in Spain, and its only solid foothold in Europe was gained when an Asiatic people, the Ottoman Turks, took Constantinople in 1453.

But to go back to the Catholic or Universal Church - its great power is principally to be explained by the fact that it convinced the masses of people that only through its teachings could they hope to obtain salvation. The 

Church was also a well-organized body, with the Bishop of Rome or Pope at its head (the institution was known as the Papacy), and it had its own laws, courts, and even a system of taxation. In the eighth century the Pope acquired some land encircling Rome, becoming thereby a territorial prince, for such was deemed essential to his defense in an age when barbarous neighbors might be tempted to attack his residence. The clergy, who performed the work of the Church, were for a long time the only educated people, and that was no doubt

an additional cause of the tremendous influence of the Church. There was not only religious unity under the Church but intellectual as well. Foremost among men of learning were some of the monks, a particular type of clergy members of a religious order which imposed upon its members strict vows and rules of life.

A good deal might be said, if we had space, about the influence of the Church in the Middle Ages. Some popes were forceful personalities and laid down the law to some of the most powerful princes. It was largely due to the papal influence that many princes in the West took part in the famous Crusades, which were efforts to wrest the tomb of Jesus in Palestine from the Mohammedans or Moslems. It is interesting to notice, moreover, that aside from religious wars, the influence of the Church was exerted to restrain violence in what was essentially an age of violence. In general, the Church tried to get people to be less worldly, and to think rather of the future than of the present life. Few people had the learning or the desire to question its teachings. 

Those who did so were known as heretics and might be condemned to be burned at the stake, though by long-established custom it was some prince, rather than the Church, who carried out the dreadful sentence. treatment of heresy, however, is just one illustration of the deep reverence for authority in the Middle Ages. In the field of religion and, for a long time, in the field of learning as well, the Church held absolute sway. 

The Feudal System 

This While the Church gave the Christian world or Christendom a sense of unity for a holy end, politically the world was for a long time cut into innumerable fragments. In place of the enormous Roman Empire there arose a number of states, and each of these states, under a prince who might have assumed the title of king, came to be split into further divisions; here is where we encounter the feudal system. 

Feudalism was another institution characteristic of the Middle Ages. Viewed in one aspect, it was a system of holding land, but it also had a definite military object, and something to do with government as well. 4944

A prince or lord bestowed lands (known as "fiefs") on some of his followers, and to these vassals, as they were called, he owed protection in return for military and other services. 

Chiefly it was a device for giving a prince some fighting forces, though a vassal owed money to his lord on certain occasions, as well as the duty of giving him counsel and of assisting him to judge crimes. The feudal tie was thus really a kind of partnership, the terms of which were fixed by custom. fixed by custom. Hence a prince was not supposed to impose his will on any of his vassals. 

He was not their master. His power was, in fact, strictly limited by the terms of the feudal contract. But had there not been this bond of loyalty, disorder would have been far greater than it was. For some time during the Middle Ages the feudal state was all that served to hold people together. 

There was also an under layer of feudal society that we must mention. While princes and nobles formed the fighting class and the clergy might be called the praying class, the peasants, as tillers of the soil, furnished the

Groups of peasants usually lived about the castle of some lord, and he was supposed to give them protection in return for such services as labor on his estates. 

Any services owed by the peasants are also commonly spoken of as "feudal," since they were rendered to a feudal lord; and originally the peasants were bound to the soil - in other words, serfs. After a time, however, the peasants in England, and most of those in France, secured emancipation, and were able to leave their villages if they chose. For their labor obligations a certain proportion of the crop came to be substituted. 

Such in its essentials was medieval society. 

But not much time elapsed before there were signs of change. There were things which seemed to point to the gradual coming of a new era.

Times. Some writers pick 1492, the date of the discovery of America, as marking their beginning. But dates for beginning periods are usually no more than pegs chosen for convenience. THE RISE OF THE MODERN STATE The Problem of Creating a Modern State 

We noticed what a loose and disorganized thing was the feudal state. Only when substantial unity was attained could this hodgepodge be converted into what is known as a modern state.

There had to be one supreme law to which all the people of a state were clearly subject.

Let us picture the problem as presented by the feudal state. No prince who called himself king, as in France, for example, could be satisfied with such limited authority as feudalism gave him. He would want to wield absolute power, so that his own laws and justice would be respected by all his vassals, as well as the vassals of his vassals, and the thousands of peasants scattered throughout his kingdom. Instead of a band of knights serving for only a stipulated time, he would prefer to have his own army, subject to his will alone. He would want to impose what taxes he saw fit for the support of his growing interests. How, then, was he to accomplish this transformation? How was he to convert his vassals into subjects and in fact bring all the population of his kingdom under his own direct control?

France Becomes a Modern State 

The story of how kings accomplished this purpose is a very long one, and we cannot tell it in detail in these pages. From about the twelfth century the kings of France slowly but steadily extended their power. They seemed to take every chance that was presented to encroach on the rights of their vassals. Sometimes they persuaded the great lords to give them money, instead of the fighting forces required by feudal custom. Then these kings would employ hired soldiers mercenaries as they were called to do their fighting for them. Toward the end of the fifteenth century a French king felt strong enough to levy a direct tax upon his people, and with the money thus obtained he supported a standing army, which was capable of putting down a rebellious nobleman. Sometimes, too, the territory of one of his vassals was acquired by marriage or by conquest, and thus added to the domain of the Crown. By the end of the fifteenth century all these greater nobles, possessing enormous fiefs, had ceased to exist, and the royal authority was felt throughout the land. True, there were lesser nobles (descended from former vassals of the greater nobles) who sometimes defied the king; but most of the time the king's will was obeyed. 

He had his own paid officials, his own courts, and his own army, and all were simply instruments of the royal power. 

Rise of Other Modern States 

There was a similar development in Spain as in France, and much later in the petty German states, which were loosely held together in the Holy Roman Empire, a feeble imitation of the ancient Roman Empire. England, too, became a modern state, though here the greater nobles managed to co-operate with the Crown instead of trying to become virtually independent. From the thirteenth century the English Parliament, consisting of two chambers, the House of Lords and the House of Commons, served as a check on the royal power by virtue of the fact that for running the government the King was largely dependent upon Parliament for money. In short, England tried the experiment of a limited monarchy, while remaining a unified state under a central government and a common system of laws.

Only in certain communities, such as Poland and the Holy Roman Empire (that is, Germany and certain outlying regions), did feudal rights still prevail. feudal rights still prevail. So weak, indeed, was the authority of this elected feudal monarch, the Holy Roman Emperor, that we shall often speak of "Austria" instead; for it was in 

Austria, his hereditary archduchy, that his power really lay. From 1438 the imperial throne was held by a member of the House of Hapsburg; and in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries Spain and Austria were both ruled by members of that dynasty.

When a region comes to recognize one to recognize one supreme authority we have what is known as the modern state; and the modern state began as a monarchy, which, with the exception of England, was becoming more and more absolute. Indeed it was only by virtue of the supreme power of the monarch that the disorganizing character of feudalism could have been ended, order been enforced, and the state unified into a single, compact whole. This was very clearly a sign of progress. 

But there was also a parallel movement we must now consider.

THE RISE OF THE MIDDLE CLASS 

Another factor which brought the world nearer to modern times was the rise of the middle class, as it is called. The name is derived from the fact that this class held a position midway between the clergy and nobility above them and the peasants below them. The middle class was the business element, that is, merchants and manufacturers and, in course of time, bankers. Professional people and officeholders, unless they happened to belong to the upper classes, were also lumped in this same group, the middle class. 

Merchants and Manufacturers all people had got their living from the land, and even the crude manufacturing of such things as clothes and furniture was done entirely by peasants. But after a time some enterprising people began to see the value of trade and of setting up little shops for the purpose of making and selling things. Thus we came to have merchants and manufacturers, and that is how towns emerged here and there usually with fortifications to protect them from the violence of the nobles.

The manufacturers or artisans generally formed themselves into guilds. These "craft guilds," as they were called, consisted of those who were engaged in a certain trade, or, as they used to say, "craft," such as bootmaking or tailoring. Each master artisan, the man who owned his business, employed a few workmen, known as journeymen and apprentices.

The apprentice worked under contract for a certain number of years, after which he was supposed to know his trade sufficiently to become a journeyman, or skilled worker. A journeyman had a chance to become a master if he passed an examination that tested his skill. The masters who made up the guilds were not supposed to compete with one another except in so far as one displayed a greater skill than another. None was supposed to pay any higher wages to his men or to charge any lower prices for his wares than any of his associates. As a rule, the upper classes got their wants sufficiently met by the nearest town. But there was also some exchange between towns; and goods were even brought from across the seas. 

Bankers and Capitalism 

After a while much ready money came to be needed for carrying on trade, and banking was developed. Thus there rose a new element in the middle class the middle class the bankers or financiers.

Bankers made loans on which merchants or others paid interest, and money was thus used in the form of capital. A merchant was no longer forced to limit his business by the amount of cash on hand. He could borrow money on the strength of his personal credit that is, the belief that his business would be prosperous enough to enable him to repay the

At first during the Middle Ages, practically loan when demanded.

THE COMING 

13 

OF MODERN TIMES 

The system which enabled people to get ready money, which other people, wishing a certain return for the use of their money, were willing to lend, is known as capitalism. 

Sometimes people who wanted to invest their money acquired a direct interest in a business by buying shares of its "stock." In that case they were entitled to a share of the profits in proportion to the amount of stock they had purchased. A business which got capital in that way was known as a joint-stock company. 

By the extensive use of capital some merchants conducted large undertakings and sold their products in many lands. Doubtless the richest members of the middle class were some of the bankers. Two brothers, by the name of 

Fugger, at Augsburg, in southern Germany, lent money to a Spanish king on condition of receiving a share in the rich cargoes from America.

Importance of the Middle Class 

It is easy to imagine how the existence of a middle class would make for progress. They supplied the world not only with certain necessities but in many cases with luxuries as well; and the standard of living naturally rose in consequence. Since many of those who were merchants traveled widely, they were able to spread ideas. They thus seemed to infuse a new life into medieval society. Some of the members of this class lent money to needy monarchs and provided the means by which these monarchs built up their military power. 

Many of them, too, served princes in governmental positions, since they were likely to be more loyal than the upper classes; and gradually, too, they were getting an education that rivaled that of the clergy. They were given representation in the old feudal assemblies, such as the Estates General in France and the 

Imperial Diet in Germany, and in England they came to form (with the lesser nobles) a separate chamber, the House of Commons. 

But outside of local affairs the middle class did not acquire political power, since, like the upper classes, they were subject to the royal will.

It was also largely due to the middle class that the sphere of the known world was greatly extended.

THE GREAT EXPLORATIONS The Opening of the Outer World 

The ambition to amass wealth led merchants far afield. We need not review here the story of the circumstances which led to the discovery of America and the opening of the all-water route to India round the Cape of 

Good Hope. These and similar exploits are spoken of as the "Great Explorations." You have probably read that the Spaniards went west; that the Portuguese went east; and that soon afterward the English, French, and Dutch also engaged in voyages of discovery and opened up many lands across the seas. The 

Portuguese brought in the products of the East, such as spices, precious stones, and fine fabrics made in India. The Spaniards made their fortunes from the gold and silver mines found in Mexico and Peru. Farther north, furs and fisheries attracted the French, and to some extent the English, though the latter devoted most of their attention to farming or raising tobacco. But we shall not pause to review the colonization of North America, which belongs, rather, to a study of American history. Here we are more concerned with the bearing of all these activities upon Europe. 

Imperialism and Mercantilism 

Obviously such a movement was of great importance to Europe, which now seemed to embrace the whole world. Sometimes people settled in distant lands; sometimes trading companies merely set up fortified posts, where trade was carried on with some of the natives. In any case, we use the term "imperialism" to designate a movement of national expansion to remote and backward regions. Spain, Portugal, Holland,

France, and England all founded colonial empires; and all these European states were in consequence enriched. 

Naturally enough, national governments now took more interest in commerce, no longer leaving its organization to individual towns. 

In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries there developed the theory of national selfsufficiency. Each nation aimed to produce all that it needed; and to this end a colonial empire was considered of immense value.

Following the lead of Spain, all the colonial powers monopolized the trade of their colonies, while at the same time strictly prohibiting them from producing anything that was likely to compete with the home land. Colonies were supposed to supply not only products for home consumption but also the raw materials needed for manufacturing goods to sell abroad. 

Each country made every effort to sell as much as it could to another, while at the same time imposing tariffs, often prohibitive, on another's goods. Such a policy led naturally to the regulation of industry, already subjected to the strict rules of the guilds, as we have noticed. It was important, for example, that woolen goods of the best quality should be offered for sale abroad; hence it was necessary that the guilds should maintain their high standards, and to that end they were often subjected to governmental inspection. All this system of control and regulation, with a view to making a country economically independent and even profiting at the expense of its rivals, came to be known by the term, "mercantilism" or "mercantile system."

Promotion of Capitalism 

Another important effect of the explorations and imperialism was the promotion of capitalism in Europe. New fields of investment were opened up, such as sugar plantations in the West Indies, and joint-stock companies trading with distant lands. Thanks to the influx of gold and silver from America,

there was now much more money in circulation and more ways found of putting it to profitable use. Since money was plentiful, interest charges dropped from ten per cent or higher in the Middle Ages to as low (sometimes) as three and one half per cent. Banking ceased to be merely an individual or family affair and came to be carried on more and more by a company known as a bank. 

In 1607 - to look ahead a little the Bank of Amsterdam came into being, and much of its capital was used to back Dutch commercial companies. In 1694 the Bank of England was founded, primarily as a means of enabling the government to obtain loans. Because of the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver in large quantities, paper money, as well as other instruments of credit, came more and more to take the place of bullion in business transactions.

Social Changes generally in the making of clothes than wool or silk.

Thus the Great Explorations and the movement we have called imperialism had noticeable effects on the social life of Europe. 

In the meantime another movement had its part in ushering in Modern Times, and that was the Renaissance.

THE RENAISSANCE 

Literally Renaissance means "re-birth," and this movement was, in a sense, a revival of learning, which began in Italy in the fourteenth century. But its significance was broader than that, as we shall see; and nothing, perhaps, had greater importance in shaking up the placid old medieval world. 

A World Asleep 

We must realize that people did little thinking for themselves in the Middle Ages. With rare exceptions the only educated people were

A natural consequence of these developments was a great increase in the number of wealthy men, many of whom in the seventeenth century bought titles of nobility and entered the upper circles of society. Thus to some extent the lines between the upper and middle classes became obscured. But there was a darker side of the picture. The quantities of gold and silver brought from the New World cheapened the value of money, and all prices rose accordingly. This was naturally very hard for the journeymen, whose wages NZ rose very slowly, and in all European towns there was much poverty and distress. 

But for those who could afford the good things of life, the opening of new lands had much to offer. There were new luxuries added to the table, such as the potato and tomato, as well as tropical fruits. Spices were now to be had more cheaply, while sugar came to rival them for seasoning. Coffee, tea, and cocoa also added new delights, and the smoking of tobacco, or, what was more usual, taking it as snuff, became a diversion of the upper classes. Meanwhile houses were rendered more attractive by rugs and articles of furniture made of wood brought from the East; and eventually cotton, because of its cheapness, came to be used much more EX Bettmann lo-pocras

the clergy, and the Church was interested only in such knowledge as had to do with God's relationship with man and the course which man must follow to save his soul. 

This world was regarded simply as a sorry stage until the releasing hand of Death started the soul on its way to the "Great Hereafter."

Naturally, then, people had but little understanding of the marvels of Nature, declaring that these were the acts of God, and that was sufficient. Humble obedience to authority (and for a long time the Church was the sole authority in the realm of thought) was a virtue always stressed in these early days. 

No one seemed to wonder about things. In certain ways the world seemed actually asleep. 

The Awakening and Its Significance 

Yet there were signs as early as the twelfth and thirteenth centuries that people were beginning to waken and wonder a little. An 

English monk, named Roger Bacon, stressed the importance of learning things by observation. Some knowledge, too, was brought into Europe by the Arabs, who at the time were better scientists than Europeans. nally, during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, many classical works, long lost to the world, were rediscovered, and they added still further knowledge. This was, of course, Fi- the Renaissance; and its principal significance lay in its "spirit."

In the first place, speaking generally, the Renaissance altered the individual's outlook upon life. The Ancients, as you may know, had thought little of what was beyond this present life; they sought their satisfaction here on earth. Now the people who read their writings at this time seemed to catch this worldly spirit. They felt a new joy in life and thought of man as something more than a creature seeking forgiveness for his sins and looking solely to Heaven for his reward. The individual yearned to express what was in him, whether this urge happened to be art, or science, or scholarship, or just the love of adventure. Thus the Renaissance stressed a secular attitude of mind. One should make the most of this world (the Latin word saeculum means "world") and give its varied interests as much weight as thoughts of God and the saints beyond.

Such a spirit was obviously suited to men of ambition. It was shown by national monarchs when they pursued the interest of the State above that of the Church. 

It was shown by the middle class when it pursued objects of gain. It was shown by great painters like Raphael, or great sculptors like Michelangelo. The beautiful Gothic churches and stained-glass windows, which were the glory

That same worldly spirit was shown by scholars who pursued investigations, unhindered by traditional ways of thinking. Thus Copernicus, the Pole, gave positive proof that the sun rather than the earth was the center of the universe; and 

Galileo, the Italian, was able to devise a telescope to aid him in learning more about the stars. 

Thus the Renaissance may be said to have encouraged a spirit of inquiry. But it also developed a critical spirit. Many felt that traditional beliefs were not of necessity sacred; some of them might be wrong. Certain scholars began even to turn a questioning eye on religion. We shall presently see the significance of this trend. But first we should also note that the invention of printing by movable blocks the work of two German artisans in the fifteenth century—meant that literature was no longer confined to books written laboriously by hand, and that henceforth new ideas, whether good or bad, could spread with great rapidity. 

Already, perhaps, you can see how the

Renaissance paved the way for the Reformation. 

THE REFORMATION 

A final movement which contributed along with the others to give us Modern Times was the Reformation. When we use the term "Reformation," we must give it a broad meaning. It included the revolt of a large portion of Christendom from the Catholic or Universal Church, and the substitution of other creeds and organizations. This phase of the 

Reformation is what is known as the Protestant 

Revolt - "Protestant" because it represented a protest. But the movement also included an eventual reformation of the ancient Church itself. The final result of all this was the reforming of religion in certain respects, some people reforming even their beliefs, while those who still remained loyal to the old Church reformed and elevated its spirit and thus enabled the Catholic faith to meet the challenge of its opponents. 

Causes of the Reformation 

The causes of the Reformation are too long a story to examine in much detail in a chapter dealing with so many factors that brought on Modern Times. In a body as large as the clergy, it was natural that there should be many who did not lead spiritual lives. Such persons very often are more conspicuous than the greater number of persons who are faithful to their calling. Moreover, it was the misfortune of the Church that among the most worldly were certain popes, some of whom unhappily displayed the all too prevalent vices of their day. Then, too, because the papal expenses were heavy, questionable means were often employed to raise money. Church offices were sometimes sold; and it was said, whether justly or not, that anything could be got at the papal court for a sum of money. 

On occasions, too, the money collected supposedly for a crusade would be spent for a political object, though, in all fairness to the Papacy, it must be recalled that the Pope was a territorial prince, who had to defend himself against his neighbors. At all events, many thought of the Pope as a powerful Italian prince, who extorted money from the faithful more to advance his personal interests than to promote the welfare of the Church of which he was head. That the high standards of the 

Church were often ignored may be judged from the fact that even many of the clergy declared again and again that the Church needed "reform in head and members."

Along with the questionable practices which had sprung up in the Church, there was a feeling among certain scholars that some of the teachings of the Church needed to be reexamined in the light of the New Learning. 

Renewed study of the Bible led some to believe, rightly or wrongly, that the spirit of the Master's teachings was misunderstood. Some felt, indeed, that religion, as it was taught, allowed real devotion to be lost because of the emphasis placed on certain forms and theories. "How pure, how simple," exclaimed Erasmus, one of these scholars, "is the faith that Christ delivered to us!... The Church, divided and tormented by discussions and by heresy, has added to it many things of which some can be omitted without prejudice to the faith." Most

FIGURE 17. LUTHER AT THE DIET OF WORMS 

Which man is Luther? What was his profession? Who sits on the throne? of these men of the Renaissance were unwilling actually to break with the ancient Church, desiring, rather, that certain existing practices, such as pilgrimages to shrines and holy relics, should receive much less stress. Such views, to be sure, were not voiced by the majority of churchmen. Yet this critical attitude of mind tended to weaken, among many persons, that deep respect for its traditions which the Church had always exacted. When people begin to question, there is never any knowing where they will stop.

The Protestant Revolt, in fact, was the result of all these kinds of dissatisfaction. It began in Germany because there the papal exactions were most resented. Moreover, it was 

Germany that produced Luther.

The Reformation in Germany 

In 1517, Martin Luther, a German monk, who had become a professor at the University of Wittenberg in Saxony, made an attack upon one of the means by which the Papacy raised money. His arguments, put into print and distributed widely, met with an almost instant outburst of applause, for it seemed that now at last had come a leader who could voice the German people's discontent. Luther was an earnest and courageous man, but he was also a man of strong emotions, violent and impulsive. impulsive. In the quarrel with the Papacy that followed his onslaught upon the Church, he was soon expressing views that beyond all doubt branded him as a heretic. In 1521, he was summoned to a hearing before the Imperial Diet at Worms, and his works were formally condemned. But the movement which he had started grew in strength until probably more than half the German people followed his lead. Prominent among converts were certain princes, who utilized their position to seize the lands of the Church that lay within their dominions.

Yet there is little doubt that the movement would have been crushed but for the fact that most of the Catholic princes of that period were much of the time at war, and there was also need to stem the advance of the Turks, who were seriously threatening Christendom from the East. (The map, page 25, will

show you how large and formidable was the Turkish or Ottoman Empire at that time.) 

In the end a compromise was reached, the Peace of Augsburg, in 1555, which allowed every German prince to choose between the Catholic faith and Luther's doctrines contained in the Augsburg Confession, as the Lutheran creed was called. The Peace of 

Augsburg, though in a certain sense a compromise, was also something of a triumph for the Protestant Revolt, since heresy thus gained a sort of legal recognition.

The Reformation in England Luther's attack on the Church produced some followers in England, but in any case the Papacy had long been unpopular in that country, and thus the ground seemed prepared for action similar to that in Germany.

The lead, however, was in this case taken by the king, Henry VIII, who, unable to get the Pope to annul his marriage, got Parliament to acknowledge him as sole head of the English, or Anglican Church. Thus England definitely separated from Rome.

Few changes, however, were adopted either in creed or in the form of worship in Henry's day. Indeed, Henry put to death many

Catholics on the one hand, and Protestants on the other. But during the reign of his successor, Edward VI, the Anglican faith, as distinguished from the Catholic, was definitely adopted. Though England renewed her allegiance to Rome under Edward's sister, Mary, this reaction was only brief; and under 

Elizabeth, who followed her sister on the throne, the Anglican creed was re-established and received its final form.

In a few countries in the sixteenth century the population was predominantly Catholic or Protestant. In others there was a division of opinion. Notice which faiths are in conflict in each country. not till somewhat later that Protestantism in that land received definite organization. At 

Geneva, John Calvin, a French refugee from persecution in France, became the founder of another branch of Protestantism, commonly known as Calvinism. 

One of the most conscientious men that ever lived, but also exceptionally stern and bigoted, Calvin seldom if ever allowed his will to be questioned and was cruel and relentless toward all who disagreed with him. Thus Calvinism differed from all the other branches of Protestantism in standing for an unusually stern morality. At Geneva people were forced to go to church, and sleeping during a sermon or criticizing it afterward was punishable by fine. Card-playing, dancing, and the theater were strictly forbidden, and no form of diversion was allowed on the Sabbath Day. 

Fines, imprisonment, and banishment and for graver offenses, death-were freely imposed as penalties by Calvin's judges on those 

who broke the moral law. Spies pried into everybody's business, looking for trouble; and even the minutest things, such as the manner in which women arranged their hair, were strictly regulated.

Calvin also prohibited the observance of Christmas, and he refused to allow churches to be made artistic or vestments to be worn by any of his ministers. The more simplicity, he thought, the more the Christian would turn to God. Before he died, in 1564, he thought he had made Geneva a model city, though, after his stern presence was felt no more, there was something of a reaction against the rigidity of his rule.

Nonetheless, the moral influence of Calvinism was manifest in all the Protestant sects which it produced. Simplicity of worship, a reverential Sunday, and a distaste for frivolous pleasures were conspicuous among the Presbyterians of Scotland and also characterized the English Puritans, who tried, as we shall see, to remold the Anglican Church.

Men of Calvin's faith were also noted for perseverance, since, believing as they did that they were especially favored by God, they felt the utmost confidence in themselves. Finally, Calvinism imparted a spirit of freedom, for its church organization was essentially democratic, and people accustomed to manage their own affairs in the sphere of religion were less contented with autocratic rule in the sphere of politics. It thus had a powerful appeal for the middle class in many countries. 

Spread of the Reformation 

Lutheranism spread throughout Germany, had a strong foothold in Poland for a time, and definitely won the Scandinavian countries, Sweden and Denmark. But Calvinism spread even more widely. Besides making thousands of converts in Hungary, England, and France, it became the dominant religion of Holland and Scotland, as well as some of the Swiss cantons, and gained a number of princes and towns in Germany.

But the spread of Protestantism was ultimately checked, and some of the lands which it had gained were finally lost. Let us now ascertain the reason.

The Catholic Reaction and Reformation 

The success of Protestantism in many lands roused the followers of the old Church, the Catholics, to take action. Gradually a movement got under way to fight Protestantism and regain the lost ground. It was a sort of crusade, waged not against the Moslem but against the heretic. Its inspiration came from Spain, where there was probably the most intense devotion to the Church, and where there was also a very real desire for reform; for a reformation of the Church was, indeed, an important aspect of the movement. 

We may pause here to say that many of the practices in the Church, of which Catholics as well as Protestants had complained, were condemned in 1562 by a great council of the Church, the Council of Trent; and by restating Catholic doctrine and making the difference between the teachings of Catholics and Protestants clear and sharp, this council gave the forces of the Catholic Reaction a greater feeling of unity for the struggle. 

But undoubtedly the greatest instrument of the Catholic Reaction was a religious order, the Company or Society of Jesus, founded by a Spaniard, Ignatius Loyola. These Jesuits, as they were called, were rigidly trained for their work, not only receiving a thorough education but learning to stifle all personal desires and to bury themselves entirely in their cause. They probably made hundreds of thousands of converts, and did the greatest work for the Catholic Reaction. It was chiefly through their efforts that southern Germany and Poland were recovered for the Church. 

But conversion was not the only method of the movement. Force was also frequently applied; and here is where the armies of a secular prince served the purpose. It was the task of Philip II, King of Spain, to lead the forces of the Catholic Reaction in western Europe. Spain was at that time the most

Philip was a man of limited intelligence, and he exhausted the strength of his country by his wars.

In any case, his task was probably too great for any man. He tried to put down the Protestant Dutch in the Netherlands, to prevent the heretic Henry of Navarre from gaining the French throne, and to force the return of England to the Church. It was remarkable, to be sure, that Elizabeth escaped the many plots against her. She felt forced in self-defense to place a ban on Catholic worship and to make attendance at Anglican services compulsory; it was even made high treason to convert any of her subjects to the Catholic faith. In 1587, she executed her rival, Mary of Scotland, whom Philip was seeking to place upon her throne. 

But except for recovering his hold on the southern provinces of the Netherlands (which came to be known as the 

Spanish Netherlands), Philip failed in all quarters; and at his death, in 1598, he left 

Spain a pitiful wreck. She lost forever her position as the greatest power of Europe. (To understand Philip's relation to the rest of Europe, look at the chart on page 22.)

The Wars of Religion 

The Wars of Religion, as they were called, were the collision of the two great movements, the Protestant Revolt and the Catholic Reaction, and the result was a terrible period of plots, persecution, and bloodshed. The struggle involved, at one time or another, Spain, France, England, Scotland, Germany, and even Poland and Sweden. If the drama were made into a series of moving pictures, we might imagine that we could see Mary of England sending scores of heretics to the stake; then the Dutch in Holland, cutting their dikes and flooding their fields to save their towns from the Spanish soldiers; then 

Henry of Navarre fighting a battle to get his throne, his white plumes waving his followers to victory; and again, Mary, Queen of Scots, struggling to keep her hold upon Scotland, or waiting in prison to hear her sentence of death. Or perhaps we might see Elizabeth herself, sister and successor of Catholic Mary, worrying her ministers by her indecision, or making one of her state journeys to court the favor of her people, or sending off some freebooter to pillage the galleons of gold Spain was fetching from the New World. And finally we might glimpse the patient man in the Escorial, that immense, gloomy palace near Madrid, pondering over the great fleet, the Invincible Armada, which he is sending against the English, only to be scattered by the tempests or sunk by the English seamen. And meanwhile, with these graphic scenes before us we might see somewhere in the background massacres of Protestants by Catholics and

Catholics by Protestants. Such is a fleeting impression of a tangled period, when lust for wealth and political ambition combined with religious fanaticism to make war more terrible even than usual.

It is evident that life was cheap in the sixteenth century. The nobility of the period were still passionately fond of fighting, and probably most of them expected a violent death sooner or later. Plots and conspiracies abounded at every court, and it was not an uncommon practice to hire an assassin to kill an enemy. It was not until well into the seventeenth century that the nobleman began by degrees to acquire a polish that properly fitted him to become a courtier. Another fact which added greatly to the horrors of the Religious Wars was the general employment of mercenary troops. These soldiers, made up of foreigners, generally riffraff or adventurers, had little or no interest in the country whose prince they served. Feeding themselves, as they went, and mainly intent upon booty, they devastated fields and plundered towns. Occasionally, too, a garrison was put to the sword, like the brave defenders of Magdeburg in 1631. But perhaps the most eloquent example of the cruelty of the age was the readiness with which people killed one another in the name of religion. The Wars of Religion seemed to prove that Europe was only gradually emerging from the bigotry and roughness of the Middle Ages.

It was Germany that staged the last and undoubtedly the most terrible of the Wars of 

Religion, the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648).

FIGURE 22. GUSTAVUS ADOLPHUS (1594-1632) OF SWEDEN 

Historians speak of this Swedish king as a great general and a wise statesman. See what you can learn about his life and then decide whether you agree with this opinion. 

The Peace of Augsburg had broken down because the government of the Holy Roman Empire had been too weak to enforce it. 

Catholics and Protestants contended bitterly for the mastery until at last they took up arms, and all Germany became involved. Indeed, most of Europe itself became involved, as foreign powers intervened, using religion all too often as a cloak for political aims. Thus 

Germany became the battleground of Europe. 

When Christian of Denmark had failed in his efforts to aid the German Protestants against the victorious Catholic forces, Gustavus Adolphus, King of Sweden, adventurous, ambitious, and fervently Protestant, invaded Germany, and was successful until his untimely death in 

1632. Three years later Catholic France entered the war, but as she pitted herself against the Catholic Emperor, it is obvious that her object was political and not religious. 

She sought to keep the Emperor from dominating Germany. Two foreign powers, France and Sweden, decided the issue of the war, which ended finally in the Peace of Westphalia (1648). Practically every part of Germany had been ravaged; and it is said that the country went back in civilization a hundred years.

The Peace of Westphalia 

The Peace of Westphalia, which confirmed in general principles the Peace of Augsburg, left Germany almost equally divided between the two great battling religions. Roughly speaking, northern Germany remained Protestant, and southern Germany, Catholic.

The old Holy Roman Empire, which had proved so utterly helpless to protect Germany from foreign invasion, now ceased to have any importance, the Emperor centering his power in his hereditary possessions on the Danube, while all the German princes were independent in all but name. Meanwhile France gained territory on the Rhine, and Sweden got possessions across the Baltic in northern 

Germany. The outstanding result of the

Wars of Religion was the fact that Protestantism had managed to survive; and hence the 

Reformation as a broad religious movement had been achieved. And now what is the importance of the Reformation? 

Results of the Reformation

A general result of the Reformation, which included, we must remember, a reformation of the ancient Church, was the development of a clergy (or, as Calvinists would say, a ministry) more earnest in the performance of their work; and it is probable that for a time most of the people in western Europe were more religious. But that very zeal for religion and the compulsion in many cases to fight for one's faith led to a much more bigoted attitude, Catholic or Protestant, than the old Church had shown. Few as yet believed in toleration as a principle. Instead of one church, there were several different churches, each professing to stand for true Christianity; and those who did not conform to the ruler's religion were always liable to persecution. 

Moreover, before religious peace had come again, a series of terrible wars had wracked Europe, as we have seen.

It is only after this bloody period is over that one may realize the full importance of the Reformation. The fact that there were several forms of religion being taught meant that people were beginning to exercise their judgment in the matter of religion. Whether a privilege of that sort is good or bad depends upon whether one is a Protestant or a Catholic. 

But at least the fact that several religions managed to hold their own made an attitude of tolerance easier of attainment; and when, in a later period, certain writers held the view that nothing, human or divine, was really settled, the time of religious tolerance had finally dawned. It is chiefly by looking ahead that one sees the Reformation as a religious revolution, ultimately bringing religious liberty to man. 

Finally, the Reformation may be said to have a broad political significance. By shattering forever the medieval conception of the world, it put the finishing touches on the creation of Modern Europe. No longer would national monarchs look to Rome as an influence making for unity and peace. There was no longer in western Christendom a common church with a common head. Hence the various national states, such as France, Sweden, and so on, must henceforth adjust their differences as best they could; and on them must rest responsibility for peace. There was nothing even approximating a superstate. 

Each state was legally sovereign; that is, it recognized no higher power than itself. And that unfortunately meant that the world, considered as a whole, was really in a state of anarchy, nations being free to fight one another, without any more respect for their plighted word than they chose to observe.

Such is, perhaps, the chief tragedy of Modern Times. 

In the meantime, let us become more closely acquainted with the people of Europe during this period of religious upheavals. 

D. How People Lived in the 

Sixteenth Century 

Domiciles, Dirt, and Diet

The common people of the sixteenth century were the peasants and humbler artisans. The peasants lived in little thatch-roofed huts with

THE COMING OF 

27 

MODERN TIMES 

no more than two rooms and perhaps a single window. Even the pigs and cattle were often housed under the same roof. There was no furniture save, perhaps, a rude bench and a wooden chest, often no fireplace at all, and nothing to sleep on but straw. The diet of the peasants consisted mainly of bread and beer, perhaps some salted meat during the winter, and certain of the commoner vegetables and berries. Most peasants, in spite of long hours of toil, were barely able to subsist, and famines were not uncommon. In

The well-to-do people were the wealthier merchants and artisans and most of the landed aristocracy. Their dwellings, whether in towns, as in the case of the merchants, or in the country, as in the case of the nobles, were sometimes very handsome. In countries, like 

England and France, where feudalism had declined, they began to build their mansions to look like homes rather than castles, as had formerly been the case. The interiors (including kitchens, see page 26) were quite ornate and the furniture beautifully made. Carpets, however, were still an uncommon luxury. most houses the floors were still strewn with rushes, and, as these were seldom changed, the dirt undoubtedly accumulated for months. 

Glass was commonly used now in the windows, but as it was still rather costly, windows were not very numerous. A stove or open hearth furnished the heat, but the great baronial halls and the interior of churches must certainly have been bitterly cold during the winter. 

There was, of course, no running water in the homes. All water had to be brought from a near-by well, but in any case there was very little drunk and still less used for washing.

Even the upper classes seldom bathed; and no one seemed to mind any of the discomfort that resulted. An English writer of the nineteenth century penned the comment, "Gentlemen, there can be little doubt that your ancestors were the Great Unwashed." The nobility of the day could stand one another only by the liberal use of perfumes.

Because of lack of sanitation, epidemics were very frequent. All sorts of things were thrown into the streets, and the odor of such towns as Paris and London was notorious. In certain towns it was the rule that refuse should not stand in front of a house more than a certain number of days, but the narrow streets were ⚫ so filthy that few people went about at night; for there was as yet no street-lighting, a fact which also made holdups frequent. As carriages were only just beginning to appear, most of the aristocracy still went about on horseback, a lady often sitting behind her husband.

Medical science was in its infancy. Doctors knew little about the treatment of disease, and the commonest "cure" was bleeding. Luther adopted any sort of remedy for his ills that anyone chose to suggest, and some of these concoctions did much more harm than good. 

Such doctors as there were seemed to confine their practice to the court and the upper classes. Nature alone had to minister to the poor. 

A nobleman's household was large. Besides his own family there were stewards and clerks, scores of servants, and not infrequently, a corps of musicians. The younger sons of noblemen often made up the retinue of some lord, sharing his pleasures and even performing quite menial services without any loss of dignity. Thus we read of a young nobleman who did all the carving of meat at a lord's table.

In the households of the upper classes breakfast was probably served in bed. Dinner was held in the great hall, usually an hour or two before noon. It was a heavy meal, consisting of several courses. Meat, game, fish, and eggs, as well as different vegetables, such as lettuce, spinach, cucumbers, and cabbage, were placed on the table, and fruits, such as apples, peaches, and oranges, were passed around later. As coffee, tea, and chocolate were still unknown in western Europe, noblemen drank a great deal of wine - often as much as a quart at a single meal. Tobacco, which was just beginning to be known, was looked upon chiefly as a drug. The English were considered unusually heavy eaters, and they seem to have sampled almost everything, even porpoise being a delicacy on some tables. 

People for the most part ate with their fingers, though spoons and knives were beginning to come into use, and wooden plates were gradually supplanted by china. 

---

MODERN TIMES THE COMING OF Costume 

The nobility in those days dressed in very gay attire, and the male of the species was more gorgeous than the female. Bright colors were the vogue, especially at the court of 

France. Men wore long jackets known as doublets, at one time belted and flaring out like skirts, while a long mantle or cape, lined with silk, was sometimes thrown over the shoulders. A huge pleated collar, known as a ruff, enclosed the neck. Trousers were short and often very full, and silk stockings were worn the full length of the leg. Shoes were of leather or velvet. The hat was usually of velvet with sometimes a feather in front or on the side. Gloves were long like gauntlets and usually of fine leather, beautifully embroidered. Silk, satin, velvet, and fur were all used in making a gentleman's costume, and the doublet was usually embroidered and sometimes adorned with jewels, not to mention a series of gold or crystal buttons. Men often wore necklaces, too, as well as rings for ears and fingers; and their swords were jewelhilted. (The first sketch in the group below will help you to imagine how such a man looked.)

Women laced in their waists, which, by the time of Queen Elizabeth, were very small.

The skirt, as a rule, flared and hung to the ground, and for more formal occasions tapered into a train. Toward the end of the century, skirts became hooped, and a lady could rest her arms on her skirt quite as if it had been a table. (A picture of a woman dressed in this fashion appears below.) The hair was usually dressed in little curls about the face, and headgear at first was something like a hood, later to be replaced by a stiff hat. Elizabeth in her later years wore an auburn wig to resemble the color of her hair as a younger woman, and the fashion of wearing false hair was taken up by others.

Women, like men, wore a ruff, but later this was abandoned for a stately lace collar, broad and high at the back of the neck. Shoes were usually of satin and sometimes cut out at the instep to show the silk stockings of the wearer. 

Jewelry was worn by the upper classes in great profusion. Some women wore so much on grand occasions, in addition to their heavy clothes, that they actually could not walk and had to be carried. Elizabeth being extremely vain, her skirts were covered with embroidery and literally studded with jewels. Every lady of quality felt it necessary to have an immense number of gowns, and probably at no period was there more extravagance in dress than in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. But, as a rule, women were rather less colorfully

Manners and Diversions

In the sixteenth century, manners were still medieval, that is, rough. Some monarchs, it is true, attempted a little etiquette. (For example, everyone was required to kneel before 

Elizabeth, and one French king, Henry III, had homage paid even to his sword.) But, for the most part, society took little pains to cultivate any polish. Manners were especially crude among the Germans where dinner parties often ended by the guests pelting one another with crusts and bones. Little respect was paid to women during this period and they were expected to be always submissive to their husbands. Even wife-beating was perfectly legal and not uncommon.

Obviously there was little self-control in "polite society." Noblemen indulged in frequent intrigues and acts of violence. Little value was placed upon life. Not only were duels frequent, but the hiring of assassins to kill an enemy was a very common practice, as we have said. To a large extent such crimes were left unpunished, since a king, save, perhaps, in England, was hardly strong enough to lay down the law to his nobles, and even in England, a nobleman with an escort of armed knights sometimes forced a court of justice to yield in his favor. We should realize, too, that kings themselves displayed great ruthlessness at times. Some of the people whom 

Henry VIII brought to the block were not even given the benefit of a trial. The violence one associates with the Middle Ages not only persisted but was sometimes practiced even by the State.

However easy the law may have been with the nobles, for commoners the royal justice was often cruel, and torture was freely used to extract confessions or information. As stated by one writer, "blinding, branding, scourging, cutting off noses and ears, and amputation of hands were among the milder punishments." 

One of the commonest forms of capital punishment was breaking on the wheel. A great many petty crimes were punishable by death. 

At Augsburg, in Germany, for instance, a woman was burned to death for adulterating spices, an interesting relic of the medieval insistence on the quality of the goods. Suffering and death apparently contained no horrors for people of the sixteenth century, for ladies of the highest rank attended the public executions.

Wickedness was probably not more general

TIMES THE COMING OF MODERN 

then than now, but people were more open about it. Language was apt to be coarse, and there was nothing too disgusting for one person to call another, whether as a joke or as an insult. The virtues of good taste and refinement belonged, rather, to a later period. 

Family life in the upper circles of society was hardly likely to be happy, for marriage was contracted for convenience rather than prompted by inclination. Some matches were made for political objects, others for financial reasons. Few husbands pretended to be faithful to their wives, and though women were usually shielded, there were some whose private lives were as bad as their husbands'. In the event that a man grew tired of his wife or wished to take another for political reasons, he could sometimes get his marriage formally annulled, but as this privilege in Catholic countries could be granted only by the Pope, it was difficult and always expensive to obtain. 

In certain Protestant countries, but not in England, divorce came to be recognized as an alternative solution, though Luther, following Old Testament examples, went on record as preferring bigamy in exceptional cases. In

Holland the civil marriage, that is, marriage by a public official, was established, but in most countries marriage was still exclusively an affair of the Church. Families were generally large, though the death rate among children was very high.

SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

Aside from fighting, the nobility of the sixteenth century found their chief diversions in jousts or tournaments (which, however, went out of fashion during the last half of the century along with armor), hunting, tennis, cards, and dice. There were also court entertainments, especially in France, where gentlemen and ladies mingled for dancing or elaborate masquerades; but Elizabeth, always jealous of any rival, kept her court almost exclusively for men. Some forms of diversion display the brutality of the age. Lunatics were sometimes employed at house parties to afford amusement, and the burning of alleged witches gave the public occasional diversion. 

The amusements of lesser people were much less costly. Many of the towns had pleasure grounds, where spear-throwing, archery, running, and wrestling were freely enjoyed. In 

England, pageants (costume affairs to illustrate certain themes) and even strolling actors were a source of entertainment for the common people. Medieval superstition lingered on in most of Europe, and most people still believed in a personal devil. Nearly everyone felt that his future could be told by the course of the stars (that false science known as astrology), and many princes determined their conduct accordingly. People believed in revelations of all sorts, and the time was yet to come when the thought of the next world had ceased to haunt men's minds.

CHAPTER II The Modern State as an Absolute Monarchy: 

THE EMERGENCE OF GREAT POWERS IN EUROPE - THEIR STRUGGLES AND AMBITIONS 

How did Bourbon France become the most powerful state in Europe? 

What were the characteristics of the absolute monarchy (France under Louis XIV)?

To what extent were the rulers of Prussia, Austria, and Russia able to organize their states after the French pattern?

Why were the great questions of parliamentary supremacy and religious toleration settled differently in England from on the Continent? 

YOU WILL REMEMBER that the chief means by which the modern state evolved from feudal disorder was the development of the royal power. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries absolute monarchy on the Continent became realized in practice. Strong within, the greater nations then proceeded to expand, seeking to obtain better geographical positions. 

During this period England alone of the "great powers" refused to organize herself as an absolute monarchy. Here, indeed, was the tradition of a limited monarchy (the united one-law state under a constitutional monarch); and though it is true that even here the monarch almost succeeded in adopting the Continental type of government, the English people, in the end, settled the issue by definitely placing in Parliament the supreme political power.

France under the House of Bourbon was the leading modern state of the seventeenth century, and she set the clearest example of the strength, as well as the weakness, of absolute monarchy. 

A. The Ascendancy of France in the Seventeenth Century The Work of Henry IV Out of the Religious Wars in France there emerged a new dynasty, the House of Bourbon, the last of the previous dynasty having died in 

1589. The first of the Bourbon kings, Henry 

IV, had been earlier known as Henry of

Under this king the power and magnificence of absolute monarchy reached its height. He it was who announced simply, "I am the state." Who paid for the royal display of gorgeous jewels and immense palaces staffed with hundreds of servants? 

Navarre, leader of the Protestant cause toward the end of that struggle. Having at last obtained the throne after hard fighting, he changed his religion and became a Catholic, since the great majority of his subjects belonged to the old faith. Yet, true to his old comrades, he issued the so-called Edict of Nantes, in 1598, giving the Huguenots,' as the French Calvinists were called, freedom to worship as they pleased in certain places, and even a number of walled towns for their own defense. Henry was a very popular king, jovial and kindly, yet firm and practical. He restored his kingdom, wracked by thirty years of bloodshed and disorder, to the condition of a prosperous and contented state. The Work of Richelieu and Mazarin

Richelieu knew that no such object could be attained until he had made the King absolute master at home. When the Huguenots 

When the Huguenots rebelled (for some of their leaders were nobles), he wisely took away their walled towns, though he was liberal enough to leave them their religious rights. He also destroyed the castles of the nobles, and whenever they dared to defy him, he had them beheaded. At last the nobles were made to feel the power of the King's law. Richelieu even established certain officials, known as intendants, throughout the kingdom to enforce the royal will. Thus

France was now centralized as never before an absolute monarchy in fact as well as in theory. 

In foreign affairs Richelieu sought to obtain for France the "natural boundaries": the

Rhine, the Alps, and the Pyrenees. A keen diplomatist, he took advantage of the Thirty Years' War to give his support to certain princes, such as Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, in their struggle with the Emperor; and in 1635 he finally brought France herself into the war. 

Though his policy was successful, neither he nor Louis XIII lived to see the fruits of his work, for the Cardinal died in 1642, and the 

King, the following year. Fortunately for

France, Richelieu's policy was carried on to a successful conclusion by his able pupil and successor, Cardinal Mazarin, the chief minister during the minority of Louis XIV. By the Peace of Westphalia with the Emperor, in 1648, France secured certain territories in the east, including most of Alsace, which gave her a stretch of frontier on the Rhine. By the 

Peace of the Pyrenees with Spain, in 1659, she acquired certain provinces on the French side of the Pyrenees, thus making that range a natural frontier in the south, and likewise certain districts in the northeast, which widened the distance considerably between 

Paris and the Spanish Netherlands. Only at one point had Mazarin failed to reach his objective. He was unable to get the districts of

Savoy and Nice, which would have made the Alps the boundary on the southeast. But beyond a doubt France was now the strongest power of Europe.

The Ascendancy of France under Louis XIV 

Louis XIV, who had come to the throne at the age of four in 1643, was twenty-two years old when Mazarin died in 1661. As a child he had been badly spoiled, and had had but little training for his coming responsibilities. 

But now, on Mazarin's death, he at once took the reins of power into his hands, and gave his whole attention to the duties of his position. 

Tall, graceful, and majestic in bearing, Louis seemed every inch a king. One of his courtiers has told us that one had to get used to his presence in order to avoid feeling embarrassment; and certainly Louis never forgot for a single moment that he was king. Yet he was far from a mere ornamental monarch. 

Though a man of hardly more than average intellect, he worked hard and long, and in that way set an example to his ministers. "One must work hard in order to reign," he once remarked, "and it is ingratitude and presumption toward God and injustice and tyranny toward men to reign without hard work." 

He was too sure of himself ever to feel that he needed any minister to exercise the chief responsibility he wanted no Richelieu! he was exceedingly well served by such men as Colbert, who had been trained in the service of Mazarin. The kingdom was more rigidly centralized than ever, the intendants occupying permanent positions throughout the land enforcing the royal will. 

But

Thanks chiefly to Colbert, who managed the finances, the industrial and commercial development of the country made great strides, and much attention was given to colonization in North America. 

Louis had an exalted conception of kingship.

He believed that he was divinely authorized to rule, and he exacted a loyalty from his subjects that amounted almost to worship. 

Court etiquette was made more rigid than ever. Above all, Louis made a business of having the most magnificent surroundings.

At the huge and stately palace which he constructed at Versailles (about eight miles from Paris) was gathered his sumptuous court. 

Now the court was composed of nobles. 

Louis gave them no longer a chance to do any plotting against the Crown. While he had them all at court, he kept them under his eye; and he noted every absence. Moreover, garbed in their beautiful costumes, they formed the proper background for his own unique splendor. Some of them, indeed, were forced to perform very menial services on the theory that it was an honor to serve the King. 

When he rose at eight, there were specially favored courtiers who handed him his garments. Then, when he attended mass, his courtiers followed him; and when, this service ended, he entered his cabinet to hold his council, they waited outside the doors until the conference was ended. It was often very wearisome, as there were few chairs to sit on, and in winter the great corridors were very cold. Thus low had fallen the sons of the men who had once defied Richelieu.

Yet Louis's inordinate vanity cost his country a terrific price. The extravagance of his court and the cost of his numerous wars brought misery to his people. Unwilling, moreover, that any of his subjects should worship in a manner different from his own, he reversed the wise policy of Henry and

Though he gained some notable success in his wars (he extended the eastern frontier, even acquiring Franche- Comté, and later, the rest of Alsace), the time came when he had to face a formidable resistance from nations which feared to lose their independence, and France became exhausted under the strain. Before the end of the reign the sun of Bourbon France had lost much of its splendor. In 1715 the great king died at the age of seventy-seven after the unprecedentedly long reign of seventy-two years. He was succeeded by a great-grandson, Louis XV (17151774).

The Origins of Prussia 

The modern state of Prussia evolved from two separate states, Brandenburg and Prussia, each of which had its own history. 

Brandenburg had long been the possession of an ambitious family, the House of Hohenzollern. Its ruler had held since 1413 the title of "elector," which meant that he was one of a group of princes which had the right to elect the Holy Roman Emperor, of whom he was nominally a vassal. During the troubled period preceding the Thirty Years' War,

Brandenburg extended her dominions, which included a solid footing on the Rhine. 

Prussia was originally an ecclesiastical state.
