Brandenburg-Prussia, as this state must now be called, was able to acquire most of Pomerania in the course of that dreadful war. It was still a rather weak state, however, its two main divisions, Brandenburg and Prussia, being separated from each other by the kingdom of Poland.

The Rise of Prussia 

The first distinguished ruler of Brandenburg-Prussia was Frederick William, generally known as the Great Elector. Finding at his accession, in 1640, a poor country, a backward people, and a state still under feudal domination, he achieved a remarkable work of reconstruction. He promoted industry, tamed the nobles, established a centralized government on the model of that of France, and formed a standing army, large out of all proportion to the resources of his country. Rough, unscrupulous, and domineering, the Great Elector made Brandenburg-Prussia a modern state. heathen natives of that region. These knights (shown on the march in the picture on page

Prussia, under the grand master of the order, became a very powerful state, much feared by all her neighbors; but later she declined, and lost part of her dominions (West Prussia) to the

King of Poland. In the sixteenth century the knights renounced their faith and became Lutherans. The grand master became then an hereditary duke, and the knights, founding families, became the landed aristocracy of Prussia.

His son and successor, Frederick William I (1713-1740), a gruff and boorish person like the Great Elector, spent much of his time with his army, and he made a practice of getting the tallest soldiers he could find. Since he was also exceedingly stingy, he left plenty of money, as well as an efficient army, to his able son and successor, Frederick the Great. 

Little by little Prussia had grown considerably in extent (as you will see for yourself on the maps, page 42) under her cautious but grasping rulers. But it was left for Frederick the Great (1740-1786), a man of great military talents, to make Prussia a really formidable power.

As the result of a struggle with her great German rival, Austria, he acquired the province of Silesia, thus obtaining a mountain barrier on the south; and later, by taking part in the dismemberment of Poland, he got the territory required to link Brandenburg with (East)

Prussia. Thus his kingdom became a much more compact state. 

Frederick the Great was one of the most celebrated rulers of his day. By nature hard and ungenerous, with something of a contempt for most of mankind, he was, however, a very painstaking ruler, and, unlike any of his predecessors, a man of wide learning. Thanks to his achievements, Prussia was looked upon as a power of the first rank.

The Progress of Austria Austria was the principal possession of the 

Hapsburgs, and her ruler, as you remember, bore the title of Holy Roman Emperor. Since the Thirty Years' War had ended forever the dream of making Germany a unified state under their sway, the emperors centered their interests in Austria and Hungary, the latter being recovered from the Turks about the beginning of the eighteenth century. 

Austria's misfortune, however, that some of her possessions, the Milanese and the Netherlands (both acquired in 1714), lay at a considerable distance from Vienna, the seat of government; while all her numerous possessions were but loosely held together. c. The Rise of Russia 

Russia Before Peter the Great 

Russia was formed of a number of different states which had been welded into one, and the ruler was known as the czar which is the Slavonic form of caesar. Most of her civilization, such as it was, had come from the ancient Byzantine Empire, which had lasted down to 1453, and the rulers of Russia regarded themselves as the true heirs of the Byzantine emperors and the protectors of the Orthodox faith. But the Russians did not advance in civilization like the people of the West, since for more than a century and a half they were subject to an Asiatic tribe, known as the Ta- 

Down to the time of Peter the Great, despite some occasional intercourse with the West, Russia continued to face eastward. tars. 

The czars ruling at Moscow in central 

Russia were powerful rulers if they happened to be men of strong personality. But ordinarily the Russian nobility had a great deal of power. They filled most of the offices, and on some occasions were able to lord it over the czars themselves. It was through their influence, moreover, that the peasantry had been converted into serfs. The Russians lived almost entirely apart from Europe. Their only outlet to the sea was in the frozen north the White Sea, as it was fitly called, for it was covered with ice three quarters of the year.

AS AN seemed to care for nothing but youthful pleasures. Then all of a sudden, his brother having died, he decided to assert himself, and in 1696 he began his personal rule. Almost his first act was to engage in a Turkish war; and he got the port of Azov though he was forced to relinquish it later. 

Peter was one of the most striking personalities that ever sat on a throne. He was, to begin with, six feet, eight and a half inches in height, with a splendid physique and exceptional muscular strength. His will and his temper seemed to fit these vast proportions, and it is hardly to be wondered that people feared him. Like most Russians of his day,

Peter lacked all sense of refinement. He was slovenly in his dress and coarse and vulgar in his manners; and none but a very strong man could have stood the long career of dissipation in which he indulged. His sense of humor was clownish. He delighted in offending the dignity of people, as when he forced an ecclesiastic to caper about in fancy dress. He loved a practical joke, and once on All Fools' Day he sounded the fire alarm, and made the people of St. Petersburg turn out in a veritable panic, thinking the city was on fire. He was absolutely insensible to the feelings of others, and anyone who crossed his will did so at his peril. 

Yet at least it can be said that he was not crafty or deceitful, and he was capable of being friendly and even gracious. He had, apparently, never learned any self-control, and he usually followed his impulses good and bad. 

He was also very restless. He was eternally doing something. Not a man of exceptional intellect, he was, nevertheless, eager to know the world and try out every novelty he saw.

The Work of Peter the Great The Europeaniza tion of Russia

How did Peter manage to learn the ways of the West? Partly by bringing in foreigners. 

He invited Western artisans to come to Russia and gave them every encouragement in their work. Then he got many of his nobles to send their sons to the West to be educated. He also gained a seaboard on the Baltic, and opened closer trade relations with the West. 

He built a new capital, St. Petersburg, near the sea, and though it was situated in swamps and very unhealthful, he forced his court to reside there, and made it the great center of 

Russian life. 

Above all, Peter himself traveled to the

West. He made two long journeys, visiting 

Holland, France, and England. He went to the dockyards of Holland, and, having acquired some skill in carpentry, he learned the art of shipbuilding. He got a tremendous thrill when he watched some maneuvers of the British navy.

Perhaps because Russia had thirsted for water so long, he was never so happy as when he at last obtained a seaboard on the Baltic. 

And what did all these contacts mean to 

Russia? Peter made up his mind that the

Russian people should behave like people of the West. He forced the men to cut their long beards and to give up wearing cloaks. (The picture suggests how forcefully he carried out his ideas.) He forced the women to come out of their customary seclusion and mingle freely with men. Having learned to dance in the West, he taught his people dancing. He eagerly imported anything that made for progress as he understood the term. In other words, Russia needed a better geographical position, with outlets less blocked by ice. She wanted access to the sea on the west and south because she could then trade more easily with the West. Also by coming farther west and by advancing farther south toward the Mediterranean, she would become a greater power in the world, more able to take an active share in European politics. Finally, she had an interest in the Christian peoples in the south, who also professed the Greek Catholic faith, and had long been in subjection to the "Infidel Turk." We shall tell about them later.

Peter began this policy of expansion when he suddenly challenged Sweden, a country whose scattered possessions partly the result of the Thirty Years' War were difficult to hold together. The "Northern War" (1700-1721), as it was called, was a hard struggle, but Peter finally won it, and gained a Baltic seaboard, as we have said. After his death in 1725 no ruler appeared who was able to continue his work till in 1762 a German princess, wife of the mad czar, Peter III, ascended the throne as Catherine II. This lady, who had lent herself to the plot to dethrone her husband, was an able and ambitious monarch, and she determined to carry on the work of expansion. 

Catherine's opportunity seemed to lie in two directions. To the west was Poland, a country which had long been in a state of anarchy. The king was elected by a feudal diet composed entirely of nobles, and every measure brought before this body had to pass by a unanimous vote. Naturally the government was practically at a standstill. The king was so weak that he had no army, and the nobles were so selfish and corrupt that they thought only of the interests of their class.

D. England Rejects Absolutism 

It would have been strange indeed if England had not felt the tendency of the age toward the creation of absolute monarchy. Such a tendency, already noticeable in the sixteenth century under the strong monarchy of the Tudors, reached a definite and crucial stage when the Stuart monarchs threatened to follow the example of Bourbon France. The issue was finally settled by the rejection of every form of absolute monarchy by the English people themselves after a long and patient struggle. 

Henry VII THE TUDOR MONARCHY 

In 1485, a new dynasty, the House of Tudor, came to the throne in England. (If you turn to page 50 you will see how this house was connected with the Hapsburgs. 

The chart shows you the House of Tudor and its successors.) The founder of this dynasty, Henry VII, was a wise and strong king, who sensed that the English people wanted order above all things and that therefore they would be willing to follow the lead of a strong monarch. Fortunately, too, for Henry, most of the nobility had lost their lives in the civil wars that had raged before his accession, and he wisely filled their places with a new nobility made up of men who had belonged to the middle class. He also saw the political wisdom of pursuing a policy in the interest of the business part which England played in the Great Explorations. Moreover, Henry did not try, like his fellow monarchs on the Continent, to centralize his kingdom to the extent of overriding' local feeling. He preferred to employ members of the country gentry (the lesser nobles who had no right as such to sit in the House of Lords) to serve without salary as justices of the peace. These officials, content with the honor of serving the Crown, were largely relied upon to keep order. 

Henry was never quite an absolute monarch, for he did not venture to rule without Parliament. But as he got much of his revenue by forced loans from the older nobility, and as his rule was economical in the extreme, he was never very dependent upon Parliament. 

There was nothing at all showy about Henry VII, and he was sometimes crafty and mean, but his subjects, in general, appreciated his wise and cautious policy. 

Henry VIII 

Henry VIII, high-spirited, fond of show, strong-willed, and sometimes cruel, had none of his father's thrift or quiet force, but he did possess a measure of his father's tact. When on one occasion Parliament refused to grant him the money he wanted, he had the good sense to yield, and often he got his way by flattering Parliament into believing that his wishes always hinged on its approval. Then, too, when he seized the property of the monasteries, much of this wealth passed to members of the middle class or to nobles and gentry who held seats in Parliament. It was by such means that Henry seems to have bought the approval of Parliament for his break with Rome. It might be said that Henry was an autocrat with parliamentary backing. Elizabeth

The reigns of Edward VI and Mary were both brief; had they lasted longer, Parliament might have taken some advantage of the weakness of these sovereigns. Elizabeth, on the contrary, had much of the family shrewdness, and she deliberately made a point of convincing her subjects that their interests were always hers. Even the long struggle with

ABSOLUTE MONARCHY 

the Catholic Reaction brought wealth in the shape of plunder from Spanish galleons; and as Elizabeth's wise counselors had brought England through a period of great peril, the English felt a real devotion for their queen. 

Even when she violated Parliament's right of freedom of debate, her subjects regarded her action as one of her customary fits of temper and quickly forgave it.

But would Parliament always display the meekness it had generally shown toward the 

Tudors? The answer would come with the accession of a new dynasty.

THE STUART MONARCHY Accession of the House of Stuart 

Elizabeth was succeeded in 1603 by her cousin, James I, of the House of Stuart. He was the grandson of Henry VIII's sister, Margaret, who had married James IV, King of Scotland. His mother was that romantic figure, Mary, Queen of Scots. There were other claimants to the throne, but none that had so good a claim by birth, and it seemed, on the whole, wiser to accept James, who had been working hard for the succession, than to risk a war with an offended king of Scotland.

Besides, his accession to the throne of England meant that England and Scotland were linked by a common sovereign, and England need not fear continued strife on her northern border. known as the Puritans. They wished, it seems, to "purify" the Church by bringing about a simpler form of worship and making the Church itself more democratic. They were plainly influenced by Calvinism, though not disposed, like the Calvinists, known in England as Presbyterians, to sever their connection with the Established Church.² James, however, refused to treat their wishes with any courtesy for he likened all these people to the Presbyterians, whom he felt to be disloyal to the Crown. He remembered the stormy days of his youth in Scotland, when parsons would grasp his cloak and call him "God's silly vassal." Thus to him this

Puritanism smacked too much of Presbyterianism. Unfortunately for James, Puritanism was strong in the middle class, which in Tudor times had been the staunchest ally of the Crown.

Both the King's foreign policy and his attitude toward Catholics intensified ill-feeling. 

Since danger from the Catholic Reaction was now at an end, James made haste to close the long struggle with Spain; but the consequence was that the nation no longer felt the need of rallying to the Crown in its own defense.

At the same time, many missed the profitable raids on Spanish commerce. Then, when

James attempted for a while to secure a Spanish bride for his son, he was thought to be currying favor with a Catholic power.

More tolerant than most of his subjects, James was lax in enforcing the existing laws against James I and the Beginning of Resistance to the Catholics, and this was, of course, an addi- Crown James I was a man of some intelligence, but so proud of his kingly position that he would never lower himself to flatter opponents to win their good will, as Henry VIII and Elizabeth had done. Unfortunately for him, the times called for a man of extraordinary tact, more than even Elizabeth had possessed, and James was quite deficient in that quality. 

Indeed, the arrogance of the Stuarts was probably the principal cause of their undoing.

A further cause of trouble was the religious question. During the reign of Elizabeth an element had arisen in the Anglican Church,

The cost of government had greatly increased by the seventeenth century, due to the lowering of the value of money, and the King's ordinary resources would not go nearly so far as had normally been the case under the Tudors. 

For that reason James was particularly dependent upon Parliament, which, as the money-raising body, could alone meet his needs. But James was always his own worst enemy. He explained at great length to his first Parliament the doctrine of the "divine

Parliament failed to give him the money he needed; for James threw some of its members into prison, thus showing that he did not propose to respect Parliament's freedom of speech. In his later years, it is true, he was granted some money, but never enough; and when he died in 1625, middle class and gentry and even some of the nobles were filled with a spirit of resentment against the Crown. 

Charles I and Parliament 

Charles I, son and successor of James I, was much less sociable in disposition than his father, while he possessed even more than his father's arrogance. (The portrait in the chart, page 51, suggests the Stuart pride.) All the difficulties we have noticed in the previous reign became now much more acute. The quarrels over religion became more serious, since Charles wanted to bring the forms of worship in the Anglican Church into greater similarity to Catholic forms. Relations between Crown and Parliament became more bitter, for Parliament had lost all confidence in the royal leadership and the King refused to consider that body as worthy of his respect. 

Charles tried three parliaments in turn, and got little out of them.

He was therefore driven to the alternative of raising money without its consent. From 1629 on he was determined, if possible, to rule without any parliament at all.

Meanwhile, Charles would brook no opposition. When he imprisoned certain members of the House of Commons, he was violating their cherished right of freedom of debate; and one of these illustrious victims, who died in prison, was looked upon as a martyr to the cause of political liberty. Not only were members of Parliament so mistreated, but one reads of a rich merchant who was imprisoned for six years for refusing to pay a tax which the Crown had imposed. Others suffered similarly for merely criticizing the King. 

It was no wonder that the country was deeply stirred. There was strenuous opposition to the alterations made in the Anglican prayer book and to the drastic steps taken to prevent all discussion. Hence a great many persons who had never been classed as Puritans were now bitter against the King. Some believed, as the result of the favor shown to Catholics (for the Queen was an ardent Catholic), that Charles intended to restore the Catholic Church. In any case the King gave needless offense even to the more conservative Anglicans by putting into their form of worship certain novelties they did not like. Meanwhile, the Puritan element was gradually parting company with the Church, and thousands of "God-fearing folk" trusted their lives to the stormy Atlantic in order to find in America a refuge where they could worship as they pleased. The people who settled New England were fugitives from the England of James and Charles. There is little doubt that the Puritans were a difficult people; they were prejudiced against the court, and just as intolerant as Charles and his Anglican clergy; but a tactful king would have shown a more yielding spirit and refrained from driving everything to extremes. 

But to all this opposition Charles was indifferent as long as he could manage to have his way.

When dismissing his third Parliament with the warning that he would manage to get money somehow, he declared to the astonished members, "Take this not as a threatening, for I scorn to threaten any but my equals." It was evident, indeed, that England was on the verge of absolute monarchy. 

Was the opposition earnest enough and strong enough to avert it? One could not tell.

It might be suggested, of course, that some were merely grasping at an excuse not to pay taxes, and it is clear enough from the amount that was paid in taxation thirty years later that the country could have afforded to contribute a great deal more than it did for the support of the government. It might be true also that fairly good times induced Englishmen to hesitate long before resorting to armed rebellion. Then, too, there were no newspapers circulating throughout the country; so people in one part of England knew little. of what was going on in another. But grievances were accumulating; and if the country's accustomed mouthpiece, Parliament, were

AN ABSOLUTE MONARCHY 

called again, resistance might prove bold enough to win. After all, Charles lacked the most important means of becoming absolute. 

He had no standing army. That is why he made a fatal blunder in picking a quarrel with Scotland, for it forced him to call a parliament against his will.

The Short Parliament 

Charles, it seems, had tried to force the new Anglican prayer book on the Scots, with the result that they had revolted. For the moment the King gave in, but he was persuaded by his advisers to call a parliament in the hope of getting the money to raise an army.

Charles traded on the belief that a feeling of patriotism would rouse the English people to come to his aid against the Scots. 

When Parliament met, however, it refused to grant any money until its grievances had been met. After three weeks of wrangling the 

King dissolved it.

Yet this parliament, known as the Short Parliament, was important for three reasons. 

In the first place, the various members, gathered from all parts of England, came to appreciate how widespread was the opposition to the Crown after so many years of misrule. 

In the second place, they found an ally in London. Rioting in the capital showed the temper of the middle class and was a warning to the stubborn king that his policy might lead to revolution. In the third place, the

Scots perceived that the English people were not behind their king. Hence, after Charles had failed in an effort to raise an army, the Scots invaded England and informed him that the price of their withdrawal was the promise of an indemnity. After much hesitation the 

King bowed to the inevitable. He called another parliament; and this time, of course, the odds were heavily against him.

The Long Parliament and the Outbreak of Civil War The Parliament, which now met in November, 1640, was known as the Long Parliament, for it lasted, with some interruptions, for nearly twenty years. From the first, this resolute body knew that it had the King at its mercy, and took full advantage of the fact. The most hated advisers of the King were driven from office and eventually put to death. Most of the evils complained of were done away with; the King was forced to admit that he could not levy a tax without Parliament's approval; and a bill was passed to the effect that Parliament could not be dissolved without its consent. To break the royal obstinacy, a parliamentary leader, John

Pym, had enlisted the support of the turbulent elements in London; and it was fear of mob violence, more than any other factor, that shook the King's confidence at this juncture. 

Yet Charles was not easily overborne. On 

January 4, 1642, he attempted in person to arrest five members of the House of Commons. 

Warned of the danger in time, they were not present in the house when the King arrived. 

As he passed through the hall the commoners stood, silent and aghast, at this extraordinary performance. Finding that the "birds had flown," Charles left without a word. His counterstroke had failed.

But the agitated commoners felt now that only force could decide the struggle; and those who loved their liberties began immediately to take up arms. Charles, too, saw that the die was cast, and on January 10, 1642, he fled to the north of England, whence he called all loyal followers to support him. Thus began the Civil War. 

The Civil War The English Civil War, or Great Rebellion, as it is also called, lasted for four years, 16421646. The supporters of the King were known as "Cavaliers"; those of Parliament were popularly dubbed "Roundheads,” a term applied to shopkeepers in London. Most of the aristocracy (that is, nobles and country gentry) decided when the crisis came that their duty was to support the King. Most of the middle class, as well as a few of the nobles and gentry, stood by Parliament. After a hard struggle the Roundheads won decisively, and Charles was taken prisoner. 

The reasons for the outcome were three. 

In the first place, with the towns on their side, the parliamentary forces had more money at their disposal than the King. In the second place, they found a capable leader, Oliver Cromwell, who organized an army, the so-

called Model Army, which under his able direction came to outclass the royal troops.

In the third place, Parliament obtained the assistance of the Scots, to whom it promised that the Presbyterian Church should become the established church of England. 

It was the decision to make England Presbyterian and to grant no freedom of worship to any other Protestant body that spoiled the victory of Parliament over the Crown and spread dissension among the victors themselves. It seemed that people never would learn the lesson of toleration. The great majority of Anglicans were powerless, of course, since those who had sat in the Commons had left to serve in the King's army. 

But most of the soldiers in the Model Army were known as Independents; they wanted the privilege of belonging to any sect, and, for all except Catholics and Anglicans, they favored toleration. They were also naturally furious when Parliament tried to disband them without pay. On December 6, 1648, a detachment of soldiers forcibly expelled all

Presbyterians from the House of Commons. 

The remaining members were known as the "Rump Parliament."

The Rump Parliament, which was anything but representative, then took a most questionable step. It set up a special court, which tried King Charles, and sentenced him to death. Meeting his fate with courage, Charles was beheaded on January 30, 1649. Then the

Rump proclaimed England to be a "commonwealth," in other words, a republic. Of all this policy Cromwell was the prime mover. 

England under a Republic 

For three years Cromwell ruled as the leading member of a council of state, chosen by the Rump. All Protestants except Angli cans were now tolerated, but the government

depended chiefly for its support upon the army. England was under a military dictatorship.

Cromwell was a man of strong personality, thoroughly sincere and not extreme in most of his views, but often very ruthless in his methods. Since his immediate task was to bring both Scotland and Ireland into submission, he lost no time in accomplishing it. 

Ireland was promptly subdued by fire and sword. Scotland was treated more leniently and gave no serious trouble, though the Scots did not approve of Cromwell's tolerance of the different sects. As soon as the British 

Isles were finally pacified, Cromwell fought a war with Holland and another one with Spain, which enabled him to take the island of Jamaica. In 1653 he was given the title of "protector," having declined the title of king.

But the Protectorate was never very popular. Cromwell offended many by his Puritan regulations, such as the ban against "vainly and profanely walking on the Sabbath Day"; and, depending on the army to enforce obedience, he antagonized a peaceably minded people. When Cromwell died in 1658, people wanted the Protectorate abolished. After a year of confusion and disorder, one of Cromwell's military henchmen, General Monk, summoned the Long Parliament, including the Presbyterians once expelled, and this body, which met early in 1660, called back the House of Stuart to the throne.

The Restoration and the Policy of Charles II 

Apparently everyone welcomed the Restoration. The beheading of Charles I, which, as you will remember, was the work of a small minority, had shocked most people profoundly, and everyone seemed tired of military rule. 

A nation which had never known a standing army naturally felt that their political liberties were endangered by a dictatorship. Moreover, Puritanism had seemed to lose its charm when it tried to regulate morals and fetter the conscience. Once more people rejoiced in the old pastimes even on Sunday! The theaters opened again, and men drank hearty toasts to the "Merry Monarch." Finally those who had fought and bled for their king, many of whom had suffered in consequence the loss of their lands, were naturally anxious to see the monarchy restored. Anglicans, of course, wished to see the Anglican Church re-established, and even Presbyterians preferred monarchy, with the Anglicans in power, to the disorders which had followed Cromwell's death. All seemed to feel that the legitimate king, eldest son of Charles I, would bring the country back to peace and order. 

So the new king, Charles II, arrived from his exile in Holland, with everything in his favor. (The scene on page 56, depicting his arrival shows the pleasure of his subjects.) 

Charles was an easygoing person, fond of his leisure and his vices, and a witty and delightful companion. He was, however, much more shrewd than people realized, as they were later to learn to their cost. 

For the time being Charles made a point of making himself agreeable. Religious matters were not, of course, his problem. He had promised to leave the religious settlement to Parliament, and the first Parliament, elected on his accession, restored the Anglican Church, while other religious creeds were denied. freedom. Later in the reign both Catholics and Dissenters, as non-Anglican Protestants were called, were, in effect, excluded from both Parliament and public office, since only by taking communion in accordance with the Anglican rite could a person be considered eligible. Charles himself, being tolerant and rather inclined to sympathize with Catholics, naturally disapproved of these measures, but he was powerless to prevent them. Religious bigotry lingered on in the seventeenth century.

Yet a struggle between Crown and Parliament could hardly have been averted. Parliament had no check on the royal authority except by the traditional method of withholding funds, and the King soon found a means of avoiding the necessity of asking for money. 

He formed a secret alliance with his cousin, Louis XIV, who exacted England's assistance in a war with Holland and a promise from Charles to reinstate the Catholic Church in England.

A rival group, the Whigs, was inclined to be suspicious of the King and especially of any favor shown to Catholics. 

These two groups marked the beginning of political parties. Meanwhile, the King, who kept his real design to himself, watched their rivalry with interest, secretly hoping that the Whigs, who controlled the Commons, would come to grief. This hope seemed likely to be realized in 1678. 

A certain rascal named Titus Oates claimed to know of a Catholic plot to kill the King an affair which is known in history as the "Popish Plot." Excitement became intense, and such was the fear of Catholics (an inheritance from the stormy days of Elizabeth) that a veritable panic prevailed, especially in London, and more than fifty Catholics were done to death. The Whigs deliberately encouraged this fanaticism and tried to get through Parliament a bill to exclude James, the King's brother, from the succession on the ground that he was a Catholic. Unfortunately for their purpose, Charles obtained some timely gold from Louis XIV, and in March, 1681, he dissolved Parliament. Then a genuine plot against the King was unearthed, and three of the Whig leaders were found guilty of conspiracy. Two of them were beheaded, while the third fled into exile. The party was wholly discredited. 

Charles was now at last free to act, and with the Tories blindly following his lead, he laid plans to make himself absolute. By arbitrary changes in the method of electing the House of Commons he saw to it that the Tories would be sure of having control. Meanwhile he dispensed with Parliament altogether, having enough of Louis's gold to meet his needs. In case of trouble he had at hand a small standing army, granted him at the beginning of

But after four years of personal rule Charles died rather suddenly in 1685. The outcome of his policy was left to be determined by the conduct of his brother, James II.

THE REVOLUTION OF 1688 The Crisis under James II 

James II resembled his brother in wanting to be a despot, but, unlike Charles, he lacked the necessary skill. He was as stubborn as his father, Charles I, and had even less intelligence. Certainly at the outset the chances were all in his favor. He had not only a subservient parliament but a standing army, soon to be raised to the number of 16,000 men. 

But James made the mistake of throwing his whole soul into the task of making Catholicism supreme. No one could justly blame him for wanting to free his co-religionists from the penal laws which had cramped them since the bygone days of Elizabeth, but when he also gave them positions in the Church, people naturally thought — and perhaps they were right that he meant to make Catholicism the only legal religion. The mad terror which followed the Popish Plot of 1678, as well as his own unhappy relations with the Whigs, should have deterred him, but James was never one to understand the public temper. 

In deliberately stirring up anti-Catholic sentiment he took the means most likely to bring about his own fall.

In 1687, James issued what was known as a "declaration of indulgence," suspending the penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters. 

The favor shown to Dissenters was, of course, a blind, and it really deceived no one. As people 

As people saw the Catholics holding their services quite openly, and even monks walking the streets of London, they felt sure that James was surrendering to Rome. Popular feeling became intense. 

The only hope for England seemed to lie in the fact that James's two daughters had both been reared as Protestants; and consequently, when the King should die, the danger would disappear. But even that one hope was of short duration; for on June 10, 1688, the 

Queen gave birth to a son, and this presum- No wonder, then, that a group of prominent men decided to call in a man who perhaps might rescue England from her plight. This man, though a Dutch prince, was also a Stuart by blood,' and married to the elder daughter of James himself.

William III and the Glorious Revolution 

William of Orange had long been watching the gathering storms in near-by England, fearing that if James should become an ally of France, as his brother had been, Dutch liberties were doomed. To save his little Holland from destruction he was willing to dare anything, So he welcomed the invitation to rescue England from the tyranny of James. 

It was the case of a country about to be invaded of its own free will.

When William landed in England on November 5, 1688, he probably expected that his coming would lead to a civil war. The King would certainly regard him as a meddler and resent his published demand for a free parliament. And it seemed likely that many would object to the dethronement of a legitimate monarch, if such were attempted. But James was so distracted that he made no appeal whatever to the loyalty of his subjects, and his army was so mutinous that he knew that he could not trust it. So he suddenly gave up the struggle and fled to France. Thus William secured the throne, and England had staged a bloodless revolution.

The Revolutionary Settlement 

Steps were now taken to see that England would never again be subject to the danger of absolute monarchy. The Crown had lost in its struggle; Parliament was now supreme and meant to keep that supremacy. William and Mary (whose pictures are seen in the chart on page 51) were given the throne as joint sovereigns, and it was clearly understood that they owed their position to Parliament. 

By the Bill of Rights, in 1689, all the arbitrary acts of the House of Stuart were declared illegal and a standing army in time of peace was prohibited. Since a small army was

needed in the colonies, it was decreed, in the Mutiny Act, that the money for its support should be voted for only a year. Thus Parliament was certain to be called in annual sessions.

Eleven years later it was determined by the Act of Settlement that the throne should pass to Mary's sister, Anne (for William and 

Mary had no children) and then to her cousin who ruled the little German state of Hanover.¹

Thus the son of James, as well as that son's descendants, was excluded from the succession. 

By this action the English people felt that their Protestant religion and political liberties were now rendered doubly secure. 

William III proved a loyal and wise king.

He was quite willing to be a constitutional monarch and never tried to stretch any of his rights. Being a Calvinist at heart, he would have liked to see Dissenters given the chance to enter Parliament, but he did not press the point. He was glad, of course,. that nearly all Dissenters (the one exception being Unitarians) were given freedom of worship by the Act of Toleration in 1689. Rather cold

SUMMARY of Important Concepts never very and uninspiring, William' was popular in England. He was aware that some of his subjects were actually disloyal, many of the Tories in particular feeling that James was the rightful king. There were 

Stuart adherents in Scotland; and the intensely Catholic population of Ireland was also loyal to James. When, in 1690, James, with France's backing, landed in Ireland, William defeated him in the battle of the 

Boyne, and quickly subdued the Irish. He also made the Scots profess allegiance. And this, as events were to show, was preliminary to union.

The Union with Scotland 

Under William's successor, Anne (17021714), complete union with Scotland was finally achieved in 1707. The Scots gave up their Parliament and were henceforth represented in the Parliament at London. From then on we speak of "Great Britain," a term which is meant to include both England and Scotland. Similarly also we speak of the "British Empire," which we must now take time to consider.

CHAPTER III The Making of the British Empire 

Why did rivalry for colonies and commerce develop following the great voyages of exploration? 

Why was Great Britain victorious in this struggle?

How did social and political life change in eighteenth-century Great Britain?

WHILE THE CONTINENTAL 

POWERS were mainly though not wholly expanding on land, England, as an island nation, was looking across the seas for the extension of her power. The result of her activities and of her triumph over her rivals was the development of the richest colonial empire in the world. In order, however, the better to understand its evolution, we must dwell a little upon the circumstances out of which it rose.

A. The Background and Rise of British Imperialism The Spanish and Portuguese Monopolies 

As the result of a papal decision in 1493 Spain was supposed to be entitled to all discoveries west of a certain parallel, and Portugal to all that happened to be east of that line. By the middle of the sixteenth century, Spain had taken possession of Mexico, Peru, most of the 

West Indies, and the Philippines. Portugal established posts at strategic points on the shores of Africa and southern Asia, as well as in some of the East Indies, and, in the Western Hemisphere, Brazil. The Spaniards were mainly seekers of the precious metals, gold and silver, while the Portuguese, though they also looked for gold in western Africa, reaped most of their wealth from Oriental products such as spices. 

Spain ruled her colonies through officials known as viceroys, who were given a good deal of power, though they were always made to realize that the government was watching their conduct, and they often received orders from the "Council of the Indies," which had been specially created to oversee the colonies. 

Only the merchants of one port, Seville, were privileged to engage in the oversea trade; and though they were independent traders, they had to obtain a license from the government and to submit to the most rigid regulation. 

The government itself profited greatly from the trade, for besides the customs duties, it always received a fifth of the gold and silver. 

Accordingly, since the shipments of precious metals from America attracted pirates, the government provided merchant vessels with ships of war as escort. All foreigners were strictly debarred from trading with the colonies, which were maintained for the exclusive benefit of Spain.

The Portuguese had much more trouble in establishing themselves than did the Spaniards, for the Arabs, who had long brought the produce of the East to the Venetians, did not want to lose their old position as "middlemen," and put up a stiff resistance. But, in 1509, the Portuguese managed to rout them, and then established fortified posts, which enabled them to trade with the interior. Like

Spain, Portugal ruled her scattered empire through viceroys; like Spain, too, she claimed a monopoly in the lands and waters allotted to her by the Pope.

In 1581 the Spanish and Portuguese empires were united under the rule of Philip II, who had inherited the Portuguese throne, and this union was to last almost a century.

England, Holland, and France had never accepted the idea that the sea was closed to all but Spain and Portugal. Both the 

French and the English had been active in exploration, as we have noticed, and the English even interfered directly with Spanish trade. The English pirates of Elizabeth's day had made a profitable business out of plundering Spanish galleons, and English merchants later carried on a lucrative trade by smuggling their wares into the Spanish colonies, which the mother country had never adequately supplied. Unfortunately for herself, Spain lacked the strong naval power needed to protect her treasures.

Meanwhile, the Dutch were intruding on Portugal's sphere. Formerly they had gone to Lisbon to get the spices which the Portuguese had brought into Europe. But after 

Philip II had debarred them from that port, they went direct to the Spice Islands themselves. These islands, which they eventually took from Portugal, were included in the spoils known later as the Dutch East Indies.

The decline of Spain had been due partly to the character of her people and partly to the unwise policy of Philip II. The Spanish nobility despised business as something quite beneath their notice, and those who engaged in trade wanted to retire as soon as possible and pass for men of leisure. Spain had few thriving industries, and consequently much of her gold had to be used to buy from foreign countries the things that Spaniards needed. 

Moreover, Philip made conditions a great deal worse by taxing business so heavily that the middle class could derive but little profit. 

Portugal, a comparatively weak power, found it quite impossible to defend her scattered empire, and annexation to Spain meant simply sacrifice to the interests of her neighbor.

In the meantime, France and England had both founded colonial empires. Early in the seventeenth century the English established trading posts in India, a country then divided

THE MAKING OF THE 

65 

BRITISH EMPIRE 

among a number of native princes. Long famous for its native-wrought fabrics, as well as its jewels, perfumes, spices, and other luxuries, India had been the chief goal of the explorers, and was destined to become the richest stake in the struggle between England and France. Meanwhile, furs, fish, and agricultural products were the attraction in 

North America.

Though the English had gained the upper hand over the Portuguese before the French had penetrated India, the two rivals began their pioneering in America at about the same time.

The first settlements established by the French in Canada, or New France, were 

Port Royal in 1604 and Quebec in 1608.

The first settlement by the English was made at Jamestown in 1607. In the course of the seventeenth century more and more of the English crossed the ocean to try their fortunes, and some of them, as you know, were refugees from religious persecution. Unlike most of the French, who were content to make their pile and return home, these English stayed and established permanent settlements. In the meantime, with the decay of Spanish power, many of the West Indies had fallen to England and France, though the French islands were the more valuable because of their greater production of sugar. Of great advantage to the English, on the other hand, was the contract, acquired from Spain in 1713, to supply the Spanish colonies with 

African Negroes to work as slaves. 

Generally speaking, the French colonies were autocratically governed, whereas in the British some degree of self-government was usually permitted. In general, both countries adopted a monopolistic policy toward their colonies, of which the example had been set by Spain; that is, colonies were conceived of as exclusively for the benefit of the mother country a a characteristic feature of the mercantile system. But, unlike Spanish usage, trade was generally carried on by companies.

The Joint-Stock Company 

It was, in fact, a hazardous thing in those days to engage in the oversea trade. There were pirates ready to prey on rich merchantmen; there were native princes who often resisted the foreign intruder; and there were frequent losses from storms and other causes.

Quite early, therefore, the English had seen the advantage of organizing themselves into commercial companies, which, because of their collective responsibility, would greatly lessen the risk to individuals.

The joint-stock company was the usual solution of the problem. solution of the problem. Members of such a company owned shares or stock in the enterprise and profited in proportion to the amount of their investment. The company sent out merchantmen in fleets, always escorted by warships to furnish protection. 

Each company had a charter from the mother country, which gave it a monopoly of trade in a certain zone and empowered it to found colonies if the land were suited to settlement or to establish trading points in the case of a country with a large native population. 

It had even the right to make war or negotiate treaties with native princes. By thus giving these companies political rights the mother country shifted the burden of empire-building to groups of private individuals. Rivalry between companies of different nations in the same zone often led to actual hostilities, without, however, involving the national governments.

The English and Dutch companies never seemed to have any difficulty in obtaining capital, but the French companies were usually partly financed by the government, as the French were much less interested in the oversea trade. Among these maritime nations of the seventeenth century Holland deserves our special attention.

The Brief Commercial Ascendancy of Holland and 

Its Collapse The Dutch were a people who made their way against great odds. They helped even to make their own country, for much of it was below the level of the sea, and the water could be kept out only by well-built dikes. 

They had always been great fishermen, and during the Middle Ages they had supplied much of the fish eaten on fast days. Naturally, too, shipbuilding was in Holland a leading industry. But the chief interest of the Dutch

Portugal the monopoly of the spice trade, they were also the chief distributors of coffee to the West. Above all, they enjoyed for a time a virtual monopoly of the carrying trade; for their freight charges were lower than those of any of their competitors. Any merchant wishing to ship his wares from London, let us say, to Naples, would be likely to engage a 

Dutch shipper to carry them. The old saying, "It beats the Dutch," carried with it a sort of acknowledgment of business supremacy. Even in manufacturing, the Dutch were exceedingly active. Their cloth and linen industries were thriving institutions, while in bookmaking and printing they led the world. Finally, during her prosperous days Holland was the banking center of Europe, where all who desired loans could obtain them on comparatively easy terms. In no country were the interest charges so low. 

No wonder, then, that this nation, as a whole, was very rich. Wealthy merchants and bankers gave direct encouragement to the arts, and gloried in having their portraits painted by artists such as Rembrandt or van Dyck. Perhaps because they were practical business men the Dutch were rather more tolerant than other people of this age. Refugees from persecution found a welcome asylum, and everyone was free to write as he pleased. Naturally science flourished, and it was a Dutchman who invented the first pendulum clock.

But the greatness of Holland was really out of proportion to her size and population. 

When all due credit is given to Dutch intelligence and vigor, much of their success must be explained by the fact that their natural rivals were preoccupied at home. England in the early Stuart period was weakened by internal quarrels and France under Richelieu and Mazarin was seeking "natural boundaries." But after the Great Rebellion and the beginning of the personal rule of Louis XIV, the situation changed. England fought three wars against the Dutch, and quickly forged ahead as a commercial power. Between 1713 and 1783 some important territorial changes took place in North America. The British colonies had gained their independence and extended their territory west to the Mississippi. France had lost all her territory on the continent of North America either to Spain or to Great Britain. In

As Governor-General in India, he made friends with the powerful native rulers. He hoped by building strong political friendships for France, backed by military force, to drive the English out of India. 

Who was his English rival? Why did Dupleix fail? south of the Great Lakes and even a large expanse west of the Mississippi. All this tract, with the exception of Canada, was known as Louisiana, the eastern frontier of which was an object of dispute with the British colonists. 

In fact, apart from the town of New Orleans, founded in 1718, only a few scattered trading posts and forts gave force to the French claim based primarily on exploration. Great Britain, having acquired New York as the result of one of her naval wars with Holland, held all the Atlantic seaboard as far to the south as Florida, and these British colonies were much more densely settled than the French. 

1750, the French population of North America numbered scarcely eighty thousand, whereas the British colonies contained about a million white inhabitants.

In In India the two companies, French and 

British, competed vigorously for the trade of the native princes. It was not, however, till 

1740, when France chose as her governor-general Joseph Dupleix, that rivalry became seriously acute. (His portrait appears on this page.) A daring and farsighted man, Dupleix believed that the only way for France to get the better of her rival was to bring the princes completely under her sway. He took a more active part in the native quarrels than any previous agent had done, and he enrolled native troops, known as Sepoys, which, officered by Frenchmen, gave him a powerful force to push French interests. But the government of Louis XV failed to appreciate Dupleix and gave him but meager support. In the meantime, the 

British company found an exceptionally able man, Robert Clive, to pit against the formidable Frenchman, and the latter lacked the strength to sustain the position he had won. 

At the same time, the French company began to complain of Dupleix's schemes on the ground that they were too costly, and as both the French and British governments still deluded themselves into believing that peace could somehow be maintained, Louis XV abruptly recalled him. Thus, in 1754, France threw away her best chance of success, and just at the time when the two nations were coming to grips.

The Decisive Struggle: The Seven Years' War 

As a matter of fact, it was practically certain that Great Britain would soon pursue a more active policy. The landed aristocracy which controlled the British government was almost as interested in trade as the middle class. 

The British, moreover, appreciated the importance of naval power, which, as soon as the test should come, was likely to prove decisive. 

That test was the Seven Years' War. This name is applied primarily to a struggle between Austria and Prussia (1756-1763) over Silesia; but, as it happened, France was then allied with Austria, and Great Britain with Prussia. Between the two colonial rivals the war was waged chiefly in India, in North America, and on the seas; and in North 

America it had begun in 1754. The dispatch of some regular troops the following year to support the colonists showed that Great

THE 



MAKING OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE 

7333 Britain was now ready to wage direct war on her rival.

We shall not relate the story of this war in detail. Wiping out some early defeats, British policy, under the direction of William Pitt (afterward Earl of Chatham) was brilliantly successful. The British navy swept the seas. British arms conquered Canada and expelled the French from India. Though 

France, in desperation, brought Spain into the struggle, the outcome was unchanged. 

By the Peace of Paris (1763), which ended the war, Great Britain acquired Canada as well as that part of Louisiana which lay east of the Mississippi, and, in addition, some scattered spoils of minor importance; she also obtained Florida from Spain. France regained her trading posts in India, but only on condition that they should not be fortified - a stipulation that gave Great Britain a free hand in the conquest of India. Since 

France had ceded the rest of Louisiana to Spain in compensation for the loss of Florida, she no longer retained an acre on the North American continent. The struggle for colonial supremacy had been finally won by the British.

The British Empire Loses and Gains 

One might feel that the story of the colonial struggle should end right at this point. But hardly was the Seven Years' War ended before trouble came to Great Britain from within her empire itself. You know the story of the 

American Revolution - called in Europe the 

War of American Independence. France, as you know, gave aid to the revolting colonists, and some believe that this aid was the decisive factor. Oddly enough, France recovered only very little of what she had lost in the Seven Years' War, but the British Empire had lost what was, perhaps, its choicest portion. 

Yet the British Empire continued to grow in size. Gradually but steadily the British extended their holdings in India until they finally got that whole enormous country under their sway.

Meanwhile, as the result of exploration, Australia and New Zealand began to be colonized; and, following a war with 

Holland, Great Britain acquired in 1806 a per-

And now let us become more acquainted with the people who made this empire.

Régime of the Landed Aristocracy 

General Character of British Politics 

The landed aristocracy had long dominated both houses of Parliament, but until the Revolution of 1688 they had had to share power with the King. After the enactment of the Bill of Rights these aristocrats had become the controlling power in the state. 

William III never attempted to play the part of a Stuart monarch, and the liberties of England were not again endangered. Several efforts were made by the Stuarts to recover the throne, but all of them met with failure, and

Great Britain therefore maintained the line of succession as established in William's day.

William was succeeded in 1702 by Anne, the younger daughter of James II, and she, in turn, was followed in 1714 by George I of the House of Hanover. He was a great-greatgrandson of James I on his mother's side. (See the genealogical chart, page 168.) 

The ministers, as well as a large majority of both houses of Parliament, continued to be members of the landed aristocracy. The 

House of Lords was composed of both lay and ecclesiastical lords that is, the hereditary peers and the bishops of the Anglican Church. 

The House of Commons was elected, but actually very few possessed the vote. There were two divisions of the kingdom which elected members of the Commons- the counties and the boroughs. Those chosen for the counties were elected by the nobles, the gentry, and the small independent farmers known as the yeomen. The boroughs were the towns, and there the electorate, that is, the people who voted, were usually the town governments or a limited number of citizens with high property qualifications, though in a good many boroughs the members were actually picked by the Crown or by some nobleman who had long possessed the privilege. Eng- land was not, therefore, democratically ruled, even the House of Commons being very unrepresentative.

Now we mentioned in the last chapter that as early as the reign of Charles II two parties, the Whigs and the Tories, came into being. (See page 56.) Gradually the leader of the numerically stronger party began to wield considerable authority. Sir Robert Walpole, who was the King's chief minister from 1721 to 1742, had an absolute majority in Parliament on which he could depend. Some of the members of the Commons had got their seats by government influence; some of them on occasions sold their votes; while others, perhaps a majority of the House, were holders of offices or pensions which the Crown was able to bestow. This system of corrupt politics continued down to about 1784. During the reign of George III, who ascended the throne in 1760, the King himself took a direct hand in the traffic, and through his minister, Lord 

North, successfully "packed" the House of

Commons in order to make his wishes prevail. 

Rise of Cabinet Government 

As a rule, however, the King did not suggest what Parliament should do. Long ago there had gradually developed a small body known as the Cabinet, composed of some of the ministers and others, who met the King in conference and found out what he wanted.

Since these men were either commoners or lords, they were also able to keep the King in touch with Parliament's wishes. An important change took place, however, with the accession of George I. This German never managed to learn English, and so he ceased to attend the meetings of his Cabinet. Henceforth, in fact, the Cabinet met without the King, and thus developed a policy of independent action. The 

Prime Minister, or Premier, who guided the Cabinet, of which, of course, he was a member, was supposed to be able to command a majority of votes in the House of Commons. 

If the King should choose a Cabinet that failed to have or maintain the support of the Commons, then it would have to resign, as otherwise government and legislature could not act together. Thus, in choosing his Prime Minister, the King was virtually restricted to the

choice of a party leader, who happened to enjoy the backing of Parliament. This system is what is known as cabinet government, and it included, of course, the idea of ministerial responsibility, for the most important ministers held seats in the Cabinet, were answerable for their acts to the House of Commons, and resigned with the rest of the Cabinet if it lost the 

Commons' support. 

British Policy in the Eighteenth Century It

Under this parliamentary régime, controlled by the aristocracy and guided by commercial interests, Great Britain steadily prospered. Her major attention, as we have noticed, was devoted to empire-building. was only toward the close of the eighteenth century that a few British statesmen, notably 

William Pitt, the Younger, and Charles James

Fox, began to see the need of reforms in the internal life of the country. Fox became a champion of what was known as "parliamentary reform," a changing of the electoral system in such a way as to make the House of 

Commons more representative.

Pitt sup- ported the same principle; but their efforts to persuade Parliament were vain, and the issue was not seriously revived till well into the nineteenth century. Nevertheless, a liberal spirit had somehow awakened in the days of the "unreformed House of Commons." 

Pitt was a capable man who, as prime minister, got along with George III and also had the confidence of Parliament and public. (The portrait shows him in middle life-conscientious, patient, and intelligent.) One of his most important acts was to bring about the union of Great Britain and Ireland in 1800. Henceforth the Irish people were represented in Parliament. Pitt would have liked to give 

Irish Catholics the right to membership in

Parliament, since the vast majority of the Irish, being Catholics, were thereby disqualified by the old laws against Catholics, dating from the reign of Charles II. But the 

King was so opposed to any change in this regard that Pitt did not persist, though he felt compelled to retire from office for a time. 

It was the last occasion when a king was allowed to balk the wishes of Parliament; and 

Pitt yielded the point only because George

In the period just discussed, men still belonged to one or the other party, Whigs or Tories. The Whigs were in power from 1714 to 1762, chiefly because the Tories were then suspected of secretly favoring the Stuarts. After 1762 the Tories enjoyed a long term in office.

Both parties, however, were equally the voice of the landed aristocracy, a class which ruled not only the political but also the social life of the British nation. 

THE LIFE OF THE LANDED ARISTOCRACY The Education of a Gentleman 

The English aristocracy differed somewhat from its counterpart on the Continent in being rather less formal and less polished, though the influence of France was always felt more or less, and English society as a whole was hardly more democratic than the French.

What institution in our day corresponds most closely to the coffee-house of the eighteenth century? 

The oldest son of a peer would usually be sent on tour with a tutor, sometimes spending as much as three years in seeing the world.

Younger sons, as a rule, were taught at home by a private tutor, though some were sent to school, and a few, perhaps, finished at a university. The oldest son was, of course, predestined to manage the family estates and embark on a political career. To the younger sons, the Church, the army, and the navy were practically the only fields open, since careers in business and the professions were considered rather beneath a nobleman's dignity.

The There were also more casual ways in which the upper classes acquired an education. 

Newspapers and journals, usually appearing weekly or monthly, had made their appearance as early as the beginning of the seventeenth century, and had multiplied greatly during the period of the Civil War. As news sheets they hardly amounted to much, but they usually gave an idea of what was happening at court or in Parliament, and contained much serious discussion. Parliament itself was no doubt a source of political education for its members, but it was not till fairly late in the eighteenth century that debates were regularly reported.

The dress of the upper classes distinguished them as a rule from their "inferiors." peasant, the workman, the small shopkeeper, and the domestic servant would never have thought of donning the showy frills of the upper classes, even if they had had the money to do so. 

Wealth alone and that not always -enabled a person to rise above his station. 

Some members of the middle class managed to "break into" society, but there was always a good deal of prejudice against such "newcomers. دو 

Probably fewer aristocrats in England had a taste for arts and letters than was the case on the Continent. But having in England a chance to run the government, they were much more interested in politics. They were also probably, as a whole, better educated. 

Another means of molding opinion (as well as furnishing diversion) was the coffeehouse. Dating from the middle of the seventeenth century, this institution attained its height of popularity in the reign of Anne, and some were as regularly frequented by Whigs as others were the cherished haunts of Tories. 

Coffee or chocolate was served, and stronger drink if one desired it. Gambling was also frequently indulged in, but the coffee-house was famous chiefly for its political discussions as well as for the retailing of any stray gossip that was going around. Toward the end of the eighteenth century tea dethroned coffee as the favorite beverage, and, along with this change, the coffee-houses began gradually to develop into private clubs. Those which did not so change became less and less exclusive and soon lost their old individuality. The type frequented by the lower classes were mainly for drinking purposes and came to be known as taverns.

Homes 

The interior of the homes of the well-to-do had undergone some changes in the course of two centuries. Carpets had largely replaced the dirty rushes on the floor. Windows were now more common since glass was cheaper. 

Wallpaper, another borrowing from the East, covered the plaster on the wall unless the wall happened to be paneled. Furniture was of fine wood and richly upholstered, and seats, having acquired backs since the sixteenth century, were much more comfortable to sit on. 

A long line of portraits exemplified family pride, while a profusion of bowls and vases offered variety to the eye. Much of the decoration was for show rather than because the head of the house was a lover of art, but such is the way of fashion. Many of the aristocracy had a "town house" in London as well as a mansion on their estates. 

It is an interesting fact that people had become much cleaner in their personal habits. 

The daily cold bath had become an established practice by the eighteenth century; and the use of soap, quite rare a century earlier, was now fairly common for bathing as well as for washing underwear and shirts. All this, of course, applies rather to the aristocracy and the upper middle class than to the masses of the people; but even among the masses the wearing of underwear and the use of bedding had come to be fairly general - due mainly to cheapness of cotton in the eighteenth century. 

Costume 

Much time and thought in those days was given to costume. The Puritans had tried to introduce simplicity of dress, but most of the aristocracy kept their love of gorgeous display. 

Charles II introduced the long coat, which fell nearly to the knees, and which showed the long embroidered or jeweled waistcoat only when the coat was left unbuttoned. The coat had short sleeves, generally ending in lengthy cuffs; and a sash girded the waist. Breeches were full and fitted to the knee; stockings were still worn and shoes, for a time, high-heeled, displayed a bow of ribbon at the instep. Over the coat was usually worn a long wrap. At this period (as the first sketch shows) the wig was generally a mass of curls. This monstrosity was succeeded in the eighteenth century by the periwig, much smaller and bound at the end with ribbons, or fitted into a dainty black silk bag. 

The cocked hat in the eighteenth century took the place of the jaunty beaver with its graceful feather. Buckles had, in the meantime, replaced ribbons on the shoes. Breeches (as the

All such costumes were usually in bright colors, for women had no monopoly of gorgeous plumage in those days. In the seventeenth century women wore large hooped skirts, tight-fitting waists, and full sleeves (as the second sketch, page 75, suggests). Much attention was paid to curling the hair and sometimes fashion required it to be piled high on the head. Both women and men wore plumes in the seventeenth century, but these became less common in the eighteenth, though hats were still large. Hoops began to grow smaller in the latter century until they finally disappeared. Children's dress became simplified in the late eighteenth century. The boys were no longer dressed like miniature men and the girls were no longer corseted. But skirts and trousers were long and not too comfortable. 

Diversions and Manners

The amusements of the upper classes were varied. Hunting was still popular in the country, the hunting of foxes by hounds and men on horseback being the chief innovation of the eighteenth century. Tennis retained its popularity, but archery and fencing gave way to rougher sports, such as football and boxing. (Scenes showing eighteenth-century tennis and boxing will be found at the top of this page.) Horse-racing was popular from the early Stuart period, chiefly for the excitement it afforded gamblers. For evening entertainment, cards and the opera or theater served to while away the hours.

The time had long since passed when moral scruples stood in the way of any pleasures. 

During the period of the Long Parliament, when Puritanism held sway, dancing, cards, and the theater had been much frowned upon,

THE MAKING OF THE

BRITISH EMPIRE 

and any amusements on Sunday had been held in grave disfavor. But the strong reaction which accompanied the Restoration made it proper for anyone to do pretty much as he pleased after the morning service was over, and the court of Charles II set an example in freedom which characterized the life of the aristocracy down to the end of the eighteenth century.

Manners underwent little change during this period.

People became accustomed to using forks and ceased to use them to pick their teeth. It became less common in the eighteenth century to wear hats at table, and when chairs with backs generally supplanted benches, one could eat in greater ease and devote more thought to conversation. 

Charles II's time, wit was anything but clean, and later, on the accession of the German Hanoverians, conversation grew extraordinarily coarse, and manners became rather boorish. After the middle of the eighteenth In century, the world of fashion decreed that its members should be more careful of their outward behavior. Yet throughout this period there was considerable drinking in society, and violent brawls were not an uncommon occurrence. As far as morals were concerned, there was no social stigma attached to anything. 

Women had still an important place in society, but as the court was not popular under the Hanoverian kings, mixed company was probably less usual than under the Stuarts. One lady complained that the men were likely to stay on one side of the room and the women on another; and, for her part, she thought that the women were quite capable of taking part in the conversation. But women's education was still a thing very little considered. The daughters of the aristocracy learned needlework and dancing, and possibly French, but the main idea was to give them a certain charm that would enable them to capture a desirable male. a few ladies ventured to open their houses to men of intellectual tastes. These were the socalled "Blue-Stockings," who imitated a custom already current in France, where the salon, an intellectual circle presided over by some lady, had been popular since the time of

Travel

The greater social intercourse among the aristocracy resulted from the improvement in modes of travel. In earlier times, the ordinary country gentry, who never used to come to London unless they happened to be members of Parliament, were described as an uncouth lot, almost as boorish as the man of the street. 

But by the eighteenth century more and more families of this class made visits to London to "see the sights." A system of stage-coaches (like the one found in the second sketch on this page) had been opened about the middle of the seventeenth century, which linked the capital with some of the provincial towns. Heretofore it had been necessary for the provincial to travel in his own coach with a retinue of servants, partly to ward off bandits and partly to maintain the owner's social position. Later in the century, hackney coaches (illustrated in the first sketch), drawn by two horses and accommodating six persons, might be had for hire, though they were usually confined to London and near-by points. Since the roads were very bad, all such modes of travel were quite fatiguing, especially since it was not till near the end of the eighteenth century that coaches were blessed with springs. The fast mail coaches, introduced in 1784, carried travelers, and made possible more frequent visits to the capital. It soon became noticeable that people in the country were patterning their lives after the examples set in the metropolis. For shorter distances, travel by horseback was still common, a woman (like the one in the third sketch) often riding on the pillion behind her husband.

Yet throughout the eighteenth century traveling was dangerous. People with private coaches arranged to travel together if possible, for highwaymen were everywhere; and even 

London streets were not very safe, though street lights had been introduced in the reign of Queen Anne. Many a lady of the time made a point of carrying with her a purse of bad money in case a freebooter should stop her carriage. 

Crime and Philanthropy

The increase of crime in the eighteenth century is hard to explain unless it was due to the general laxity in a long period of prosperity.

Thieving was punished by hanging, and even so slight an offense as being unable to pay one's debts was usually punished by imprisonment. But there was a certain ad- 

But there was a certain admiration for a notorious bandit, and some of them seemed to ply their dangerous profession through sheer love of adventure. Doubtless the immense number of people gathered to witness a public hanging was a proof of the low state of public morals, though a similar morbid curiosity is not unknown in America today.

Certainly, the London populace tended to be rowdy. Members of the nobility were often insulted in the streets, and popular manners were rough, to say the least. On the occasion of the funeral procession of the mother of George III, the crowd, which thronged to watch it, shouted huzzahs, though the lady in question was scarcely known to the public. 

Hard drinking, partly due to the comparative cheapness of some of the brands of strong liquor, had probably much to do with the ugly temper of the London populace; and there was even mob violence on certain occasions. 

In 1780, after some of the oppressive measures against Catholics had been repealed, members of Parliament were assaulted and several Catholic churches were destroyed before the riot could be quelled. Yet the upper classes themselves were not innocent of lawless acts. 

Dueling was common, and some of the most distinguished public figures were sometimes involved. It was not until well into the nineteenth century that this practice finally died out.

Society in the eighteenth century was lacking in a stern sense of duty. The upper and middle classes were satisfied to live in comparative ease, and did not want to be bothered either by thinking of their own self-indulgence or by trying to make life easier for the less fortunate classes below them. There was little interest as yet in the common people, who were expected to be ignorant, since ignorance, it was supposed, made them all the easier to manage. There was also little done to relieve poverty. Private charity, of course, helped somewhat, but Parliament was quite indifferent to the problem. It would seem as though the Church should have played a more vital part in helping people to lead better lives; but unfortunately many of the clergy were creatures of habit, and made of religion a cut-anddried affair.

Yet toward the end of the century one finds a genuine stirring of a nobler spirit. An Anglican clergyman, John Wesley, though a stern disciplinarian who frowned upon innocent pleasures after the manner of the early Puritans, was the founder of a movement to arouse

the common people into leading a more Christian life. Both he and his associate, Whitefield, exerted their influence by preaching. 

Since, however, their, eloquent appeal to the emotions of their hearers was something new in the Church, they found themselves excluded from most pulpits. Consequently Wesley was driven to found a new sect which, because of its methodical habits, became known as the "Methodists." One writer has called Methodism "the religion of the neglected poor.' 

SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

There were a few people outside of religious circles who showed a nobler spirit than characterized the great majority. John Howard spent his life in trying to reform prison conditions, and William Wilberforce worked for twenty years for the abolition of the slave trade. On the whole, little headway was made in the eighteenth century toward abolishing social evils, but a movement was beginning, which was in time destined to produce many needed reforms. 

1. Following the great explorations, Spain and Portugal attempted to monopolize trade with the New 

World and the Far East. a. Colonies were planted in sparsely settled regions; trading posts established in those already heavily populated. b. The practice of monopoly made conflict with other sea powers inevitable. 

2. The struggles for commerce, colonies, and sea power paralleled the great wars on the Continent. a. First England, France, and Holland broke the monopolies of Spain and Portugal in the New 

World and in the East. b. Then England and France reduced Holland to the position of a second-rate power. c. Finally, the threat of French supremacy on the Continent enabled England to find powerful allies in a series of wars which left France exhausted and defeated. d. Although British expansion in the New World was arrested by the revolt of the Thirteen Colonies, it continued unchecked in Asia, Africa, and Australia. 

3. An increase in national wealth and the growing importance of the middle class, generally speaking, characterized the colonial powers. 

4. In England, after 1689, the government was controlled by the landed aristocracy and was guided by commercial interests. Although living conditions improved greatly for members of the middle classes, these groups showed little interest in the welfare of the common people.
