GAINING Skill A. Where to Get Information. Most of your knowledge of history is gained through reading. In some cases, however, it is possible to visit a museum and view relics (clothing, utensils, coins, weapons, and so on) or even to make an excursion to some place of historic interest (Mount Vernon would be an example) or to a reconstruction of such a place (Fort Ticonderoga). Perhaps you will be able to make a field trip in order to get information about topics discussed in this chapter. If you are, plan your trip carefully. (1) Do background reading. (2) Get in mind what you want to learn. (3) Take notes on and make pictures of what you see. (4) Get suggestions for further reading. (5) Discuss your findings in class.

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. In Part I considerable emphasis has been placed on how people lived and dressed in various countries at various times. 

1. The organization of such information need not be restricted to oral and written reports. Indeed, one of the most effective ways to show change is through a series of drawings. Still another way is through the construction of model sets. Boys can make model furniture, houses, tools, and conveyances; girls can dress dolls in correct costumes for the various periods. Such projects, needless to say, are valuable as permanent displays. 

2. The foregoing suggestions raise another question which perhaps has been troubling you. How can one keep in mind the dates when important events occurred, relate these events one to another, and get a clearer picture of happenings in various countries at about the same time? 

Unquestionably one method is to memorize a few important dates-events; another is to construct time-lines. Thus you may draw a time-line five inches long and say that it represents 3000 years B.C. and 2000 years A.D. On such a line, how much space would be equal to a thousand years? Where on the line would you place the discovery of America by Columbus? Where the outbreak of the Second 

World War? Would it be better to use a longer line? Why?

We recommend that a committee prepare such a time-line and post important dates-events discussed in the first three chapters. After that is done, the committee should keep the time-line up to date. It is better not to include too many events. 

It may also be desirable to make multiple time-lines. For example, for the period after 1450 the text treats briefly the history of many nation-states: England, France, Portugal, Spain, Russia, Poland, and so on. Can you see any advantage in drawing parallel time-lines, one for each country, and all to the same scale?

You may want to organize a committee to do this work. It is better to use a large scale, and to draw the time-lines on large sheets of paper or on the blackboard. 

Can you think of another classification of history that might serve as a basis for the preparation of time-lines? Some might favor a topical plan, that is, an organization to include topics such as discovery and exploration, religious developments, governments and constitutions, science and invention, and so on. Perhaps you may want to make still another set of multiple time-lines according to this plan. 

Do you see how you can use time-lines to advantage in the study of history?

C. How to Evaluate Information. Even when a person is unprejudiced, he may still reach conclusions which are not valid. For example, there are many reasons why one of you might not form a correct opinion of the caliber of your football team. You might not be an expert in football, you might not see all of the games, you might not sit where you can accurately observe the play, you might be so excited that you can't tell exactly what happens, you might not have seen enough good teams play to know exactly what to expect, and so on. Can you see, therefore, why, in a theme which you might write to describe the play of the team, you might give the reader some wrong impressions? Are writers of history sometimes handicapped in the same ways? Think, for example, of the difficulties correspondents have encountered in accurately reporting the Second World War. Now can you see some reasons why historians are unable to write with authority about all events that have transpired? What kind of topics do you think that they can treat most adequately? Why?

DIVISION TWO The Age of Revolution 

Preview 

WE HAVE ALREADY LEARNED how in "The 

Age of National Upbuilding" the power of the king increased in the countries on the Continent at the expense of the Church and the feudal nobility. Although the churchmen and the nobles lost much of their political ascendancy and no longer "protected" the common people as during the Middle Ages, they nevertheless continued to enjoy such privileges as exemption from direct taxation, the right to collect feudal dues, and a preferred position at court. Since governmental expenditures were increasing, the economic burdens bore heavily on the peasantry and the middle class. 

Meanwhile, in the period following the

Protestant Revolt people became increasingly critical of existing conditions, and many intelligent persons began to question the value of maintaining privileged groups and an absolute king. In France, the failure of the privileged classes to accept voluntarily a part of the tax burden led to bankruptcy and compelled the King to call a meeting of the Estates General, the first in one hundred and seventy-five years. The French middle class grasped this opportunity to enact social and economic reforms and to establish a constitutional monarchy. This was the French Revolution.

The overthrow of the old order in France alarmed absolute monarchs in other countries, and, fearful of foreign interference, the French Revolutionists plunged their country into war. 

Under the pressure of the Paris mob, the radical leaders then established a republic, which, because of the national peril, soon developed into a temporary despotism based on terror, and it was this despotism, known as the "Terror," that restored order and saved

France. After the crisis was surmounted, a more moderate régime was set up, but unsettled conditions continued for several years. 

Tired of unrest, the French finally welcomed a strong government established by a military leader, Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon did not believe in government by the people, but scrupulously preserved equality of opportunity and equality before the law. The wars he inherited from the revolutionary governments, together with his vast ambition, led him to embark on a series of conquests which made him supreme on the Continent. In the end, however, the financial resources and naval strength of England, plus a rising spirit of nationalism in Spain and Germany, combined with military reverses to bring about his downfall. But first he had spread many of the revolutionary reforms to neighboring lands. 

The victorious powers compensated themselves for their losses, in general restored the larger states which had existed before 1789, and laid plans to prevent another revolutionary outbreak. Their peace settlement failed entirely to satisfy the craving of Germans and Italians for national unity, and a series of unsuccessful revolutionary attempts followed. 

Unrest also prevailed in various countries on the Continent because of the failure to establish democratic government. Only in Great 

Britain among the major powers was reform accomplished through peaceful means. 

Finally another Napoleon made himself 

Emperor of the French. Seeking to take an active part in foreign affairs, he fought a war with Austria which enabled the great Italian statesman, Cavour, to all but complete the unification of his country. The unification of 

Germany, in turn, was accomplished by Bismarck through a series of wars, the last of which was fought with France and resulted in the downfall of Napoleon III.

Thus by 1871 the spirit of nationalism, which had begun to burn so fiercely almost a century earlier in the days of the French Revolution, had won some glorious victories. But democracy had made but slight progress except in Great Britain and France.

CHAPTER IV The Old Régime in Europe: 

THE BACKGROUND, CAUSES, AND OUTBREAK OF  

What were the political, social, and economic conditions which characterized the Old Régime? 

What were the basic evils of the Old Régime?

Why did people become critical of the Old Régime when they lost respect for authority?

What were the immediate, as contrasted with the underlying, causes of the French Revolution?

WE MUST NOW MAKE a survey of the institu tions of Europe as we find them in the eighteenth century, for a great revolution will soon be coming, which will sweep many of them away. The government and society of this period are commonly known as the Old Régime. Most of its characteristics were centuries old, for civilization was still moving very slowly. But discontent was gathering, and this was to end in revolution; and then the world was to move on much more rapidly. 

Later we shall notice that in England there was a parallel revolution, known as the Industrial Revolution, which was also to lead to farreaching changes. In this chapter we shall explain the conditions that led to the French Revolution. 

A. Political Conditions under the

Old Régime 

Character of the Absolute Monarchies

Most of the European states were absolute monarchies. A few of the smaller states, Holland for example, were known as republics, since they were not ruled by princes; but actually they were ruled by a group of rich business men and were not at all democratic. 

Great Britain was a monarchy, but power rested in the hands of her landed aristocracy. 

Poland was a feudal state with only a shadow king, and she was therefore no match for her strong and aggressive neighbors — all of them, modern states. 

The great Continental powers, Austria, Prussia, Russia, and France, were absolute monarchies, and the same was true of scores of smaller states. All power resided in the sovereign, and it was exercised in his name by a multitude of officials. Every such government was therefore highly centralized. Orders issued by the central government were carried out by officials in the various provinces, intendants in France, stadholders in Prussia, and so on. Anyone who defied the king got into trouble with the police who served these officials, and if he were too powerful for the police, the king would use the standing army at his disposal. An absolute monarchy always rests on military power. It has force at its command.

Yet in most of the absolute monarchies there were to be found certain relics of the old feudal state. In Austria, Prussia, and France there were still provincial assemblies or feudal diets which went through the form of voting money to the king. In France, it is true, they always voted the sums which the Crown demanded. 

In Austria they had almost as little choice in the matter. In France and Prussia many of them had been suppressed or indefinitely suspended. But they present an interesting example of the fact that change came very slowly in the Old Régime.

FIGURE 62. COSTUMES IN FRANCE AT THE TIME OF THE REVOLUTION 

From left to right: Bishop and parish priest; courtier, poor country noble, and judge; bourgeoisie and peasants. 

The Prevailing Lack of Uniformity 

Another characteristic of the Old Régime was the lack of uniformity in institutions. Some provinces retained assemblies and some had lost them. Hungary did not contribute as much to the support of the common government as did the rest of the Emperor's dominions. In France some parts were taxed more than others, not because they were richer but because of age-old customs that had never been revised. Each state had grown up a hodgepodge since feudal days. The same weights and measures were not in use throughout a nation. Different systems of coinage were still employed in the Hapsburg lands. There were not even uniform laws concerning property. In France there were nearly three hundred codes of law. A man might inherit a piece of land in one province because he was the eldest son and in another province he might be forced to share the inheritance with brothers and sisters.

This lack of uniformity was, of course, very confusing. But it was sometimes worse than confusing. Some classes were exempt by feudal tradition or special favor from paying the land or income taxes; and that meant that the weight of taxation had to fall on other classes as a matter of fact, the poorer classes in the realm. The rulers of Austria and Prussia were partly successful in breaking down the privileges of the Church or the nobility in 

this connection, and sometimes the French kings attempted, though rather half-heartedly, to make the privileged classes share the burden of new taxes. But the fact remains that in 

France they paid next to nothing; in Prussia and Austria, little in proportion to their wealth; and in Russia not a penny. Generally, indeed, kings preferred to let well enough alone rather than hurt the pride of the classes which seemed to add dignity to the State. There was, of course, as wide a difference in the type of costumes in this period as the difference in income and interests in the various classes. Thus the splendor of the bishop was a contrast to the simplicity of the parish priest, as the first two sketches in Figure 62 show. 

And the courtier's elegance was not matched by the poor country noble, as may be seen in the third and fourth sketches. The judge in the fifth sketch wears still a different kind of costume. The well-to-do middle class or bourgeoisie dressed much better than the needy peasants, as the last two sketches demonstrate. 

Let us consider these privileged classes and turn to another side of the Old Régime. 

B. Social and Economic Conditions under the Old Régime Social and economic conditions can be best treated together because certain classes of society had interests which belonged to them as

classes. In other words, their manner of making a living depended largely on their position in society. They also had certain functions as members of society, which are strictly social conditions. We shall deal first with the classes especially identified with the land, and then with the class associated chiefly with business. 

Another distinction, however, may also be made. It was customary in France to divide society into three different classes or "estates," as they were called. The clergy were the first estate, though we shall find two divisions among them. The nobility were the second estate, though here again we shall note two inner divisions. The middle class and peasantry were lumped together as the third estate; but, as they differed greatly in economic condition, we shall treat them under separate heads. 

We shall here make our distinction between the landed or agrarian elements and those concerned with business.

The Clergy 

The clergy, or first estate, were privileged in taxation, as we have said, and even in France, where they made certain donations, they contributed very little to the royal treasury pitifully little if we consider the Church's wealth. On the other hand, they did carry on much of the social work which nowadays is the function of the State. 

In this class we must make a distinction between the higher and lower clergy. The higher clergy, which included bishops and archbishops, as well as the heads of monastic houses, were great landed proprietors who derived their means from the toil and income of peasants. The lower clergy, on the other hand, made up largely of parish priests, served as best they could on the wage which the higher clergy paid them, and it was usually pitifully small. Just as the higher clergy were drawn, as a rule, from the nobility, the lower clergy were men of humble extraction, usually from peasant families. Except for their relation to the Church, these two elements had little in common, and in France the time was to come when the parish priest, who toiled among the poor, and was poor himself, would feel much closer in sympathy to the third estate, whose blood he shared. 

The clergy, of course, played a supremely important rôle in society by ministering to the religious needs of humanity, pointing out to them the way to eternal life. They also provided most of the schools, hospitals, and asylums, though much more money might well have been contributed to these ends. Unfortunately the higher clergy had a social position to maintain, and many of them lived at court or in lavish splendor on their estates with little thought of their duties as Church officials. 

Those who did the most good were the lower clergy, who came in daily contact with the people.

In England, the Anglican clergy got their support partly from lands belonging to the Church, partly from voluntary contributions, and partly from a special tax. In other 

Protestant countries the clergy drew their salaries from the State, or, if Calvinists, through the support of their congregations. None of the Protestant clergy were landed proprietors; but in England the Anglican bishops held seats in the House of Lords, and none but the Anglican Church had the privilege of a special tax for its support. 

The Nobility 

The nobility, or second estate, got their income chiefly from land, though a favored few drew pensions from the Crown; and all enjoyed the same immunity from taxes as the clergy. They no longer enjoyed the political rights of the bygone feudal days, since every office was now derived from the Crown, but they were, nevertheless, of considerable political importance. They held most of the high offices in the government, as well as the diplomatic posts and the commissions in the army and navy. Moreover, the most influential nobles constituted the court, thus following a profession which was then considered necessary to royalty, namely, that of courtier. 

France, more than in any other country, to belong to the court was the highest social honor, and many courtiers managed to get royal pensions which enabled them to live in elegant style. One noble family, though already immensely rich, drew enormous sums in pensions. Some, however, could not have maintained the social pace without the aid of a In

pension; and others, who did not come to court at all, were actually poor. But, on the whole, the nobles in every country were a wealthy class. Only a few of them, moreover, performed any useful public service.

Yet the daily life of the courtier was not one of unqualified pleasure. Etiquette hedged 

Etiquette hedged him in at every turn. In every company he must know exactly how to address each person, and always pay the most scrupulous regard to differences in rank. The young noble who was about to make his plunge into society found it well to take some lessons on the manner in which he should carry himself. One of them wrote in his memoirs, "No actor can have been as nervous as I was when I made my first appearance on the social stage." One old courtier gave some shrewd advice to a newcomer, "You have only to do three things: say nice things to everybody; solicit every post that is likely to become vacant; and sit down when you can." In such an atmosphere it was difficult to be natural, though we should remember that in every age there are people who talk sweetly in order to advance their personal fortunes. Most of the French nobility were unfortunately a class which knew little about anything but etiquette and war. Their education was limited, and whatever they learned of the details of public business they had to pick up from experience, a fact which may account for much misgovernment in the Old Régime.

They impress us, on the whole, as a frivolous and useless class. Perhaps because they had lost their political power (in the feudal sense), they made the most of their empty pride of birth, and were arrogant in dealing with all whom they deemed beneath them. As they thought of nothing but class or personal interests, they exerted a bad influence over the king, unless he happened to be one who perceived the national interest and forced his nobles to follow his lead. Even most of the intendants were by this time of noble rank. 

Of course, the English nobility were markedly different from those on the Continent, since they were accustomed to assume political responsibility. And far from being immune from most of the taxes, they really bore the brunt of them. But they were also as a rule wealthier than the nobility of France.

Some nobles were descended from wealthy men who had bought their titles, but these upstarts, in spite of possessing landed estates, were hardly accepted as equals by the men of ancient family. Still less could those nobles in 

France, who owed their rank not to land but to office, hope for any social eminence. This official nobility - numbering, it is said, four thousand consisted of those who held certain offices that carried with them noble rank, and officially were regarded as belonging to the second estate. We mention them here, not because they belonged to the landed classes (though some of them did, it is true, own country estates), but because it is easier to get acquainted with all the nobles at one time. 

The Peasantry 

The peasantry constituted the mass of the population in every country. Their position varied greatly; for in eastern and central 

Europe most of the peasants were still serfs and could not leave the land which they tilled for their lords. In England, however, serfdom had long since disappeared, and in France there were probably not more than a million serfs out of a peasant population of twenty million.

In England, where feudal rights had also died out, there were even some small free proprietors (the so-called yeomen), though they were rapidly becoming extinct as a result of the enclosure movement. Backed by acts of 

Parliament, large landowners succeeded in getting more and more of the arable land as well as the common lands which the peasants had used for pasturing their stock, and fenced them off, or "enclosed" them, so as to create large-scale farms tilled by scientific methods. 

No doubt such a change was to the national interest, since it insured a greater food supply than could have been possible under a system of small and scattered holdings and large commons. But the peasants, having lost their common lands, were now compelled to utilize some of their tillable land for pasture, and had even less of this at their disposal. Though they received a slight indemnity for their loss, they were undoubtedly in a worse position than before; and they could not hope to rival the large landowners with their ready store of

OLD RÉGIME IN EUROPE THE 

capital and their modern methods of farming. 

Many of this former class sold their plots for what they could get and became tenants of these wealthier landlords. Still others - probably most of them-sank to the position of farm hands, working for the landlords at a wage.

As was said earlier, the English peasants were at least free of feudal burdens. Their 

Continental brothers, from time immemorial, had owed obligations to some lord, such as paying a sum of money which was equivalent to rent, or handing him a certain specified portion of the crop. In some parts of France the peasants had also to pay toll to the lord on roads which they had to travel in order to bring their products to market. Nearly all peasants, at least in France, had to use the lord's mill for grinding their wheat into flour and his oven to bake their bread and his winepress to make wine. It was said that the winepress was often busy and the peasants' grapes spoiled while they waited. In each case a fee had to be paid, and in some cases the lord's miller failed to return all the flour that was the peasants' due. Moreover, it often happened that the peasants had to wait before marketing their wine until the lord had marketed his. 

In addition, they suffered greatly because of the nobles' hunting privileges, since the deer kicked up the fields and the rabbits fed on their crops. But there was, of course, no redress; the peasants might neither kill these pests nor do any hunting themselves. Some of them were even compelled to grow thornbushes to serve as cover for the game in order to make the chase more thrilling; and such bushes were, of course, an obstacle to tillage. 

And in most of Europe, outside of France, the peasants had also the additional duty of furnishing labor to their lord.

All these duties were feudal in origin relics of the day when the peasants paid a lord for protection in an age of violence. But since the modern state now furnished all the protection needed, the peasants were obviously

The French peasants, though better off in the main than the serfs of central Europe, must have had a pretty hard time making a living. In addition to the feudal exactions, a tax had to be paid to the Church and several taxes to the State. They even had to furnish the State with several days of free labor (anywhere from twelve to forty days a year), which might come at a time when they needed to harvest their crops. Many were forced by poverty to enter into a sort of partnership with their lord, receiving from him some capital, such as implements and livestock, and paying him with a certain proportion of the crop. 

Most miserable of all were the farm hands, the rural laborers, who even at best could barely make a living, and many of whom were forced to become vagabonds and beggars. 

Yet in spite of the wretched condition of most of the peasantry, it is probable that there was a smaller percentage of extremely poor folk than had been the case a century before, since France was relatively prosperous in the 

This prosperity, late eighteenth century. however, was chiefly felt by the people of the towns. Financiers

The financiers were perhaps the wealthiest of the middle class. They were the bankers and the people who in France collected taxes as a private business, a practice we shall presently discuss. Many old aristocrats were glad to marry their sons to the daughters of these wealthy commoners and thus bring money into the family. The union of birth with wealth was becoming more common than ever before. Merchants

Next to the financiers in point of wealth ranked the merchants. The oversea trade had naturally made many fortunes; and the decline of the chartered companies, due to mismanagement and other causes, had made it possible for a greater number of merchants to participate in this trade. Some merchants took the place of the manufacturers and Bettmann

This was the so-called domestic system, and in England it was more important than the manufacturing under the direction of the guilds. There were also wholesale merchants who took the wares of the artisans and sold them in different localities, charging a commission for their service.

Yet commerce in the Old Régime had many noticeable drawbacks. The roads were poor, and most of the hauling was done by pack horses or oxen. Besides, on most of the roads and canals tolls were charged at various points, especially near the towns; and, save in England, tariffs were usually imposed on goods carried from one province into another. 

Thus merchandise shipped from Brittany, in

northwestern France, paid duties seven times on the way to Provence in the southeastern corner; and to make any profit at all a pretty high price would have to be charged in Provence. Manifestly such duties hampered trade and greatly restricted the market for manufactured wares.

While pack horses or oxen provided the usual means of transportation on land, the wind had to furnish the motive power on sea; and that meant that maritime journeys were long and arduous affairs. It sometimes required two years for a merchant fleet to sail to the East and return. Moreover, piracy wealthier manufacturers even opened large establishments, which were something like modern factories, employing several hundreds of workmen and even using machinery. The plight of the workmen under these industrial conditions was very grave, as we shall see when we later describe the Industrial Revolution. 

c. The Two Basic Evils of the Old Régime: Privilege and Absolutism 

Privilege was still a danger to be encountered; though Old Régime, it is not hard to find grounds for 

As we look back upon the conditions in the the British navy, it is true, had done much to lessen that evil.

Manufacturers The ancient manufacturers were the socalled artisans, among whom the master artisans were divided, as we have seen, into guilds; and in all industries organized in this way only the members of the guild had the privilege of manufacturing. Obviously in such a system there was no such thing as free competition. Moreover, the guilds were so exclusive that few of the wage-earning artisans, the journeymen and apprentices, were able to secure admission, and hence were debarred from setting up establishments for themselves.

But while the guilds were still exceedingly strong in most of Europe, they had gradually been losing much of their old importance in France, for the Crown had allowed new industries to develop without compelling them to conform to the old system. Doubtless it was being realized more and more that the guilds were quite unsuited to the times. The rise of the domestic system, which meant the employment of many more persons, and thus the production of a much greater volume of goods, seemed to show that the old régime of little shops and rigid rules was out-of-date. 

Capitalism was demanding a more efficient means of supplying trade with articles to sell. 

In England most of the guilds had died out, and many of the merchant-manufacturers now engaged in the domestic system were former members of a guild. Some of the dissatisfaction. Inequality was certainly the besetting sin. The upper classes were privileged members of society. In all countries they held the chief offices and in Great Britain they dominated Parliament. On the Continent they were able to dodge almost all of the taxes and in France many of them drew their main support from the royal treasury. Even in the matter of punishment, certain degrading forms, such as flogging, were reserved for the lower classes. People were not equal before the law. Where "Privilege" also invaded business. chartered companies existed, they were supposed to possess a monopoly of trade in a certain zone; they held a privileged position. 

And where guilds were strong, they possessed a monopoly of making a certain product; they, too, had a certain privileged position. Moreover, the guild itself was composed of masterartisans; journeymen and apprentices had little chance of admission. "Privilege," it is true, was breaking down somewhat in the economic world, but in politics and society it still held full sway.

Absolutism 

Absolutism was not, perhaps, so oppressive as privilege, yet it usually upheld privilege. 

It was the absolute king who protected the nobles and sometimes the guilds in the privileges they enjoyed.

Moreover, absolutism had certain vices of its own. It squandered money which the poor man had paid in taxes. In some coun-

tries, like Prussia, it conscripted men for the army and paid them next to nothing for this service. It stood in the way of freedom of speech and usually prohibited religious freedom. Its administration of justice left much to be desired, and too often it subjected the people to domineering officials over whom they had no control. It was at times, indeed, It was at times, indeed, very inefficient, for the person who sat on the throne got his position through inheritance, and it was just a happy accident if he showed himself a good and able sovereign. 

But people for centuries had meekly borne these evils without much protest. They seemed to feel that things had to be as they were. How, then, did people finally become aroused?

It was not because the Old Régime was worse in the eighteenth century than it had been, let us say, in the sixteenth. 

In fact, it was somewhat better, for strongly centralized government was better than feudal disorders and civil war, and in France at least, where revolution was brewing, the middle class had gained in wealth and numbers. But many gradually came to believe that all these various evils which still persisted need not be endured forever. Then arose a strong demand for some reform. It was because reform when it came was totally inadequate that men were finally swept into revolution. Let us now consider the movement which enabled people to realize the weaknesses of the Old Régime.

D. Rise of Dissatisfaction with the 

Old Régime, the Underlying Cause of the French Revolution

The Enlightenment: Its Meaning and Origins 

The movement which showed up the follies of the Old Régime and led many people to hope for better things is known as the Enlightenment. It was a wave of intellectual protest, steadily gathering force as it went on, and merging in the end with a strong emotional reaction against the antiquated social, economic, and political system. It was a movement long getting under way, and to discover its origins we must go back a century or two.

To begin with, we remember that the Renaissance had fostered a certain critical habit of mind, a feeling that one did not have to believe all the things which had been handed down as settled. This conviction led many to doubt some teachings of the Church, a factor, as we have seen, in the Protestant Revolt. Certain beliefs in the realm of science were also questioned, as we have noted. (See page 17.) Now, after the Wars of Religion and the English Civil War had come to a close, certain men found the leisure in which to think of the world about them, the world of Nature and of man, and to discover some new truths. Many of the things that science tells us today date from this period.

The telescope and microscope, inventions of the seventeenth century, brought men nearer to things which had formerly lain beyond their vision; and advances in mathematics led to a greater degree of accuracy in scientific work. (The picture on page 92 shows an early demonstration of the use of the telescope.) Unquestionably the greatest scientist of the seventeenth century was Sir Isaac Newton, an Englishman whose genius overcame his humble extraction and won for him a professorship at the age of twenty-seven. Newton discovered the law of gravitation, explaining the attractive force which enabled the earth and all the planets to stay in their orbits about the sun instead of just "running wild" throughout the universe. Of immediate practical value was the discovery of an English physician, Edward Jenner. In the eighteenth century he found by experiment that the dreaded disease of smallpox could be averted by vaccination. It has been estimated that sixty million people had died of that scourge in the course of a century, and it was particularly dreaded by women, because, even if they recovered, they were likely to be terribly scarred. Rightly Jenner was hailed as one of the noblest and most distinguished men of his time. tinguished men of his time. (The picture on page 93 shows his first vaccination.) scientific discoveries of the seventeenth century naturally paved the way for others in the eighteenth; and it was partly as a result of scientific study that the steam engine was invented. Thus this intellectual awakening gave rise to another great movement, the The

What was really natural one could not always help; one could not wholly defy the laws of Nature. But what appeared to be unnatural might just as well be thrown into the discard. 

How, then, was one to know what was unnatural? More and more thinkers came to believe that human reason should make this test; and the test of an institution was its utility. Thus any institution which stood in the way of men's happiness was unnatural and irrational. Human reason would not accept it. And reason, as John Locke, an

English philosopher, believed, was likely to be the product of experience. Thus Nature and human reason should shape the life of man.

Now it is clear that all have not the same ability to reason, and that is where the rationalists, as they were called, were weak in argument. They seemed to think, moreover, that good laws were all that were needed to make men happy, regardless of the fact that people may be quite too wrong-headed to obey these very laws. 

But the idea that human reason should be the method of testing all existing notions and institutions was the central idea of the Enlightenment. It was the magnifying glass through which the Old Régime was Industrial Revolution, which we shall study in being viewed. a later chapter.

All these facts would seem to show that certain people at least were doing some thinking, and it was natural enough that some should turn to social and political questions and ask themselves if some of the things man suffered at the hands of his neighbor might not also be out-of-date.

Particularly were thinkers impressed by the basic discovery of Newton. This scientist proved that the universe (our world and many others) was not a mysterious thing which God was moving according to His pleasure, but that it ran according to certain natural laws. 

Hence it was natural to believe that man himself was also subject to natural laws as for instance that the length of his life was partly explained by the condition of his body. The realm of the supernatural, on which the Church had laid great emphasis, seemed to 

There was, however, another factor which contributed to the Enlightenment - one that appealed somewhat to the feelings as well as to reason. The horrors of the Religious Wars had led many to feel thoroughly tired of creeds and opinions that people had to accept merely because someone said that they were right. 

Hence all these rationalists felt that it was most unjust to punish people for what they believed. In other words, they all stood for religious toleration. 

The Critical Philosophers as Representatives of the 

Enlightenment

Except for Locke, who advocated a limited monarchy and certain "natural rights," such as the right to own property, the critics of the seventeenth century were not at all famous as such in their day, and we shall consequently omit them, though their critical attitude of

mind had some influence on later thinkers. 

But in the eighteenth century an influential group, the "Philosophers," most of whom were Frenchmen, thought and wrote. One of the earliest, Montesquieu, wrote a famous work, The Spirit of Laws, published in 1748, in which he set forth the advantages of a limited monarchy. He made himself famous for his opinion that the executive, legislative, and judicial arms of government should be distinct from one another an idea known as the "separation of powers." Being a judge, and therefore a member of the official nobility, Montesquieu did not venture to attack privilege, but he denounced religious intolerance, unjust punishments, and other evils. 

Another critic, Diderot, edited a great encyclopedia, in which he and other contributors deliberately attacked things they did not like, such as feudalism, guilds, and religious intolerance. Twice the government tried to put a stop to the work, and once a whole volume was suppressed; but Diderot had endless patience and courage, and brought the work to completion in 1772. 

There was also a group who called themselves the "Economists," and leveled their chief attack at mercantilism, insisting that all business should be free of regulation. Laissezfaire (let alone) was their watchword. They believed in what they called "natural law," and by that they meant that the business man should be left to his own judgment as to how he should do business. The manufacturer should make things as he pleased and the merchant in turn should be free to decide where he should find his customers and what he should charge for his goods. They disapproved of all tariffs, guilds, and monopolies. Turgot, an able intendant, was one of the leading members of this group. Another, a Scottish thinker, Adam Smith, known for his book,

The Wealth of Nations (1776), showed how mercantilism cramped and impeded commerce, and he is regarded as the father of free trade.

But undoubtedly the most famous man in his day was Voltaire. This celebrated Frenchman was a tireless writer, and people enjoyed what he wrote because his style was clear and witty. He hated superstitions of all sorts, FIGURE 66

Naturally kind-hearted, he could not bear to see anybody a victim of injustice; and he devoted much of his time and money to righting people's wrongs. Though he felt that class differences were inevitable, he did not approve of the crushing feudal burdens, and he denounced the tax exemptions of the nobility and the clergy. No other author of his day was so widely read, and people who followed his arguments could hardly help being shaken in their respect for the Old Régime. 

In the wake of these famous writers there were many others. Many of these men were not opposed to absolutism in theory, but they yearned for a freer life for the individual one in which he might write and believe as he chose, and not be ground down by useless burdens.

The Romantic Philosopher: Rousseau 

(He is shown Jean Jacques Rousseau was a native of 

Geneva, the son of a poor watchmaker. His mother died at his birth, and he grew up a rather neglected boy, with naturally vicious habits. He was apparently never taught any self-control, and was always too ready to follow an evil impulse. Twice he ran away from his employer, and he lived the life of a vagabond most of his days. Naturally given to solitude, he usually found it hard to get on with people. He seemed always to be looking inside himself, conscious of his talents, yet shy and morbidly sensitive, and feeling himself the victim of a hard and cruel world. If he had only been blessed with a saving sense of humor and been able to laugh a little, he might not have taken himself or the world quite so seriously.

Yet there was something about Jean Jacques that seemed to draw people toward him, and he managed to make some friends among the Philosophers, who knew him to be brilliant and were willing to overlook his boorish manners. In 1749, when he was thirty-seven years old, he read that a learned society was offering a prize for the best answer to the question:

Has the progress of the arts and sciences contributed to corrupt or purify manners? After weeping from stress of emotion, Rousseau decided to enter the contest in support of the first conception and wrote a bitter tirade against civilization. "Nature," he said, "made man happy and good, but society depraves him and makes him miserable." He seemed to feel that only primitive man was really worthy of admiration. In the world that he saw about him he seemed only to be impressed by the hollow and artificial. the conveniences of life increase, as the arts are brought to perfection, and luxury spreads, true courage flags, and virtues disappear."

So wrote Rousseau, with a thought, no doubt, of the people who enjoyed the products of civilization without doing a bit of good for their fellowmen. His views were so unusual that he won the prize, and people looked with wonder at this strange and discomfited soul who wrote with clearness and vigor and yet seemed at times to be not quite sound of mind. "As

Rousseau wrote other works, the most famous of which was called The Social Contract (1762), in which he argued that people had originally set up a government merely for convenience and that really it was they themselves who possessed power; they could even use this power to abolish their government if they wished. From this theory one might gather that even revolution might sometimes be justifiable; yet Rousseau often contradicted himself, and he did not always trouble to think

what his teachings seemed to imply. He believed that fundamentally man was good. "Man is born free and everywhere he is in chains" was his lament.

The people alone should rule. He did not, however, believe in any parliament to make the laws, and he seemed to feel that the majority's will should rule a condition that might be hard on the minority. He also believed as far as possible in equality of wealth.

Piecing together the views, poured out haphazardly in his writings, one might feel that Rousseau preached equality and democracy, or something pretty close to these principles. 

To the downtrodden he held out the hope of a new life.

The Middle Classes as the Champions of Reform 

It was not to the masses, however, that Rousseau brought his gospel, much as he had them in mind. We cannot suppose that many of the common people read his message, for few were able to read well enough for that, and those who could would hardly have been able to follow his wordy arguments. Some workmen in the towns may have heard his views discussed, and we learn of one occasion when an orator tried to interpret The Social Contract on the street corners in Paris. one cannot say that the masses were moved by Rousseau, and it was certainly not the masses, for all their acute distress, that began the French Revolution. 

But

It was, rather, the middle class that was deeply stirred by the Enlightenment, not, of course, because it was poor and downtrodden quite the contrary. This was a class that was in the main comfortably off, and it was because of that very fact that it looked with a critical eye on the misgovernment of a king who surrounded himself as a rule with worthless favorites. What could be more significant than a financial system no business man would endure! The middle class wanted reforms, and, provided reforms were made, most of them probably would not object to absolute monarchy itself. taire himself had said that he would rather be ruled by one lion than two hundred rats.

Vol- But privilege was something the middle class genuinely hated. They resented the airs of the nobles and felt themselves deserving of social equality. When a certain Madame 

Roland, on being invited to remain for dinner at a nobleman's residence, learned that she was expected to eat it in the servants' quarters, her resentment was bitter and deep. The middle class were well aware of their own importance - how they brought trade to the country, lent money to the Crown, and held most of the posts in the administration. In learning and practical experience they far outclassed their privileged superiors. Naturally they felt that worth rather than birth should be the basis for recognition. The highest political honors should no longer be reserved for an arrogant and idle aristocracy. The middle class should reap the rewards they so justly deserved.

Hence, Rousseau's principle of equality meant much to the middle class. They did not, it is true, think highly of the classes below them, but as far as the nobility were concerned, it was for them a class struggle. Perhaps if they ousted the nobility, they might even try to run the government itself, and at least they expected to be treated on a par with the nobles. Thus the middle class, who had furnished most of the critics of the Old Régime, were ready and eager for change.

In the meantime, all over France were formed societies which met and discussed the views of the philosophers of the Enlightenment. Gradually a public opinion was being shaped and after a while the Old Régime was shaking under its force. Would an absolute monarchy that upheld the system of privilege see the danger? Could it be moved to adopt sweeping reforms as the only possible alternative to revolution?

E. The Immediate Causes and Outbreak of the French Revolution 

An immediate cause of the French Revolution was the failure of the monarchy to institute a really complete housecleaning; another was an acute financial crisis which made necessary an appeal to the people to come to its rescue.

These facts we must now consider.

THE WEAKNESS OF THE MONARCHY AND THE FAILURE OF REFORM Two Incompetent Kings 

The weakness of the monarchy was partly due to the character of the king and partly due to the blighting influence of the nobles, which stood in the way of the reforms most urgently needed. He

Louis XV was king at the time when the Enlightenment had got well under way. was a man of some intelligence, but too lazy to employ it. All his life he seemed to care for nothing but dissipation. He squandered money on favorites and left the government hopelessly in debt. There were a few competent ministers one of them was able to add Lorraine to the kingdom, and another, Corsica - but these were exceptions. Most of the time the government seemed to be run in hit-or-miss fashion. During his last days the King himself realized what a sorry state he was leaving to his successors, for he is said to have remarked, "After me, the deluge."

When his grandson, Louis XVI, ascended the throne (1774), people felt that perhaps better things would come. But Louis, while a nobler man than his grandfather and naturally kind and amiable, had, unfortunately, little intelligence or force; and he was much influenced by his wife, an Austrian princess, Marie Antoinette. There was no one quite so unpopular in France as this queen. was frivolous and extravagant, and perhaps because she was a foreigner, the public liked to think that she was to blame for all the She monarchy's misfortunes. It would possibly be more just to condemn the court. 

The Influence of the Court 

A great many nobles were holders of royal pensions, and at the court they amused themselves by indulging in petty intrigues and, in fact, behaving as idle people are only too likely to do. Of course, this was the usual condition at the French court, but the fact remains that these courtiers exerted a very unfortunate influence over a pleasure-loving queen and a king who had so little will of his This idle element was closest to the own.

reforms! Truth to tell, Louis XVI was amiable enough to play the rôle of a reformer even if he did not have the mind to understand the philosophers. Accordingly, some of his ministers were permitted to enact reforms, and one minister, Turgot, whose work we shall presently discuss, seemed likely to give the monarchy a new lease on life. But alas, the influence of the court was much too strong to permit any reduction of privilege. And it was privilege that was ruining the monarchy. 

For it was the influence of the privileged classes that was bankrupting the monarchy and also keeping it from saving itself by thoroughgoing reform.

THE FINANCIAL CRISIS 

Impending Bankruptcy

The bad state of the finances was of long standing. Louis XIV had left a great deal of debt, and Louis XV had made it larger. 

When Louis XVI came to the throne, the government owed an enormous sum on which it had to pay a high rate of interest. Moreover, there was always a heavy deficit; that is, the money raised in taxes was less than the sums expended.

Much of the trouble resulted from the extravagance of the court. 

Louis XV had never considered the amount of money in the treasury and how much could be spared for royal extravagance. A king was accustomed to draw as much as he pleased, not even bothering as a rule to leave a record of his spending.

Yet this heavy load might perhaps have been borne if the system of taxation had been more efficient. The fact that most of the taxes did not reach the upper classes has been mentioned again and again. This meant that a great deal of wealth was quite beyond the reach of the State. Furthermore, many of the taxes themselves were very unwisely handled. It was customary to allow some financiers to collect certain of the taxes for the government, keeping a rich commission for themselves. In this way the government was able to get ready cash, since these tax collectors were expected to make payment in advance of collection. But the State was, of

Turgot Does His Best Was

To straighten out the financial tangles of the government was a problem that called for a man of exceptional ability and courage.

Such a man was Turgot, a member of the group known as the "Economists," who had made an excellent record as an intendant. 

Louis made him director of the finances and promised him his entire confidence.

Turgot readily grasped the fact that the deficits must be met by strict economy and that taxes must fall upon those who were able to pay. By careful economy he reduced the annual deficit by more than a third. He also did away with many of the old restrictions on trade and abolished the monopoly of the guilds. Though he did not as yet improve the system of tax collection, he abolished the tax in labor paid by the peasant, meaning to substitute a tax that would fall on all in accordance with their wealth. But in attempting to levy on privilege, he antagonized those very classes which were strong enough to defeat him by the method they generally used that of intrigue. They persuaded the Queen to induce the King to dismiss him. "Do not forget, Sire," Turgot warned Louis, "that weakness cost Charles I his head."

Revolution may be said to have contributed in two ways to the downfall of the Old Régime. It put the monarchy deeper into debt, and inspired many Frenchmen with a love for more liberal institutions. When Benjamin 

Franklin visited Versailles he charmed society with his unaffected manner and genuine love of freedom. Many French nobles - for example, the Marquis de Lafayette played a part in the American Revolution and returned to France with the feeling that the Old Régime was out-of-date.

Living from Hand to Mouth 

Meanwhile the financial condition of the government had been growing steadily worse. 

A Swiss banker named Necker was placed at the head of the treasury, but his only plan was to borrow more and more money. In order to make it easier to float a loan, he published, in 1781, what was supposed to be a complete report on the finances. It was not, however, complete, and consequently not honest; for, in order to show a balance in the treasury, he entirely omitted the expenses incurred in waging the American war. 

This report attracted a great deal of attention, for it listed the enormous sums spent on pensions for the nobility. So, naturally, it deepened the discontent.

Necker only made matters worse by such expedients. "Do not expedients. Other directors of the finances struggled to lessen the growing deficit, but in vain. One of them, Calonne, as a desperate resort, got the King to call a meeting of an

Assembly of Notables, as it was called, a select group of the privileged classes, hoping that these gentlemen would allow themselves to be taxed. Having lived off the King's bounty, could they now refuse to aid the King in distress? What happened as the result of this step neither Louis XVI nor Calonne could well have foreseen.

These words were strangely prophetic. 

Turgot was the one man who might, by radical reforms, have saved the absolute monarchy.

Had he, in fact, been able to undermine privilege, he might have given the monarchy a new lease on life. But the King lacked the courage to withstand the pressure of his court, and all of Turgot's reforms were swept away after his fall. 

Influence of the American Revolution

It was after Turgot's fall that France embarked on a venture far more expensive than any she had attempted in many years. She took a hand in the American Revolution by waging war on Great Britain, the War of

THE COMING OF THE ESTATES GENERAL AND THE OUTBREAK OF  The Privileged Classes Turn Against the Crown 

The Assembly of Notables met in 1787, and 

Calonne besought their approval of a tax that

would fall on all persons in proportion to their wealth. But all appeals were vain. The privileged classes declined to approve of a tax that took no account of class differences. 

What they wanted, indeed, was to increase the embarrassments of the Crown, hoping that in the end they might control the monarchy, as their forefathers in feudal days had done. Some of them clamored for the summons of the Estates General, a feudal assembly which had not met since 1614.

The Summons of the Estates General 

A new head of the finances had no more success than Calonne.

The government was now bankrupt, and the King was at his wits' end. So loud was the agitation that Louis finally yielded, and summoned the Estates General.

Was it possible that this ancient institution, now revived in a time of crisis, would assume a new importance and create a new France?

The Middle Class Assumes Leadership 

As soon as it was announced that elections were to be held for the Estates General, the middle class became active. This class resolved to control the Estates General if it could possibly do so, and hence it was greatly pleased when the government announced that the third estate should have the same number of deputies as the other two estates combined. 

If some of the lower clergy should vote with the third estate, provided, of course, that the three estates should meet and vote in one assembly, then the middle class would control the Estates General. 

This class, accordingly, took a most active interest in the elections, and it was chiefly they who were elected to represent the third estate. Then, as each estate was authorized to draw up petitions, one of the time-honored privileges of the Estates General, the leaders of the middle class made it their business to instruct the people what to demand. These petitions give us a good clue to the state of public feeling. Heavy taxation, court extravagance, and feudal burdens were among the things most complained of; and there was a strong demand for a constitution. Though Though there was a good deal of distress in the country at this time, partly because of a bad harvest and partly because of an increase in unemployment, the elections were held without violence, and people seemed to feel that in some way or other all their grievances would be met and that a new and better France was in the making.

The Opening of the Estates General 

The Estates General was summoned to meet at Versailles, where the King and court lived. The opening session was held on 

May 5, 1789, all estates meeting together to be formally received by the King. 

It must have been a very interesting sight. 

The nobles were there in their handsome and colorful attire; the clergy, in their long and stately robes; and the third estate, clad in simple garb (black coats and breeches), must have felt quite out of place in such a throng. 

Most of the latter had never before been anywhere near the court, and now, as their eyes took in the hall, with its marble columns, its gilded ceilings, and its beautiful paintings and tapestries, one can readily guess how dazed they must have been. Then, as the King himself rose to address them in all his majesty, how wonderful it must have seemed to them to be there! And to think that His Gracious

Majesty had actually called them to help in the task of governing his kingdom! 

But it was not very long before the third estate grew puzzled and rather distressed. 

What could His Majesty mean? He said nothing about giving them responsibility, and he warned them that they must not think of tampering with privilege. He did not even say that the Estates General was to meet in one body; and they knew that if the estates were to meet separately, the privileged classes would control the situation, since the first and second estates could invariably outvote them.

Apparently the Estates General was in some mysterious way to save the King from bankruptcy by filling the national treasury. Presumably it was expected to approve some tax the government wanted. But no suggestion was made that the Estates General should act as a true partner of the Crown in carrying out any of the reforms so much demanded.

THE MIDDLE CLASS RESORTS TO REVOLUTION 

Formation of the National Assembly On one thing, however, the third estate 

SUMMARY of Important Concepts held firm. It would not meet separately as one of three bodies. So, while the other estates met to take up matters of business, the third estate spent most of its time in trying to persuade the first and second estates to join them. A few of the lower clergy decided to come over, but most of the clergy remained in their own meeting, and all the nobles, of course, held aloof. It was evident that the third estate must now take some drastic action if anything substantial were to be accomplished.

So the third estate took a momentous decision. On June 20, it declared that, representing as it did ninety-six per cent of the nation, it was the only body qualified to express the national will, and it constituted itself the "National Assembly." In other words, the other estates could join or not, as they pleased; the third estate in any event was the one body which represented France. (The cartoon on this page reflects the feeling of the middle class that the third estate supported the other two.)

But the third estate had not a particle of right to determine how the Estates General should hold its meetings. Any such decision belonged to the Crown, which was legally the sole source of power. 

Thus the third estate was clearly taking the law into its own hands. 

And in this momentous step we may well mark the outbreak of the French Revolution. 

What would the outcome be? At the moment one thing was clear. The middle class was to lead in the work of reform. 1. The failure of social, political, and economic institutions to adapt themselves to new conditions caused widespread dissatisfaction in the second half of the eighteenth century. Fundamentally the Old 

Régime was unpopular because of a. Privilege: groups within each estate enjoyed rights the majority of the people lacked. b. Absolutism: the king and the government in effect owed an accounting to no one for their acts. 

2. Opposition to the Old Régime developed from a. The Enlightenment which made people critical of existing conditions and much less likely blindly to accept authority. b. The insistence on more nearly equal treatment by the increasingly powerful middle class. 

3. In France, dissatisfaction with existing conditions turned to revolutionary demands for reform largely because of a. The inability of the king to introduce efficient government. b. A financial crisis which made necessary a sweeping reorganization of the tax system and the placing of a fair share of the tax burden on the privileged classes.

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. When you were in the grades you probably expected the teacher to ask you questions and felt lucky if you could recall enough of what you had read in the textbook to give a satisfactory answer. But in high school you probably have discovered that the superior student before he goes to class knows the very questions around which the class discussion will center. 

There is no magic about this mind reading. 

1. Skillful readers grasp what a textbook relates. Before they begin to read they see if there are any clues to what is being discussed. (Do you use the guide questions at the beginning of the chapter?) Then they read the selection rapidly and ask themselves what are the big ideas in the chapter. (Do you feel that these are made clear in the "Summary of Important Concepts"?) Next they ask themselves what is the important information that must be focused on each big idea. (Don't you think "How Carefully 

Do You Read?" suggests this information?) To get essential knowledge in mind requires serious effort to recall information plus re-reading if recall proves inadequate. 

2. In this textbook we help you to study effectively, but, needless to say, you should learn to do for yourself the things we are doing for you. You can gain skill by choosing a subject in which you are

interested and giving an oral report to the class. Take notes on what you read, make an outline to include major points, and carefully think through what you are going to say. When you report to the class, refer to your notes only if you want to quote some important material exactly. Learn to keep your outline in mind and to speak without notes. 

The following subjects will suggest a topic for your oral report: feudal customs under the Old Régime, the privileged classes, a French reformer (Rousseau, Voltaire, Turgot, and others), the greatest abuse of the Old Régime, and the cahiers. 

C. How to Evaluate Information. If you have a chance, read Arthur Young's Travels in France or extracts from this book published elsewhere. You will discover that Young finds much to criticize about farm practices and rural life in France under the Old Régime. 

As you read Arthur Young or some other writer who is describing what he actually saw or heard, notice that part of the time he states facts; part of the time he states his opinion of what these facts imply. Do you see clearly the difference between fact and opinion?

For example, your teacher might say, "The thirty pupils in this class are the most co-operative group in the school." Which is fact; which is opinion? Analyze a paragraph in some history book you are reading to discover statements of fact and opinion. Is that distinction easy to make? 

If a classmate were to say, "It was 10 above at eight o'clock this morning," would that be a statement of fact? To decide this question you would need to know whether your classmate actually looked at a thermometer at 8 A.M., whether he read it accurately, whether the thermometer was so placed that it accurately measured the temperature, and whether indeed it was an accurate instrument. In other words, your classmate might have looked at a thermometer and yet not have learned the truth. He might have implied that he looked at one without actually doing it. Conceivably he might be so expert at judging temperature that he is always close in his estimates and often makes them exactly right. 

As you read, therefore, remember that statements of fact may be incorrect, that implied statements of fact may be only statements of opinion, and that statements of opinion range in validity from extremely unreliable to highly reliable.

CHAPTER V The French Revolution: 

THE PEOPLE PROVE THEMSELVES WILLING AND ABLE TO CARRY OUT SWEEPING REFORMS

THE 

HE FRENCH REVOLUTION was a movement that shook Europe to its foundations. Though it was only France that was turned upside down, it really challenged the Old Régime everywhere. We shall later consider its effects upon Europe. Here we must trace its stormy course in France, watch it sweep away the entire Old Régime, plunge the nation into anarchy, set up a curious despotism of "terror" in order to save itself, and finally because the work of destruction was carried much too far for most of the nation - observe a return to more settled conditions under a moderate liberal régime. It was the fate of the middle class to begin the Revolution, lose control of the movement, and finally rise to power once again.

A. The Revolution Becomes General 

If nothing had happened in France beyond a successful defiance of the King by the middle class, we should still have called the affair a revolution. The breakdown of absolute monarchy after nearly two centuries is quite enough to justify the term "revolution." But the movement was much more powerful than that. It not only altered the form of government, but it created in some respects a new society. All this took place in the course of the first year of the Revolution. And now let us pick up the thread where we left it in the last chapter.

THE MIDDLE CLASS STARTS THE REVOLUTION The Middle Class Decides to Make a New Mon archy and Defy the King

We have noticed how the middle class put itself at the head of the movement called into being to rescue the monarchy from its financial plight; and how it took upon itself the right to speak for all France. Naturally enough, the government was amazed, and the King resolved to hold a meeting of all three estates in order to force them to respect him. In the meantime he commanded that the estates should suspend their sessions. 

But for some reason this announcement was not delivered promptly to the third estate, and when this body repaired to its hall as usual on 

June 20, they found the doors barred and several guards posted outside. At once they suspected that the King had decided to dismiss the Estates General, and they were furious at what they believed to be a conspiracy hatched by the court. Without taking time for thought, they moved to an indoor tennis court near the palace, where they took the famous Oath of the Tennis Court. after another these deputies solemnly swore that they would not end their sessions until they had made a constitution for the French nation. (See page 104.) Thus the middle class announced its decision that the absolute monarchy must end. One
