The King Yields 

We do not know the King's feelings when he heard of this bold proceeding. As a matter of fact, the Dauphin' had just died; the court was therefore in mourning; and probably the significance of the act was hardly appreciated for the moment. On June 23, the King held the meeting of all three estates, as he had intended.

Following custom, the first estate entered the hall, and then the second. As it happened to be raining, the third estate, standing outside the palace, got very wet and very impatient, while they waited for their turn to file in. When all were finally seated, the 

King addressed them. He told them that they were to meet in three estates as hereto- I The name given the oldest son of the King of France. fore, and warned them again not to disturb privilege. Certain reforms he promised (only promised!), such as the approval of all taxes by the Estates General and his sanction of the abolition of tax exemptions of the upper classes as soon as the latter had renounced them; but he did not admit, of course, that the deputies had any right to make a constitution, and his manner was very gruff, as if he looked upon them as spoiled and unruly children. 

When he had finished his brief address and left the hall, an officer of the King declared the meeting at an end. The first estate filed out, and then the second. But the third estate, when the time came for them to go, did not budge. They remembered that they had made themselves a legislative body, and they did not mean to leave at the King's command. "The King bids you disperse," said the officer

with some impatience. Then up rose one of the men of the third estate, a big, burly fellow, the Vicomte de Mirabeau, who, though a member of the nobility, had been chosen a representative of the third estate. "Know you," he declared in a thunderous voice, "that the commoners of France will never disperse save at the point of the bayonet." Hearing these bold words, the third estate lost all fear, and not a deputy stirred until it was voted to suspend the session.

It proved, indeed, a great victory for the third estate. When told of their disobedience, the King declined to try any discipline. "Well," he sighed wearily, "let them have their way." He even gave orders that the other two estates should join with the third estate to form one assembly. Thus on the question of organization the third estate had won its point.

Getting Down to Business Formation of the 

Constituent Assembly 

A few days later, on July 6, the Assembly appointed a committee to draft the provisions of a constitution. By so doing it assumed the authority of a "constituent" assembly, meaning an assembly whose chief business was to make a constitution. Until this constitution should be put into effect, giving France a new legislative body, the original assembly would make the laws.

Thus, unless it were sharply checked, the Revolution would make an end of the absolute monarchy. But the King had not yet 

Isaid his last word.

THE PEOPLE OF PARIS TAKE A HAND IN THE REVOLUTION The King Attempts to Stop the Revolution 

On the same day that the King gave in to the wishes of the third estate, he prepared a surprise for them. Some twenty thousand soldiers were ordered to Versailles. The meaning of this was fairly clear to the Assembly; he intended to use this force either to frighten it into submission or perhaps even to abolish it altogether. In vain the members protested. The King answered blandly that this force was to protect them. But it did not take much wisdom to perceive that the court was at the bottom of this design and that what it really wanted was to undo the Revolution. 

While the fate of the Assembly and the hopes of the middle class thus hung in the balance, the King dismissed his liberal ministers and replaced them with some men of reactionary views. 

Paris to the Rescue

But Paris came to the rescue of the Revolution. The hard-pressed Assembly was saved in a curious way by the men of the street.

Every great city has a lot of rough characters in its midst, and Paris was at this time. overcrowded, since tens of thousands of peasants had swarmed into the city. There had been a bad harvest in the autumn, followed by an unusually hard winter, so most of these peasants were hungry. There were also thousands of workmen out of work, for a commercial treaty with England had let in English woolens to compete with the domestic product, and accordingly many shops had closed their doors. doors. A large proportion of the population, which was over six hundred thousand, was, therefore, suffering want; and it would not take much to turn these wretched creatures into a mob. 

The Attack on the Bastille When the news of the King's acts reached the city on July 12, it was ready for an explosion. Thousands, it seems, were collected in a public park, when a journalist jumped upon a table in front of a restaurant and shouted at the top of his lungs, "The soldiers are killing the patriots. To arms! To arms!" This seemed to be all that was necessary to rouse the assembled crowd. It did not march to 

Versailles to defend the Assembly, but it needed no further encouragement to start a riot. Bakeries were pillaged by the hungry, and gun-shops were entered by many in search of arms.

As the guardians of order, half-sympathizing with the rioters, seemed unable to keep order, some leading citizens petitioned the King for the right to form a guard. But unfortunately, before there was time to complete arrange-

FIGURE 71. STORMING THE BASTILLE, JULY 14, 1789 

This picture appeared in a newspaper shortly after the Bastille fell. On the ramparts the defenders have hoisted a white flag indicating their readiness to surrender. ments, there was a fresh outbreak of rioting. 

On July 14, another crowd, made up, for the most part, of criminals and mutinous soldiers, gathered in search of arms. They plundered all the gunsmiths and even got some weapons from the veterans' home. 

Then someone suggested that arms could be got from the Bastille, a prison, once used as a fortress, which stood in the heart of the city. 

The people of Paris had long hated the Bastille, since it seemed to them a symbol of royal tyranny, though at this time only seven persons, all of them common criminals, were confined within its walls. That this mob could have taken it by storm is highly unlikely, but after scattered firing from both sides, the commandant was persuaded to surrender "with the honors of war." (An artist's conception of the storming of the Bastille appears on this page.) Unhappily the commandant was brutally done to death, as were other officers of the King. The whole episode was a terrible forewarning of the power that lay in the masses.

Nonetheless, the violent action of the people really saved the Revolution, for the King sent away his troops and restored the ministers he had dismissed. No wonder France has celebrated this day, July 14, brated this day, July 14, as her great national holiday.

There were important results besides the King's abrupt yielding. A new city government, known as the "Commune," was now organized; and a citizen guard, the so-called 

National Guard, with Lafayette as its commandant, now kept watch over the city. The middle class had come to realize the danger that might surround private property unless the people were held in check. Many of the nobles, too, were genuinely frightened, and some of them fled from France the beginning of a long series of emigrations. "The rats are leaving the sinking ship," said one of the revolutionary journals. And finally, the uprising of Paris led to widespread disorder in the provinces. The Revolution, as the result of the July Riots, was now sweeping over the nation.

THE PEASANTS COME INTO THE REVOLUTION 

The Countryside is Affected by a "Great Fear" You have learned already that there was much distress in the country; and even before the July Riots the peasants had been much wrought up. A panic, which started somehow, became worse as time went on and spread throughout France. Someone would shout, "The bandits are coming!" and then a whole village would be in an uproar. The people did not know of whom they were afraid, but they believed that someone would manage to get their small stock of food. It was an unreasoning fear, but it kept the country people in a chronic state of excitement. 

It might be compared to a rapidly spreading forest fire, and it did not burn itself out until well into the autumn of the year. 

The Attacks on the Châteaux 

When the news of the July Riots reached the countryside, it was like the setting off of a powder magazine. Everywhere the peasants attacked the châteaux, the residences of their lords, and in many cases destroyed them. For to the peasants the châteaux were the symbols of feudalism and of the many oppressive burdens they endured. Now at last they felt free to turn on their lords. Some of them even made bonfires of the feudal records which listed the various services they owed. Not many lives were lost, though some noblemen, millers, and tax collectors were murdered.

The intendants were quite unable to put a stop to the insurrection, and it was citizen. guards from neighboring towns who usually restored order.

Thus the peasants, like the mob of Paris, violently attacked the old order. Another class had entered the Revolution. What was to be the result? 

The Downfall of Privilege

The Constituent Assembly was busily engaged in drafting a declaration of human rights when the news of these wild disorders came to its attention. A committee was appointed to investigate these tumults, and when it reported in full this story of violence and disorder, the Assembly was deeply stirred. 

One of the nobles present moved the complete abolition of feudal rights. He was promptly seconded by another, who declared, "The people are trying to shake off a yoke which has weighed on them for centuries, and we must confess that this uprising, illegal as it was, can find its lawful excuse in the grievances of which they have been the victims." 

Aroused to a high pitch of enthusiasm, the Assembly virtually put an end to privilege. 

Noblemen and clergy rivaled each other in sacrificing the rights which feudalism had given them. They even abolished many other things, such as serfdom, and the taxes known as tithes which the Church drew from the peasants, and special hunting privileges. 

Long after midnight the tired assembly finally wound up its famous session by voting the astonished king the "restorer of liberty."

Yet, amidst all this sympathy for the peasant, there was a sober second thought that seemed to say that he should be required to pay something for his redemption. Thus, before these acts were given the King to sign, it was further decreed that the possessors of feudal rights should be given some compensation. It was not till a later assembly that this provision was repealed.

Nonetheless it may be said that feudalism had perished, for the peasants no longer respected any of these ancient obligations.

REVOLUTION THE FRENCH 

About the same time the tax exemptions enjoyed by the Church and the nobility were abolished; likewise the special penalties reserved for commoners. Privilege was practically demolished. A new and great principle had come into being: equality before the law.

But already the middle class was at work establishing a new order. The Old Régime was vanishing through the process of legislation.

B. The Making of a New France The Declaration of the Rights of Man 

Ever since July the Assembly had been solemnly deliberating the proposed constitution. The first thing to be settled, so the 

Assembly thought, was the determination of man's "natural rights." None of the people had previously possessed any rights, and the middle class was now to put into force some of the things which it had learned from Rousseau and other thinkers. 

"All men are born and remain free and equal in rights," was the first statement of this charter. The natural rights of man were declared to be "liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression. All citizens were declared to be “equal before the law" and eligible to any office for which their "virtues and talents" qualified them. No person might be punished except according to law. 

Sometimes a limit was set on the freedom of the individual in the interest of society as a whole. Liberty was defined as "the power to do anything that does not injure others."

Property could be taken from the individual only when a public necessity demanded it and always under condition of a just payment to the one deprived. "Security" meant that no one might be arrested save in accordance with the law; and every man was presumed to be innocent until he was found guilty. Freedom of opinion, religious or otherwise, was permitted, but not to the extent of disturbing the public order. Taxes should be "equally apportioned among all citizens according to their means."

Such were some of the striking features of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen. Probably most of us would agree to all the principles there pronounced; and this charter of liberty was to stand as a kind of model for many future generations. And yet one might regret that the Assembly did not also frame a declaration of duties as well as rights, for "rights" has a selfish sound, while "duties" implies self-sacrifice. Mirabeau said that the veil had been lifted too quickly, for the people, when they found that they enjoyed so many rights, would be certain to abuse them. It was also soon to be proved that the body which passed this act was not yet sure that it meant to carry it out in all particulars. 

Finally, one must realize that, while the Assembly was busily defining these rights, the nation was greatly in need of strong action to end disorder. The old order was collapsing, while a new order had yet to be erected. The intendants were quite helpless. Taxes, old or new, were almost equally hard to collect. It was almost as if the country had been swept by a kind of madness.

The Constitution of 1791 In 

The Declaration of the Rights of Man was the preamble or introduction to the new constitution. The general purpose of the constitution, commonly known as the Constitution of 1791, was to set up a limited monarchy under the control of the middle class. working out its plan, the Assembly had no thought of following England as its model. 

The constitutional committee, to be sure, had proposed a legislative body composed of two houses after the fashion of the English Parliament; but the Assembly could not imagine an upper house that was not made up of clergy and nobles, and the middle class would have no body like that. The legislature was, therefore, to consist of a single chamber, and it was to be elected in such a way that the men of wealth and property would control it. This was obviously not in accordance with the Declaration of the Rights of Man, which had declared for equal rights; and it showed the intense distrust which the middle class felt for the populace. 

The executive was to be weak. No one, of course, thought as yet of doing without a king, but there was no idea of allowing him

any power. When someone proposed that he be given an absolute veto over legislation, the 

Assembly would have none of it. "What is a veto?" exclaimed one of the revolutionary journals. "You lift up a bowl of broth to your mouth. 

Then someone comes up and دو dashes it away. That is a veto." On the other hand, neither the King nor any of his ministers was to be allowed to suggest a law; and the King was even prohibited from choosing any of his ministers from the ranks of the legislative body. Thus the Assembly was to some extent influenced by Montesquieu's idea of the "separation of powers." On the question of the veto it compromised by giving the King the right to hold up a law until it was passed by three assemblies. Such a privilege gave the King the chance to irritate the Assembly without permitting him to guide it. One of the greatest changes was in the government of the country at large. The old centralized system with its intendants was abandoned, and France was now divided into departments, as they were called, of fairly equal size, the officials of which were to be chosen by election. (See the maps on page 

110.) The men who were to enforce the laws throughout the country at large had no connection whatever with the central government. 

Along with provincial officials, all the ancient courts of justice were swept away and replaced by others. Judges were to be elected, with salaries paid by the State. And now what about the finances?

Solution of the Financial Problem 

One of the hardest problems to be tackled by the Assembly was that of straightening out the finances. It will be remembered that it was this problem that had brought about the crisis which produced the Revolution. 

Naturally all the old taxes were speedily abolished, but it was hard to levy new ones and have them respected when most people seemed to think that all their obligations were now at an end. When new taxes were tried and failed, the government asked for a "patriotic" gift. Some people gave their silver. All sorts of curious things were sent to the treasury, such as horses and casks of › See page 93, wine; a little girl even donated her doll's furniture. But the money that found its way into the empty treasury was quite insufficient to run the government, much less pay off the huge and mounting debt. "You sit deliberating," cried Mirabeau to the Assembly, "while bankruptcy, hideous bankruptcy, is at your doors."

At last someone had the shrewdness to suggest the seizure of the Church lands, and with Mirabeau's vigorous support the measure carried. As all this land could hardly be sold at once, it was decided to issue paper money called "assignats" to the value of the amount unsold. (A facsimile of an assignat may be found on page 111.) Though the sums thus raised did not dispose of all of the immense debt, they did enable the government to meet its expenses for a while. But the policy was to lead eventually to another crisis. rose.

The trouble was that the government found it too easy to "make" money, and it issued more than was covered by the value of the land. Hence the value of this money rapidly declined, or, in other words, prices rapidly This is what is known as inflation, and it is always hard on people whose earnings fail to keep pace with prices. It was also hard on the government in the end because the value of its money diminished until its financial situation was as bad as before. Moreover, the

State had to pay the clergy and to support the various charitable institutions, since the Church no longer possessed any sources of income. Thus the duties of the State were much enlarged, and its expenses grew accordingly. 

One other important result of the confiscation of the Church lands was the enrichment of many private individuals. People might turn in this money and receive in return its equivalent in land, and as the value of the money declined, many snatched at the chance to acquire land very cheaply. Though some of the people who benefited were well-to-do peasants, it was chiefly the middle class who speculated profitably in these lands. Such people would have to be loyal to the Revolution, for their right to these lands depended on keeping the Church from ever regaining them. 

The Revolution was consequently strengthened.

In the meantime, the economic power of the Church had been swept away, and it was soon to lose the rest of its independence. 

The Civil Constitution of the Clergy 

By the so-called Civil Constitution of the Clergy the Assembly decreed that the clergy should be elected, no longer appointed by the King, or anyone else, and, contrary to all tradition, the Pope was not invited to confirm those chosen. The clergy were to be paid salaries by the State, like all the other government officials; and, incidentally, the lower clergy were to be given a decent wage. 

As a

The Pope was naturally hostile to a measure which took no account of his position as head of the Church, and he forbade the clergy to accept it. Hence it became impossible for a clergyman to be loyal to the State and to the Church at the same time; and most of the clergy, when told that they must take an oath to this constitution, refused to do so. result, these clergy had no legal right to carry on their work, and since the great majority of people sympathized with their scruples, the religious life of the nation was sadly upset. 

The Assembly underestimated the strength of the Catholic Church when it passed this radical measure.

It is now time to review the work of the Assembly and to estimate its importance. 

Estimate of the Constituent Assembly and Its Work 

The Constituent Assembly was probably made up of the most enlightened men that could have been found to perform the task of remaking France. They were also very earnest and enthusiastic, as all reformers are at the outset, and they followed their own convictions. There were no political parties to tell them what to do. Each man was free to vote exactly as he pleased. But as we have already stated, they lacked all practical experience for such a task; and naturally some deliberately tried to win the favor of the galleries, where sat the "sovereign people" closely following the proceedings.

Yet the Assembly did pretty well if we consider its handicaps. They abolished all the glaring inequalities of the Old Régime, such as tax exemptions, tithes, guilds, and feudal TOOOOO

Try to translate the writing on the assignat. obligations; they swept away the tariffs which divided the provinces from one another; they curbed the extravagance of the court, with its liberal pensions, by fixing a definite allowance for the King; they did away with the corrupt and antiquated system of justice; and they even tried to give the lower clergy a square deal. They also put an end to the absolute monarchy, and gave France a government, which, though not democratic, was at least responsive to the will of a large section of the population.

But they also committed many serious mistakes. First, they made co-operation impossible between the executive and the legislature, and the King's "suspensive" veto was calculated to irritate the Assembly and weaken his own position. Secondly, the separation of the departments from the central government made it more difficult to keep order in a country that was torn by revolution, and thus trouble was stored up for the future. Thirdly, the issuing of a great amount of paper money rapidly increased the cost of living, which, in turn, contributed to popular unrest. And finally, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy made the Revolution distasteful to hundreds of thousands, including even the King, who felt that he had violated his conscience when he ratified this act. In fact when the King began again to plot against the Revolution, the monarchy was divided against itself. 

Another blunder of the Assembly was a decree that none of its members should be

FIGURE 75 HONORÉ GABRIEL RIQUETTI MIRABEAU 

(1749-1791)

Mirabeau was a Provençal nobleman elected to the Assembly by the third estate. So ugly in appearance that he could boast it an asset, he was a forceful speaker to whom the Assembly listened. He was a gifted leader, and a practical statesman. Had he been able to conceal his contempt for many of his colleagues or to resist the temptation to voice unpleasant comments he might have enjoyed the great rewards to which his ability entitled him. eligible to sit in the legislature created by the constitution. This resolution, instigated by 

Robespierre, an impractical idealist, shows that the members of the Constituent Assembly felt distrust of one another, fearing corruption by the court. Of course the property qualifications for voting insured that the middle class would control this new assembly just as it had the old. If assemblies were still to guide the Revolution, this class would stay in power. 

Yet this security of the middle class was not nearly so great as it seemed, as events were soon to show. 

c. The Plunge Into Anarchy From the time of the Constituent Assembly the Revolution swept on until it plunged France into anarchy, and, bursting its borders, threatened other countries and finally provoked war.

But we must first go back a little and try to understand how the populace came to control the Revolution. Long before the close of the Constituent Assembly, the weakness and insecurity of the monarchy had become apparent. We must go back for a moment to the year 1789.

THE MONARCHY IN PERIL The March on Versailles: the People Get the King into Their Power 

You will remember the July Riots and how the populace of Paris took the law into its own hands and saved the Revolution from being crushed. No doubt this element then realized its strength for the first time — the strength that lay in numbers. But the National Guard managed to keep order for the next few months. All was likely to go well, unless, as in July, something should make the people desperate.

There was still a good deal of want in the great city. Some of the makers of luxuries had to close their little shops, as more and more nobles, their best customers, left France; and so there were thus thousands of workers out of employment. Besides, many more peasants had flocked into the city, and the food supply was insufficient for all. Meanwhile, at the beginning of October it was learned that troops were again being called to Versailles, and that during a party at the palace the famous tri-color, the red, white, and blue flag of the Revolution, had been insulted. On 

October 5, 1789, a hungry crowd, mostly made up of women, began to gather in the streets, and after a time straggled to Versailles to ask the "royal baker," as they impolitely called the King, to reduce the price of bread. 

Doubtless they felt that if they should have the King in Paris, he would be forced to remain faithful to the Revolution and at the same time give them bread. In the crowd were some rough men dressed as women, some of them even dragging along a cannon. Lafayette with the National Guard followed the crowd, but he did not dare to stop this strange procession, for some of the guard were friendly to the rioters, and possibly, too, the marquis saw a chance of becoming a hero - playing to the mob on the one hand, and protecting the King on the other. We do not really know what he had in mind. 

When these thousands of market-women,

tired and drenched by a driving rain, reached Versailles, they pushed their way into the hall where the Assembly was holding its sessions, and forced that body to lower the price of grain. They cut all sorts of capers, some of them even compelling an august bishop, who was presiding, to stoop and kiss them. They also vowed that they would hack the Queen to pieces. "I'll have her head!" "I'll have her thighs!" some of them shouted. Partly in order to quiet them, wine and bread were distributed; and some of them, who drank too much, became really dangerous. Toward nightfall, as they gathered about the palace, some of them espied an open door and passed through, killing some guards who barred the way. Lafayette, who was summoned in the nick of time (he had been taking a nap at the inn), now cleared the palace. 

But the mob triumphed anyway when the King, probably persuaded by Lafayette, graciously agreed to go to Paris. It was a weird procession that now took the roadthe royal family escorted by the National Guard and by the howling, cursing women, shouting, "We have the baker, and the baker's wife, and the baker's little boy! Now we shall have bread!"

This was the second time the populace of Paris had taken a hand in the Revolution, and the result was just as momentous as before. 

For the removal of the King to Paris meant that the Assembly had to follow him. Thus the seat of government shifted from quiet Versailles to the center of popular unrest. 

The Assembly would find it hard to stand its ground against popular pressure, and the King might shortly find himself the prisoner of his people. 

Mirabeau Fails to Check the Revolution

The Revolution was going too far, in the opinion of Mirabeau (whose portrait appears on page 112). He tried to persuade the King to leave turbulent Paris, and, setting up his government at Rouen, look, rather, to the provinces for his support. But the King would never listen to wise counsel, and rejected his proposal.

The greatest statesman of the Revolution, Mirabeau, was probably its greatest orator as well; and it was due to his powerful voice that in the early days the Assembly had held its ground against the King. But he felt convinced that the King, if his powers were greatly reduced, would be unable to preserve order, and that the very acts of the legislative body might themselves promote disorder. Thus he had urged, though in vain, that the Crown should at least be allowed an absolute veto. 

He hoped for a time that the King would choose him as one of his ministers, so that he might keep the King and the Assembly on friendly terms. But his hopes were disappointed; for, on the one hand, the Queen distrusted him and kept the King from listening to his advice, and on the other hand, the Assembly was too jealous of his abilities to permit a minister to be chosen from among its members. Finally, his health broken by overwork and dissipation, Mirabeau died on 

April 2, 1791. He had tried to stem the tide of the Revolution, but he realized before his death that he had fought a losing fight. see so clearly," he said, "that we are in the midst of anarchy and sinking into it deeper every day." He was perhaps the one man who might have been able to save the monarchy had his leadership been followed. 

The Growth of Popular Unrest 

“I There were many things which tended to make the people more and more restless. 

While the Assembly had made a business of putting many thousands to work, there was always plenty of distress which the authorities never reached, and the rise in the cost of living, due to the decline in the value of money, naturally sharpened this distress. Strikes had been made illegal by the Assembly, and the time might come when the needy would resort to physical violence as their only hope of relief. For the present there were a good many people only too ready to listen to any writer or orator who clamored for radical changes.

Some of the newspapers, of which there were literally hundreds, no doubt did much to keep the people excited. They printed little news, but they expressed a good many opinions, and some of them were fiery in their language.

Politics. France.

From Paris. 

Tuesday, June 21, 1791, 10 A.M.

The king was carried off tonight about two o'clock without anyone knowing the route that was taken. As soon as the 

Municipality was informed of his departure, it took the most prompt measures to discover his route. The National Assembly and the Directory of the Department have been notified. 

The National Assembly has taken all the measures which the circumstance demands; it expects from the citizens the calm necessary for their execution. The Assembly of the Council of the Commune has been convoked; notices are being sent to departments and municipalities to be on guard against internal enemies; all good citizens are asked to be brave and especially to maintain order. Consequently, the Council decrees that the fronts of all houses be illuminated tonight and following nights; it asks all citizens to obey this order faithfully. 

Signed, BAILLY, Mayor; DEJOLY, Secretary.

But as the champion of "popular rights," the people might forget that he had once been the friend of "privilege"; for, after all, devotion to the monarchy was strong in France. 

Louis was never a good politician, and his conscience was sorely tried by some of the things he had had to accept, especially the 

Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Moreover, he naturally felt himself a prisoner of the Revolution. Possibly instigated by the Queen, he had secretly appealed to foreign monarchs for help, though no one in France as yet suspected that he had gone to such extremes. 

At all events, he resolved to make a personal effort to crush the Revolution and become a free man again.

The King's plan was to leave Paris in the dead of night and travel by coach to Lorraine, where a commander of certain regiments stood ready to furnish him the troops needed for his purpose. On June 21, the royal family slipped out of Paris and started their journey for the east. Unfortunately, at a village where his coach was forced to stop for a change of horses, the King's identity was discovered by a man who was familiar with the engraving of his head on the paper money, and he was stopped a few miles farther on at the village of Varennes, and there detained.

Some members of the National Guard were hastily summoned, and they escorted the royal family back to Paris amid the jeers of the people in the villages along the way. The 

King's plot had failed. 

The "Flight to Varennes," as this episode is called, greatly weakened the King's position. 

People now were certain that he was a traitor to the Revolution; and for the first time the opinion was openly expressed that France no longer needed a king. Some weeks later, there was a serious riot in Paris, and several people were shot by the National Guard. 

Needless to say, it would not be soon forgotten that the middle class had shed the blood of the people.

End of the Constituent Assembly 

But what of the new monarchy which the middle class was striving to establish? Its position was steadily weakened. In September, certain foreign powers declared that the cause of Louis XVI was the cause of all monarchs; and now many began to suspect that the King was seeking foreign aid to put an end to the Revolution. About this time also the 

Constitution of 1791 was finished, and, the King having finally approved it, the Constituent Assembly came to an end. A con- stitutional monarchy had been created, but the events of the last two years had left it in grave peril.

THE UPRISING OF THE MASSES THE DOWNFALL OF THE MONARCHY AND OF THE MIDDLE CLASS 

The leadership of the middle class, who sought to guide the Revolution by legislation, was coming to be more and more challenged by the populace, who stood ready to use violence to carry out their will. It was a difficult situation for the Assembly called into being by the Constitution of 1791. Moreover, foreign powers were beginning to regard the Revolution as a threat to their own safety, and the French nobles who had taken refuge in foreign courts were urging intervention.

And all the while the populace of Paris (ruined merchants, idle workmen, starving peasants, and out-and-out criminals) were being led by the radical clubs to think that the monarchy had no place in a revolution.

The Legislative Assembly and the Middle-Class Conspiracy Against the Monarchy 

The Assembly, elected in accordance with the provisions of the new constitution, is commonly known as the Legislative Assembly.

It had actually been elected before its creator, the Constituent Assembly, had ended its sittings, since it was feared that if one day intervened between the sessions of these two bodies, the King might do some harm to the 

Revolution. So the Constituent Assembly ended its session September 30, and on October 

1 the Legislative Assembly began its meetings.

This new body was much less fitted for its task than its famous predecessor, for, thanks to the resolution that none in the old assembly was eligible to re-election, the Legislative Assembly was composed of men with hardly a shred of political experience. Conspicuous in

this body was a group known as the Girondins, many of whose leaders came from the department of the Gironde in southwestern France.

They were invariably men of means, since only men of means could have been elected under the suffrage qualifications as set forth in the constitution. As was natural, then, they shrank from any thought of popular violence as a means of accomplishing their aims, though these aims were really radical in the extreme. Rather, they hoped by legislation to keep the Revolution in the hands of the middle class, from which they sprang. Some of them were gifted orators, but few of them were blessed with any common sense. one who chiefly inspired them was a charming lady, endowed with great enthusiasm but passionate in her hatreds, Madame Roland.

It was possibly due to her hatred of the nobility that the lands of the emigrant nobles were confiscated by the Legislative Assembly. The Most of the Girondins distrusted the King, and they were bent, it seems, on ruining him, some of them wishing to go so far as to establish a republic. All this, in spite of the fact that they had been elected to office under a constitutional monarchy! Out of 

Out of a wish to show up the King, whom they suspected of being disloyal to the Revolution, they determined to involve France in foreign war. 

Thus, they reasoned, would the King be forced to reveal his true colors (that is, he would side with the foreign monarchs!), and then he could with justice be dethroned. What they expected next to accomplish most of the Girondins probably did not bother to consider.

There were ample grounds for war, as we shall explain later, but there was no need for the Girondins deliberately to hurry it on. In any case the Assembly was easily swayed by fiery speeches, and on April 20, 1792, it formally declared war against Austria. Little did the Girondins foresee the consequences of their acts!

The Beginning of Mob Rule 

It was the populace who were destined to be moved by the war to terrible deeds, but it was not the war that incited them against the monarchy at this time. In June the King vetoed certain measures of the Assembly which the Girondins had sponsored, and this group was furious. What could be done with a king that thwarted the will of the Assembly? 

The people gave the answer. On June 20 an immense crowd broke into the palace in order to force the King to withdraw his vetoes. But 

Louis was no coward and he stood his ground. 

Little by little the mob dispersed.

As events were to show, this episode of June 20, 1792, was the beginning of a year of mob rule. The Assembly was no longer a free agent. The supremacy of the middle class was at an end, and power was now centered in the Paris populace, led by base and unscrupulous ruffians and sometimes by men of the 

Jacobin Club. 

The National Crisis and the Downfall of the Monarchy 

Popular excitement was greatly intensified by the war. The army was in no condition nate. to fight, since most of the officers, noblemen, of course, had fled from the country, and the common soldiers, taking literally the principle of equality, were thoroughly insubordi- 

When the first brush with the enemy ended in defeat, one of the generals was actually murdered by his men. On July 11, the Assembly declared the country to be “in danger." Volunteers poured into Paris. A battalion of the national guard of Marseilles arrived, singing their famous song, the Marseillaise, which henceforth became the anthem of the Revolution. Excitement became intense. 

Expecting and dreading invasion, people turned against the King, the hated "enemy within the gates." Robespierre harangued the Jacobin Club, demanding the King's immediate dethronement and the election of a new assembly to clear the way for a republic. 

Excitement was further fanned by the news of a declaration issued by Austria and Prussia, the so-called Brunswick Manifesto, threatening the city of Paris with destruction if any harm befell the King. Another popular outbreak was at hand. 

On August 10, a mob attacked the palace. 

The royal family, warned in time, found refuge with the Assembly, but most of the Swiss guards who defended the palace were

killed. The palace itself was sacked, and more than a hundred servants were done to death. A little band of ruffians, abetted by the Paris Commune (the city government, now composed of members of the populace), had engineered the attack, but the man who openly boasted of having "prepared" it was the popular leader, Danton.

Balked of its prey, the mob now thronged to the hall of the Assembly, and entering it, forced that body to vote the King's immediate dethronement. The royal family was then lodged in prison. The populace had put an end to the monarchy.

The Establishment of the First Republic and the Climax of Mob Rule 

The abolition of the monarchy naturally ¹ brought the Legislative Assembly to an end, and a new election was held. Although practically universal suffrage prevailed in theory, there was so much intimidation that only a small proportion of the citizenry went to the polls. The new assembly, known in history as the National Convention, had the double task of making the necessary laws and of drafting another constitution for France. 

For the present France was a republic, and on 

September 21, the day after the opening of the

Convention, the republic was duly proclaimed. 

Yet France was still in a state of anarchy, for the new government was weak, and the populace were able to do as they chose. 

Danton, as minister of justice, might possibly have maintained order, but he was much too afraid of risking his popularity to do anything that was likely to offend the people. And the mob was only too liable to resort again and again to violence and bloodshed.

In September, the border fortress on which the safety of Paris depended fell to the enemy.

Danton inflamed the Assembly by his famous speech, "Daring, daring, still more daring, and France will be saved!" But the populace gave way to a spasm of blind and unreasoning terror. Some suspected people, mostly nobles and clergy, had been jailed by the Paris Commune as an act of precaution; but the cry was raised, "What if they should break ¹ Since the constitution, which had provided for this assembly, was now at an end.

A mob broke into the prisons, and more than thirteen hundred were butchered in cold blood, some of them in the most brutal manner imaginable. This episode, "The September Massacres," was the most terrible mob outbreak of the Revolution.

But the populace were still enjoying their triumph. When the King was tried for "conspiracy" before the Convention, the galleries were packed to the doors by a grim and excited rabble, which held the Convention completely in its grip. Many of the deputies, for fear of losing their lives, did not dare to cast their vote (for voting was oral) against the death penalty. Louis XVI was duly con-

21, 1793, he was executed on the guillotine, a beheading machine which a certain Doctor Guillotin had invented. Louis met his end calmly. Whatever might have been said against this ruler, he was not deficient in courage.

But the Girondins' turn was coming. They had never approved of the anarchy and the bloodshed which had tainted the Revolution, and they hated and despised the populace. 

Yet they seemed not to sense their danger, and one of them even threatened Paris with destruction if the populace should again resort to violence. On June 2, 1793, a mob broke into the hall where the Convention was meeting and forced that body to decree the arrest of twenty-nine of its members, as well as two ministers. Practically all the proscribed were 

Girondins, and most of them soon met their fate on the guillotine. The words of Madame

Roland, as she mounted the scaffold, have often been quoted: "Ah, Liberty, how many crimes have been committed in thy name!"

Most of the Girondins who managed to escape from Paris were hunted down, and were either driven to suicide or sent to the guillotine. The leaders of the middle class, who had stood for parliamentary rule and an orderly revolution, were dead or in exile. 

Yet the episode of June marked the end of the period of anarchy if not of bloodshed. A new government had risen which would hold the mob in check and save France.

D. The Terror 

The "Terror" was a means of lifting France out of anarchy and civil war and enabling her to defend herself against a hostile Europe. It is extraordinary how quickly the change took place. In just a few months, France was transformed from a country drunk with liberty to a stern and savage despotism the like of which the world had never seen.

THE EVOLUTION OF THE TERROR The External Crisis 

The crisis facing France in the spring and summer of 1792 was as grave as can be imagined. Her army was in no condition to fight. If her enemies had followed up their victories and brought up all their forces to invade France, the struggle would have been decided very quickly. France could not at the time have saved herself. Happily Austria was slow to get into the struggle, and Prussia was chiefly interested in Poland, which Russia was threatening to seize in its entirety. It was truly lucky for France that at the time when she fell into anarchy, her enemies seized upon Poland rather than upon her. Indeed, the attack by Prussia and Austria was so halfhearted that France was not only able to check the invasion, but even to take the offensive for a time. 

But would such luck continue? In February, 1793, France had broken with Great Britain, and during the spring the First Coalition was formed, Great Britain, Prussia, Austria, and other powers combining to dismember France. The odds were now tremendously unequal, and Poland had ceased for a time to serve as a distraction. As a result, the French army in the Netherlands was disastrously defeated in March, 1793, while the army on the Rhine was likewise compelled to retreat. France was again threatened with invasion.

And at this time France was in no condition to withstand a strong attack. Faced with invasion, the country was woefully disunited. 

The Internal Crisis 

In March, 1793, a serious revolt took place in the west of France. The peasants in the valley of the Loire rose in arms against a government which they felt had been unjust in dealing with the Church, and was now trying to force them into the army. volt spread very quickly, and France plainly threatened with civil war. The re- was In the meantime, some of the larger towns, dismayed by the decline in business and disgusted with the mob-ridden government at Paris, were just on the verge of revolt. As

GEORGES JACQUES DANTON (1759-1794) 

In Danton's character several traits warred. was, on the one hand, wise and farseeing. derstood clearly the need for vigorous leadership and would in crises act ruthlessly, but he was also convinced that tact and moderation should be practiced when possible. Easygoing and careless, he tended to laziness and sometimes failed to act promptly. He was, moreover, in many respects lacking in integrity.

France no longer possessed a centralized government, it was easy for civil strife to gain. headway. In April it looked as if France were falling to pieces.

The government at Paris was evidently not strong enough to meet the crisis. The Convention was the scene of constant wrangles and the populace were liable at any moment to get out of hand. Something had to be done if France and the Revolution were to be saved.

The Radicals Face the Crisis 

One man at this juncture seemed to tower above all others, and that was Danton. With the face of a ruffian and a clear, bellowing voice, a born leader of the mob, he was nevertheless at heart a fervent patriot, and in spite. of his seamy past, a practical statesman. Easygoing and even somewhat lazy, he, nevertheless, displayed at times a ferocious energy. 

He saw that only through strong government and desperate measures could France weather the crisis.

In March, even before the military disaster, a court known as the Revolutionary Tribunal was set up at Danton's suggestion to deal with traitors; also members of the Convention were sent "on mission" to various departments to raise troops.

In April, the so-called Committee of Public Safety was established, a special body to deal at first with national defense. These instruments were part of what was soon to be known as the "Terror," though it was not until September that its whole elaborate machinery was perfected. 

CHARACTER, ORGANIZATION, AND OPERATION OF THE TERROR Purpose and Character of the Terror 

The Terror was an emergency despotism.

It was a government set up by patriots, most of whom, like Danton, had once been popular leaders, for the purpose of forcing the nation to stand united against dangers within and without. It took no account of the liberties once proclaimed in the Declaration of the 

Rights of Man. No constitution defined or restricted its powers. It could do anything it pleased. But its purpose was patriotic. object was to save France from herself and from the invader.

Its The method of this dictatorship was terror. 

If people would not be loyal from love of country, then they must be loyal at least from fear. Death was the punishment for anyone guilty of conspiracy or of promoting any disorders that might hinder France in fighting her foreign enemies. More than that, people who had simply incurred suspicion of disloyalty were jailed, given the briefest trial, and executed. It seemed as if a sword were suspended over the nation, ready to strike any-

one who did not serve the republic with his whole heart.

But this was organized terror, not the haphazard, brutal terror of the mob. When 

Danton urged the establishment of the Revolutionary Tribunal, he had said, "Let us be terrible in order to relieve the people of being terrible." The period of anarchy, when the Swiss guards were slaughtered and the prisoners massacred, though terrible enough, is not what is known in history as the "Reign of Terror." The Reign of Terror was the period during which death was coldly and deliberately dealt out by a court, which was organized for that purpose. 

There is no doubt that such a government was cruel. More people were put to death under the Terror than had lost their lives in the August and September massacres. Moreover, many innocent people were done to death - people whose only fault was their noble blood or the fact that they were known to be moderate in their views. Some also suffered merely because they had happened to incur the hatred of the men in power. People lived in an atmosphere of fear, and no one who had been in politics could really feel secure during this period. The safest thing, at least for the middle class, was to shun the limelight. 

One who lived through that period declared that "not a single carriage was then to be seen in Paris. The whole of people's lives were centered in their homes, where they spoke little, in a low voice, and with doors securely closed. No one was sure of what the next day would bring forth. Women did not go out at all, men rarely." Yet the great majority of people went about their daily tasks, and an inconspicuous person had no cause to feel afraid. At least the nation realized what it was facing, and the stern discipline of the Terror seemed to steel men to self-sacrifice. 

No government in history has been stronger, and few have been so efficient. And it accomplished its prime object - it saved France. 

The Machinery of the Terror 

The machinery of the Terror was elaborate, though we shall mention only those organs that were most important. Leadership centered in the Committee of Public Safety, FIGURE 82. MAXIMILIEN MARIE ISIDORE DE ROBESPIERRE (1758-1794) 

Robespierre was called the incorruptible, in recognition of the rigid honesty which distinguished both his private and public life. This admirable quality made it difficult for him to accept compromises. 

When in power he ruthlessly brought about the execution of those whom he regarded as enemies of the Revolution. twelve men who controlled the ministers and the Convention, and who really governed France. The Deputies on Mission, two members of the Convention sent to every department and every army in the field, enforced loyalty and order. They were the long arms of the government. The Revolutionary 

Tribunal and other courts similarly organized tried cases of treason. A Committee of General Security, as it was called, had police powers which enabled it to hunt down "traitors" and determine who should be tried. By the terrible Law of Suspects, every person in any way connected with the Old Régime and, indeed, any person whose language or conduct was not pleasing to the authorities, was open to suspicion. Besides, many got into trouble simply because of an unsupported accusation, perhaps by a personal enemy. 

Very few who were actually brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal escaped the penalty of death.

The Terror Gets Under Way 

The first activities of the Terror took place before its whole machinery was developed.

The revolt of the peasants in the west was crushed, and many thousands were put to death. At Nantes people were bound together and put on boats which were sunk in the river Loire. When, during the summer, various towns broke out in revolt, punishment was equally severe. Civil war was speedily brought to an end by a policy that was as merciless as it was swift.

At Paris there were endless executions. 

Nobles and others who had served the monarchy, priests who had refused to swear to the 

Civil Constitution of the Clergy, politicians like the Girondins who had quarreled with the men in power and stirred up revolts in the departments, and, of course, the unhappy Queen - such were some of the persons who went to the guillotine in the summer and fall of 1793. Every day saw people driven in carts to a public square where the guillotine did its work. It was a long and tragic procession, but almost all met their fate bravely, many with a smile. The prisons were always full, and people were chosen by lot for the public show. No doubt the Terrorists reasoned that these spectacles were a very wholesome warning to the country. Unity and loyalty must prevail on pain of death.

The Terror in Operation 

At the same time France was making strenuous efforts to raise and equip armies to defend her soil, and heavy taxes were levied on people of wealth to pay the cost. There were few, indeed, who were not called upon to make some sort of sacrifice to the cause. But in the end the enemy was beaten, and France emerged victorious.

And at home she was reunited. There were no longer popular outbreaks. Certain noisy extremists who clamored to raze church steeples because they violated the principle of equality and loudly demanded the confiscation of all property by the State, and who had tried to substitute the worship of Reason for that of God, were sent to the guillotine in March, 1794. This element had found its strength in the Paris Commune; but the Commune had had its day, and the government meant to teach it a lasting lesson. While an effort was made to relieve the sufferings of the poor, the populace were not allowed to overawe the government. 

But, oddly enough, a division appeared within the ranks of the Terrorists themselves. 

Robespierre was the leading member of the Committee of Public Safety. He wished to continue the Terror until he had established what he considered an ideal society, a "republic of virtue," as he expressed it. Remembering Rousseau's belief in the idea that all people should be as nearly equal in material things as possible, he wanted to take the property of the wealthy and divide it among the poor. poor. Naturally the middle class was greatly alarmed, and it found a champion in Danton, though the latter had lost his position on the great committee and only voiced his opinions in the Convention. Danton himself was rich, and many suspected that he had made his fortune dishonestly; but he was also a practical man, and he felt that by now the Terror had done its work: the enemy was defeated, and now was the time, he thought, to go back to normal. Thus Danton forced the issue. 

He demanded that the Terror be brought to an end.

This was not to Robespierre's liking. Sincere, honest and industrious, but exceedingly self-righteous, a grave little man, who thought that any person who disagreed with him must be crooked or disloyal, he cordially disliked the easygoing Danton, who had so few principles and laughed at danger. Robespierre was a fanatic who could see but one object and one means of attaining that object. The ideal republic, he felt, could be established only by keeping up the Terror. So Robespierre and his friends finally had Danton accused of treason. It was a travesty of justice, for Danton was as true a revolutionist as his rival. But Robespierre had his way, and 

Danton and his friends were sent to the guillotine in April, 1794. lotine in April, 1794. "Show my head to the people," Danton had said to the executioner. "It is worth it.”

After Danton's fall the Terror stiffened. A new law made it virtually impossible for an accused person to put up any defense, the question of guilt being simply left to the "conscience" of the jurors; and even a member of the Convention might be suddenly sent

to his doom. People wondered with tense alarm whom Robespierre would strike next. 

The End of the Terror 

But Robespierre had plainly overreached himself. The Convention was roused against him, and when he tried to defend himself, their shouts drowned out his words. "See," someone cried, "the blood of Danton chokes him." Robespierre was suddenly arrested and placed in confinement. A popular movement to save him having failed, he and his friends were sent to the guillotine in July, 1794. Thus the Terror came to an end with the death of its principal champion. 

E. The Middle Class to the Front Again - The Directory 

The Thermidorean Reaction With the overthrow of Robespierre, France parted definitely with the Terror. All its machinery was abolished, and many of the leading Terrorists were sent to the guillotine they had used so often against others. Even the Jacobin Club was closed; and in some places armed bands attacked the radicals who had been agents of the Terror and killed them in batches. All this was part of what is known as the Thermidorean¹ Reaction. 

This reaction was characterized by reckless extravagance of all kinds. People felt so glad to be rid of the Terror's discipline that they went to the other extreme. At no time in the history of France was wickedness more open ¹ Because the fall of Robespierre had occurred in the revolutionary month of Thermidor, the revolutionary calendar had twelve months of thirty days (and five special days), with every tenth day a holiday. It was supposed to begin with the founding of the Republic, September 22, 1792. Thus the first year of the Republic was called "the year I."

SUMMARY of Important Concepts and unashamed. A certain hardness, too, is shown by the fact that children were given toy guillotines to play with, and what was known as the "victim ball" became very popular, each person who wanted to attend being expected to use the death warrant of a relative as a ticket of admission. People had stood so many terrible ordeals that they were ready to laugh at horrors. But the populace were still in dire want, for prices were higher than ever. 

Indeed, the flaunting of wealth and the riotous living of the well-to-do contrasted sharply with the misery of the poor. 

The Constitution of the Year III 

But the middle class was again asserting itself, and what it chiefly wanted was settled government. Some even wanted a king; but the Convention, having executed a king, could hardly risk the return of any of the Bourbons.

Finally, in May, 1795, a constitution, the socalled Constitution of the Year III (that is, the third year of the republic), was drafted and put into effect. The government was put into the hands of a body of five known as a directory (which gave the name, the Directory, to the whole régime), and the legislature was composed of two "councils," both elective. 

The executive was weak, but France was fairly well centralized, as the acts of local bodies, still elective, were supervised by officials appointed by the government. The suffrage was carefully restricted to men of means; and this meant that the middle class had returned to power.

Thus France remained a republic, a middleclass republic, instead of a middle-class 

How well this new experiment monarchy. would work no one could tell. But for the moment France was victorious in war, and no one expected the coming of another despotism, the work not of civilians but of a soldier.

You may want to arrange a showing of some historical movie which was issued before your time. 

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. When you go to the theater you usually go to be entertained. 

Viewing a film tends to be much like reading a mystery story. That is you are not chiefly interested in getting all the facts or in evaluating them. On the whole you are satisfied to get a general impression of what happened. Indeed you may deliberately "skip" the descriptive bits and concentrate only on

the action, or unfolding of the plot. Should you want to study a film it will be necessary to proceed somewhat as follows: 

1. Find out in advance about the story and setting of the film, and decide exactly what you expect to get from viewing it. This can best be done by having a committee preview the film. 

2. When you view the film, look for information that relates to the points in which you are interested. 

You may need to view the film more than once. 

3. Discuss your conclusions in class to get the advantage of what other pupils saw. 

4. Contrast what you saw in the film with pertinent information that you have read. If necessary, do further reading to check the accuracy of the film version.

Organize your information and report your findings to the class.

THE REVOLUTION WAS TOO BIG to confine itself privilege, it was but natural that the other to France, and hence it came to involve Europe. Meanwhile, out of the war with foreign powers there emerged a military genius, Napoleon Bonaparte, who, while he ended liberty and re-established absolutism in France, held firmly to the principle of equality which the Revolution had stood for. Abroad he continued the war of the French Revolution with foreign powers, and all Europe was made to feel the force of a nation reinvigorated by revolution, and led by one of the greatest captains in history. When the storm had finally passed, both France and Europe felt the abiding influence of the French Revolution. 

A. The French Revolution and 

Europe

For a time the relations between Revolutionary France and the rest of Europe were peaceful. The men of the Revolution were too much occupied with setting France right to care to meddle with the rest of the world, and they would not even countenance any alliances. But geography was against them. 

France belonged to the Continent of Europe, and she had neighbors on three sides. could hardly produce a great explosion without its affecting other nations as well.

CAUSES OF THE STRUGGLE The Underlying Causes 

She 

Europe came to fear and hate the Revolution.

When the French destroyed absolutism and monarchies in Europe should feel themselves threatened. How could they keep their own subjects from wanting those very things which people in France were now enjoying? How could they expect any longer to keep their peasants in serfdom when the French peasants had freed themselves from all their old burdens? In short, the Revolution was a challenge to the old order. 

Then the revolutionists themselves - would they not want to spread their doctrines to other lands? Convinced that they had found the key to happiness in the establishment of individual freedom, would they not insist that all Europe should enjoy this priceless boon?

When the other monarchies of Europe began to show their disapproval of the Revolution as less moderate leaders came to shape the policy of France, it was natural that these champions of "liberty, equality, fraternity" should make of these words a battle-cry.

After ending the Old Régime in their own land, they would want to bring it to an end everywhere else. "Let us fling down to the kings the head of a king as gage of battle!” cried Danton.

In short, Europe was not large enough to harbor two social systems so fundamentally different as the old order and the new. A conflict between them was practically inevitable.

neighbor was her treatment of the question of Avignon. This was a little district on the 

Rhone which had been ruled for many centuries by the Pope. Surrounded by French territory, it seemed as if it ought to belong to France. Moreover, the people themselves were French in the sense that they spoke the French language and were of much the same character as the people in the kingdom of France. But what about the legal rights of the Pope? At first the Constituent Assembly felt that it did not want to interfere with Avignon. Even after the Avignese begged to belong to France, the Assembly tried for a year to evade the question. But under continual pressure it finally yielded, and in 1791 Avignon was annexed. Naturally the old monarchies felt that the legal rights of princes were not respected by the Revolution.

The emigrant nobles, moreover, did their best to rouse the fears of the old monarchies; and it was chiefly at their persuasion that Austria and Prussia declared the fate of the French monarchy a matter of common concern. They were led to believe that monarchy was in danger in France, and that if it fell in France, it might not survive in other countries. Moreover, Marie Antoinette was an 

Austrian princess, and her brother, the Emperor, did not like to think that she might lose her throne, if not her life.

On their side, the French revolutionists bitterly resented all signs of interference, and some perhaps suspected that the King was in treasonable contact with foreign powers.

When the Girondins came into power, they deliberately provoked war, largely because, as we have seen, they wanted to ruin the monarchy in France. There were many grounds for complaint on both sides, but it was France who finally precipitated the struggle. 

Thus in April, 1792, war was formally declared against Austria. That other powers in 

Europe would ultimately be drawn into the struggle was a foregone conclusion. 

The Break with Great Britain 

The position of Great Britain, however, was not precisely the same as that of the Continental monarchies. She was not an absolute monarchy, and she did not suffer from guilds On or feudal privilege, as the French had long suffered. Some of the more liberal Whigs, Charles Fox, for example, showed a very real enthusiasm over the freedom which the French had won from evils of which the British had managed to rid themselves long before. the other hand, a great Whig orator, Edmund 

Burke, sharply denounced the Revolution as "a strange chaos of levity and frivolity and of all sorts of aims jumbled together with all sorts of follies." 

In fact, as the Revolution developed, more and more Englishmen began to feel that Revolutionary France was headed for anarchy, and the conservative elements began to fear the influence of the new doctrines on the unenfranchised masses in Great Britain. 

So great were British fears that William Pitt, who was Prime Minister at the time, restricted freedom of opinion and kept a watchful eye lest his fellow-countrymen should start a revolution of their own. Relations were also strained by the French occupation of the 

Netherlands; for no doubt you will remember that it had always been a principle of British policy that no strong power should occupy territory so near the English shore. Finally, in January, 1793, occurred the execution of Louis XVI; and the British, forgetting, it seemed, the fate of their own king, Charles I, were evidently so shocked that Pitt immediately ordered the agent of France out of the country. So deep was resentment at Paris in consequence of this insult that the National 

Convention, on February 1, 1793, declared war.

FRANCE AND THE FIRST COALITION Formation of the First Coalition 

The outbreak of war with Great Britain meant another enemy for Revolutionary France. Prussia had already allied herself with Austria; and by March, 1793, the First 

Coalition was formed, composed of Austria, Prussia, Great Britain, Holland, Spain, and Sardinia. This was not merely a league to restore monarchy in France.

The powers meant, if successful, to dismember France.

How could France in her present condition expect to save herself from destruction?

France Meets the Emergency 

When the allies, Austria and Prussia, invaded France in the fall of 1792, only the fact that Prussia was mainly interested in the Polish question saved France from complete disaster; for she was in no condition to fight, as we have noticed. As it was, the Prussians waged a half-hearted fight and the French managed to check the invasion at the battle of Valmy. 

Taking advantage of their victory, the French armies advanced into the Netherlands and into Germany as far as the Rhine. After Prussia and Russia had finished with Poland (this was the Second Partition of Poland in 1793), Prussia placed a stronger army on the Rhine, and Austria planned to reconquer the Netherlands. Since the French armies were badly equipped and short of officers, they were defeated and forced to retreat. Worse than that, France was about to be invaded. On 

Then, as we noticed, came the Terror. the Committee of Public Safety was an unusually competent man, Lazare Carnot, the "organizer of victory." Under him every branch of the military service was practically made over, and by conscription thirteen armies were put in the field, numbering 750,000 men. 

Moreover, merit was made the basis of promotion, and every private had a chance to become an officer if he deserved it. Instead of friction between officers and soldiers, the army was soon a model of teamwork and discipline. 

The men who marched into battle, singing the Marseillaise, felt that they were fighting for their country and for the principles of the 

Revolution. Rarely had the world seen so staunch and ardent a patriotism. 

And now what were the goals sought by the French?

The French Achieve Their Objects 

At first the French were concerned about the national defense, but as soon as they had saved their country from invasion, more ambitious objects were sought. They wished not merely to free themselves, but to free all other peoples desiring freedom. The Revolutionary soldiers were to march and fight as crusaders in a great movement to spread liberty and equality throughout Europe. As the French won more successes, still a third

B. The Rise of Napoleon Bonaparte 

Napoleon was the man who capitalized the fighting spirit of the French, and also used the Revolution to further his own interests. But who was this man, Napoleon? How was it possible for him to bend first France and then 

Europe to his will?

EARLY LIFE AND CHARACTER OF NAPOLEON BONAPARTE The Man from Corsica 

Napoleon was born at Ajaccio on the island of Corsica in 1769. Though his family was 

Italian, as was true of most Corsicans, Corsica itself belonged to France; and so Napoleon took a course of military training which brought him eventually a commission in the artillery service of the French army. Winning distinction in the service, he was promoted in 

1793 to a general's rank.

While gaining military experience, Napoleon also broadened his knowledge of other things. Whenever he was not engaged in active service, he devoted his time to diligent reading. Little by little he was forming his opinions. Always a dreamer, he thought much about the world in which he lived and how he would like to change it. Yet Napoleon probably learned much more from experience than from books.

Napoleon at Paris 

Napoleon had many direct contacts with the Revolution. He had visited Paris on several occasions, and once when he was in temporary disgrace he had been so poor as to have to pawn his watch. Often he played politics, even talking like a radical when it seemed to suit his interests. suit his interests. It was in Paris also that he took his plunge into the pleasure-loving society which had followed the Terror. He was not then particularly attractive in appearance, for he was careless in his dress, and his face was very thin. His manners were far

A GREAT EUROPEAN 

131 

UPHEAVAL 

from polished, and he seemed lacking in the art of conversation unless matters pertaining to the army were being discussed. Yet he always impressed people with his earnestness and ability. He also made useful contacts, and his ability was recognized by Carnot, a competent judge of military skill. It was in Paris, too, that he married Josephine de Beauharnais, who felt that he was a rising man, and seemed to see in his eyes the power to bend men to his will.

But Napoleon was sometimes served by sheer luck. After refusing a military assignment (in consequence of which he was suspended from his command), he was given the chance to direct the forces which saved the National Convention from a Paris mob. 

Naturally he was restored to favor, and shortly afterward, in March, 1796, he received through Carnot's influence the command of the Army of Italy. At last he was to have the chance to show his talents to the full.

But what manner of man was this young officer, destined to make so great a name in history?

The Character of Napoleon 

In stature Napoleon was short (he was only five feet, three), but he carried himself well, and his face was very animated and expressive. His steel-blue eyes were perhaps his most striking feature; they seemed to dominate the people with whom he talked. The firmness of his chin also seemed to show the iron strength of his will.

Napoleon's nature was hard. There were few persons for whom he seems to have possessed any affection, for he regarded people in general as mere instruments in his hands, useful as long as he needed them, discarded when they ceased to be of use. Loyalty and efficiency were the virtues he always demanded, and he was always ready to reward faithful service. He did undoubtedly inspire great devotion, especially among his soldiers, and sometimes his very presence aroused fear. 

He was a man whom common folk regarded as a little more than human. 

In the final analysis, his greatness may be attributed to three qualities: his industry, his will, and his genius.

Endowed with an unusually strong constitution, Napoleon stood for more than fifteen years a strain that would have floored most men. He schooled himself to reduce his hours of sleep to five or six. He loved his work, and every waking hour found him at it. 

He eagerly seized every occasion to gain information, whether by observation, conversation, or reading. Despite his power for lofty planning, he always gave attention to details, though never allowing them to obscure the larger things. scure the larger things. He was a living example of the fact that brilliance is never enough without diligence if a man is to become great; and, hard as he drove his men, he himself worked hardest of all. "How could one possibly have shown the slightest negligence," one of his officers exclaimed, "when we were set such an example of indefatigable energy in the highest quarter!"

And everything seemed to yield to his over-
