mastering will. It drove him on to achievement, and drove the people who served him to do his bidding without question. It was 

It was partly, no doubt, his unbounded confidence in himself that sharpened his will and made him sure that he would succeed. "Impossible," he is alleged to have said, "is not a 

French word."

But underneath it all was a genius that is granted to few people. Great creative talent has been manifested by many men and women in the course of history, but few have shown the marvelous versatility of Napoleon. A brilliant warrior and diplomat, he was also a shrewd and farseeing statesman. He had the gift of imagination as well as a practical sense of realities the realization of what was suited to human beings as he found them. 

One may not admire Napoleon because of his egotism, an egotism that cost millions of lives, but of his marvelous mental powers there can be no doubt. Such a man is cast for a great career.

NAPOLEON'S OPPORTUNITY 

The Basis of Napoleon's Opportunity Outside of his personal abilities Napoleon's opportunity to mount to supreme power in 

France lay chiefly in two circumstances: (1) the war, which gave him the chance to show his genius and to become a popular hero, and (2) the weakness and incompetence of the civil government in France. 

Napoleon's Military Fortunes, 1796–1799

Napoleon took over his new command with the greatest eagerness. He had already planned how he could vanquish the First Coalition and make France supreme in Italy. 

Realizing the importance of arousing a warlike spirit in his soldiers before leading them into action, he deliberately held out hopes of fame and spoils. "I will lead you," he said, "into the most fertile plains in the world. 

Rich provinces, great cities will be in your power. There you will find honor, glory, and wealth. Soldiers of the Army of Italy, shall you be lacking in courage and perseverance?"

It was during the Italian campaign of 17961797 that he showed to a striking degree his extraordinary gifts of strategy. 

He managed to separate the armies of Austria and Sardinia, and, defeating the latter, detached her from the coalition. Then, after several brilliant victories he forced peace upon Austria. When he returned to Paris in the fall of 1797, he had already won a fame far greater than that of any other French general.

The following year he was sent to Egypt in the hope of gaining for France the country which was the threshold to the East. Though 

Egypt belonged to Turkey, this move was really directed against Great Britain, the leading commercial power in the East, and now the only active enemy of France. Unfortunately for his plans, Lord Nelson, the commander of the British fleet in the Mediterranean almost completely destroyed the French fleet in the battle of the Nile; and Napoleon and his army were thus cut off from France, their base of supplies. Seeing that his position was hopeless, Napoleon eventually abandoned his army and returned to France, barely escaping capture by the British on the way. 

He had learned, meanwhile, that his services were badly needed in France, for that country was in the greatest peril.

Much had happened in Europe during Napoleon's stay in Egypt. The Directory had pursued a very aggressive policy, and a new coalition had been formed against France, composed of Austria, Russia, and Great Britain. Though Russia had later withdrawn, this Second Coalition had won considerable success, and all Napoleon's recent conquests in Italy had been lost. one point France had actually been invaded, though it should be noted that the tide had definitely turned before Napoleon's return. 

Napoleon felt, however, that a chance had thus presented itself of winning new glory by vanquishing the Second Coalition. At

But Napoleon did not go directly to the front. First he seized the opportunity to make himself master of France.

The Weakness and Incompetence of the Directory The Directory was one of the most unpopular régimes that régimes that ever governed France. 

Power fell into the hands of unscrupulous politicians who seemed to care for nothing but

staying in office, and gave the country nothing but bad government. Though the old paper money had long since become worthless, a new issue was attempted; but having little to back it, this money steadily declined, and the government once more became bankrupt. 

Naturally there was suffering among the poor, as prices rose higher than ever; and business conditions were thoroughly unsettled. There was widespread dissatisfaction with a government so corrupt and inefficient. 

It is even said that the war was continued largely because the government was afraid to let the soldiers come home. They might turn the politicians out.

Nonetheless the civil government largely depended on the army for its existence. It was the money levied on conquered states by Napoleon that had rescued it from bankruptcy. Napoleon, for his part, had fully realized his power, and in Italy he had made what treaties he pleased without the slightest regard for the government., Of course the directors naturally mistrusted Napoleon's ambitions; and it seems likely that the young general's popularity accounted in part for their sending him to Egypt, since at least this would remove him from the scene.

Yet the time must certainly come when the army would overwhelm the civil government, if only some leader, such as Napoleon, would point the way.

NAPOLEON BECOMES MASTER OF FRANCE The Overthrow of the Directory 

When Napoleon returned to France in 1799, he found that a plot had already been hatched to overthrow the Directory. After careful consideration, he placed himself at its head.

There was little difficulty in getting rid of the directors. One of the councils, however, refused to be shunted aside, and Napoleon very narrowly escaped being outlawed. the end, however, soldiers came to the rescue, and as they entered the door, most of the deputies hastily left by the windows. Friendly members of both councils were then induced to put into effect a constitution which Napoleon and one of his henchmen had already In drafted. The whole affair is known as the 

Coup d'État of Brumaire - - a coup d'état meaning a change of government by violence, and Brumaire, one of the months of the revolutionary calendar.

The Establishment of the Consulate 

The new régime was known as the Consulate. The executive was composed of three consuls, though the second and third consuls had duties of little importance. There was a legislature, made up of several chambers, but its functions were so divided among them all that it was really quite powerless. One body proposed the laws; another discussed them; another voted or rejected them; and a fourth decided whether they were constitutional. 

Napoleon had said that he wanted a legislature that was dumb, and he had apparently obtained one. Practically all power rested in the hands of the First Consul who was none other than Napoleon himself.

Thus the popular hero of the army became the civil government. France was placed under a military dictatorship. After the people had voted approval in what was known as a plebiscite it was announced that the French Revolution was at an end. 

But Napoleon's upward climb had only started, as we shall see.

The Establishment of the Life Consulate 

The Consulate was only the first rung on the political ladder. Napoleon's tenure as First

Consul was limited to ten years, but his ambition demanded more, and it can fairly be said that he earned what he wanted. He was successful against the Second Coalition, and in 1801-1802 he gave France a period of peace for which she had yearned. He had also earned her gratitude by certain reforms, which we shall describe later. So in 1802 he was given the position of consul for life, with even the privilege of naming his successor. 

The Establishment of the Empire 

Still Napoleon's ambition was unsatisfied. 

He wanted the grandeur befitting a ruler who was practically absolute. He must be mon- 

¹ A plebiscite was a referendum. The word and the usage were derived from the practice of the Roman republic.

arch now in name as well as in fact. Moreover, since in the event of his sudden death, disorders might occur (perhaps even the return of the Bourbons), it was generally felt that his rule should be made hereditary. An unsuccessful plot against his government served as the pretext for such a change, and in May, 1804, Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor of the French.

Even the Pope was summoned to crown him, though in the end Napoleon thrust the Pope aside and crowned himself. His rule was now hereditary, and though he had no child to inherit the throne, a Bonaparte dynasty was assured. Many of the emigrant nobles, feeling that a return of the Bourbons was out of the question, came back to France and were welcomed by her ruler. Court life and ceremonial were restored, and France was again a monarchy with all the splendor once associated with the Old Régime. 

But was not this rather curious? How shall we explain the fact that France, after tasting political liberty, should willingly go back to a form of absolute rule?

How It Came About That Absolutism Was Restored in France

The explanation is perhaps threefold. 

In the first place, the French people were weary of the many political changes they had undergone. They were tired of the endless elections, tired of self-seeking politicians, tired of the chronic financial disorder and of uncertainties in the nation's economic life. 

Napoleon, a military man, seemed to stand for law and order. The middle class was willing to barter its liberties for the security his rule seemed to promise.

In the second place, the French people cared most for the social benefits of the Revolution, and these were perfectly safe under

Napoleon. Those who had acquired the confiscated lands felt sure that they would be able to keep them, since the strong rule of Napoleon prevented a Bourbon restoration. And the claim of merit, rather than birth, to receive recognition was now assured. Had not

Napoleon himself risen from poverty to the first position in the State? Able politician Able politician that he was, Napoleon was careful not to infringe on the old spirit of equality. With gorgeous liveries and costumes all about him, he himself usually dressed with a soldier's simplicity. He also asked the approval of the 

French people every time he made a change in the form of government, and thus he claimed that his power really rested on the popular will. The fact that he was Emperor of the French, not of France, seemed to reflect this relationship. Even the word republic was employed beside the designation, “empire," and the tri-color was retained beside the imperial green and gold. Napoleon felt that he had not destroyed, but had consolidated the Revolution.

In the third place, Napoleon had certainly captivated the public imagination. No soldier of France had ever won such triumphs, and the French are a people who eagerly follow the banner of a great leader. Napoleon himself sensed the vanity of the people he was ruling. "Give them glory," he once remarked, "and you can lead them anywhere.' وو But, in truth, he had given them much more than glory. He had established for them a wise and enlightened government. 

NAPOLEON REORGANIZES FRANCE 

Reorganization of the Government 

Napoleon was not only a military genius; he was a statesman. As soon as he became 

First Consul, he set about the task of giving France a much-needed reorganization. 

The legislative bodies had become a mere sham, nothing more than the rubber stamp of the executive. All trace of local self-government disappeared. Over each department an officer known as a prefect was placed, and the prefects were responsible to the First Consul. 

France was centralized once more. At the same time judges were no longer elected, but were appointed, like the prefects, by the First Consul.

One of his greatest services was to unify and codify the laws. In place of the numerous codes of the Old Régime, France was given a uniform code of civil and criminal law. This great compilation, the Napoleonic Code, as it was called, was the work of a corps of experts, but Napoleon himself, though possessing little

A GREAT 

135 

EUROPEAN UPHEAVAL 

technical knowledge of law, greatly influenced its work. Certain features, like the strict subordination of women to men, might well be criticized, but civil equality, religious toleration, trial by jury, and many other benefits of the Revolution were preserved. There no longer was any confusion as to what the law provided.

Napoleon also straightened out the financial tangle. The Revolution had swept away the old inequalities, but taxation had been fitful and badly managed during this period. 

Napoleon not only distributed the burden fairly equally, but made his subjects realize that taxes, however unpleasant, were a civic obligation. He put the finances in order, and restored the national credit after ten years of disorder. In 1800 he established the Bank of

France, which enabled industry to find the needed capital to expand. 

Economic Policies 

Napoleon made a determined effort to build up manufacturing and commerce. He established technical schools, offered liberal rewards for invention, and subsidized important industries. He hoped by defeating Great 

Britain to secure the Continental market for

French goods, but he realized that he must first develop a thriving industry in France. 

As an aid to internal commerce he constructed canals and built a splendid system of highways; and, to capture the world's trade, he strove, though without success, to erect a great colonial empire. In 1800 he got Louisiana from Spain, but, as we shall see, could not keep it.

Reorganization of the Church One of his greatest reforms was the reorganization of the Church. Ever since 1790 the clergy who had remained loyal to the Papacy had been hounded and ill-treated; and so many churches had been closed that the religious needs of the people had not been met. 

By a treaty with the Pope, known as the Concordat of 1801, Napoleon got the Papacy to recognize the transfer of the lands of the Church to the State. Henceforth the government should appoint the higher clergy, but papal sanction was required for every appointment. The lower clergy were to be chosen by the bishops, subject to the approval of the government. Peace was now restored in the religious world.

Other Activities 

There was hardly any feature of the national life that did not receive Napoleon's attention. 

He established a great system of education, centralized under the government. He did not, it is true, allow freedom of opinion; indeed he established a strict censorship that stifled all criticism. But probably, in the main, he knew, better than did his subjects, what they needed. He gave much attention to beautifying Paris, constructing broad boulevards, and making it a center of art, having despoiled the Italian states of many of their treasures. 

On the whole, Napoleon's policy was well conceived, for it gave the people the things they most wanted. "My policy," he said, "consists of governing people as they wish to be governed. That, I think, is the way of recognizing the sovereignty of the people." 

Napoleon and the Revolution

Of course this was not "sovereignty of the people," for the full responsibility reposed in one man. But he gave the French people the régime of order which they had wanted. 

And, above all, he symbolized to them the idea of social equality, as the term was understood; that is, equality of opportunity, or the "career open to talents." He was quick to reward talent when it appeared, and the establishment of the Legion of Honor was an example of Napoleon's recognition of merit.

Titles were given to men for conspicuous service, and they were sometimes made hereditary; but there was no privileged class of the old type.

Napoleon may be said to have consolidated the Revolution. He kept and protected the benefits which the people most prized: equality before the law, equality of opportunity, religious freedom, and the recognition of the property rights which had come down from the Revolution.

But he was also the distributor of some of the benefits of the Revolution to other lands in a way that we shall notice later. And he

c. Napoleon and Europe

The position Napoleon made for himself in Europe was quite a different thing from his position in France. In France his work satisfied certain needs, and most of it met with the approval of his people; in Europe his work was based largely upon conquest, and was therefore less enduring, though it had some important results which we shall consider at the end of the chapter. 

NAPOLEON BECOMES MASTER OF MOST OF EUROPE 

Napoleon's Reorganization of Central Europe Everywhere Napoleon went, he made important changes. The people of northern

Italy hailed him as a liberator, for they were glad to be rid of Austrian rule, and Napoleon gave them a republic (which he afterward converted into the Kingdom of Italy). Some of the Italian princes had to pay indemnities to keep their independence; and eventually 

Sardinia lost all her mainland territory. In 

1805 Napoleon dethroned the Bourbon king of the Two Sicilies, but though he made himself master of Naples without difficulty, he was never able, for lack of a fleet, to take possession of Sicily. Mainland Italy he held from north to south.

Meanwhile, Germany experienced an even greater upheaval. In order to secure some allies in Germany, Napoleon handed over most of the smaller states to the larger ones. 

Some of the princes, like those of Bavaria and Württemberg, were raised to the rank of king. 

The Holy Roman Empire, reduced from over three hundred states to less than a hundred, was finally abolished by a declaration of Napoleon's in 1806. The Holy Roman Emperor accepted the situation, and took the title of Emperor of Austria. 

By his German policy Napoleon gained two things: Austria and Prussia accepted the 

Rhine frontier as France's boundary to the east, and all the German states south of the Main were formed into a vast defensive league (the Confederation of the Rhine), allied to Napoleon and bound to furnish him with armies and supplies. Even Prussia, in the hope of greater spoils, contracted a secret alliance with France, but Napoleon did not mean it to be permanent, for he intended to humble the Hohenzollerns as he had already humbled the Hapsburgs.

The Struggle with Great Britain The enemy hardest to beat was, of course, Great Britain. Napoleon had inherited the struggle with Great Britain from the period of the Revolution. She had been a leading member of the first two coalitions. 

She was formidable because of her sea power and her money, the latter being used to provide her allies with munitions of war. Napoleon knew that he could never hope to establish a colonial empire until he had humbled this age-old rival. But while other powers suffered successive defeats, Great Britain had been able

to hide behind her navy, and Napoleon could not reach her. Her enmity to Napoleon was assured, for she had never allowed a power to become too formidable on the Continent. 

There was, however, a brief interval of peace. Great Britain and France signed the 

Treaty of Amiens in 1802. Thanks to Napoleon's skill in diplomacy, it was a more profitable peace for him than for Great Britain. 

He was not required to cease his aggressions in Europe, and his evident designs on Holland roused the British to new fears. After considerable friction the two powers again drifted into war in 1803. Further aggressions of Napoleon on the Continent had led Great Britain to keep in her hands the island of Malta, which she had promised to give up. 

Napoleon seems to have welcomed the renewal of the struggle, though he was forced to part with Louisiana (selling it to the United States for a mere fifteen million dollars). He knew, of course, that if he kept it, it would fall to the British navy. He was able, however, to strike some telling blows. He occupied 

Hanover, which belonged to the King of England; induced Prussia to close her ports to 

British trade, thus preventing any alliance between the two; and even scared the British into thinking that he intended to invade their island. To prevent the execution of this plan, Pitt bent all his efforts toward building up another coalition. But this Third Coalition,

Great Britain, Russia, and Austria, fared as had the others. Napoleon smashed it in the decisive battle of Austerlitz in December, 1805. 

Peace with Austria followed, and Russia became for some time inactive.

But one event marred Napoleon's triumph. 

In October, 1805, Nelson destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets in the battle of Trafalgar. True, Nelson did not survive his great victory, but the French navy would never again be able to cope with the 

British. Trafalgar was a crushing blow to the 

Emperor's fond dream of a colonial empire.

And it had, in consequence, an important effect on Napoleonic policy. 

Convinced that he could not hope to defeat

Great Britain by force of arms (for her navy was a safeguard against invasion), Napoleon made up his mind to crush her in another way. 

He would close the ports of the Continent to 

British trade, and this "nation of shopkeepers," as he expressed it, would "slowly bleed to death." He had already begun this policy by closing to the British all ports from Hamburg to the tip of Italy. Henceforth he made it the cardinal feature of his program. This plan was known as the Continental System. 

Where it would lead him no one could know.

Meanwhile England, although mistress of the seas, was powerless to check Napoleon on the Continent. Austria had been humbled, and it was now Prussia's turn.

The Peace of Tilsit-Napoleon's Power at Its Zenith

In 1806, Napoleon broke with Prussia. 

He had nothing but contempt for the Hohenzollerns and he goaded them into war. After a victorious campaign, he entered Berlin in triumph, the royal family taking refuge in Old

Prussia. Nothing, perhaps, afforded him so much pleasure as this crushing humiliation of the land of Frederick the Great. After

Russia had failed to be of much help to Prussia; and now it was Russia's turn. a hard campaign, Napoleon decisively defeated the Russian army and in June, 1807, Czar 

Alexander sued for peace.

There was no more dramatic episode in the Napoleonic period than the meeting of the two emperors, Napoleon and Alexander, on a raft in the river Niemen, which separated the two armies. We do not know precisely what took place between the two, but we know that the impressionable Czar was simply overcome by Napoleon's fascination. As a matter of cold fact, he had become Napoleon's dupe.

The Treaties of Tilsit were signed, one of them between France and Russia and the other between France and Prussia. Besides considerable loss of territory, Prussia was forced to close her ports to British trade, and by a later agreement was compelled to make an alliance with Napoleon and to reduce her army to 42,000 men. With Russia, France had signed a close alliance, and by one of its terms the Czar agreed to help enforce the 

Continental System. 

The Peace of Tilsit in 1807 marked the zenith of Napoleon's power. All of central 

Europe except Austria was in his power, and 

Austria, thrice humbled, could not dream of a resistance. Russia was his ally, and Russia was now to help him crush Great Britain. 

Yet Tilsit was, in a sense, a turning-point in Napoleon's fortunes. For the Continental 

System proved a snare and a delusion, as we shall see.

EUROPE OVERTHROWS NAPOLEON 

Causes of Napoleon's Downfall

There were several reasons why Napoleon lost his empire in Europe. One was the Continental System, particularly because it led him into steps that were fatal to his position, as we shall see. A second was the nationalist uprising, which was largely the result of a blunder committed in Spain. And the third was his belief that he could triumph against every obstacle.

Hence he committed the disastrous blunder of invading Russia, the effects of which could never be undone. 

The Continental System and Its Effects 

The Continental System, as we have noticed, involved the closing of the ports of the Continent to British trade. The British naturally retaliated by subjecting the coasts of France and her dependencies to a blockade, thus cutting them off from intercourse with countries outside Europe. This blockade bore very heavily on neutral powers, whose ships were liable to seizure if they carried goods to France. Napoleon retaliated by declaring the 

British Isles in a state of blockade and seizing any ships which had stopped in a British port. 

The system was also hard on the French and their allies. French industry was not sufficiently developed to satisfy all Continental needs, and Germans and Italians sighed for British cotton goods and many other things of which they were now deprived. Napoleon was very resourceful, to be sure. As cane sugar was no longer to be had, beets were raised in France for the sake of their sugar.

Likewise chicory was cultivated to take the place of coffee. But substitutes were hardly satisfactory, and the French began to feel the cost of the struggle in which they were engaged. Much more hostile was the attitude of various people outside of France. The discontent resulting from the enforcement of the Continental System had much to do with increasing opposition to Napoleon in Germany.

In any case the policy failed of its aim. 

While it did injure Great Britain, it was very far from ruining her. For one thing it was quite impossible to close the whole Continent to British trade, and British goods continued to enter at distant places, such as Saloniki on the Aegean. Then smuggling was so profitable that merchants were often ready to take great risks, and no amount of vigilance could stop it completely. It was to get direct control over more and more of the coast that Napoleon annexed so many of the lands which had already been under his sway. An ardent patriot himself, Stein worked ceaselessly to foster national pride in Prussia. Napoleon, aware of the threat such a leader offered his plans, forced his dismissal as prime minister. system, all the coastline of Europe was in his hands from the Adriatic to the Baltic. Even the Papal States were annexed to France; and the Pope, refusing to submit to Napoleon's dictation, was for a time, imprisoned. Most of northern Europe, though independent, was also involved in the system. 

In the meantime, Russia had joined France in attempting to impose the system on neutral powers. This meant specifically Denmark, Sweden, and Portugal. Denmark complied willingly. Russia having humbled Sweden (from whom she wrested Finland in 1809), this country also submitted. Portugal likewise yielded, but compliance did not save her from attack; for Napoleon meant to pick a quarrel with Portugal, and he dictated further terms, which that country could not accept. The truth is, Napoleon was launching a plot against Spain in which Portugal was to play a certain part. 

The Nationalist Uprising in Spain Napoleon had secretly promised Spain a part of Portugal in return for the right to send a French army across her territories to conquer her little neighbor. Once this army was in Spain, Napoleon resolved to use it, instead, to drive the Bourbons from the Spanish throne. It is not known with certainty why he wished to get rid of the Bourbons, for Spain had long been serving him just as faithfully as any other dependent state. At all events, he took advantage of a quarrel between the King of Spain and his son to invite them to a conference at Bayonne on French soil. There he announced his decision that neither father nor son should wear the Spanish crown, which he proposed to deliver to his brother, Joseph Bonaparte.

Napoleon had an uncanny skill in making fools of princes, but for once he went too far. 

The people of Spain bitterly resented this high-handed performance. Badly as they had been governed by the Bourbons, they did not want a foreigner forced upon them; and though Joseph tried to give them a good government, enacting many reforms, the people would not have him. Everywhere they rose in fierce rebellion; and as the country is very mountainous, the insurgents, darting from every direction, were able to reduce the French to serious straits. Moreover, a British force arrived to aid the insurrection. 

Napoleon himself now rushed to Spain, and to all appearance put down the uprising. But actually he had not done so. As soon as he left, the revolt flamed out again; the British arrived in greater numbers, commanded by 

Sir Arthur Wellesley, afterward Duke of

Wellington; and slowly but steadily the French were driven back. What is known as the 

Peninsular War had begun. It kept a large 

French army engaged in Spain, and thus materially helped to weaken Napoleon's position in Europe. Well might Napoleon say at a later time in recollecting how badly this struggle had sapped his resources, "It was the 

Spanish ulcer that ruined me."

The Nationalist Movement in Germany 

The Spanish revolt was the revolt of a nation, a demonstration of nationalism. A people had risen in arms against foreign dictation. And it proved to be the beginning of a general nationalist movement throughout Europe. So far Napoleon had dealt only with princes, who obeyed him either through fear or hope of favor. But now at last he had to reckon with a people.

For some time there had been signs in Germany of an aroused national spirit. Under two patriotic ministers, Stein and Hardenberg, Prussia had put through various reforms, designed to make her people feel a greater sense of unity and common interests, and, as a result, a greater devotion to the common cause.

In 1807, serfdom was abolished, and by later laws the differences between classes were much reduced. The middle class were allowed to acquire property; the peasant himself was able to become a free proprietor; and the nobles, who in Prussia were known as "Junkers," were no longer excluded from business. With the removal of such restrictions the old medieval class system was obviously breaking down. 

But Prussia did not appeal to the German people to take up arms against Napoleon. 

Despite their manifest discontent the Prussian King was far too timid to assume the leadership of such a movement. But Austria was arming; and the revolt of the burly mountaineers of the Tyrol, who had objected to being handed over to Bavaria by Napoleon, was a fine test of the loyalty of her people. 

Believing that Napoleon's hands were effectively tied in Spain, Austria started a new war in the spring of 1809. Her commander issued a resounding proclamation. "The freedom of Europe," it declared, "has sought refuge under your banners." It was undoubtedly intended as an appeal to the German people in the hope that they would compel their princes to join in a general rising. a hard campaign defeated the Austrians in 

July, 1809. Peace was then followed by an alliance, since Austria wanted to counterbalance the Franco-Russian alliance, and

Napoleon wanted an empress. Because Josephine had failed to bear him an heir, Napoleon had divorced her, and was anxious to marry again. The result was his marriage in 1810 to the Archduchess Marie Louise, daughter of the Austrian Emperor. A year later a son was born and given the proud title, King of Rome. Now the future of the First Empire seemed assured.

Napoleon, to all appearances, had reached the pinnacle of success. But appearances were deceptive, for underneath the surface a new and dangerous force, an intense nationalism, was undermining his power. Moreover, the 

Czar had come to feel that his alliance with Napoleon was too one-sided. 

The Russian Tragedy

Napoleon and Alexander fell out over many things. The Czar had come to realize that he had been duped, and Napoleon, for his part, wanted to teach his ally a lesson. He was too jealous of his own power to accept a partner on any terms of equality for very long; and he was confident that he could humble the Czar and add him to his long list of dependents. Napoleon had come to believe himself invincible. Drunk with power, he felt that every prince must bow before his will.

Both sides were well aware that war was coming. By the summer of 1812, Napoleon had amassed probably the largest army so far known in history. It was an army not only of Frenchmen, but of Spaniards, Poles, Danes, Germans, and Italians. Prussia and Austria were still allies of Napoleon, but all that he demanded from them were small forces to support the main army. With the "Grand 

Army" itself he invaded Russia.

The story of this tragic venture has often been told. The Russians avoided a decisive battle, and Napoleon pursued them for six

The horrors of the retreat can only be imagined. Hungry and exhausted, suffering from intense cold, often losing their way in the blinding snow, and continually harried by the pursuing Russians, the Grand Army was a pitiful wreck when it reached Germany. 

Out of the 450,000 soldiers that Napoleon had led into Russia only a few thousand were with him at the end. Most of this sorry remnant were unarmed and in rags.

The significance of the Russian disaster can hardly be exaggerated. Not only was a large army practically wiped out, but the legend that Napoleon was invincible had been shattered. Napoleon's enemies took courage. 

The War of Liberation 

Napoleon, for his part, left his broken army and hurried back to Paris to raise another. 

Russia and Prussia, in the meantime, formed an alliance to liberate Germany; and when

Napoleon returned with an army of nearly 250,000 men (mostly raw troops), he was able to do no more than hold his own. Prussia had at last dared to assume the leadership in 

Germany; and the War of Liberation had begun.

Gradually it became clear that the fate of Napoleon's empire in Europe was at stake, and that he was fighting a losing struggle. 

The odds were too great against him. The

The decisive battle was fought at Leipzig, in October, 1813. Napoleon was defeated; the Confederation of the Rhine quickly collapsed, and the French army retreated across the Rhine. The Allies then offered Napoleon terms that would have allowed him the "natural boundaries," but he refused to admit defeat; so the Allies crossed the Rhine. Now at last the French were compelled to defend their own land against invasion. 

There is no need to tell the story of the desperate fight that Napoleon made in the hard campaign that followed. His military genius could not avail against the superiority in numbers on the side of the Allies. When the 

Prussians managed to elude him and took Paris, there was nothing for him to do but to abdicate his throne. The War of Liberation had been won. resolution formally branding him as an outlaw. Napoleon knew that he would have to fight in order to maintain his position; that is, fight against his enemies abroad. With all speed he put an army into the field and took the offensive. THE HUNDRED DAYS AND THE END OF NAPOLEON Napoleon's Return 

By the terms of the abdication, Napoleon had been sent in exile to the little island of Elba, off the western coast of Italy. There he remained not quite a year. Carefully informed of all that was going on in Europe, he learned that the Allies were quarreling over the spoils, and that the Bourbons, who had returned to the French throne, had made themselves thoroughly unpopular. Hence he reasoned that he had a chance to recover his old power. The Allies, he believed, would not unite their forces against him, and the 

French would welcome him back.

Napoleon was mistaken about the Allies, for as soon as they learned that he had escaped, they ended their squabbles and united in a and the battleground was the Netherlands, or Belgium, as it was now usually called. This little land was once again the “cockpit of the nations." 

As neither Wellington nor Blücher, the respective British and Prussian commanders, had expected so swift an attack, they were far from ready to meet it. Napoleon's plan of campaign was, as usual, masterly. He divided his forces and strove to throw back the two armies along diverging lines so that the farther they retreated, the farther apart they would be. Then he expected to destroy them piecemeal.

The plan succeeded fairly well in the beginning. Wellington brought up a portion of his troops, but they were speedily thrown back. Blücher, meanwhile, advanced and was badly beaten. Unfortunately for Na-

Meanwhile Napoleon, exhausted from the strain of the past few days, had lost most of a day in preparations to fight the British. 

This delay enabled Wellington to take up a strong position and Blücher to get in touch with him.

The battle of Waterloo began at about noon on June 18, 1815. Napoleon tried desperately to dislodge the "Iron Duke," as Wellington was called, and the charge of the French cavalry is one of the most heroic and picturesque incidents in modern history. But they could not shatter the British lines, and charge after charge failed. By the late afternoon the 

Prussians at last arrived, and Napoleon was compelled to detach a force to meet them. A final attack was made at about seven o'clock, in which Napoleon used every available soldier. Perhaps he might have succeeded if he had not had to engage the Prussian forces on his flank. At any rate, the last charge failed, and then it was Wellington's turn to order an advance. "The Old Guard dies; it never surrenders," was the proud boast of the Frenchmen who stood their ground on this occasion. But most of the army broke and fled from the field. Napoleon had staked everything and lost.

Yet, even if he had won, it is unlikely that he could have held his ground against a united Europe.

Saint Helena 

Reaching Paris, Napoleon wanted to continue the struggle, but his followers saw that it was hopeless, and he was again forced to abdicate. Since the armies of the Allies were rapidly approaching the capital, he made for the coast; but here, of course, he was faced with the British blockade. He, accordingly, negotiated with the commander of a British cruiser, was taken on board, and brought to England.

In the meantime his fate was being decided. 

Though Blücher would have had him shot, the British government insisted upon exile; and this time Napoleon was sent to faraway Saint 

Helena, a little island in the South Atlantic

Ocean. His enemies took no chances of his coming back again.

At Saint Helena, Napoleon spent the last years of his life. He mainly occupied himself with dictating an account of his principles and plans to the men who accompanied him in exile. Thus arose the "Napoleonic Legend," not what Napoleon had believed, but what he wanted the world to think he had believed. 

He was the friend of peace, he said, and of human liberty. All this was meant to assist his son some day to ascend the throne. It is an evidence of Napoleon's foresight and his knowledge of the French people that his plans were to bear fruit. 

But the great man him Napoleon II, more commonly known as the Duke of Reichstadt, never reigned. He died at Vienna in 1831.

self soon vanished from the world's stage. 

After many months of suffering, which he bore with great fortitude, he died, May 5, 1821, at the age of fifty-two.

The Lesson of Napoleon 

Stern autocrat though he was, Napoleon belonged in spirit to the Revolution. He had no patience with privilege and taught not only France but much of Europe the lessons of efficiency and equal opportunity. For individuals in the mass Napoleon cared little, but the capable individual he honored, and to him was given a chance to prove his worth. 

And now that this period of stress and struggle was ended, just what had the Revolution achieved, and just what is its real significance in the history of civilization? 

D. The Results of the French 

Revolution When the Bourbons returned to power, one might feel that all the achievements of the Revolution were at stake. But however the men of the Old Régime might try to undo its work (and these efforts will be mentioned later), the experience through which the French people had passed since 1789 had given them a consciousness of their strength which could never be destroyed. And throughout 

And throughout

Europe as a whole, though the spirit of progress was held in check for the moment, the Old Régime could never get back its former influence and strength.

Let us note the immediate and more definite results of the French Revolution and then consider its wider significance. 

In France

IMMEDIATE RESULTS 

In the first place, France possessed, and would continue to possess, a written constitution. This constitution might be anything but liberal, but at least there were certain definite rights proclaimed in black and white, which no king could ever expect to override without encountering resistance. If the mid- 

If the middle class did not return to power in 1815, we should remember that they had not been in power since 1799. But even Napoleon had given the French people a constitution; so 

Louis XVIII could hardly have done less. 

In the second place, the principle of equality had triumphed to the extent that all people were equal before the law. This meant that penalties for crime were the same for all classes; that no person was debarred from holding office because of his position in society; that any person was free to work at his trade without restriction; and that the peasants were emancipated from feudalism. Those who had obtained lands as a result of the Revolution still retained them; and a person of the lowest station had now a chance to rise to a position of prominence. Napoleon had saved the principle of equality in its most practical sense equality of opportunity, the "career open to talents."

In the third place, religious freedom was now achieved. The time when people were prevented from believing or worshiping as they pleased was apparently over for all time. 

Freedom of speech and press and the right to hold public meetings were not yet guaranteed. 

In the fourth place, France was a far more unified nation than in 1789. The old administrative divisions, the patchwork of legal codes, the internal tariff walls, and the numerous special rights of favored classes had all been swept away. The Revolution had destroyed the old order; the Revolution and more especially Napoleon had built a new and better nation. The state was centralized, with prefects governing fairly equal territorial divisions, the departments. There was one law for all, the Napoleonic Code; a uniform system of weights and measures (the metric system); and a tariff only on merchandise imported from abroad. The complexity of the 

Old Régime had given way to simplicity and uniformity. 

In Europe

In Europe the immediate results were not so evident, and some of the changes made by Napoleon's hand were not preserved. Yet in most cases his work stood its ground. In 

Italy, and in various German states, feudalism and serfdom were abolished, and taxes were

imposed without regard for customary exemptions. The Napoleonic Code, with certain slight modifications, was introduced into many lands; and that meant, among other things, equality before the law and religious toleration. Government had been generally efficient under Napoleonic rule, and this lesson of efficiency was not lost after his hand had been withdrawn.

Prussia was not reformed by Napoleon, but she had followed France's lead to a considerable extent. (See the account of Prussian reforms on page 141.) One might say that she caught the spirit of the French Revolution. To a certain extent Bavaria and Württemberg did likewise. One writer has said that "no country that had been touched by French influence became ever again quite what it had been before."

SPIRITUAL SIGNIFICANCE OF THE REVOLUTION 

In France

Already the spirit of fraternity, expressing itself in nationalism, had entered deeply into the hearts of the French people. Their country's defense and their country's welfare were matters in which they would take the keenest interest from now on. There were also many Frenchmen, particularly of the 

SUMMARY of Important Concepts middle class, who believed in political liberty and would not be content until that principle had been established. 

In Europe

Upon Europe as a whole the French Revolution had made a deep impression. People who had witnessed a demonstration of government by the people wished to see it put into operation again; and in almost every country there were little groups working and sometimes plotting to that end. A seed had been sown which was bound to bear fruit before long. What has been said of democracy can also be said of equality.

Fraternity in the sense of nationalism, had been greatly promoted by Napoleon. Sometimes his work had been conscious and deliberate. Thus the Italian people were given a sense of unity they had hardly known before. 

Sometimes, however, his work had been unintentional. German nationalism, for example, was born of the struggle to free Germany from his sway.

Unquestionably nationalism was to prove the strongest force which the Revolution unchained.

And finally, the effect of the great upheaval was to make people sense that society was changing, that the world was broadening out, and that progress would be much swifter in the future. 

1. The zeal of the French in extending their doctrines and governmental system to neighboring peoples alarmed the crowned heads of Europe and caused them to attack France. a. Their hope of partitioning France ended in defeat at the hands of the fiercely patriotic French citizen-soldiers. b. In the long wars many soldiers rose to fame from the lower ranks, but none had the ability of 

Napoleon Bonaparte. c. Weary of disorder and inefficiency, the mass of the people approved Napoleon's overthrow of the Directory.

His efforts to enforce this boycott plus a rising tide of nationalism led to wars which ended only with his complete defeat.

GAINING Skill A. Where to Get Information. Music often helps us to a better understanding of history. The words of a song may tell us what happened or afford a clue to how people felt long ago. 

Sometimes a melody stirs faintly within us the same emotions that were experienced by the people who first sang the song; at other times the music helps us sense what happened. Many songbooks classify songs by historical periods as well as in other ways. Your local music dealer will have catalogues that list available recordings. You may see for yourself how music illuminates history if you read the words of the Marseillaise and then play a recording of that stirring song. Perhaps you have heard a soloist sing "The Two Grenadiers" by Schumann, a song that throws light on the hardships experienced by Napoleon's veterans and their deep feeling of loyalty to him. You may want to play the "1812 Overture" by Tchaikovsky. 

Though you probably have heard it on the radio, the music should mean more now that you have read about Napoleon's campaign in Russia. 

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. It is important that you not only learn to organize ideas effectively orally or in writing, but also that you learn to evaluate and to refute the arguments of others. 

This valuable experience you can acquire through informal debate or discussion. Select a subject which is controversial and for which material is available. Be sure to inform yourself about both sides of the subject so that you know in advance what arguments your opponents are likely to make. 

1. For example, you may want to discuss in class one of these questions: the Terror was necessary to save France; a substantial reform program sponsored by Louis XVI would have saved France from violent revolution; Napoleon was greater in peace than in war; Napoleon was the forerunner of the twentieth-century dictators; when a radical party comes into power it becomes conservative; or, sea power defeated Napoleon. 

2. You may want to give an oral or written report on one of these topics: Napoleon in Egypt; Napoleon as "a child of the Revolution"; Napoleon's reform program; Lord Nelson, an English naval hero; or, how nationalism defeated Napoleon. 

3. Find the account of the battle of Waterloo in Les Misérables by Victor Hugo and read extracts to

the class. Does this reading help you see why one needs a great deal of information about past events if they are to seem real?

C. How to Evaluate Information. Have you found conflicting estimates of Napoleon in your readings? 

How do you account for these differences in opinion when all the authors had access to much the same facts? Can you cite similar differences in opinion with respect to present-day men and events? 

1. As a class project let various students write character sketches of Napoleon, Metternich, Wellington, Lord Nelson, and other important personages of this period. For each personage, have one student give the Allied, another the French, point of view. Might there be more than one French point of view, depending on the date and the group involved? 

2. Draw a cartoon to make clear the nature of the struggle between Napoleon and England. Or make a drawing to give point to the words of the captured Russian officer who answered Napoleon's question about the best route to Moscow by saying, "Many roads lead to Moscow. Charles XII went by the way of Poltava." How do you interpret these words?

THE REVOLUTION laid a train of dynamite in Europe, and henceforth absolutism, privilege, and foreign rule were doomed to lead an uneasy existence. 

Explosions with increasing violence would continue to shake Europe until very little of the Old Régime would be left. 

During the period we are entering (from 1815 to 1871) nationalism won its most brilliant triumph in the making of two new national states, Italy and Germany. Only in Great 

Britain did progress come about through legal and peaceful methods. First, however, we must give our attention to the reconstruction of Europe following the downfall of Napoleon.

A. The Old Monarchies Make a New Map of Europe The Treaties of Paris 

Since France had been finally beaten in the European struggle which had developed out of the French Revolution, it was the task of the old monarchies to make a new territorial settlement. The First Treaty of Paris, signed with France after Napoleon had been sent to Elba, was canceled by his return; and, following his final defeat, the Second Treaty of 

Paris was concluded, November 20, 1815. It was less liberal than the previous treaty had been, and of all the gains made under the Revolution France retained only Avignon. 

She was also compelled to pay a war indemnity, and until this requirement was met, she had to submit to a large army of occupation.

The Vienna Settlement 

To dispose of various lands outside France was a harder problem. For that purpose representatives of the powers had met in Vienna in 1814, and their work was finally completed in 1815 about a week before the decisive battle of Waterloo. There was no "Congress of Vienna" in the sense of formal meetings. Rather, the settlement was the result of various deals between the great powers, Russia, Prussia, Austria, and Great

Britain. But a good deal of time was devoted to the entertainment of the various monarchs or their ministers; and someone remarked, "The Congress of Vienna does not advance; it dances." The courtesies which Austria, a bankrupt state, extended to her guests, cost approximately $16,000,000. 

All the great powers which had combined to defeat Napoleon made territorial gains. 

Austria, not wanting to receive back the Netherlands, acquired Lombardy-Venetia, an enlargement of her former possession, the 

Milanese. Prussia, besides recovering her former possessions, received Swedish Pomerania and a portion of Saxony; and Russia, already in possession of Finland (since 1809) and Bessarabia (gained in 1812 after a war with Turkey), received some of the Polish possessions acquired by Austria and Prussia in the Second and Third Partitions of Poland. 

Great Britain, as usual, added to her store of colonies. There had been a good deal of squabbling over the spoils, and it was because of the greedy efforts of Russia and Prussia that France, though recently humbled, was able to

It is noticeable that the Congress had little regard for nationalism, that force which had been so powerful in the overthrow of Napoleon. The German people were not given a national state, but received once more a loose federation of princes, known as the Germanic Confederation, under the leadership of Austria. 

Norway, a former possession of the crown of

Denmark, was handed to the King of Sweden, and Belgium was given to the King of Holland. As special safeguards against France (still thought of as a possible danger to the peace), the merging of Holland and Belgium into the Kingdom of the Netherlands was designed to serve as a bulwark at the northern end of her eastern frontier, while an enlarged Sardinia was supposed to serve the same purpose at the southern end. Between the two lay the Germanic Confederation, which had the means of raising an army, and the mountain republic of Switzerland, which was formally neutralized - an act which meant that the powers pledged themselves never to invade it. Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia also entered into a defensive alliance against France.

Such were the precautions taken against a renewal of French aggression. But what about the danger of revolution?

B. The Revolutionary Forces Versus the Old Order Democracy as One of the Revolutionary Forces 

Two forces, bred of the French Revolution, produced an undercurrent of revolutionary unrest and seemed perpetually to challenge the old order. These forces were democracy and nationalism. Democracy, as you know, means literally government by the people. 

It does not mean, of course, that everybody governs. There is always an age restriction, and until more recent times there was a sex restriction as well. The nearest the citizen actually comes to governing is when he votes. 

Ordinarily, of course, he does not vote directly on a public question, though the French people did on special occasions when they ratified changes of government made by if the candidate which the citizen votes for does not win, then it cannot be said that the government represents him. It represents the majority. This was as far as Rousseau carried the principle of democracy, and most countries even today identify democracy with majority rule.

In 1815 there was little evidence of democracy in Europe. Owing to property qualifications, only a small proportion of the citizenry was able to vote, even in France, and the same was to be true of various countries where constitutions were granted during this period. Other benefits, associated with democracy, such as freedom of the press and freedom of public meeting, were still to be obtained in most of Europe. 

But the French Revolution had presented democracy to people as an ideal. Hence those persons who did not enjoy its application first, the upper middle class, then the lower middle class, the peasantry, and the workers were certain to engage in a struggle workers for political rights.

Nationalism as One of the Revolutionary Forces 

Nationalism must not be confused with democracy. A people which does not possess any political rights may yet fully express the sentiment of nationalism, as the Spaniards did when they revolted against Napoleon. 

Nationalism, then, applies to a group of individuals wishing to preserve their interests as a group against outsiders. Such a group is commonly termed a nationality. 

But what, we may ask, makes a nationality?

Usually it is the fact of a common experience. 

People who have shared the same customs, the same trials, and perhaps the same language, feel themselves to be one, and they want to stay one, and to manage their own affairs. The Dutch spoke the same language and most of them were Protestant in religion, and thus they felt themselves different from

Savoy, being French, wanted to share the same government with the people of France. 

They were imbued with the spirit of nationalism.

Unfortunately, little regard was paid for this spirit by the men who had just remade the map of Europe. The old idea that a state properly comprised the territories of a ruler, quite regardless of the character of the population, was still the principle generally accepted in 1815, rather than the principle of nationality. Yet nationalism had manifested itself so powerfully in the French Revolution and in the War of Liberation that it had come to inspire most of the peoples who were still living in subjection to foreign rule. Of all forces unchained by the French Revolution, this was the strongest.

The Concert of Europe and Its Failure 

To organize resistance to democracy and nationalism, the statesmen of the old order devoted their time and thought. Led by the 

Austrian foreign minister, Prince Metternich, the great powers, Austria, Prussia, Russia, and Great Britain, formed the so-called Concert of Europe, sometimes popularly known as the Holy Alliance; and congresses were held from time to time in order to watch over the peace of Europe. After France had paid her indemnity in full, she was admitted to the Concert. In fact, France under the restored 

Bourbons was most unlikely to disturb the peace. It was, rather, the outbreaks of revolution in other countries that caused these diplomats concern. Austria, acting for the 

Concert of Europe, put down revolutions in Italy, and France disposed of one in neighboring Spain. But when it was finally proposed to suppress Spain's revolting colonies in the New World, Canning, the British foreign secretary, objected; objected; and Great

Britain definitely withdrew from the Concert of Europe.

It was because of this threatened intervention in the New World that President Monroe, in 1823, proclaimed the Monroe Doctrine, according to which Europe was explicitly warned not to interfere in the affairs of the western hemisphere, while the United States, on her part, promised not to meddle in Europe. In point of fact, however, the British navy was the principal means of keeping Europe at bay. 

At all events, the Concert of Europe had shot its last bolt. Events were to show that the forces of revolution were far too strong for the old monarchies.

The Revolutionary Unrest 

In the Balkan Peninsula nationalism gained some signal triumphs. The Greeks revolted in 1821, and after a long struggle obtained their freedom in 1830. The Serbs by repeated revolts were able in 1830 to gain

autonomy that is, limited self-government under Turkish rule. The Rumans, living in the Danubian Principalities, acquired a similar status in the previous year. Curiously enough, Russia, staunchly autocratic as she was, aided these movements because she saw in the Balkan States convenient instruments of Russian policy against the ramshackle Ottoman Empire. 

But the revolutionary forces were not confined to the Balkans. In 1830, France dethroned the Bourbons, replacing Charles X by his cousin, Louis Philippe, who promised to rule as a democratic monarch. As the revolution had taken place in the month of July, the new régime was usually known as the July Monarchy. It was certainly not democratic. 

Just as the Bourbons had always favored the old nobility and the Church, the July Monarchy rested for support on the rich bankers and manufacturers in other words, the upper middle class. Discontent finally ended in another revolution in 1848. Louis Philippe was overthrown, and the Second French Republic was proclaimed. This democratic régime was, in turn, overthrown by a clever politician, who knew how to make capital out of his name. This was Louis Napoleon Bonaparte, a nephew of the great Napoleon. 

Having become the master of France as the result of a coup d'état in 1851, he was proclaimed Emperor of the French the following year. It seemed as if the French people, shaken as they had been by their experience with the French Revolution and Napoleon, would never be willing to settle down.

Just as had been the case with the great French Revolution, these later revolutions at Paris had immediate effects in other lands. 

Belgium won her independence from Holland in 1831, and in order to save her from falling a prey to her neighbors, she was neutralized by international treaty. The Poles revolted, too, though without success. In Germany and Italy, both composed of a collection of states, various uprisings occurred; and in 

Austria, where several nationalities were bound unwillingly together, a violent upheaval took place in 1848, and it was only with great difficulty that the Hapsburgs were able to keep their empire intact. 

To all appearance, by the middle of the democracy had

But in any case democracy and nationalism had grown considerably in strength as the result of the experiences we have mentioned, and were almost certain to triumph in the end. One of the principal gains was not political but social. Feudalism had perished throughout all of central Europe. 

It was only in the political sphere that the old order, battered though it was, had, generally speaking, managed to survive.

Europe, as we shall see. c. The Unification of Italy 

Italy in 1815

Italy, in 1815, was composed of a number of political divisions. At the southern end of the peninsula was the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, ruled by a Spanish Bourbon prince. 

Farther to the north were the Papal States, extending across the peninsula and including not only the city of Rome but certain outlying districts, such as Romagna.¹ Northwest of the Papal States were the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and two smaller duchies, Parma and Modena, all three under Austrian influence. 

In the northwestern corner of Italy was the 

Kingdom of Sardinia, comprising Old Savoy, 

Nice, Piedmont, and the island of Sardinia.

Finally, north of the Po was the Austrian province, Lombardy-Venetia. Most of the 

Italian princes, being absolute monarchs and very incompetent, depended mainly upon

Austria to protect them from revolution, and, in fact, Austrian influence ruled the peninsula from end to end.

The Awakening of Italy 

But the Italians were gradually awakening. 

They wanted a freer life and national unity. 

Those in northern Italy had once enjoyed a kingdom of their own under Napoleon, and this taste of unity had made them feel that they all ought to be united in a single state. 

There was, consequently, much unrest and even occasional revolts. An ardent patriot, Giuseppe Mazzini, founded in 1831 a society, known as Young Italy, and inspired his fellow- Italians with an intense devotion to the cause. 

Unfortunately, the Italian people were not united and had yet to learn the lesson of cooperation; and when most of them revolted in 

1848, they failed before the superior strength of Austria. Yet the leadership of Sardinia in that struggle seemed to point to her as the state most likely to guide in the unification of 

Italy. Moreover, Victor Emmanuel II, who ascended the throne of Sardinia in 1849, was 1 On the Adriatic; a part of the States of the Church which are shown on the map on page 156.

Cavour as the Guide for Unification 

Count Camillo di Cavour was a nobleman, distinguished for business ability and a journalist by profession. He was liberal in his views, and had aided in drafting the Sardinian constitution the only constitution to be found in Italy at that time. A man both practical and daring, and an exceptionally hard worker, Cavour was also a genius in weaving intricate plans and carrying them out. Having promoted the economic development of Sardinia, he enabled her to increase her fighting forces; and meanwhile he made her set an example to Italy as a liberal and progressive state. He particularly wanted Europe to observe the progress that was being made. And underneath it all Cavour cherished a definite purpose.

Cavour Seeks an Ally for His People What Cavour wanted was an alliance with a foreign power that would be willing to fight Austria in the cause of Italian freedom. 

Either Great Britain or France would serve that purpose; and when both these powers engaged in a war with Russia, he boldly brought Sardinia into the struggle in the hope of winning French and British favor. After the war Cavour made visits to London and Paris and in that way came into contact both with the English ministers and the Emperor Napoleon III. Since Great Britain proved unwilling to assist him, Cavour was forced to appeal to Napoleon III.

Cavour Makes a Bargain with Napoleon III 

Napoleon III was a person not easily understood. He often showed exceptional skill in maneuver, but, essentially a dreamer, he sometimes strove after things that perhaps a more practical mind would have known to be unattainable. Yet it was something that he was a man of imagination. Though he was totally out of sympathy with democratic institutions, he was liberal and progressive in certain ways. He was by conviction a freetrader and he fully believed in the principle of nationality. Autocrat as he was (for universal suffrage meant practically nothing when his parliaments possessed no power), he was anxious to justify his rule to the French people, and by furthering their economic interests he assured them a period of exceptional prosperity. It was thanks partly to his backing that the French engineer, Ferdinand de Lesseps, constructed the Suez Canal, opened in 1869.

It was Napoleon's misfortune, however, that he would always be compared to Napoleon the Great. He knew that the French people expected him to make their country once more the greatest in Europe. So he joined Great 

Britain in waging the Crimean War (18541856), a struggle occasioned by Russia's aggressive policy in the Near East. Though the Allies mismanaged the war, they were victorious in the end, and Napoleon's influence was paramount in drafting the final

peace. 

Certainly, in 1856, France loomed highest among the powers. The Second

Some of the powers, suspecting his motives, tried to patch up a reconciliation between Austria and Sardinia, and as Cavour could not deliberately provoke war, he was so distracted that his friends were afraid that he would actually lose his mind. But Austria's patience was also becoming exhausted, and when she made an unreasonable demand, Cavour felt able to reject it in the hope that the world would judge Austria the aggressor. 

The War for Liberation began in April, 1859, and was over in less than three months. 

The Franco-Sardinian forces were successful, and almost all Lombardy was conquered. 

Then, in the hour of triumph, when everyone was expecting an advance on Venice, the news was flashed that Napoleon had made a separate peace with Austria. Italy was not to be freed "to the Adriatic."

And now Cavour was tempting Napoleon 

III to greater exploits. The Emperor of the 

French, being a Bonaparte, had no love for the Vienna Settlement, and he imagined himself making a new Europe based on the principle of nationality. In the summer of 1858, Cavour met him, as if by accident, in a resort in the Vosges Mountains, and there the two statesmen entered into a conspiracy against Austria. Though he was still unwilling to see 

Italy a united nation, since Catholic influence deterred him from any attack on the Papal States, Napoleon agreed to liberate Italy from the Alps to the Adriatic, in return for which he was promised Savoy and Nice, which would at last give France the Alps as a natural boundary. He also insisted that Austria should appear responsible for the coming war.

Parliaments, newly established in all these states, demanded union with Sardinia. But 

Victor Emmanuel did not dare to annex these lands to his kingdom lest such action might embroil him in another war with Austria.

1860, he returned to office. Cavour realized that all depended on Napoleon III, and he was willing to buy his favor with the surrender of Savoy and Nice. Agreement was reached in March, 1860. France acquired Savoy and 

Nice, and Sardinia got her compensation by taking over Tuscany, Parma, Modena, and Romagna. Napoleon warned Austria that she was not to interfere. Meanwhile, plebiscites in Savoy and Nice ratified their annexation to France.

The Completion of Italian Unity 

It was now the turn of a soldier to contribute to the unification of Italy. Giuseppe 

Garibaldi, a hardy mountaineer, who had figured in many a desperate revolution, enrolled a band of volunteers to attack the King of the Two Sicilies. It hardly seemed humanly possible that this little band of redshirts, totaling little more than a thousand, would invade and conquer a kingdom; but the rule of the Bourbon king had been oppressive and his subjects were in revolt. After taking possession of Sicily, Garibaldi crossed to the mainland, and proceeded to capture Naples. He would then have advanced on 

Rome; but, in order to prevent a clash with a 

French garrison which Napoleon had kept in Rome since 1849 to protect the Pope, Cavour now intervened. The Sardinian army conquered the remaining territories of the Pope save Rome itself and some small surrounding districts.

Only Venice and Rome remained to be won. 

We shall see the former acquired in 1866 by the Seven Weeks' War and the latter gained in 1870 as a result of the outbreak of the 

Franco-Prussian War. 

Meanwhile, on March 17, 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was founded, Victor Emmanuel being proclaimed "by the grace of God and the will of the nation King of Italy." It had been under the banner of Sardinia that the work had been accomplished, and thus Sardinia merged herself with Italy. 

Without foreign aid the unification of Italy would hardly have been possible, and that is where Cavour had shown his diplomatic skill. 

But unity was in part the work of the Italian people themselves. By plebiscites the people

D. The Unification of Germany 

Germany in 1815

Germany in 1815 was almost as disunited as Italy. The only suggestion of unity was the Germanic Confederation, and this cumbersome organization had very little authority over the individual states. Such was the sorry reward which had been given the German people after the War of Liberation. Austrian influence was dominant in Germany, and Austria preferred conditions as they were. 

The rivalry between the two great powers,

AND SOME REFORM MORE REVOLUTIONS 

Austria and Prussia, seemed to make it all but impossible to create a united Germany. 

Austria did not want to unify Germany and she would not willingly allow Prussia to do so.

A Forward Move and a Lost Opportunity 

But especially among the middle class the hope still lingered of attaining German unity. 

The gradual evolution of a tariff union between the various German states (Austria excepted) seemed to pave the way for ultimate political union. Finally, in 1847, a movement was set on foot for a national assembly which should plan a constitution for a united Germany. The fact that Austria, the enemy of such a movement, was engulfed in revolution the following year, seemed to promise complete success for such a movement, and an assembly, chosen by universal suffrage, met at Frankfort in May, 1848. Unfortunately these liberals felt that a monarch was a necessity, and the logical person for the throne of a united Germany was the King of Prussia.

But the Hohenzollern king was both too timid to offend Austria and too autocratic to be willing to accept a crown from the German people. Hence the assembly, known as the "Frankfort Parliament," failed. United the

German people would become in course of time, but the chance to become united on a liberal basis was definitely lost. Democracy and nationalism were soon to part company.

Prussia as the Power to Lead in the Work of Unifi- cation 

Yet Prussia was the power most capable of unifying Germany. She was not at all democratic, it is true; indeed, everything was done to stifle democracy in a country where the army and police were everywhere in evidence. But Prussia was becoming a prosperous state, capable of putting a large army in the field. Unfortunately for Prussian policy, the

middle class was afraid that a large army might be used to strengthen the power of the Crown. Illiberal as the constitution, granted in 1850, undoubtedly was, it at least provided a parliament which had the right to vote on financial matters; and this parliament enabled the middle class to thwart the will of the King to increase the army. William I was in despair, and was almost ready to abdicate his throne. Then appeared on the scene the man whom the German people so badly needed as their leader in the work of unification. 

Bismarck at the Helm 

Otto von Bismarck was a Prussian Junker, who had already acquired considerable political experience. He had been prominent in the politics of the Germanic Confederation and he had also served in diplomatic posts. 

In 1862 he accepted the King's offer of the premiership of Prussia.

Bismarck was a man of tremendous force. 

Yet he was also a man of wonderful perception, who planned his course with care and could be cautious or courageous as required. 

With democracy he had no patience. He was a true Prussian in believing firmly in absolutism and the power of the sword. Military power in the hands of an autocratic state was the weapon on which he relied. "Prussia must keep her strength intact," he declared in a public speech. "Not by speeches and party resolutions are the great questions of the day decided, but by blood and iron."

And it was by blood and iron that he was destined to unify Germany. 

Bismarck Sharpens His Sword

But Bismarck was thinking not so much of the German people as of Prussia. He meant that Prussia should dominate Germany and wrest the supremacy from Austria. Consequently he realized that Prussia must have, above all, a strong army. When the King, unable to get the funds he needed for this purpose, talked of abdicating, Bismarck told him frankly that the thing to do was to ignore the constitution. The government, accordingly, levied the usual taxes, and the money was expended to equip an army of 450,000 men.

Bismarck Fights Denmark and Plans for War with 

Austria 

And now that he had sharpened his sword, what did Bismarck purpose to do with it?

Sooner or later he knew that Prussia must fight her rival, Austria, to decide the question of German supremacy. 

The opportunity came out of a quarrel with Denmark, who in 1863 annexed the 

Duchy of Schleswig. Since Schleswig was mostly peopled by Germans, there was great resentment in Germany over this action. On the ground that the annexation was a breach of a treaty which had fixed the connection of Denmark with Schleswig as a purely personal union - that is, the bond of a common ruler and no more - Bismarck persuaded Austria to join Prussia in threatening Denmark with war unless she yielded the point within fortyeight hours. He knew that Italy greatly desired Venetia, which was Austria's last possession on the Italian peninsula, and that Prussia and Italy had, therefore, something in common. So in April, 1866, a treaty of alliance was signed with Italy. 

Meanwhile, he was quite indifferent to public opinion. Few really believed in the necessity of fighting Austria, and the thought of war between Germans seemed abominable in the extreme. "I know that I am generally detested," he exclaimed. "Fortune is as fickle as the opinions of men. I am staking my head. 

But I shall play the game through if it brings me to the scaffold." Thus Bismarck, once he had carefully made up his mind, did not flinch. But he did believe that he ought to make it appear that Prussia was fighting in a just cause. Consequently, in order to "correct" the popular belief that the impending war was purely for the sake of grabbing the two duchies, he proposed a thorough reform of the Germanic Confederation, knowing, of course, that Austria would be bitterly opposed. 

And true enough, it was Austria now who made up her mind to fight, feeling that this was the "last straw" in a series of irritations.
