The publication of the news threw public opinion in France into a frenzy. The idea of having a Hohenzollern in Spain, while another member of the family, the King of Prussia, ruled on the Rhine, was enough to infuriate a The Sensitiveness of France as a Cause of the Franco- people already touchy because of their recent 

Prussian War

In fact, ever since 1860 the prestige of the Second Empire had greatly declined. Napoleon attempted in 1862 to found an empire in Mexico, but the affair was badly managed and ended disastrously. When he tried to appease his people by giving his parliament greater power, it was apparently too late. Above all, the French people felt that Prussia's astounding triumph was as much a blow to France as it was to Austria. They were sensitive in the extreme about their country's loss of prestige. 

If Prussia should wound their feelings, it would undoubtedly take but little to provoke a war. 

Bismarck's Policy as a Cause of the Franco-Prussian War

Bismarck knew the state of mind in France and resolved to take advantage of it. He felt that France would never willingly allow him to bring the South German states into the empire he was creating; and he was inclined to believe that a war was needed to make the Germans thoroughly desire unity. Meanwhile, France herself played into his hands. 

It seems that Napoleon, hoping desperately for compensation for Prussia's recent territorial gains, had demanded of Bismarck some 

German territories on the Rhine. Seeing his opportunity, Bismarck cleverly divulged the scheme, and thereby induced the South 

German states to ally themselves with Prussia. 

Thanks to these alliances, he knew that he could count on a united Germany in case of war. It only remained now to provoke 

France into declaring war. 

The opportunity came with the choice of a new king in Spain. This country selected 

Prince Leopold, a member of the Hohenzollern family and a cousin of the King of 

Prussia, to fill its vacant throne. Leopold himhumiliations. It was decided to have the 

French ambassador at Berlin request an audience with the King of Prussia, then vacationing at Ems, in order to demand the prince's withdrawal. Not wanting war, himself,

William intimated to the ambassador that he did not approve of the prince's acceptance of the throne; and a few days later the prince again declined it. France gloated over her victory, while Bismarck was so dejected that he almost reached the point of resigning from office. All his planning seemed to have been in vain.

Then the unbelievable folly of the foreign minister of France changed the entire situation. 

He insisted that the Prussian king should promise never again to allow the Hohenzollern candidacy to be renewed. To this unreasonable request William replied by a firm but courteous refusal. Then he telegraphed an account of the affair to Bismarck at Berlin. 

Bismarck received the "Ems Telegram," while dining with two of his friends, one of them Moltke. He was feeling much depressed over the entire failure of his plans. Then the telegram arrived, and after reading it, his mood suddenly changed. mood suddenly changed. He took a pencil and shortened the message in such a way as to make it appear that France's request had been sharply and roughly rejected. When he showed the result to Moltke, the latter exclaimed, "That turns a defeat into an offensive." Bismarck then gave the telegram, as he had changed it, to the press. 

The Ems Telegram was the immediate cause of war. Paris went wild with excitement. The French ambassador had been insulted, and nothing but war would salve the national pride. Napoleon, for his part, was far too sensible a man to desire war, but he was ill in mind and body and his ministers

were bent on teaching Prussia a lesson. On July 

19, 1870, France declared war against Prussia.

The Franco-Prussian War 

The Franco-Prussian War was one of the most one-sided struggles in history. France was in no way prepared to meet the crisis. 

The army was badly organized and badly equipped. Everything seemed lacking. There were insufficient rations for the men, insufficient means for transporting troops, and in some cases cannon without ammunition. One general wired headquarters that he could not find his brigade: "What shall I do?" he wailed.

A state of greater confusion can hardly be imagined. Prussia's army, on the other hand, was a splendid fighting machine. France also had the misfortune of being greatly outnumbered. Prussia could muster 450,000 men against France's 300,000.

With such conspicuous advantages on the side of Prussia, the outcome was never in doubt. Two Prussian armies invaded France, and the French were badly defeated. Napoleon himself was taken prisoner along with 83,000 men. He was allowed to take refuge in England, where he died a few years later. 

Meanwhile, changes were taking place in Paris. Napoleon's defeat and surrender were the death-blow to the Second Empire, and a group of patriots in Paris proclaimed a republic. The socalled Committee of National Defense was set up, the leader of which was Léon Gambetta, not only a dauntless patriot but an able organizer.

But by this time the Germans had begun the siege of the capital itself. Gambetta, who escaped from Paris in a balloon, did wonders in raising armies to break the iron ring that was encircling and strangling the city. the Germans were far too powerful, and Paris was finally starved into submission. But

An armistice was signed in order to enable the French to elect an assembly which should decide the question of peace. This body, the Bordeaux Assembly, was made up of men who saw that the war was lost and were ready now for peace. 

Gambetta and other leaders of the republic, who wanted to prolong the resistance, had been decisively defeated. 

By the Treaty of Frankfort (1871), which closed the Franco-Prussian War, France was

Uneasy as long as the Germans were encamped in the country, the French people dug deep into their pockets, and paid the indemnity in less than two years. 

The Results of the War

The results of the war were momentous. 

Three countries were vitally affected: In the first, German unification, if we except the Germans in Austria, was completed. The 

South German states had been made to feel

In the second country, Italian unity, if we except a few Italians in the Tyrol and across the Adriatic, was also completed. When the

In the meantime, without recourse to revolution, Great Britain had gradually been setting her house in order.

E. Reform Instead of Revolution in Great Britain 

Great Britain Still a Land of Privilege

Great Britain had been, previous to the French Revolution, the most liberal country in Europe, and so the people of the Continent had recognized. Montesquieu and Voltaire had received much of their inspiration from visits to that land. It was the one country which possessed a vigorous lawmaking body, the British Parliament; and no one, not even a Catholic, was persecuted for his opinions. 

Except in a time of peril the press was free and the right of public meeting generally respected. 

No one could be arrested without warrant or imprisoned without trial. In all these respects Great Britain set an example to most of the Continent.

Yet at the beginning of the nineteenth century Great Britain was still in some respects a land of the Old Régime. Parliament

MORE REVOLUTIONS 

165 

AND SOME REFORM 

was anything but representative, for only five per cent of the adult men possessed the vote. 

While the so-called "rotten boroughs" still existed, some of the largest towns, like Manchester, had no representation at all. The landed aristocracy still controlled both houses of Parliament.

Naturally this aristocracy pursued a policy in its own interest. There was little sympathy for the workers or for the poor in general. Though a depression followed the 

Napoleonic Wars (due largely to the sudden falling off of a war market), with low wages and unemployment as natural results, the government treated discontent with nothing but severity. Moreover, a high tariff on wheat, dictated by the interest of the country gentlemen, so increased the price of bread that the masses could barely eke out an existence. 

The First Reforms 

Fortunately, among the Tories, who controlled Parliament at that time, there were a few liberal statesmen, the most important of whom was Sir Robert Peel. The son of a wealthy manufacturer, Peel was able by virtue of his wealth to enter politics. He was extremely shy and reserved, and O'Connell, one of his contemporaries, said that his smile was like the silver plate on a coffin. But he was a fairly broad-minded statesman, and his abilities made him the leader of his party. When the Irish, ably led by Daniel O'Connell, seemed on the verge of revolution because Catholics were still excluded from Parliament and public office, Peel persuaded Parliament against its will to pass the measure known as Catholic Emancipation. This measure, passed in 1829, had been preceded by a similar act, extending the same legal privilege to Dissenters.¹

For the short adjournments of Parliament his lordship said, that sufficient grounds had certainly existed, but that they now no longer existed in such force as to render it necessary for ministers to detail them to the House.

the need of factory reform, Peel achieved a notable service in his sensible attitude toward crime. In a day when little thought was expended on trying to remove the causes of theft and murder, the government tried to protect society by making the criminal fear the severity of the law. Sir Robert's sense of justice was offended by the thought that petty thieving was punishable by death, and in 1823 he got the repeal of the death penalty for more than a hundred minor offenses. For the protection of London he established in 1829 the 

Metropolitan Police Force. These policemen, armed with clubs instead of firearms, were typical of a country which hated military domination.

Parliamentary Reform 

But the greatest issue of the time was parliamentary reform. For some time the masses had been clamoring for the right to vote, and they were fortunate in having a leader, William Cobbett, whose paper, The Weekly 

Register, enlisted thousands for the cause. (See facsimile on page 165.) After a time the

Whigs, who were then the party of opposition to the government, came out definitely for parliamentary reform, and they won the general election of 1830. A reform bill was then introduced in the House of Commons. 

The chief obstacle, however, was the House of Lords, where the Tories remained entrenched. So great was the fear that the

Lords would reject the bill that riots broke out in the country, and many of these hidebound aristocrats began to fear revolution. After an exciting struggle the bill was finally passed in 1832 by both houses. It had been understood that if the Lords rejected the bill, the King would appoint enough new peers to insure its passage.

It is unnecessary to describe the First Reform Bill in any detail. It abolished the "rotten boroughs" and for the first time gave representation to a number of thriving towns. 

The main thing to remember is that the suffrage was so widened that the upper middle class got the right to vote. The future would determine whether the masses would receive the reward they deserved for their efforts. 

Some further reforms followed, such as the abolition of slavery in the colonies and some factory reforms, to be mentioned later. We might add that in the meantime a new monarch came to the throne in 1837, the youthful Queen Victoria. It was the beginning of a long and prosperous reign. (To understand the succession to the English throne, see pages 

168 and 169.)

The Establishment of Free Trade 

Since, however, the Whigs had seemingly lost their appetite for reform, the Tories under 

Sir Robert Peel recovered power in 1841. 

Peel, an excellent business man, devoted his attention chiefly to economic questions. The 

Tories during their earlier tenure of office had opened the British colonies to the ships of other countries, and Peel reduced the tariff on hundreds of articles of manufacture. It was now contended by leading manufacturers that British interest lay in importing wheat

MORE 

167 

REVOLUTIONS AND SOME REFORM 

and raw materials from abroad in exchange for British manufactured goods. In other words, Great Britain should adopt free trade. 

Hence there was a growing agitation for the repeal of the Corn Laws, which had established the duty on wheat (which in England is called "corn"). "In France," said one orator, "there are millions willing to clothe themselves in English garments, and you have millions of hungry mouths to take their corn." 

While the Tories remained deaf to all such arguments, the news arrived of a terrible famine in Ireland. The vast majority of a population of 8,000,000 depended normally on potatoes for their subsistence, but in 1845 the potato crop failed. There was not enough wheat at hand for these starving millions, and the tariff virtually excluded foreign wheat. 

Peel now rose to the emergency, and, in 1846, with the aid of the Whigs and some liberal Tories, he carried through Parliament the repeal of the Corn Laws. The Tories got their revenge by promptly forcing him out of office, but a momentous step had been taken in the direction of free trade. The Whigs continued the policy, and by 1860 only a few duties were still retained, and these were for revenue only. 

To all intents and purposes Great Britain had adopted free trade.

Great Britain as the Workshop of the World 

Great Britain reaped full advantage from this policy. Her cottons, woolens, hardware, pottery, and glass were sold in immense quantities throughout the world. It was only after 

Continental countries began to speed up their industrial development under the protection of high tariffs that the margin of British supremacy began to shrink. To the Germans in particular the British lost some of their markets both in Europe and in the world at large. 

Yet, even so, they continued to command the market for most goods of superior quality, and in the whole volume of their trade they kept the lead. Rightly was Great Britain spoken of as the "workshop of the world."

The vast extent of her commerce also promoted her shipping industry, which was greater than that of any other country. 

Moreover, thanks to the wealth amassed from industry and commerce, the British had the largest store of capital and the largest investments abroad. Loans could be made more readily in London than anywhere else. More than any other country, Great Britain was the world's banker.

For the original impetus that led to this prosperity we must go back to the free-trade movement and to the leading place which Great Britain had taken in the Industrial Revolution a subject we reserve for the next chapter.

In the meantime, let us look more closely at that class, which, as the nineteenth century advanced, had come to assume a leading position.

F. The Middle Class Begins to Set the Tone of Society

Growing Importance and General Character of the Upper Middle Class 

More and more in the society of western Europe a wealthy middle class assumed prominence. They were the ones to benefit from the First Reform Bill in England, the 

Revolution of 1830 in France, and to some extent from the later upheavals of 1848. But once they had forced their claims on the aristocracy, they too acquired a horror of revolution. Being as a rule men with capital and property, they did not want to risk sharing power with the lower classes. They felt that they had earned the right to guide the world of the future—a future in which capital would be king. In England they flaunted their wealth and tried to outshine the landed aristocracy, who in consequence lived more quietly in the background. In France the flaunting of wealth often took the form of reckless speculation, especially in the time of the 

Second Empire. 

Compared to the Old Régime, Europe had entered a bustling age. Thanks to the Industrial Revolution, which we shall discuss in the next chapter, methods of travel and communication were becoming gradually revolutionized. The railroad, while still expensive, encouraged people who could afford it to go about more, and the opening of telegraph lines enabled them to keep in close touch with the latest things that were happening a revo-

The old aristocracy, naturally conservative, were slow to adapt themselves to the new life, but the rising middle class felt that all this progress was their own particular doing, and they gloried in it. Unlike the older society, they thoroughly approved of work hard work but they wanted the world to recognize that work had given them money, and that money was the symbol of their success. 

This mushroom society was probably less dissipated than the society of the Old Régime, but it was also much less charming. Its members were smugly self-satisfied, very moral and very religious as far as outward forms went, anxious always to appear respectable on the surface, no matter what they were covering up. They were not as yet interested in the poor, or in fact in anything at all but making money and showing off. This does not mean that every member of the class was just like that, but so many of them had these traits that we can speak of them as characterizing the class. 

Manners and Diversions

In this matter-of-fact world of the middle class there was not much room for art. Machinery was turning out much that had been done formerly by hand, and the time when men and women would spend hours in embroidering a garment for a great lady or in carving an exquisite table for a grand man-

AND SOME REFORM MORE REVOLUTIONS 

sion was rapidly passing. Indeed, skilled labor, as we shall see in the next chapter, was dying. The interior of most houses was anything but artistic. Splotches of gaudy colors on the walls, heavy horsehair furniture, pictures of flowers or fish, and stuffed birds under glass, are a fair sample of the atrocities one now found in the home. The same lack of taste was displayed in women's clothes. the time of the coronation of Queen Victoria, vivid colors which fought one another were the height of fashion. A blue satin dress and a purple scarf were combined with a bright green hat trimmed with roses. It seemed that color was somehow expected to make up for lack of workmanship. At

Manners in this age were not exactly crude, for this newly rich class was very anxious to make a good appearance. But they were rather clumsy about it, and they were apt to overdo their attempts at elegance. Everything must accord with "good form." Just as the old aristocracy had its own code of manners, so this new capitalistic society had its peculiar foibles and taboos. To be seen anywhere without gloves or to carry a parcel across the street was almost enough to disgrace one for life. The world had seemingly lost its sense of humor along with its gay and artistic clothes. It was now rather stiff and dull and very self-conscious.

Yet in certain ways there was extraordinary display. A rich banker, like the Rothschilds, when he entertained at dinner, simply loaded his table with silver. Much of the society of this time did not seem to know that overdoing a good thing is sheer bad taste. Since the middle class usually pretended to be fond of learning, a rich manufacturer's wife would make a point of inviting distinguished scholars or musicians to her dinners, either because she posed as a patron of learning or because she wanted to add a sort of finishing touch to her parties. Sentimental and romantic things also appealed to the people of this age, as though they must have emotional excitement, if only in the realm of fancy. Most of the literature of this period was either sweetly sentimental or melodramatic; and so it remained, in fact, till near the close of the nineteenth century.

Society was not so gay as in the eighteenth century. Court life in France, though glamorous in the time of the Second Empire, was hardly what it had been under Louis XVI; and it was only in Vienna that the sparkle of the Old Régime still persisted. But the new society probably had broader interests. People went more frequently to the theater and to the opera than had formerly been the case; and the improvement in the printing-press led to an immense increase in reading matter.

Newspapers were still, as a rule, more concerned with politics than with news, but at least there were a great many of them. 

Toward the middle of the nineteenth century the lowering of postal rates led people into the habit of writing letters. In 1840, Great 

Britain had adopted a uniform postage, one penny or two cents for the whole of the British Isles; so no longer was a person charged for distance, and no longer did the recipient pay for his letter. So heavy had been the charge on letters formerly that often a person would send his family simply an empty envelope as an assurance that all was well. The one to whom it was sent then escaped any postal charge by refusing to receive it. Other nations followed Great Britain in adopting a cheap postage, and thus began also the popular pastime of stamp-collecting.

There was little change in the sporting world, but dueling had practically died out before the middle of the nineteenth century. 

After all, it was only in Germany and Austria that the old nobility, who had always enjoyed fighting for fighting's sake, still lingered. The

British aristocracy and the middle class as a whole preferred horse-racing, which to this day seems to have retained its popularity. 

Costume 

It was perhaps the influence of the French Revolution that made for greater simplicity in dress. The elaborate costuming so characteristic of eighteenth-century France, seemed to have lost its popularity with the passing of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, and even the insular Englishman somewhat altered his tastes. He did not immediately adopt the long trousers, which the French Revolution had standardized on the Continent, for habits

FIGURE 110. COSTUMES OF THE EARLY NINETEENTH CENTURY 

From left to right: Man and woman of the upper class; children of the upper class; servants; man, woman, and child of the lower class. 

The formality of the period is reflected in the clothes of all but the lower class. Children's clothes were designed without regard for comfort or for the demands that healthful play would make. Compare the costumes of the eighteenth century on page 85 and with those of the seventeenth century on page 75. In change slowly in England, but he wore inconspicuous knickerbockers, black silk stockings and pumps, and long-tailed, short-waisted coats. Then, as it happened, a pronouncement of the Prince of Wales sent knickerbockers forever into oblivion, save among bishops, and henceforth trousers were worn. 

With these were worn either the cutaway coat, designed like the modern dress coat or the long frock coat with skirt all-around. addition, stand-up collar, broad tie, and silk hat were necessary parts of a gentleman's costume. With most of the men of fashion the chief attention was given the vest or waistcoat, cut low enough, when knickerbockers were worn, to reveal the ruffled shirt underneath. The short jacket finally appeared about 1850, though only for workaday wear, and ties became narrow, as at present. 

Men of the earlier period were clean-shaven, but side whiskers came into fashion toward the middle of the nineteenth century, sometimes varied by a beard, a mustache, or both. More and more, London became the fashion center for men, as Paris was for women. 

While men's costume thus was becoming fairly standardized and quite uninteresting, women's costume passed through many changes, some of which we have not space to Silk describe. At first women went back to the natural waistline, sometimes made more definite by a belt, and their chief absurdity was the wearing of huge "leg-o'-mutton sleeves," though by the forties sleeves had become fairly tight again. The hair was drawn up tightly and often twisted high on the head, but later it was knotted at the back of the neck. was generally worn, and hats became larger and larger. About the middle of the nineteenth century, the wasp waist was cultivated, ladies suffering tortures while being laced up the back. Then in the fifties someone invented the crinoline, which was a steel device to make the skirt stand out, so that the contrast to the waist was achieved without such tight lacing, which had been positively injurious. Skirts with numerous flounces, sometimes of different colors, were so huge that sitting down, or even walking, became a rather difficult art. The hooped lady also usually wore a poke bonnet, tied with ribbons under the chin. About 1867, the crinoline disappeared and skirts took another shape as we shall mention later. The American woman, Mrs. Bloomer, who tried to introduce

Oriental trousers for Englishwomen, had scant success, though her name has long survived in the garment itself.

SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

1. The Vienna peace settlement is best understood if one recalls the principles which guided the work of the Congress. a. Compensation for the victorious powers. 

b. Restoration of legitimate (pre-Revolution) dynasties. 

c. Barriers against another revolutionary outbreak in France. 

2. The settlement of 1814-1815, however, soon began to crumble. a. Great Britain and France grew lukewarm in supporting Metternich's program for suppressing revolution. b. Revolutionary movements, brought on by the spirit of nationalism and the desire for democracy, broke out in Europe, especially in 1820, 1830, and 1848. c. Of the great powers only in Great Britain did reform result from peaceful action rather than revolution. 

3. The spirit of nationalism gained three outstanding victories in the nineteenth century: a. Italy, after unsuccessfully seeking unification through revolution, was successful under the leadership of Sardinia when Cavour enlisted the aid of France. b. Germany, after the failure of the liberal movement in 1848-1849, achieved unity through the diplomatic efforts of Bismarck and successful wars with Denmark, Austria, and France. c. Austria, ousted from Italy and Germany, at last recognized the need for satisfying the nationalist cravings of the Magyars, and granted equality to Hungary in 1867. 

4. During the first half of the nineteenth century the middle class steadily grew more powerful and, in consequence, more conservative.

DIVISION THREE The Coming of the Machine and New Social and Political Problems 

THE CIVILIZATION OF TODAY differs more from that of the age of Louis XIV, about two hundred and fifty years ago, than did this earlier period from the times of the great 

Pharaohs who ruled Egypt three thousand years before the birth of Christ.

The great changes that have taken place during the last two centuries are for the most part the result of the Industrial Revolution. 

Work came to be done by machine rather than by hand, power was applied to the machine, and the production of wealth was enormously increased. 

Although the machine created fabulous wealth, the workers themselves lived in poverty. To improve their lot they organized trade unions, agitated for the suffrage, and even moved to transform all society into one great body of wage-earners (socialism). Gradually the State assumed responsibility for safeguarding workers from abuses, and finally took the initiative in protecting them from want when their earning power was lost. 

Germany and Great Britain took the lead in establishing, partly with State support, insurance funds for accident, unemployment, and old-age security. Governments also have sought to help the peasantry by promoting ownership of land and providing loans at low rates of interest.

Although the condition of many classes, therefore, has changed for the better, none has made so great an advance as that of women. 

From a position of almost entire dependence, women have come to enjoy in many countries complete social, economic, and political equality with men.

During the nineteenth century the common people in most European countries came to enjoy a greater share in the responsibility of government. Great Britain took the lead in gradually extending the suffrage to all adult citizens complete equality in 1928 and in concentrating the power of government in the hands of representatives elected by the people — responsible government. In order to develop an intelligent electorate, systems of popular education were established or greatly expanded. Of course, democracy was not equally successful in all countries, nor indeed was it given a fair trial in some of them. 

The nineteenth century also witnessed an unparalleled succession of great discoveries in science. Man learned how to combat disease and to ease pain. Practical inventions made life more comfortable for the common man than it hitherto had been for kings.

Improved communication and transportation, together with the practical demands of an industrial civilization, greatly increased the dependence of nations upon one another. 

Although conditions seemed to indicate the need for co-operation and free trade, the trend was in the opposite direction. Most nations. wanted to become self-contained (not to be dependent on others for important raw materials and manufactures). In consequence tariff barriers were erected and a feverish scramble for colonies followed. 

Large territories in Asia and Africa were brought under the direct (colony) or indirect (sphere of interest) control of the powers. 

As might be expected, rivalry led to sharp clashes of interest. There was a succession of crises (disputes nearly provoking a conflict) and occasional wars. At length the nations who had great empires tended to unite in opposing the reckless imperialism of the latecomers in the colonial field. The outlook for world peace darkened!

CHAPTER VIII The Industrial Revolution: 

MEN MAKE MACHINES AND MACHINES MAKE A NEW WORLD What were the causes of the Industrial Revolution? 

What changes resulted from the Industrial Revolution?

How did the working class in Great Britain and on the Continent attempt to secure their rights?

What steps were taken by the British government to safeguard the rights of the workers?

THE INDUSTRIAL Revolution was hardly less important than the French Revolution in changing man's position in the world. While the former gave him rights as an individual, the Industrial Revolution changed his material position. That is, it changed profoundly the conditions under which he lived and made his living. It led naturally, as we shall see, to a great increase in the wealth, power, and influence of the middle class, who were its chief beneficiaries. It also created an immense laboring class or proletariat, whose efforts to secure a fair share of the wealth which their hands produced have given us one of the greatest problems that face the world today. Just as the French Revolution was the contribution of France, so the Industrial Revolution was one of the greatest of Great Britain's contributions to the advance of civilization. Most of the everyday comforts we enjoy today may be traced to the Industrial Revolution.

A Meaning and Causes of the Industrial Revolution Meaning of the Industrial Revolution 

By the Industrial Revolution we mean the gradual displacement of hand labor by powerdriven machinery. What had formerly been done laboriously by hand came to be done by a machine, operated by hand, it is true, but requiring no skill on the part of the workers, since the machine itself furnished the skill. 

Moreover, it turned out many times as much stuff as had formerly been the case, and in a comparatively short time. 

Let us turn back a moment to the days of the domestic system. Before the Industrial

Revolution the fibers of wool from the back of a sheep, or of cotton from the boll of the cotton plant, were combed or carded (that is, cleansed and straightened by the use of cards) and spun into thread, which was then woven to make woolen or cotton cloth. Hand instruments alone were then in use, except for the spinning wheel which was operated by the foot. In the case of textile workers, spinning and weaving were a family affair, the man doing the weaving, his wife and children the combing, the carding, and the spinning. In countries where guilds persisted, the shoemaker, with his journeymen and apprentices, worked with hand tools in a little shop, which usually provided sleeping quarters as well.

The invention of machinery to supplant these crude processes brought about what is This known as the Industrial Revolution. 

machinery was first driven by water wheels (such as the one pictured on page 177); later by steam. All this combing and carding, drawing and twisting, came to be done by weaving and spinning machines. So, also, the shoemaker's tools were displaced by machinery which did the plying, sewing, and stitching necessary to make the shoe. Instead of working in their homes or little shops, as the case might be, all these workers were now assembled in general workshops known as

Some people have said that the development of machinery to do these things was so gradual that we should not speak of an industrial revolution, but, rather, an evolution, which is a gradual process of change. think of a revolution as very sudden, whereas we know that, from the time when machinery began to replace hand labor, nearly a century passed before its use became general even in England; for many inventions and improvements had been necessary to achieve this end. 

But if, on the other hand, we think of the tremendous changes produced by the general use of machinery, the movement seems so startling that no other word but revolution really fits. There had not been much difference in the way people lived between the medieval period and the middle of the eighteenth century.

But the world which men Bettmann knew in 1850, the world which the machine had produced, was very different from the world which men had known in 1750. 

In 1750, British towns were sprawling collections of cottages, each with its own gardens, near to or surrounding a market place, where local wares were displayed. To a very large extent, the masses of people supplied their own needs. needs. An English observer, accustomed to 

London, wrote in 1797 that in the north of England peasants and laborers made every article of dress that they wore with the exception of shoes and hats; and that most of the things turned out by skilled workers for sale were made for the local market. There was no better mode of travel than the clumsy stagecoach, and no means of transportation other than pack horses or oxcarts on land and sailing vessels on sea. It took some weeks for a message from London to reach a person at the northern tip of Scotland.

By 1850, many British towns had become so crowded that cottages were often built in

long rows, back to back; the gardens had disappeared; and the market place was gone. 

To the dirt which Mother Earth spread over the place were added the soot and grime from factory chimneys. Most people in 1850 bought machine-made goods from the nearest store, and such goods were also shipped in large quantities to distant markets. Railroads and steamboats carried travelers and freight; and even the electric telegraph was beginning to provide a means of communication with distant places. Such is a glimpse of the change which a century had wrought. 

Hence we may still use the term Industrial Revolution, not unmindful of the fact that it was gradual, but appreciating its far-reaching significance.

Why the Revolution Began in England and What 

Caused It

The Industrial Revolution began in England for various reasons. In the first place, Englishmen had made more money from trade than any other people, and they wanted to put their money to profitable use. When there was a chance to gather workmen into factories for the making of cotton or woolen goods, there was need of ready capital to furnish the equipment and to buy the raw materials. Isolated spinners or weavers lacked the wherewithal to buy the raw wool or the raw cotton as the case might be. But in England there were rich men, able to erect factories, provide the necessary machinery, and purchase the raw materials.

In the second place, England was abundantly supplied with streams to furnish the water power needed for running the mills; and later, when steam came to furnish the motive force, there was in England plenty of coal to make this newer form of power. 

In the third place, England laid more relative stress than the Continent on the making of textiles, such as cotton and woolen goods.

France, while she also produced textiles, was more famous for the making of luxury goods, such as watches, carriages, and furniture, which required exceptional skill and could be made much better by hand than by machinery.

It happened also that science took a more practical turn in England than on the Continent, and that in England there was a more pressing demand for invention. Since the coal mines had been dug so deep that there was water in their lower depths, it was necessary to devise some means of pumping it out. 

Since iron ore could not be used till rid of certain impurities, and since the usual method of smelting by use of charcoal was causing the rapid destruction of the forests, it was obviously necessary to devise a different process.

And since the influence of the wool merchants had prevented the importation of the cotton goods made in India, though cotton had become so fashionable for dress that people continued to demand it, it was necessary for someone to provide the means of turning out cotton goods in greater quantity. All this stimulated invention. You have probably heard the saying that "necessity is the mother of invention."

Then, too, the world itself was ready for the Industrial Revolution. Imperialism had opened new markets across the sea, where people wanted to buy what Europe produced. 

Countries outside of Europe, such as Egypt, India, or America, could supply more raw materials than were available in Europe. 

And, as we have already said, men with capital were looking about for new fields for investment. There was not enough profit in making things by hand. And finally, science had revived in the eighteenth century, and people were beginning to study it as a means of discovering better ways of doing many things.

B. Progress of the Industrial 

Revolution 

The Revolution in Production 

The first machine of which we hear in England was the stocking frame, invented as early as 1598 by an Englishman, William Lee. (A picture of this machine appears above.)

The use of this of this machine made knitting by hand unnecessary, and it is perhaps not strange that the knitters made life so miserable for the inventor that he had to leave the country. But the industry persisted, and stockings came to be made pretty generally by machinery, though the knitters probably got much less for running the stocking frame than they had formerly been able to earn by their skillful hands.

But invention did not make for change in any other industry till some time later. The greatest need was for a way to speed up spinning. After the invention of the flying shuttle (1733), which quickened the process of weaving, it took from five to ten spinners to keep the pace of one weaver. Then came a series of experiments with spinning machines, which not only increased production but improved its quality. Hargreave's spinning machine produced thread that was fine but not strong; Arkwright's "water frame" produced thread that was strong but not fine; but finally 

Compton's "mule," so-called because it combined features of the other two machines, produced thread that was both fine and strong. Similarly in weaving, the hand loom was in time displaced by the power loom, first run by water and later by steam. It should be added that the cotton industry was greatly aided by Whitney's cotton gin, the work of an American inventor, which extracted the seeds from the cotton, and made it possible for a man to accomplish in a single day as much as he had been able to do by hand in a whole year.

By 1790, both woolen and cotton goods were being made by machinery, and it was only a question of time, and not a very long time, when its use would become general. 

The use of steam as a motive power for propelling machinery was one of the greatest of all the factors that revolutionized industry. 

The first machines had made use of water power, and mills had therefore to be built near streams. (You have probably seen pictures of the great mill wheels which kept the machinery going within the mill.) fortunately water had its limitations. sometimes frozen in winter, too plentiful in the spring, and too low in the summer. The Un- 

It was greater advantage of steam lay in the fact that it was artificially created; it could be had in just the amount one wanted. 

The first steam engines seem to have been used to pump water out of flooded coal mines. 

The perfecting of a steam engine that might be used to run machinery was the work of 

James Watt, a Scottish maker of musical and mathematical instruments. (His picture on page 181 will prove interesting to compare with that of military leaders or statesmen.)

One of his contemporaries called him "an extraordinary and in many respects a wonderful man. Perhaps no individual in his age," he added, "possessed so much and such varied and exact information, had read so much, or remembered what he had read so accurately and well."

Watt examined the existing steam engines, and also made a study of what scientists had learned of the functions of steam. Though he was handicapped in his experiments by lack of money, he finally interested a wealthy manufacturer who financed his undertakings, and about 1770 he produced his first steam engine.

Later, as this engine was improved, it was used to run the machinery in factories. 

One thing which had aided Watt was the fact that iron had come to be of a better grade for making machines. The process of smelting iron ore by coal gave the iron industry a great chance of revival, for wood, as we have seen, had become scarce. By heating and stirring the iron when very hot, the process known as "puddling," most of the impurities could be removed. Cheaper and better iron could thus be made, and it was iron that was used to make machines. If we remember that coal was necessary for making steam, and that iron was indispensable for making machinery, we shall realize that coal and iron were the backbone of modern industry. Later on, about the middle of the nineteenth century, steel, a product of iron, came to be used on a large scale.

The Revolution in Transportation 

The enormous increase in production, thanks to machinery, necessitated better methods of transportation. The old method of hauling by oxen or pack horses was now too

FIGURE 114. JAMES WATT EXPERIMENTING IN THE LABORATORY WITH HIS STEAM ENGINE 

In a modern laboratory what apparatus would replace the stove? 

Notice the chair which obviously was designed for a living room. slow and totally inadequate. 

Wherever it was possible merchants shipped their goods by water, and in England there was considerable digging of canals during the late eighteenth and the early nineteenth centuries. 

Shipment by canal was better adapted for hauling large quantities of goods and hence considerably lowered their price. Yet, as production increased rapidly, canals alone proved insufficient. The three ship canals between Manchester and Liverpool were so congested by traffic that it sometimes took a month for cotton goods, intended for the American market, to reach the sea. It actually took less time to transport goods across the Atlantic than to cover the thirty miles between these two English cities. The use of steam, however, solved the problem of quick hauling, whether by land or by sea.

It was the railroad and steamboat that completely revolutionized transportation as well as travel. For some time carts had been drawn on rails (made first of wood and later of iron) from the mines to the nearest canal or Bettmann seaport town. Between 1800 and 1820 horse tramways came to be operated between a number of towns. On one of these connecting roads, seven miles long, running from Stockton on the east coast to Darlington in the coal region, George Stephenson, an engineer, got permission to use a locomotive, that is, an engine that could move itself, dragging a train of cars. This engine (a picture of which you can see on page 182) actually reached a speed of twenty-nine miles an hour. In fact, the experiment proved so successful that in 

1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railroad was opened for service. Three locomotives competed for a prize of £500, but whereas two of these broke down, Stephenson's locomotive, the "Rocket," made the trip successfully, and insured the success of the railroad as a means of transportation.

The average speed of trains was then eighteen miles an hour, and the passenger's fare ten cents a mile; but the former was soon increased and the latter decreased. By the middle of the century, cheap excursion tickets

were often issued, and it was possible to travel two hundred miles to London and back for only five shillings ($1.25). It is interesting also to observe that at first any company might use a railway line to carry freight or passengers, but after a while Parliament forced a single company to shoulder the responsibility. It is also worth noting that private steam coaches appeared on the highways, a quaint forerunner of the automobile. 

No great difficulty had been found in raising capital for railway construction, but there were often annoying obstacles to be overcome. 

Landowners sometimes charged an extravagant price for the privilege of crossing their estates. A certain peer insisted that the Liverpool and Manchester Railroad should use no engine that he considered either too noisy or too smoky. The headmaster of Eton, a school for boys, withdrew his opposition to the Great Western Railway on condition that the company maintain a special staff to see that his boys did not board any of the trains during term time. Canal companies also threatened to parallel railway lines and sometimes wrung large sums from the railway companies by way of compensation; and turnpike companies often imposed tolls when a railway crossed a highway. Yet men of wealth considered that railroad-building was a good investment, and construction steadily increased. 

Meanwhile travel and transportation by sea were similarly changed. The great clipper ships (like the one shown below), with their majestic spread of sail, were soon to be replaced. An American, Robert Fulton, made use of one of Watt's engines in his boat which steamed up the Hudson River from 

New York to Albany in thirty-two hours.

Soon afterward ferry service was opened from Holyhead to Ireland and from Dover to 

Calais. The first steam vessel to cross the

Atlantic was the Savannah, in 1819, but her fuel gave out before she reached her destination, so she had to depend upon sails for part of the way. The trip was made all the way by steam in 1838. (These ships looked much like the second sketch below.) Soon after this, the Cunard Line opened a regular service from Great Britain to the United States, the first Cunarder doing the trip in fourteen days. Since the trans-Atlantic service did not yet pay for itself, the British government subsidized it by paying generous sums for handling its mails.

The increase in business also led to better methods of communication. In 1840 Great 

Britain took over the postal system, heretofore

This cheapening of postal rates not only increased business, but in a sense brought the people much closer together. In the forties, the electric telegraph, largely the invention of an American named Morse, came into use, and business could be conducted even more quickly. In 1851, Calais and Dover were connected by a submarine cable, and in 1866, after several attempts, a trans-Atlantic cable was finally laid. Thus we see that from the beginning of the Industrial Revolution invention has gone on continuously - and it is still going on today. 

The Industrial Revolution on the Continent 

The Industrial Revolution did not make much progress on the Continent until well into the nineteenth century. In France it made little headway before the time of the

July Monarchy, but then machinery was introduced in the silk mills and to some extent in the textile mills as well. Railroad construction was meanwhile undertaken, largely financed by the government. Industrial development in Germany was retarded by political disunity, but progress was very rapid after 1850. In Belgium, which had large mineral resources, industrial progress was more rapid than in any other Continental country. The Industrial Revolution was comparatively late in reaching the other countries of Europe. 

And now let us consider some of the most important features of the transformation produced by the Industrial Revolution. 

c. Results of the Industrial 

Revolution 

Increase in Production and Wealth 

In the first place, the volume of goods turned out by the Industrial Revolution was many times as great as had been the case when people worked by hand. British exports increased nearly five times in value from 1782 to 1815. We learn that cotton goods alone almost trebled in value during the period from 1830 to 1870. In Great Britain, in 1830, there were forty-nine miles of railroad; in 1870 the mileage had risen to 15,300.

Machinery for making paper immensely in-

INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION THE 

creased the production of that commodity, and the steam-driven printing-machine increased more than fourfold the output of the earlier hand presses. Naturally, as machinery developed and improved, production correspondingly increased.

The immense increase in output led naturally to the practice of trying to get the public to buy more goods, and advertising became the common means of seeking this end. The market became less local and more national and international. Efforts were even made to civilize backward countries, partly with a view of creating millions of new customers for Europe's goods, and the revival of imperialism during the last quarter of the century, a subject we shall study later, was largely the result of the Industrial Revolution. While on the one hand the world was brought closer together through the spread of industrial products and better methods of communication, on the other hand the rivalry between the great powers became all the keener, and the factors leading to war were less susceptible to control than in the day when a single monarch decided for peace or war. Nor was prosperity as continuous as you might think. 

The machine turned out goods with such rapidity that sometimes the supply exceeded the demand; and then a depression occurred (closing factories and turning thousands out of employment) till consumption was able to catch up with the machine. Moreover, it is equally true that quality was often sacrificed to quantity. The beauty of the thing made by hand was too soon forgotten. 

And yet, unquestionably, the world has benefited in the main. In the long run goods 

In the long run goods by becoming more plentiful also became cheaper, and thus many things which had formerly been luxuries for the few became the commonplace possessions of the many. In this way life was enriched by the Industrial 

Revolution. Conveniences and comforts be came more generally enjoyed.

Naturally there was a tremendous increase of wealth. The world was able to get more value out of the land through improved methods of farming; more value out of minerals from the uses which they had in industry; more value out of industry and commerce since so many things of practical use could be made. Obviously the class to gain most was the middle class the manufacturers, merchants, and financiers, who respectively produced, distributed, and financed the fruits of this great movement.

The General Adoption of the Factory System 

In the second place, the factory system was adopted as the best means of organizing production. The new machines were as a rule much too large to be housed in a cottage worker's home; and many more hands were needed to run them than a single worker's family could provide. Moreover, much more work could be got from the workers themselves when they were assembled in one place under the ever-watchful eye of a factory foreman.

The manufacturer sought the greatest profit that could be obtained by machine production, and it was cheaper and more effective to bring the workers to the machine than to bring the machine to the workers. Thus the factory system gradually superseded the domestic system with its scattered cottage workers. 

The Flight of Population to the Towns 

In the third place, there was much shifting of population as the result of the Industrial Revolution. More and more people left the country and came to the towns, where factories had been built. Thus the towns doubled in population in a decade; and ever since the 

Industrial Revolution the urban population has grown more rapidly than the rural. This is another way of saying that industry was gaining at the expense of agriculture. Before the Industrial Revolution the great mass of the population drew their living from the soil; after the Industrial Revolution an increasingly large population obtained their living by making things or selling them. 

Widening of the Distance Between Capital and 

Labor

In the fourth place, the distance widened between the employing class and the working class.

Under the guild the journeyman had small chance to, rise from the position of a wage-earner to that of master artisan; yet he worked at the side of his employer, both of

FIGURE 117. MANUFACTURING WHEELS FOR RAILROAD CARS IN 1862 

Have you seen iron or steel being worked in a modern mill? How has equipment changed? Are conditions in such mills greatly improved? them doing the same kind of work. Thus there was close, personal contact between the two. Under the domestic or putting-out system, the employer, to be sure, did not work with his employees, but he did see them occasionally when he brought them their raw materials or returned for the finished product. 

Under the factory system, on the other hand, the owner of the factory scarcely ever saw his men. He was represented as a rule by a salaried overseer or foreman. Besides, the capital which ran the factory was in large part contributed by persons who had never seen the factory but had simply invested money in the expectation of profits. The division was thus much sharper between capital and labor. 

While both owners and workers were serving the same interest, they lacked all personal contact and understanding. And since labor was cheap, there was every temptation for the capitalist to exploit it. Too large a share of the profits of an undertaking went into the pockets of the owners.

The Character of the New Labor 

In the fifth place, the character of labor itself changed. Skilled labor was, of course, Bettmann no longer necessary. It was sufficient in most cases for a workman to turn a crank, or pull a lever, or push a button. There was, in other words, a sharp division of labor, some being employed for one process while others were busy with another. And for those who had been skilled workers this task of doing the selfsame thing for twelve or more hours a day was monotonous and deadening. No longer did a workman make the whole shoe, employing his personal skill, and watching it grow to completion in his hands; now he performed only a single process in the making of the shoe. 

The new workers were spoken of as "hands" so many "hands" required by a factory.

The brains were now provided by the machine.

The Degradation of the Working Class 

In the sixth place, the working class were certainly for a time in a worse condition than they had ever been in before. It is true that under the domestic system men, women, and children had labored at long hours for a pitifully small wage. It is true also that the cottages in which they had lived were dark and unsanitary. But they had not spun or

Most of them had spent some of their time in farming or gardening, and sometimes they had had a holiday while they waited for more material to be brought them by the merchant. Under the factory system they were forced to work long hours, day after day, at poor pay, and, in addition, were subjected to the continuous, grinding discipline of the factory. Every failure to keep the pace had to be paid for by a fine. There was an unrelenting pressure that never ceased. (Some idea of factory life in the middle nineteenth century can be obtained from the pictures on pages 185 and 186.) 

Moreover, the factories themselves were at first poorly ventilated, and workers were allowed little protection from injury while tending the machine. Besides, the hovels in which the workers lived were disease-breeding dens. Constructed back to back, with hardly any yard, and without any provision for getting rid of refuse, these cottages were foul beyond description. Small wonder, indeed, that windows were seldom opened, for the odor from the streets was quite impossible to stand. A foreign traveler, describing conditions in Manchester, wrote in part: one.

In Many of the workers even lived in cellars, where they got almost no air or light. Under such conditions it is hardly strange that they spent their brief moments of leisure in drinking, and the moral degradation of the workers was certainly greater after the coming of the factory. Slums were not unknown before the 

Industrial Revolution, but the crowding of thousands of workers into factory towns made them a common eyesore.

An inevitable result of all this squalor and degradation was a very high death rate.

A characteristic of the factory system was the employment of women and children. 

Both had been employed under the domestic system, but not in preference to men. Since, however, the running of machinery required no skill whatever, and since the labor of women and children was, in general, to be had more cheaply than that of men, they were often employed while men remained in idleness often actually supported by their wives and children. In the early cotton mills three fourths of the workers employed were women and children. (They were employed under conditions that the accompanying picture can only faintly suggest.)

But quite the most heart-rending feature of the factory system was the forced labor of

children. Those at first employed were paupers' children, taken from the public workhouse and bonded over to an employer, who was only required to give them the necessities of life. Such a system was welcomed in many localities which hoped thereby to escape supporting their children in the workhouse; and the system was important to manufacturers whose mills were located near streams in outof-the-way places where labor was scarce. 

Thus London might send several thousand children to mill-owners in the north of England.

The suffering of these factory children is almost unbelievable. They were forced to work from twelve to fifteen hours, some during the day, some at night; and on Sundays they were employed from six till noon cleaning the machinery. Very often they had to eat their meager meals while still at work; they had no place to sit down, however exhausted they might become; and some of them are known to have walked as much as twenty miles a day in the course of their work. They sometimes 

They sometimes became so tired that the only means of keeping them at work was to beat them. Besides excessive work, the children's health was endangered by working in a temperature of approximately eighty degrees without any ventilation; and they were always in danger of falling, half asleep, into the machinery. As to their few hours of leisure, some more charitable mill-owners attempted to give them the rudiments of an education, or compelled them to go to church on Sunday! In most cases they were simply left to themselves, and grew up if they ever grew up! - hardened criminals. These children having no homes to go to, were huddled together in dormitories, those on the night shift getting into the beds which those on the day shift had just left. 

There was not a soul who took the slightest interest in these waifs. 

After a while, when factories were erected in towns, the employment of bonded children became less common. But the evil of child labor still persisted. 

Weavers whose wages had sunk so low that they could no longer make a living had to send their children to the factories to help support the family. Some of

Miners had to hew the coal with hammer and chisel, even as late as 1871. these tiny workers were but four and five years old. William Pitt had seriously proposed that the working age should begin at five. 

Conditions in the factories were bad enough, but in the mines, they were, if anything, worse (as the picture suggests). Children, crawling on their hands and knees, dragged carts, to which they were chained, to the mouth of the coal mine. Some children, generally from five to eight years of age, were employed to open and shut the door that brought air into the mines; and that sometimes meant spending all of twelve hours in the dark. Such children saw the sunshine only on Sunday.

Probably the most terrible thing that a child of that time had to do was to clean chimneys; for a child, so employed, suffered terribly from burns or suffocation, and many of them lost their lives. Practically all became stunted in growth, crippled, or blear-eyed from soot. 

The employment of women and children in the factories and mines often meant that the men had no employment whatever. That was one reason why the weavers were so loath to give up their trade, for as long as they could hold out, all the members of the family could 

How is coal mined today? remain at home. Naturally the cottage workers dreaded to see their wives and children drawn into the factories, and it was only with the greatest reluctance that the workers of the eighteenth century left the country for the dirty, crowded towns. The losing struggle of the weavers against factory competition is one of the most pathetic episodes in history. 

It was no wonder that they sometimes attacked the factory and destroyed machinery. 

When the weaver was finally forced to work in the factory, it meant a wage of possibly five dollars a week, and his pay was cut a quarter if he were as much as five minutes late; if he were injured, it stopped at once. And then there was the danger of being thrown out of employment as the result of a business depression, a circumstance that would usually drive the worker and his family into the poorhouse. 

These facts sufficiently show how grave was the condition of the working class when confronted with the pitiless machine. And since human nature is pretty selfish at bottom, one may judge that the manufacturer would buy labor as cheaply as he could get it and squeeze out of it all he could. Governments might do

something we shall see that they did do something- out of a spirit of human kindness at last aroused; but the general principle of the age was laissez-faire (let business alone), and, as it was the well-to-do classes that controlled the government, there was not much chance that the workers' side would be heard. 

It looked as if they must fight their own battle.

D. The New Working Class and Its 

Uphill Struggle

The new working class, the class which the factories created, faced a long, uphill struggle. 

At the beginning of the nineteenth century they could get neither relief by legislation nor justice from their employers by such weapons as the strike. They did not even have the support of public opinion; for people as a whole were not yet interested in how the workman lived.

But the working class gradually awakened to the need for united effort. 

THE WORKING-CLASS MOVEMENT IN ENGLAND 

combinations of workmen were forbidden by the Constituent Assembly in 1791. 

It was also the way men thought at the time in England, and when, besides, there was fear of revolution in that country (for food was high, and there had been some journeymen's strikes), the British Parliament passed the 

Combination Laws (1799-1800), absolutely prohibiting all combinations of workmen. 

In Great Britain these ideas continued to hold their ground in the nineteenth century, and though hostility to unions did relax, as we shall see, it was a long time before the State took account of the plight of the workers. 

Many, in fact, believed that their condition could never be better. A clergyman scholar,

Malthus, wrote that the growth of population was normally more rapid than the increase in the food supply, and that consequently the masses, continuing to multiply, would never be better off. Some, indeed, believed that hard labor was good for the workman and probably intended by Providence. Manufacturers, forced to defend their exploitation of children, pointed to the fact that long hours at least kept them out of idleness and mischief.

To the manufacturers, of course, it was a matter of self-interest to keep the workmen The Spirit of the Times Opposed the Interests of the down at low wages and to prevent any State 

Working Class 

Unfortunately for the workers, the very spirit of freedom which in the eighteenth century did so much to undo autocracy and mercantilism deprived this needy class of any protection from the State, and even of its natural means of self-defense, that of combining in its own interests. The idea of laissez-faire meant that every business man should be free to use his every opportunity. 

The State must not interfere except to protect his property; it was not to say how much he was to pay his workmen or how long he was to keep them at work, or look into anything else that was strictly his private affair. idea of laissez-faire also meant that workers must not even combine to push their interests, for that would clearly place a restraint on the freedom of the man of business.

The This was the way the men thought who made the French Revolution, and that is why interference with working conditions. The period from the Napoleonic Wars to the late forties was a period of hard times in Great Britain, and they argued that this in itself was sufficient reason to keep wages low. The very fact that the upper middle class, such as the great manufacturers, got the chance to enter 

Parliament by the Great Reform Bill (1832) 

meant that business more than ever dominated politics. Yet the following year saw the first important factory reform, so there must have been some good influence at work. 

Already the workers themselves had begun to stir. Let us now look at things from their viewpoint.

The Rise of Trade-Unionism 

Trade-unionism is the movement whereby workers in a given trade form a union and by that means try to force their employers to grant them better conditions. It is clear that

one man cannot hope to bargain for himself; but if a group of men-say, all the railway hands act together, they can sometimes sell their labor at a fair price. If they refuse to work unless their terms are met this, of course, is a strike the manufacturer is threatened with having to close the doors of his factory and his profits for the moment Naturally much depends on the strength of the union, for its members have to live during a strike, and hence it must have some funds with which to tide them over the crisis. cease.

The idea of workmen combining to force employers to meet their demands did not originate with the Industrial Revolution. 

We read of certain wool-combers forcing their employer to grant them a minimum wage; and at various times journeymen banded to- -gether to pull off a strike in order to get more favorable conditions. But before the Industrial Revolution there were no continuous unions. Such as there were usually collapsed quickly after they had gained or lost whatever objective they had been organized to secure.

The domestic system was not likely to produce trade-unionism. Workers scattered in their cottages, had no chance to compare notes and to combine in their own interest. Trade-unionism would probably have amounted to little, had it been left simply to isolated journeymen and cottage workers.

But the factory system brought the workers together, and they could then more easily talk over their sorrows as well as realize the strength that lay in numbers. Some rioting here and there induced Parliament to pass the Combination Laws, mentioned above. But some unions of workers were formed in spite of the law, and in 1824 the Combination Laws were repealed. Unfortunately an epidemic of strikes followed, and Parliament, thoroughly frightened, made strikes an act of conspiracy and allowed the unions little more than the right to discuss their interests. 

Nevertheless trade-unionism grew to such an extent that a national federation of unions was formed in 1834, in which it is said that half a million workers were enrolled. But the movement did not prosper, partly because employers threatened with dismissal any of their men who should join a union. And by this time the workers had come to believe that their main hope lay in trying to obtain the ballot. Thus the movement shifted somewhat from the economic to the political field of action.

The Chartist Movement 

To trace the workers' part in a political movement to advance their interests we must go back a little. You will remember the acute distress which followed the Napoleonic Wars, and the government's violent suppression of discontent. You will remember, too, the success of Cobbett in rousing public opinion to such a pitch that the First Reform Bill the bill of 1832 — was finally enacted. this bill was, of course, a disappointment to the workers. They had merely helped their "enemies," the wealthy middle class, to enter Parliament. But

Yet as strikes were not allowed, and since the British workman was not disposed to violence, the movement to create a democratic Parliament was revived. This movement was known as "chartism" from the fact that a workers' charter was drawn up and presented to Parliament. Though there were many things demanded in this petition, the most important of all was universal suffrage, by which was meant the right of all adult men to vote. They hoped, after Cobbett's example, to work up a public opinion that would force Parliament to yield to their demands. But the movement seemed to lack any strong leader, and the working class became much less dissatisfied after the repeal of the Corn Laws had lowered the price of bread, while the adoption of free trade, which opened more markets to British manufactures, led to a general increase of wages. Moreover, the 

Whigs were no longer afraid of revolution and wanted no further extension of the suffrage.

It is interesting to notice that the weapons used in the British working-class movement were comparatively peaceful and lawful: trade-unionism and political agitation. It was otherwise with the movement on the 

Continent.

THE WORKING-CLASS MOVEMENT ON THE CONTINENT Rise of Socialism 

There was hardly what you might call a working-class movement on the Continent until the Industrial Revolution made its appearance; and it was long after that that trade-unionism made any headway. Unlike the situation in England, the working-class movement on the Continent was concerned with ideas of social revolution. The French as a people are much more given to theorizing than the English, and it was in France in particular that the movement became identified with socialism.

Socialism is usually interpreted to mean that all the sources of wealth, be it land, labor, or capital, should be in the hands of the State, which must be ruled and operated by the workers themselves. This would mean that everyone, whether a grocer, a doctor, or a farmer, or whatever his business might be, would be paid by the State for his services. 

Everyone would then become a wage-earner.. Bettmann

The first socialists had not worked things out so simply. They advocated co-operative communities, groups of people that worked together and shared the products of their labor; but none of these model communities met with success. One of these earlier "socialists" was Robert Owen, a British mill-owner, who had already attracted attention by his "model factories" and the founding of cooperative stores which were run on a nonprofit basis and supplied the workers' needs. 

Most of these pioneers, however, were Frenchmen. But the working class on the Continent were not yet fully awakened, and did not put their power behind the movement. 

France Rejects Socialism 

It was during the time of the July Monarchy that the workers were stirred into action. 

Those who had done the really effective work in the Revolution of 1830 felt cheated when the upper middle class reaped all the benefits. 

And as the Industrial Revolution was now coming in, with the establishment of factories here and there and the usual unhappy con-
