What is the purpose of this card? Are associations of workers international in their scope today? Can you describe a union card? ditions for the workers, there was a growing discontent, evidenced sometimes by strikes. 

A prominent socialist, Louis Blanc, championed the cause of the working class and preached the right to work, by which he meant the right to expect employment by the State. 

Blanc's chief idea was that the State should establish workshops, run by the workers themselves, which he believed in course of time would drive all private producers out of existence. Blanc did not urge that the workers should seize power; he wanted a democratic state, but in so far as he wanted a socialistic order, he might be looked upon as an advocate of revolution.

The Revolution of 1848 seemed to give the workers at last their opportunity. They were strong enough to force their will for a time on the Second Republic, and Blanc became a member of its government. He was given permission to open workshops, and a labor commission was established to propose measures of social reform.

But most of the members of the government, not being socialists but, rather, believers in laissez-faire, hampered Blanc at every turn, so that his workshops consisted mainly of thousands of men engaged in digging up the streets. There was no idea of letting the workmen operate industries. Moreover, when the elections were held for the National Assembly which was to shape the new régime, the socialists were overwhelmingly defeated.

France, as a whole, did not want a socialist republic. Soon after the elections Blanc's two creations, the workshops and the labor commission, were quickly suppressed. Driven to desperation, the workers showed fight, but their rioting was put down in the bloody "June days." There was no immediate hope of better conditions through revolution.

Yet this was the time when the working class was to find its greatest leader, Karl Marx. 

Who Marx was

KARL MARX 

Karl Marx was a German Jew, whose parents had accepted Christianity. He studied at two German universities, and then, being debarred from a professorship because of his

THE 



INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION 

liberal views, he joined the staff of a newspaper. He was a hard-working student, a deep thinker, and at the same time a born agitator. Obstinate and sometimes overbearing, naturally kind but often irritable (perhaps because of his hardships), he was absolutely unflinching in his devotion to the task which he set before him. And his task was to show the working class the way to fulfill its hopes. Marx was the man who made socialism seem possible of attainment. 

Marx at Work 

In 1843, Marx went to Paris where he became acquainted with the French socialists. 

Expelled later at the request of the Prussian government, he went to Brussels. There, with his close friend, Friedrich Engels, he founded the Communist League, which aimed to destroy the existing order of things, so oppressive to the workers. In 1848, he and 

Engels produced a famous book, the Communist 

Manifesto, in which they bitterly denounced existing conditions and called on the workers to unite in their own cause. "The proletarians," so the Manifesto declared, "have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to gain. Proletarians of all lands, unite!" 

During the same year, 1848, Marx went to Germany to help the revolutionary cause, and when revolution failed, he seemed to become convinced that it would be long before the workers would come into their own. 

Most of his exile he spent in England, where he studied each day from early in the morning till late at night, and usually under conditions so discouraging that one wonders how he managed to keep going. Often Marx was so desperately poor that his family had hardly enough to eat; not infrequently he was turned out of his house for inability to pay the rent; and the death of three of his children was largely due to the hardships and the privations his family went through. Yet he doggedly plodded on with his studying and writing, and he came to be looked upon as the leader of the working class in all countries. 

Marx's Influence 

Marx persuaded the workers that socialism was the cure for the unfortunate conditions 

FIGURE 123. KARL MARX (1818-1883) 

Marx is often called "the father of modern socialism." He was greatly impressed with the theory of the German philosopher Hegel that history is a struggle between opposing forces which leads to constant change. which surrounded them. We shall not try to understand his theories, many of which were unsound. The important thing about Marx, as had been true about Rousseau, was the spirit of his teachings. He stressed the class war, the struggle between the exploiters and the exploited, which he traced through all history. The workers, he felt, must wage a constant struggle, and eventually they would win. Sometimes he seemed to approve revolution, but often he gave the impression that the workers must be patient and that any legal means of aiding their cause, such as reform legislation, was worth their while. 

But whatever the means, he was sure that they would reach their goal in time, and thus he gave the working class a new faith and a new hope.

More than this, Marx made the cause of the workers a world movement. From the beginning he had urged that the workers should

put their class interests above national interests; their flag was the red flag of humanity, not the flag of any country. In 1864, he sponsored the organization of the so-called International to bring together the workers of all lands to deliberate for the common cause. It did not turn out to be a powerful organization, for there were quarrels among its members, and the outbreak of the Franco- Prussian War caused a breach between the French and German workers; loyalty to country was stronger than the feeling of working-class unity. Yet, although the International died, Marx had given the workers the sense of a common cause. The idea that they were a single class which must battle for their welfare against the employing class, and that sometime they would assuredly gain the upper hand that idea has never died. 

And so in all countries socialist parties were organized. Some thought that Marx expected only gradual progress toward a socialistic order, socialism by evolution, as it were. 

The capitalistic order would be so weakened by social reforms that it would finally wither away, and then the masses would find themselves in control of both production and distribution. Others, on the other hand, in token of some of his utterances, believed that Marx had approved of violent revolution, establishing the "dictatorship of the proletariat," while it was still a small minority. In other words, socialists have been split into two factions, differing not in principle but in methods. But socialism has been the chosen creed of the majority of the working class in modern Europe. And this was due to the inspiration of Marx.

Meanwhile the workers had gained a certain amount of consideration in the country where the Industrial Revolution had its beginnings. 

E. The State Intervenes on Behalf of the Working Class and though the movement was timid at first, it gradually led to the enforcement of better conditions. This reform movement was due to an awakened conscience among the people of Great Britain.

There were several factors that produced this awakened conscience. Methodism, although it did not encourage a spirit of democracy or a feeling of self-respect among the ⚫ workers, was at least full of pity for their dreadful degradation. The Methodists, being agitators, gave conditions in the factories much. publicity. Then there were places where unsanitary conditions had given rise to epidemics, which forced themselves upon the public attention, and it was a rich mill-owner, the father of the great Peel, who, learning of the evils in his own factory, introduced in 1802 the first factory act. Then the spirit of the early nineteenth-century thinkers was practical and kindly. Jeremy Bentham stressed the importance of the greatest happiness of the greatest number, and his cheery views on life were much read by the upper classes. It was a humanitarian spirit which led to the abolition of slavery in the colonies. But men who had prided themselves on this reform were forced to hear of a slavery in the factories, more terrible than anything known to exist in the tropics.

Gradually there developed a strong sentiment in favor of State intervention on behalf of the working class.. This opinion would have been hopeless if it had not possessed unusually forceful leaders; and there were some, indeed, who devoted their lives to the cause of factory reform. The wealthy mill-owner, Robert Owen, made his mill a model factory, where the working hours were limited to twelve, and he proved that this could be done without at all endangering profits. Since the first factory acts, shortening the working hours of women and children, were not properly enforced, Michael Sadler worked hard for more effective legislation. It was a com- 

A Changing Opinion in England about the Rights mittee of which he was chairman that gave of the Working Class 

Government action for the benefit of the working class did not await the extension of the suffrage to that class. The principle of letting business alone was finally challenged, the public the first vivid account of conditions in factories.

After Sadler met with defeat in the elections of 1832, his work was carried on by Lord Ashley, afterward Earl of Shaftesbury, whose

THE

picture appears on this page. 

Ashley was a typical aristocrat in some ways. He did not believe that any but the aristocracy were fitted to govern. He was opposed to political agitation on the part of the workers, and he himself was stiff, somewhat gloomy, and even tactless in disposition. But he had a deep feeling of pity for the under-dog, and a conviction that it was his mission to relieve the distress of the working class. It was due to Ashley's patient and constant pressure that the reforms most urgently needed were carried into effect. 

The Factory and Mine Acts 

The first factory acts were not well enforced, and their importance lies in the fact that they started the ball rolling, as it were, and challenged the principle of laissez-faire. The State was proclaiming its right to curb the exploitation of the workers by their employers. 

The first great factory act was that of 1833. 

It had the effect of raising the minimum age of the child worker to nine, and those between nine and thirteen were not to work more than forty-eight hours a week or nine in a single day. 

No person under eighteen was to be employed more than twelve hours a day or sixty-nine a week. The most important feature of the act was that it provided for four inspectors, who had the full right to enforce it.

In 1840, at Ashley's instance, an inquiry was held into the conditions of employment in the mines; and the public was treated to a report describing conditions more dreadful even than those in the factories. By the Coal 

Mines Regulation Act of 1842 the employment underground of women and of boys under the age of ten was altogether prohibited.

Factory reform meanwhile proceeded slowly. 

The Whigs had lost their taste for reform, and though the Tories, representing the landlords and therefore willing to impose reforms on the middle class, were somewhat more interested in factory reform, Peel, their leader, was opposed to any limitation of hours of work during a period of depression. A hardheaded man of business, he was afraid that industry would suffer if the hours of labor were reduced, and believed that any handicap to business would in the end hurt the workers 

Brown Brothers FIGURE 124. THE EARL OF SHAFTESBURY 

(1801-1885) 

What conflicting feelings did Shaftesbury have toward the working class? What reforms did he try to bring about? themselves, many of whom might be thrown out of employment. The manufacturers, of course, were always emphasizing this argument, besides pointing to the fact that manufacturers abroad were not troubled by factory acts and that these foreign producers might therefore undersell them. Few as yet realized that long hours do not necessarily mean greater output. 

But Ashley and other reformers never relaxed their fight. For a long time the great object had been the ten-hour day, and this object was finally attained. By an act of 

1847, the hours of work for women and "young persons" in the textile industries were restricted to fifty-eight a week with a part holiday on Saturday, and this meant, in effect, a ten-hour day. The result of this and some other acts was the general practice of employing workers for a maximum of ten hours.

Relief for the Chimney Sweep Curiously enough, the greatest difficulty was experienced in getting relief for the chimney sweeps, the "climbing boys," as they were called, though there was no cruelty in the world more terrible than the practice of employing these tots to clean chimneys. 

Time and time again the House of Lords prevented the passage of a law to stop this practice, and when bills of relief were passed, the penalties imposed were insufficient to do any good. The introduction of machinery to sweep chimneys had the effect of lessening the number of boys employed, but it was not till 1864 that Ashley (now Lord Shaftesbury) got a bill passed forbidding the employment of boys under sixteen to sweep chimneys; and it was not until another act of 1875 (also due to Shaftesbury) that enforcement was handed over to the police.

Poverty and Health 

The care of paupers was another problem dealt with during this period, being the occasion of an act of Parliament in 1834. All persons without means of support should be sent to a workhouse, which was made so unattractive that no one, able to earn his own living, would be tempted to enter, unless forced to it by circumstances. An unfortunate 

An unfortunate

SUMMARY of Important Concepts effect of the measure was to put persons who were destitute through no fault of their own into the class with hardened and habitual loafers. Nevertheless it relieved the local authorities from the expense of creating odd jobs for paupers, and it doubtless prompted many to do their best to earn their living in order to avoid a worse fate.

Connected with the problem of poverty was that of public health. It was argued that many of the people physically unable to work were the victims of bad sanitary conditions. 

Worse than that, inadequate drainage and contaminated water were responsible for thousands of deaths every year in the crowded factory towns. The whole question being brought before Parliament, a board of health was established in 1848; and though this body was soon abolished, it had managed in five years to spread local boards of health throughout England. A noticeable decline in the death rate proved the value of such work. 

All these social reforms showed that the State now considered it a duty to extend protection to the working class. The State no longer existed as an agency solely concerned with safeguarding the rights of those who happened to exercise power. This new kind of state, which looks after the interests of all classes of society, is sometimes called the "social state." 

1. The Industrial Revolution, the gradual displacement of hand labor by power-driven machinery, started earlier and proceeded more rapidly in England than on the Continent. a. Abundant natural resources, capital available for investment, a large supply of labor, and so on, account for England's pre-eminence. b. Transportation and communication also were revolutionized. 

2. The Industrial Revolution had many far-reaching results. a. Labor flocked to the cities; slums grew; the workers worked in factories rather than at home. b. The machine made tasks easier; this fact together with low wages accounts for the widespread employment of women and children. c. Increased production made possible lower prices, and led to increased trade. 

3. In time the English workers banded together to improve their lot. a. As long as the laissez-faire theory was accepted, little could be accomplished. b. The workers tried trade-unionism and political agitation (chartism) to little purpose. c. Living and working conditions gradually improved, however, as a result of the growing spirit of humanitarianism. 

4. On the Continent the workers were more impatient, and turned to socialism (and even to revolution) to improve their lot. a. Although no socialistic experiment was successful, Marx made the movement world-wide. b. The followers of Marx have failed to agree as to whether socialism should be achieved by violence or by gradual, peaceful penetration.

GAINING Skill A. Where to Get Information. In studying about the Industrial Revolution you will have frequent opportunities to draw on what you have learned in English and science. 

1. Ask your English teacher to recommend books which describe conditions in England or other countries during the early years of the Industrial Revolution. 

2. Plan visits to places where you may view tools, implements, and processes used before power and machinery came to characterize industrial and agricultural production. 

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. There are various ways in which you may organize and present what you have learned about the Industrial Revolution. 

1. Make a scrapbook to illustrate conditions before and after the Industrial Revolution, or to make clear the developments in transportation and communication, and so on. 

2. Make a model of an early boat, engine, machine, and so on. Do careful work so that your model may be included in an exhibit. 

3. Make an oral or written report on one of these topics: how the steam engine revolutionized transportation, the Chartist movement, Louis Blanc and the national workshops, trade-unionism in Great Britain, the influence of Karl Marx, necessity is the mother of invention, the Industrial Revolution has resulted in suffering among the masses, and an eye-witness account of the first railroad journey in England. 

C. How to Evaluate Information. You probably know from experience that conflicting interests cause management and labor, producer and consumer to differ in their outlook on many economic questions. 

1. Give some examples of different points of view. Cite statements to illustrate each. How do you account for these differences? 

2. Write dialogue for a scene in which a weaver tells his family that a textile factory soon will be opened in the town, or one in which former craftsmen discuss the work they are now doing in a factory. Make your dialogue reflect the point of view of the persons in question.

CHAPTER IX 

Political Problems of the New Age 

DEMOCRACY MAKES SOME HEADWAY AND NATIONALISM IS STILL ACTIVE 

How did the extension of suffrage and the increased power of the House of Commons promote democracy in Great Britain?

PARLIAMENTARY REFORM The Revival of Parliamentary Reform 

In Great Britain the movement toward democracy centered in the issue of parliamentary reform.

DEMOCRACY AND NATIONALISM, the two forces which came to play so important a part in the of Commons. nineteenth century, became increasingly vital issues in the period from 1870 to 1914. We shall come to know more of nationalism in a later chapter, but we shall give some attention to one of its types here. Democracy gained in strength during this period, partly because the working class had become more conscious of its strength by 1870, partly because freedom of the press and freedom of public meeting were now more generally realized in most of Europe, and partly because a public school system was being gradually adopted in most countries, with attendance usually compulsory up to the age of fourteen. So increasingly did people follow the course of public affairs that when public sentiment displayed itself for or against the policy of a government, one became used to what is known as "public opinion," which expressed itself in elections, or in the press, or in public demonstrations. 

Democracy, as an ideal, could not be realized, however, until the people could really influence the government which was supposed to represent them. Democracy was still largely a matter of experiment, and that was especially true in Great Britain.

A. Political Reform in Great Britain 

Political reform in Great Britain had two main features: (1) parliamentary reform or the extension of the suffrage, and (2) the We have noticed the decline of interest in this question, neither of the two great parties, Whigs or Tories, wishing to extend the suffrage further. Though a few of the more liberal Whigs managed to keep the issue alive, Lord Palmerston, their leader, frankly desired things as they were. Finally, in the sixties, the working class began once more to agitate for the suffrage. Perhaps their renewed interest was partly due to the 

Whig statesman, John Bright, who went about the country addressing meetings and arousing a public opinion to demand reform. At all events, the working class had awakened, as we have noticed, and it was bound to feel that it ought to possess the right to cast a vote.

Moreover, in Parliament itself they had now a new champion, William Ewart Gladstone, who, after the death of Palmerston, became the acknowledged leader of the Whigs. 

Gladstone and Disraeli

Gladstone was very dignified and serious. 

He had originally intended to be a clergyman and he seemed to feel that any demand that

THE NEW AGE POLITICAL PROBLEMS OF 

FIGURE 125. BENJAMIN DISRAELI, EARL OF BEACONSFIELD (1804-1881) 

He made the Conservative Party & constructive force in English politics. To it were attracted many men of ability. Thus when he passed from public life there were able leaders to carry on his policies. وو he made had a great moral significance. The 

Queen did not like him because his manner gave her the impression that he was scolding her. He was, however, an able leader of men, a clear and forceful speaker, and by natural taste a reformer. He had already disturbed the easygoing indifference of most of his colleagues by his attacks on the electoral system. "Gladstone will soon have it all his own way, Palmerston had prophesied. "Whenever he gets my place, we shall have strange doings." 

The ministry of which Gladstone was a member resigned in 1866 after a bill prepared by him had been defeated. Then the Tories came into power, and their leader (after 1868) was one of the most striking personalities of the nineteenth century, Benjamin Disraeli. 

Disraeli was a Jew who had been reared in the Anglican faith. When he made his first speech in Parliament, he had been laughed at, but the experience did not fluster him in the وو least. "I will sit down now," he said to the amused faces, "but some day you will hear me.'

There was often reason enough to laugh at "Dizzy," as he was called, for he was odd, to say the least. He liked to startle people by the extravagance of his statements, and he dressed in strange clothes, sometimes coupling green velvet trousers with a canarycolored waistcoat. He was as unconventional as Gladstone was the model of what was proper. He was also a smooth flatterer, and the Queen enjoyed his presence as much as she always dreaded Gladstone's. But

Disraeli was a man of great learning, a brilliant and witty speaker, and was endowed with a very lively imagination. It is hard sometimes to judge of his sincerity, for he was a shrewd politician; and no one ever played politics more skillfully. He was the only one who could rival Gladstone in debate, and between these two was many a heated battle. 

Disraeli was keen enough to see that the country really wanted reform and that the Tories ought to be something more than a party of obstruction. If they stood for nothing better than existing things, then their rivals, now that the franchise had become wider than it used to be, would be almost certain to keep their hold on the Commons. 

He therefore meant that his party should become aggressive. It should adopt a policy of imperialism; it should stand for social reform; and now at this present juncture it should bow to the public demand for parliamentary reform and thereby gain the good will of the masses. Disraeli's policy was chiefly dictated by strategy.

The Second Reform Bill and Other Reforms 

So it was under a Tory ministry that the 

Second Reform Bill was presented to Parlia ment. Some of the party, of course, would not follow this daring leadership, but there were enough Whigs to put the measure through; and though some amendments of Gladstone's largely changed the content of the bill, Disraeli did not care. His heart was with the landed aristocracy, and he reasoned that if the working class got the ballot, it would eventually undermine the middle class, of which Gladstone was the leading figure.

The Second Reform Bill, passed in 1867, enfranchised the lower middle class (such as the shopkeepers and the like), the tenant farmers, and most of the workmen in the towns. It nearly doubled the number of voters. One of its opponents anxiously called it "a leap in the dark.”

In the general election which followed, in 1868, the country seemed to credit the bill to Gladstone, for the Liberals, as we should now call the Whigs, won the Commons by a large majority. Gladstone, as Prime Minister, then applied himself with ardor to the question of more reforms. Since it was wise to have an educated electorate (someone had said of the working class, "We must now educate our masters"), a bill was passed which established a kind of public school system in England. In 1870, positions in the civil service were opened only to persons passing competitive examinations, and thus were no longer the spoils of politicians. In 1872, the secret ballot was adopted for all elections, so that men would feel that their voting was not subject to interference. Of Irish reform and the legalization of trade unions we shall speak in another connection. The reforms of the "Great Ministry," as it was called, came so fast that people actually began to weary of so much stir. Disraeli spoke of the ministry as a “range of exhausted volcanoes,” and, in 1874, the Conservatives, as we should now call the 

Tories, won the general election.

Disraeli himself was not in favor of any further political changes; and it was not till the question of parliamentary reform was again revived. In 1884, the Third Reform 

Bill was passed, the effect of which was to enfranchise most of the remainder of the working class. There were still many who, for various reasons, did not possess the vote, but, in 1918, practically universal suffrage was granted for men, and women of thirty and over were given the vote. It was not till 1928 that the age for women was lowered to twenty-one, the same as that of men. (The chart below shows in graphic form the extension of the suffrage under the several reform bills.) 

Meanwhile another political question had arisen that of making the will of the House of Commons supreme.

ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SUPREMACY OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS Character of the House of Lords 

The House of Lords, composed of bishops and hereditary peers, was naturally very conservative. There were sometimes able men in the upper house, some of whom had been promoted from the Commons, for a commoner was often raised to the peerage to crown a distinguished career; but most of the members were there merely through the accident of birth or position, and hence the mental level was rather low. Even attendance was poor. 

In any case the Conservatives were always sure of a majority in this House, and this fact gave that party an undue advantage. 

It was not so much its undemocratic character as its frequently obstructive tactics that

Damaged by bombs during World War II, the building will be rebuilt as you see it, according to present plans. gave the House of Lords a bad name especially in an era of reform. The Lords could not seem to catch up with the times. 

In 1893, Gladstone's Second Home Rule Bill, after passing the House of Commons, was thrown out by the House of Lords. The 

Liberals who came into power in 1906 encountered much difficulty in the upper house, and many of that party declared that the 

House of Lords should be "mended or ended." (The House of Lords, like the House of Commons, sits in the building called the Houses of Parliament which is shown in the picture on this page.)

Clipping the Power of the House of Lords A crisis was finally precipitated in 1909 when the Lords threw out the budget, the bill which prescribes the means of raising revenue. 

Now, this budget, framed by an able Liberal statesman, David Lloyd George, fell heavily on great wealth; and the landed aristocracy, as well as the wealthy business men, did not like it. So the Conservatives used the Lords as an instrument to thwart the Liberals. Yet it had become something of a tradition that the House of Lords should never reject a money bill, for the representatives of the people were supposed to be the best judges of the taxes the people were to pay, and none had met with defeat in the House of Lords since the reign of Anne.

The Liberal ministry were furious, and determined to put through a measure depriving the Lords of their veto power. The Lords, perceiving that the Liberals were really serious, thought that they could meet their objections by changing somewhat the character of their House, not having it include everyone who happened to hold a peerage, but making membership rest somewhat upon merit. They also went so far as to say that they would pass the budget if the ministry were able to show public support in a general election. 

In the elections of 1910, the ministry did win, though their majority was rather small.

The Lords then passed the budget. 

But this act of renunciation did not save them. The ministry determined to end the power of the Lords and threatened that if the latter refused to pass a bill with that object, they (the ministry) would get the King to create enough new peers to insure its passage. The Lords accordingly gave way, as they had done in 1832 

during the struggle over the First Reform Bill. 

The Parliamentary Act of 1911 thus restricted the Lords to a suspensive veto. A bill passed by the House of Commons three times within two years should become law with or without the Lords' consent. At the same time a money bill was to become law within one month after it was presented to the Lords, with or without their consent. 

Since, however, the Commons would gain so much in power by this reform, the measure also provided that a general election should be held every five instead of every seven years, as had been the case since 1716. One might feel that the House of Lords could now just as well have ended its existence altogether, but it at least possesses the right to hold up legislation for two years and that privilege affords the public plenty of time for reflection. Their suspensive veto at least prevents hasty legislation. The American student might well ask himself whether or not he prefers the British system of government to his own.

But what about France, where democratic theories had always been more talked about than in England?

B. Democracy Holds Its Own in the Third Republic The Critical Period of the Third Republic 

You will remember that the Third Republic was proclaimed during the Franco-Prussian War. It was the act of some staunch republicans in Paris when they heard of the defeat and capture of Napoleon III. Yet, curiously enough, an assembly which had been elected by the people of France to vote approval of the terms of peace was made up mostly of royalists, for the reason that this faction had clamored for peace and most of the people of France wanted peace. It was consequently not at all certain that the republic would continue.

While this matter was in suspense, a popular outbreak occurred in Paris, known historically as the "Commune" for the reason that the governing council of the insurgents bore that name. When internal peace was restored, the royalists of the Assembly tried to find an appropriate monarch, but for various reasons their plans met with failure, and as sentiment for a republic continued to grow, the Assembly, finally, in 1875, took the step which definitely established the Third Republic. In other words, it passed the Organic Laws.

The Organization of the Third Republic 

The Organic Laws were the constitution of the Third Republic. For the executive they provided a president, to be chosen by the legislature for a seven-year term. The royalists did not want the president elected by the people for fear that some future Bonaparte might get himself chosen and then with popular support make himself absolute. The leading executive was to be the premier, who, though chosen by the president, must be one who could form a ministry; that is, he must be able to command the support of the Chamber of Deputies, the popular chamber. Thus the 

French borrowed from the English the famous principle of ministerial responsibility. 

The legislature was to be composed of two houses, the Senate, chosen by indirect election, and the Chamber of Deputies elected directly by universal manhood suffrage for a term of four years. In practice the Chamber 

In practice the Chamber of Deputies became the more important legislative body. (A picture of this chamber in session appears on the opposite page.) 

The Progress of the Third Republic 

When the Assembly which had made the constitution retired, a thoroughly republican Chamber of Deputies was elected to take its place. Soon afterward freedom of the press and freedom of public meeting were granted by law, with certain rather unimportant restrictions. Very important for the consolidation of the republic was the establishment, during the eighties, of a national system of education. Attendance at school was made. compulsory between the ages of six and thirteen. It was also free for primary pupils, and completely divorced from the influence of the Church, which was not considered friendly to the republic.

The republic was very active in other ways, inaugurating an imperialistic policy and promoting the material welfare of both the peasants and the working class. Most Frenchmen came to feel that the form of government they now possessed really responded to their needs. 

Moreover, thousands of people put their savings into government bonds, and thus they held a sort of investment in the republic.

The Struggle with the Church More Yet the republic had its troubles. than once the royalists tried, though without success, to undermine it. The bitterest foes of the republic were a group of ardent clericals who put the interests of the Church above the welfare of the State and resented the fact that the Church had lost its hold over education. 

To the republican statesmen the attitude of the clericals seemed disloyal, for ever since the 

Concordat of 1801 (see page 135) the clergy had received their salaries from the State. In 

1900 was formed what was known as the Republican Bloc, which determined to protect the republic from the activities of the Church. 

More and more the issue became that of separation. separation. The Bloc wanted to do away with the Concordat of 1801 and to bring about the complete separation of Church and State. 

The clericals felt, on the other hand, that as the Papacy had been a party to the Concordat, it should be a party to any change, and it was known that the Papacy did not want any change. Nevertheless, separation was finally adopted in 1905, and after a bitter clerical resistance a settlement was eventually worked out in 1907. Since then the Church has supported itself in France, but the government, in turn, has nothing to do with the choice of the clergy, and the church edifices, though still the property of the State, are placed at the disposal of the Church. 

French Democracy in Practice 

France was perhaps as democratically governed as England, but she had never gone very far in local self-government. The republic was strongly centralized, keeping the system which had been devised by Napoleon I. The prefect who governed the department was responsible to one of the ministers, the minister of the interior, who, of course, held his position by grace of the popular chamber, and this prefect was a very important official. He had charge of the various public services, such as highways, bridges, and hospitals; he appointed teachers, got recruits for the army, enforced the laws, and, to a certain extent, supervised the government of the towns and villages. He was the historic successor of the intendant of the Bourbon period, though,

POLITICAL PROBLEMS 

thanks to the telegraph, he was more closely bound to the government than the intendant had ever been. The prefects and their subordinates did not change with presidents or ministers, but continued to hold office as long as they did their work efficiently; and on the whole such a system seemed to make for efficient government. It was said, however, that the prefects were often expected to work for the parties in power and in that way were not always free from corrupt influence.

The chief fault in the French system was the insecurity of the ministry. As there were a great many parties in the Chamber of Deputies, no single party was able to control it, and hence a ministry rested on a combination of parties - what the French call a bloc. 

Three or four parties, or sometimes more, were represented in the ministry. It was difficult with such a division of opinion for a ministry to hold together. If one party withdrew its support, then the ministry would, as a rule, lose control of the Chamber of Deputies and would have to resign. Ministries were constantly changing, with the result that the nation was sometimes helpless to deal with an emergency. 

But there was seldom a complete change, since some of the ministers generally found places in a new ministry. Usually there was only a little veering to the right or to the left; that is, toward the conservative end of the chamber or toward the radical. AA There was some similarity between the governments of France and Italy the latter having also a responsible ministry, likewise insecure because of the multi-party system, a king who corresponded to the French president, and a centralized administration. But for Italy the problem of working out a democratic régime was for various reasons a harder problem. c. Democracy Marches too Fast in Italy

The Organization of a United Italy 

When the Kingdom of Italy was established, in 1861, the constitution of Sardinia was simply extended to the kingdom as a whole. 

The king was the nominal head of the government, but his position was little more than ornamental. The chief executive, as in 

France and Great Britain, was the premier; and the ministry, of which he was head, was responsible to the popular chamber. parliament consisted of two houses: a senate, appointed by the king on the nomination of the premier and composed of men of distinguished merit or those who paid a certain amount of taxes, and a chamber of deputies elected by a very limited suffrage. 

Italy's Many Problems The

Italy was beset with many difficulties from the start. Something had to be done in the way of smoothing out her relations with the Papacy, since most of the temporal power had been appropriated by the new kingdom. The 

Pope was granted complete possession of a small precinct of the city of Rome and also an annual sum as compensation for the loss of the papal lands. Unfortunately he refused to accept this settlement, not only flatly declining the money, but refusing even to set his foot outside his precinct, lest he seem to be recognizing the sovereignty of the King of Italy. He also forbade his loyal supporters to take any part whatever in Italian politics. 

As this was a case of boycott rather than political intrigue, such as the clericals in France were always engaged in, Italy was not seriously embarrassed.

Another grave problem was that of develop-

A centralized form of government had given Italy the form of unity; and old political divisions like that of Sardinia had disappeared. 

Yet the people continued to think of themselves as Tuscans, Sicilians, or Venetians, as the case might be. There was also a sharp division of the population along economic lines. Northern Italy was relatively prosperous, much of the population being engaged in manufacturing. Southern Italy, on the other hand, was mainly agricultural and very backward. It was there that illiteracy was greatest and it was there that the most lawlessness prevailed.

It was only with time that the Italians would come to feel themselves one people. The centralized system of government helped somewhat to develop this feeling. Then, as more and more of the people learned to read, they naturally took more interest in public affairs. Undoubtedly the establishment of comlpusory primary education in 1877 was a step in the right direction, though there was still an insufficient number of schools. Various social reforms, the enforcement of law and order, and the conclusion of a defensive alliance with Austria were also achievements to the credit of the national government. there was also much misgovernment, and for this we must find the reason. 

Democracy in Practice 

But

Italy was apparently not ready for a democratic régime. At the time when the Italian 

Kingdom had been founded only the people of the former Kingdom of Sardinia had possessed any real experience with parliamentary institutions. Only there had there been anything approaching a democratic régime. All 

Italians elsewhere had been ruled by petty despots, and the masses were for the most part quite unfit to possess the ballot. When the suffrage, very restricted in the beginning, was somewhat widened in 1882, Italian politics became notoriously corrupt. Often a

The Germans, like the Italians, were not used to parliamentary government, but with them democracy came much more slowly. 

D. Germany and Austria Keep

Democracy at a Distance 

The Constitution of the German Empire The constitution of the German Empire was an expansion of that of the North German Confederation, and both were the work of Bismarck. It was a masterpiece of political ingenuity; for he made certain concessions both to sectionalism and to democracy, yet insured the dominance of Prussia over the empire.

The German Empire was a federation of twenty-five states, including three free cities. 

They were the states which had survived the 

Seven Weeks' War, and in local affairs they were allowed self-government. 

The upper chamber, the Bundesrath, was composed of representatives of these states, the number for each state being in accordance with its relative importance, except that Prussia was allowed only seventeen out of the total of fifty-eight. The members of the Bundesrath were chosen and instructed by the governments concerned and in each case voted as a unit according to their instructions. As most of the state governments were not very liberal, the Bundesrath was essentially a conservative body.

The popular chamber, the Reichstag, elected by universal suffrage, was Bismarck's concession to democracy. It was, however, a

POLITICAL PROBLEMS 

209 

concession that actually meant little. In the first place, there was no plan for the reapportionment of seats in accordance with the shifts of population. As the population of the cities grew much faster than that of the country, it was not long before the former were greatly under-represented. To reserve power as far as possible to the rural population was to maintain a fair safeguard against change. In the second place, the Reichstag had no control over the government, for the principle of ministerial responsibility was not applied, the Chancellor being the choice of the Emperor alone. In the third place, the Reichstag was much the less important legislative body. 

No wonder, then, that the Reichstag was commonly called the "hall of echoes." It was really one of the least important legislative bodies in Europe. Whenever it did balk, which was not often, the government could dissolve it, and then, by using its influence with the press, contrive to get a more docile body. There was nothing like a free public opinion in Germany, for there was no declaration of rights guaranteeing freedom of the press and public meeting, and a large proportion of the press was controlled by the government. 

A great deal of authority was vested in the police, who broke up public meetings on slight pretexts, and were ever ready to pounce on any editor with liberal views. It was partly because of the lack of any vigorous public opinion that the Reichstag amounted to so little.

The one important minister was the Chancellor, corresponding to the Premier in other countries, but he was responsible only to the 

Emperor, who chose him and might remove him as he pleased, and was thus in a position to shape the government's policy. The Emperor was supposed to rule by divine right, and any criticism of him was a punishable offense. 

Prussia's position in the federation was as dominant as Bismarck had wished. Her king was the German Emperor. She was able, through her influence on neighboring states, to control enough votes in the Bundesrath to command a majority in that body; and by virtue of her large population, about three fifths of the total, she had an ascendancy in the Reichstag. Finally, since fourteen votes were sufficient to block any change in the constitution, Prussia with her seventeen votes need have no fear of ever losing her grip. We know already that the traditions of Prussia were military and autocratic. Germany was therefore at best a semi-autocratic state. 

Government in Austria and Hungary The government of Austria was similar to that of Germany in so far as the ministry was largely under the Emperor's control. By a law of 1907, the popular legislative chamber was elected by universal suffrage, but owing to the number of nationalities with different interests, ministers were chosen pretty much as the Emperor wished. Hungary was even less democratic, for there the suffrage was restricted to men of wealth.

As for Austria-Hungary, the Dual Monarchy, the imperial ministry was directly responsible to the Emperor-King. A joint committee of the two parliaments, known as the Delegations, had the right to look over the work of the ministry, but nothing more. 

E. Progress in Other Countries Where Democracy Was Successful 

There was a march toward democracy in most of the other countries of Europe during the nineteenth century. The suffrage was usually limited at first, then extended to include all male adults, and in some cases granted to women. Such cases were the 

Scandinavian countries, that is, Denmark,

Norway, Sweden, and Finland (a grand duchy which enjoyed autonomy in the Russian Empire). Belgium reached what was practically universal suffrage as far as men were concerned; but in Holland the suffrage was not quite so broad. All these states were constitutional monarchies, Norway's independence dating from 1905 when she had separated from Sweden. Switzerland, on the other hand, was a republic, with a federal form of government somewhat on the model of our own.

It is interesting to note that aside from Switzerland all these states adopted the principle of ministerial responsibility. The cabinet system was also applied, as was natural, in

Great Britain's self-governing colonies, the socalled dominions.

Where Democracy Was Less Successful 

Spain and Portugal seemed less fitted for democracy than most of the countries of Europe. Though possessing constitutions, their politics were always very corrupt, and there was the same tendency as in Italy for an unscrupulous politician to become a dictator. 

Meanwhile, in eastern Europe, institutions that were mildly democratic came into existence in the Balkan States; but Turkey and 

Russia remained absolute monarchies down to the end of the nineteenth century. 

We must now give some slight attention to nationalism, reserving to a later chapter a more comprehensive study of its activities. 

F. Nationalism and the Irish 

Question

Nationalism Continues to be a Factor 

You doubtless remember nationalism as that sentiment expressed by a people having many things in common and endowed with characteristics that make it distinct from other peoples. Nationalism, by its very nature, is self-satisfied and tends to be belligerent. 

We find it in many forms. When a nation (by which we usually mean a nationality that is free) seeks to liberate and acquire people of the same nationality who are living under foreign rule, this form of nationalism is called. "irredentism" from an Italian word, meaning "to redeem." The spirit which prompted the unification of Italy is an example of this particular form of nationalism. Sometimes nationalism displays itself in much more selfish fashion. "Imperialism" is a peculiarly aggressive type, as we have seen. "Economic nationalism" is a term applied to a nation setting up tariff walls against other nations, and is obviously the opposite of free trade. 

Some economists think that people as a whole would benefit more from free trade than from the maintenance of tariffs, but at bottom, of course, the idea is self-protection — that is, protection of the home products against competition from abroad. Self-defense is at least 

Self-defense is at least natural to nations, and few will allow themselves to be injured by another.

Perhaps the form of nationalism deserving the most sympathy is that displayed by a people living in subjection to alien rule. Such was the case of the Poles, divided as they were between Austria, Russia, and Prussia; and both Russia and Prussia treated their respective Poles very badly. One of the best examples of a submerged nationality was that of the Irish, and we must now relate their story at some length. 

Irish Nationalism and Foreign Domination 

The Irish are very different from the English. They are in temperament impulsive, warm-hearted, and perhaps, as a rule, not very practical; whereas the English are deliberate, cool-headed, and, on the whole, much more practical. Most of the Irish are 

Catholic, while most of the English are Prot- They also have a language of their own, quite different from English, though English has pretty generally supplanted it. Irish nationalism sprang from difference in temperament, difference in religion, and also the memory of historic wrongs. The story of their wrongs is a long one. estant. 

The English took over a part of Ireland, the region around Dublin, in the Middle Ages. 

But there was no serious attempt to subjugate the Irish until the time of Elizabeth in the sixteenth century. Spain had tried to use the 

Irish, who were strongly Catholic, to make trouble for Protestant England, and as a result Elizabeth sent over an army which harried a large part of the island with fire and sword. 

The cruelties perpetrated on the Irish were even worse than most atrocities of that time; and much of their land was confiscated and passed into the hands of the English. Still more land was seized under James I, who founded in the north the so-called Ulster Plantation, largely made up of Scottish Presbyterians. Later, Cromwell pursued much the same course, conquering, slaughtering, confiscating; and he left behind a hatred that has lasted to this day. Finally William III, to punish the Irish for supporting the cause of James II, still further extended the English occupation. occupation. Naturally enough, the spirit of

rebellion remained; and the French endeavored to use it to their advantage during the war of Great Britain with Revolutionary France. Hence in 1800 Pitt brought about the union of Great Britain and Ireland. But it was not till 1829 that Irish Catholics were admitted to the British Parliament. Political domination may be said then to have ceased, but in other respects, economic and religious, this domination continued to be felt. 

Ireland's chief troubles were economic. 

We may leave out of the story Protestant Ulster in the north, which for the most part was industrial and got along fairly well. It was the agrarian or peasant problem that was really acute, and that concerned the majority of the population, the Catholic Irish. Most of the land was in the possession of Englishmen who were descendants of the men who had despoiled the Irish, and probably in the majority of cases they did not live in Ireland at all, but simply drew their revenues from the lands which they had leased to their Irish tenants. Since, however, these lands were not rented for a fixed length of time, the tenure of the peasant was most uncertain. If the land he tilled was needed either for pasturage or to form part of a larger holding, or if he fell behind in his rent, which was usually much too high, he was liable to be evicted. 

In case of eviction he lost any improvements he might have made, such as his sheds or other buildings. There was little incentive for the Irish to improve their holdings when at any moment they might be stripped of everything or at the least might face a sudden increase in the rent. When once a peasant was asked why he was wearing such shabby clothes, "Faith," he answered, "the last new coat cost me two shillin's sixpence more in me rint." (The picture on this page will give you an idea of how the peasants lived.) In any case the peasant was usually too poor to improve his holding, and at best he could barely eke out an existence. Most of the Irish peasantry lived on potatoes, and it was the failure of the potato crop, in 1845, that had led, as we have noticed, to the repeal of the British Corn Laws, but not until a very large number had perished. (See page 167.) 167.)

Another side of the Irish Question was religious. A certain phase of the English invasion had been the planting of an alien church upon the Irish population. At the time when Elizabeth adopted her harsh measures against Catholics, she extended the Anglican Church to Ireland in the hope of making Protestants of the Irish. Thus, staunch Catholics as they were, and miserably poor, the Irish were forced, nevertheless, to support this unwelcome Church. It was remarked that an Anglican chapel often stood empty save for the parson and his clerk, while nearly a thousand Catholics were huddled together in a miserable hovel to hear their priest. "There is no abuse like it," said one observer, "in all Europe, in all Asia, in all the discovered parts of Africa, and in all that we have heard of Timbuctoo." It was indeed

the religious question that had made Irish nationalism so bitter against the English. 

The Liberals Tackle the Irish Question 

It was hardly strange that there was periodic unrest, and during the eighteen-sixties the danger of revolt was so great that the British government was forced to give its attention to the problem. As Disraeli had no interest in the Irish Question, it was left for his rival, Gladstone, to see what he could do. Gladstone's first measure was to end the privileged position of the Anglican Church. No longer were the Irish compelled to support an alien faith out of their pittance. He also made two attempts to solve the agrarian problem. A bill passed by Parliament in 1881 secured to the peasants a fair rent, compensation for improvements if they were evicted, and reasonable security of tenure. But the Irish were not content with these concessions and clamored for the right to govern themselves.

As far back as 1873 a "home-rule league" was formed, and under an able leader, named 

Parnell, these "home-rulers" forced Parliament to consider the question. Parnell's method had been to make so many speeches on various questions that all legislative business was held up. Finally, in 1886, Gladstone, then Premier for the third time, brought in his

First Home Rule Bill. It was strenuously opposed by the Conservatives, who felt that the Irish were utterly unfitted for self-government. Salisbury, one of the Conservative leaders, compared them to the Hottentots and the Hindus. There was also a large section of the Liberal Party, who, led by Joseph Chamberlain (whose portrait appears on page 226), refused to give their support to the bill on the ground that home rule would place the Protestant Irish in Ulster at the mercy of the

Catholic majority. The secession of this group, which afterward left the Liberal Party and became merged with the Conservatives, defeated the bill. But Gladstone was not the person to give up a fight after one failure, and in 1893, now Premier for the fourth time, he introduced the Second Home Rule Bill, differing somewhat from the first. This time the bill was passed by the House of Commons only to be rejected by the House of Lords, and 

Gladstone retired permanently from political life.

The Conservatives Tackle the Problem 

The return of the Conservatives to power, in 1895, put the responsibility upon them of satisfying the Irish. Lord Salisbury, the 

Premier, was very firm in putting down disorder, but the Conservatives' plan of solving the Irish Question was to "kill home rule by kindness," as one of their opponents put it.

By several acts money was lent to the peasants to buy land, and special inducements were given the landlords to sell. In other words, the Conservative solution (the idea, as a matter of fact, was borrowed from the Liberal, John Bright) was peasant proprietorship. It was along these lines that the Irish agrarian problem was eventually solved.

The Danger of Civil War and the Rise of Sinn Fein 

Still the Irish were not reconciled, for their hopes were still centered on home rule. In 

1912, when the Liberal ministry needed Irish votes to pass its program of social reform, it was forced to present to Parliament another home-rule bill. This time the opposition of the House of Lords was not to be feared, as it had lost its veto power the previous year, and the only thing it could do was to delay passage of the bill. In the meantime, the men of Ulster were much wrought up over the prospect of home rule, which they declared would simply mean "Rome rule." They were afraid that Catholic, agrarian Ireland would persecute the Protestant section and throw the burden of taxation upon its industries. this contention they were supported by the Conservatives in England. A crisis was certainly impending, for the Ulsterites began to arm, and the Catholic Irish did likewise. 

Since the Liberals, despite the danger, were fully resolved to push the bill, probably nothing but the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 prevented civil war from engulfing the British Isles. After the bill was duly passed, the 

British government wisely declared it in suspension for the length of the war. In

Thus the Irish Question was still far from solution. The home-rulers were resentful because the government, after suspending the

home-rule bill, considered the idea of reviving it, but of exempting Protestant Ulster from its provisions; for none of the Catholic Irish would hear of a divided Ireland. Hence, a more extreme party, which wanted complete separation from Great Britain, came to the forefront. This party was known as Sinn 

Fein, an Irish expression, meaning, "We ourselves." During the war, some of this element was actually disloyal, and in 1916, an uprising took place in Dublin which aimed to establish an Irish republic with German assistance. 

This rebellion was promptly put down by the British government with so much harshness that bitterness greatly increased. Outside of 

Ulster few of the Irish had volunteered in the British service, and the government did not venture to extend its conscription law to Ireland. The Irish Question, which had become more political than economic, soon entered upon a new and serious phase. Sinn 

Fein won the allegiance of the Catholic Irish; and what they wanted was a united, republican, and independent Ireland. completely self-governing; but she was still bound by allegiance to the British Crown; she was not to have an army larger in proportion to her population than that of Great Britain; and she was to allow the use of some of her ports by the British navy. The agreement was reached in 1921, and created in 1922 what was known as the Irish Free State. It added one more dominion to the British Empire. 

The Irish Question Still Unsolved 

Were Anglo-Irish relations now finally settled? No, there were still many occasions for friction, particularly as a large minority of the Irish were not content with anything less than complete separation from Great Britain, and were even more determined that Northern Ireland, or Ulster, should be incorporated in the Irish Free State. Into the bickering of the next few years we cannot enter, though it is well to notice that Eire (as the Irish now call their country) renounced in 1933 the oath of allegiance to the British Crown, and that Great Britain, in 1938, gave up her right of using the Irish ports as bases. As in 1921, the 

The Irish Revolution and the Creation of the Irish British preferred conciliation to a policy of 

Free State

After the war the Irish waged a sniping or guerrilla warfare against the British, and a veritable reign of terror broke out in the land. 

Many of the police were murdered and there were constant acts of pillage and destruction. 

The British, of course, replied to force with force, but the country was not subdued. For several years Ireland was torn by revolution. 

Finally, the British Premier, Lloyd George, persuaded the Irish to accept a compromise. 

This compromise was really a triumph for the Irish. They did not actually win their independence, and they were separated from Ulster, which received its own government and parliament; but they secured dominion status, which was something rather better than home rule. Catholic Ireland became 

SUMMARY of Important Concepts bloody repression.

But the Second World War was to show that the Irish Question was still unsettled. The 

British sadly needed those Irish ports as bases for their airplanes sent to protect the sea lanes to 

England against German attacks on shipping.

Yet Eire, alone of the dominions, proclaimed strict neutrality in the struggle; and it was inferred that only if the British sacrificed Northern Ireland to Eire (a concession the British could not in honor make) would the Irish allow Great Britain the use of their ports. Since the fate of Eire herself was clearly involved in the fate of Great Britain, such a policy seemed to merit the severe criticism it received. 

Irish nationalism is perhaps the clearest example of that intensity of feeling of which nationalism is capable.

CHAPTER X Social Problems of the New Age: 

THE ADVANCE OF SCIENCE AND SOCIAL DEMOCRACY 

How has science served human needs and contributed to human happiness?

How has the State sought to safeguard the social and economic welfare of the common man? 

How has woman attained equality with man?

THE PERIOD WHICH ACHIEVED so much in promoting political democracy in Europe was characterized by greater changes for people as a whole than any previous period of history. 

Getting its momentum from the Industrial Revolution, science contributed more powerfully than ever to raise the standard of living for most of the people of Europe, while an enlightened public conscience served to remove many of their economic barriers. In this latter connection we mean that an important aspect of this new period was the promotion of what has been called "social democracy" the lifting of certain underprivileged classes to a position of greater security in society, with the hope of greater equality of opportunity. Social democracy was a movement of social reform in the interest chiefly of the working class and the peasantry, though the term should include the improvement of women's position in society as well. 

We shall begin with a study of some of the more important achievements of science in shaping the lives of the people of today. 

A. Science Brings Great Changes 

Origins of the Advance of Science in the Nineteenth Century

It is difficult, perhaps, to account for the great march of science in the nineteenth century; for more discoveries were made during that period and, indeed, are still being made than all which the previous history of man had produced. But, in a sense, the progress of this wonderful century was very 1 largely the result of the French and Industrial 

Revolutions. The French Revolution had greatly altered man's conception of himself as a member of society; he had now a recognized right to display his worth. right to display his worth. And the Industrial

Revolution had opened up great fields of opportunity for the individual. People seemed to feel that they were living in a time of change. Men were ever reaching out for greater wealth, and society in general was again and again startled by the achievements of the machine. In an atmosphere such as this the scientist found abundant inspiration. 

And the man who could find some great scientific truth was sure of an appreciative public. 

Character of the Advance of Science 

The scientific discoveries of the nineteenth century were so far-reaching that they altered man's conception both of himself and of the world he lived in. They taught him more about Nature and how to harness her in the service of humanity than all the discoveries which had been made since the world began. 

For reasons of space we shall be obliged to neglect the story of the theory of evolution, of the discovery of the great antiquity of the earth, and of the development of our knowledge of electricity and of matter. 

Let us merely note in passing that the sciences of biology, geology, and physics have opened to us immense fields of knowledge. And the same might also be said of other sciences.

Our chief interest will be in the story of applied science, the application of science to

Perhaps you have heard tales of putting horsehairs in a rain barrel and finding that they turned into snakes. This must include not only the various contributions of specific sciences but the mechanical inventions that have meant so much in the development of industry. Let us begin with those great discoveries that have contributed to lessen suffering and prolong life. 

Progress in Bacteriology and Medicine

One of the forms of life to receive a good deal of attention from scientists during this period was the germ or microbe, commonly spoken of in the plural as bacteria; and the study of their action is the science of bacteriology. Bacteria are the smallest living organisms. They are really minute plants, and they multiply very rapidly. Most of them, we know, are entirely harmless, but some of them are breeders of disease. They were noted in the seventeenth century in stagnant water; and the invention of the microscope enabled one to see them in countless numbers. In 1762, an Austrian physician, Plenciz, declared his belief that infectious diseases were caused by certain bacteria which floated in the air; each disease, he believed, had a microbe of its own. But his groping after the truth brought him nothing but sharp ridicule.

Soon afterward, as we remember, Edward Jenner showed the way to prevent smallpox by vaccination. He knew little, to be sure, of the cause of the disease, but in discovering by experiment the way to prevent people from getting it, he inspired others to work out the actual science of preventive medicine. 

All this problem of the disease activities of microbes, as well as the method of guarding against them, was cleared up by a great French chemist, Louis Pasteur, who lived about the middle of the nineteenth century. 

Pasteur was interested in the fact that wine readily turned sour if exposed to the air. He proved that if a cask were closed it would keep its purity, since it was not then exposed to the germ-ridden air. He also proved that by heating wine at a certain temperature the bacteria which caused the souring or fermentation might be killed. The same method came to be employed in the case of milk, and that is why we speak today of pasteurized milk. 

After a time Pasteur came to believe that many diseases of animals and men were traceable to bacteria in the air. The causes and prevention of diseases became the subjects of his constant study.

Pasteur's early successes led many to solicit his aid in combating disease. When the silk industry of France was threatened by a plague that was killing the silkworm, Pasteur devoted all his time to the problem, and after six years' study he found the remedy. Of more farreaching importance, however, was the fact that in that way he proved the "germ theory" of disease. This was in 1866, and some years later he worked out the means of preventing anthrax, a disease of sheep. He took some weakened bacteria from a sheep that had their strength. Those used effectually against typhoid are actually dead.

had the disease and injected into a well sheep just enough to cause a mild attack of the disease, which, it was found, would prevent a serious attack. In similar fashion he was able to avert the terrible disease hydrophobia. This was Jenner's method, but now the method was resting on a scientific basis. It is to 

Pasteur, indeed, that we really owe the science of preventive medicine.

On foundations such as these the science rapidly progressed. The discovery by a 

German scientist, Buchner, in 1889, that serum I drawn from an immunized animal had the power when injected to fight off the virulent microbe proved a great additional aid in preserving life. Experiments of Behring, another German, showed that diphtheria could in that way be prevented; and the causes of disease, together with the idea of securing immunity if possible, came to be foremost in importance in the field of medicine. 

Meanwhile the germ which causes tuberculosis was discovered through the experiments of a German physician, Robert Koch. It was of great importance to learn that the germs of malaria and yellow fever were conveyed by certain species of mosquitoes, that that of typhus was carried by lice, and that sleeping sickness was caused by the sting of the tsetse fly, for the war on all these pests has done much to check these maladies. Meanwhile inoculation, founded on Pasteur's principle, has been successfully adopted to prevent tetanus, cholera, diphtheria, and typhoid fever.

While we are dealing with preventive medicine we should not forget a man whose work had been done before Pasteur's. Joseph 

Lister, a British physician, taught the principle that, by observing scrupulous cleanliness in taking care of wounds, infections due to the action of bacteria might be prevented. 

Up to his day compound fractures had nearly always necessitated amputation, and a large proportion of all operations had been fatal, because of infection. Lister found that carbolic acid was an effective antiseptic, and his * Serum is the liquid which separates from the clot when blood coagulates. The discoveries of Lord Lister not only saved countless lives, but they spared innumerable victims the pain that accompanies infection of wounds. He methods, which are known as "antisepsis," have saved innumerable lives. Profiting by this contribution of Lister's, Pasteur insisted that surgeons in the Paris hospitals should sterilize all bandages and instruments. said he hoped in that way to save more people than had been lost in the Franco-Prussian War. The medical men in France at first called him an "old fogy," but he eventually had his way. 

But of all the boons to mankind there is hardly anything to compare with the adoption of anesthetics for a surgical operation. 

In 1846 an American dentist, W. T. G. 

Morton, a resident of Massachusetts, tried the experiment of using ether in order to render a patient unconscious while extracting a tooth, and the experiment proved so successful that ether was presently employed in a major operation. Soon afterward chloroform was used by a British physician for the same purpose.

Besides relieving the patient of pain, the use of anesthetics has the advantage of

enabling the surgeon to take his time in an operation and thus do his work more thoroughly.

One of the greatest revolutions in surgery has come with the X-ray, the discovery of a German physicist, Roentgen, which enables the physician to look into the body and diagnose the case without the necessity of an exploratory operation.

Progress in the Physical Sciences More associated, perhaps, with business than with health have been the two physical sciences, physics and chemistry. Applied physics had taught already the application of steam to industry. It has since enabled us to harness electricity for human uses, and has given us the telephone, wireless telegraphy, and the radio. Applied chemistry has shown what can be done by combining elements, and the result is that chemists can make many things that hitherto only Nature had been able to provide. Instead of depending upon a tree to produce indigo, this dye can now be made in any quantity by chemists. We do not have to wait any longer for lakes or rivers to freeze over to obtain ice. Artificial ice can now be made by certain gases, and there is no limit to the supply that can be had. 

All the while chemists, working in laboratories have been giving us fresh cause for wonder. Mechanical refrigeration, produced by the use of certain gases such as ammonia, makes it possible to ship meat for thousands of miles. 

The invention of photography, dating from early in the nineteenth century, led not only to a great pastime, but also to a fruitful means of educating the public, and eventually the moving picture was developed. Through the use of certain chemicals not only is the farmer able to enrich his soil and carry on what is known as intensive farming, but other chemicals enable him to destroy insects which threaten his crops. Chemists have discovered the means of ripening fruit, and purifying water, of producing the deadliest of explosives, of manufacturing perfumes (finer sometimes than those produced by flowers), and of making many synthetic products, such as artificial leather and an artificial silk, known as rayon.

Tin cans can be made from palm oil; and most of Europe now gets its sugar from the beet.

Chemists have also discovered uses for many things formerly regarded as waste products. Casein, a product of skim milk, makes the finest glues. From the cotton seed, once considered of no possible use, are now derived some eighty products, including rope, fertilizer, feed for cattle, writing paper, varnishes, soap, linoleum, and several kinds of oil. 

One of the things which had always been treated as waste was coal tar. It was of no value as fuel, and no one supposed that this black, smelly, sticky stuff was good for anything at all. Quite by accident, a British youth, William Perkin, washing up after a laboratory experiment with coal tar, found that it colored the water purplish, and before he was much older he became the founder of the aniline dye industry. As one writer has well put it, “The chemist is an economizer; it is his special business to hunt up waste products and make them useful.”

New Industries: Steel, Rubber, Oil 

Some of the greatest industries today have been the result of certain scientific experiments. Sir Henry Bessemer, a British inventor, discovered in 1856 a cheaper and faster method of making steel, thereby bringing steel into more common use. Before steel is rolled into bars or sheets, it is heated in ovens like those shown in Figure 136. Sometimes the steel is rolled into beams and used in constructing the framework of ships, bridges (like the one shown in Figure 137), and even skyscrapers. The commercial uses of rubber were made possible by an American, Charles Goodyear, who was able by chemical processes to make this product of the rubber tree durable and resistant to the pressure of heat. If one thinks of rubber boots, rubber coats, and rubber tires, one can well understand the growth of the rubber industry. Meanwhile oil from the earth was gradually displacing whale oil, as whales were becoming scarce. Products of oil, such as kerosene for illuminating purposes, and above all, gasoline, as a new source of power, gave impetus to the oil industry. The importance of oil in navigation is common knowledge.

Carrying on the Revolution in Transportation 

In no more impressive way has the science of this age shown its power than in the spheres of transportation and communication. We have mentioned the part that steel played in shipbuilding. Up to about 1860, most of the vessels that plied the sea were made of wood. 

Thereafter steel was generally used instead, with the result of making vessels both stronger and safer. As the twentieth century dawned, great ocean liners, veritable floating hotels, crossed the Atlantic. All the battleships were also made of steel.

War and travel were thus made easier and so was commerce. In this connection we should mention two feats of engineering. The opening of the Suez Canal, in 1869, and of the Panama Canal, in 1914, served greatly to shorten distances by water. Most of the trade between Europe and the East now passes through the former.

A new source of power, electricity, also facilitated transportation. For the harnessing of electricity to serve man the world is chiefly indebted to Michael Faraday. The son of poor parents, this young man was once a newsboy and a bookbinder's apprentice. 

He had, however, a great longing to become a scientist, and he finally had a chance to hear the lec-

Hardly less remarkable was the combustion engine, especially the one invented by a German scientist, Rudolf Diesel, in 1895. This engine uses oil instead of coal, and requires much less fuel than the steam engine. It is used very commonly in navigation, while others burning gasoline are employed for running automobiles and airplanes. 

Carrying on the Revolution in Communications

The telegraph and telephone have already been mentioned as improvements in the field of communication. The spreading of news has, of course, been greatly aided by the improved printing-press. All the work of producing the newspaper is now done by machinery, setting the type, stamping it on paper, even the matter of cutting and folding the sheets. But wireless telegraphy has revolutionized methods of communication more than anything else. Aided, like most inventors, by previous discoveries, a young Italian, Guglielmo Marconi, found the means of sending messages through the air without use of wires. His first message across the Atlantic, in 1901, was an epochal event. As a writer has well said, "Time has almost been eliminated as a factor in communication." Now photographs are sent by wireless, too, and what is known as television (seeing objects at a great distance) has made sufficient progress to justify the belief that it is certain to become
