Carrying on the Revolution in Industry and Agriculture There were also mechanical inventions of direct aid to production. The machine for making matches has, of course, been an enormous boon, since matches take the place of the old method of producing fire by friction. The sewing machine, the vacuum cleaner, and the washing machine have made life much easier for the housewife. Business has been aided by the typewriter, the adding machine, and the dictaphone; and agriculture has been simplified through the use of the tractor, the mowing machine, and the reaper.

There has been a veritable flood of machines, new ones as well as improvement of old ones. 

There are even automatic machines, which, once they are started, behave in a manner almost human. Such is the automatic elevator, which, summoned by pushing a button, comes straight to your floor and opens its doors to receive you. Everything in the making of woolen cloth is now done by one machine. If an old-fashioned weaver were now alive, he would undoubtedly think that a miracle had been performed.

Moreover, the perfecting of machinery has led to mass production, in virtue of which there is greater economy for the producer, though there is possibly less variety among the products offered the consumer than in the days of the handicraft worker. At all events, business has become more scientifically and systematically conducted than ever before. 

Greater Opportunities Lead to the Rise of "Big 

Business" Hav- The immense impetus given to business by the development of applied science and the progress of the machine, as well as the steady growth of capitalism, led to new experiments in business organization. Thanks to abundant capital, many industries expanded, and toward the close of the nineteenth century there was a tendency for companies not only to enter into price agreements but in many cases to unite under one management. ing larger funds to draw on, these immense combines were often able to undersell the small independent producer, and the result was the decline of the system of free competition. When a company gets something close to a monopoly of the market, we have what is termed a "trust." When we speak of these immense business combines, we often use the term, "big business." 

The chief advantage of "big business" to the buying public is that it is able, generally speaking, to charge a lower price for its goods than the small dealers are able to do, since it

is able to make its profit out of the immensity of its sales. It is also able to experiment with new things, since it can stand the risk of loss much better than the small dealer whose capital is limited. But as business is always for profit, the tendency of "big business," just as soon as it obtains what is virtually a monopoly of the market, is to charge a monopoly price. The consumer has little defense against this practice. If salt is under a trust, he will have to pay the price the salt trust imposes, unless he chooses to employ another kind of seasoning.

It is obvious that the State, which has done so much to protect labor, could do something, if it chose, to protect the consumer. Great 

Britain did intervene to fix the maximum rates on railroads, and Sweden enforced a reasonable price for the use of electric power. But, in general, democratic countries have interfered but little with the course of business. 

Though they had parted with laissez-faire to a considerable extent, they rather disliked the idea of government control as liable to prove a step in the direction of socialism. 

Germany's Rapid Growth as a Phenomenon of This 

Age 

Germany remained as the chief example of a nation whose economic life was deliberately promoted by its government. The establishment of a protective tariff was of great assistance to agriculture and industry. The State liberally subsidized its merchant marine and offered producers special rates on the railroads to enable them to meet foreign competition. 

But certain characteristics of the German people — their energy, their discipline, their talent for organization — partly accounted for the success which they attained in the business world. No people have made more use of applied science. Germany's steel production came in time to outstrip even that of Great Britain, and in her dye and electrical industries she led the world. By the end of the nineteenth century she was second only to Great Britain as an industrial and commercial power.

And now let us pause and reflect on some of the effects of all this scientific progress on the society of today.

Some Social Effects of the Advance of Science 

The effect that strikes us first is that life has become in some ways much simplified. The person of moderate means enjoys conveniences his grandparents never knew. Housekeeping is very much easier than it was even a generation ago. The merchant who has a cash register and perhaps an adding machine is saved much time and drudgery. Electric lighting has become so common that people can turn night into day if they so desire. To get anywhere one can take bus, train, or airplane and travel with greater speed. Central heating of houses has tended to become common even in Europe and eliminates the labor of building a fire in every room. Trans- 

Atlantic crossings are now marvelous in their comfort and their safety.

And all this means, of course, that the standard of living for most people has risen considerably in the last fifty years. 

If we recall improved sanitation and the triumphs of medical science, we see why the average length of life has increased. The machine has made it unnecessary for the workman to work so hard, and he has more leisure time at his disposal. Women who provide some of their meals out of cans, use a vacuum cleaner to keep their houses clean, do their washing by machinery, and wear readymade clothes instead of making them themselves, have naturally more time to spend in activities outside the home.

And there are certainly many more things to provide entertainment. The theater and the opera have usually been beyond the reach of the masses.

But the movie and the radio have brought enjoyment to innumerable per- Again, because of the radio and the moving picture the common man has a much better understanding of what goes on in the world. There is also the daily paper to relate at least the most startling things that are happening in distant countries. sons. 

Certainly the world has become much smaller in a sense. Better methods of transportation have brought the country much closer to the city, and the moving picture and the radio have broken the dull monotony of the peasant village. The Industrial Revolution, as we have noticed, had had the effect

THE NEW AGE SOCIAL PROBLEMS OF 

of making a much more unified world, but the invention of wireless telegraphy and other improvements in the methods of communication have brought all civilized peoples into even closer touch with one another. More over, the tremendous growth in the volume of international trade and the investment of much capital in foreign countries have made the world in a sense one huge economic unit. 

Such factors ought to promote mutual sympathy and understanding, and but for national jealousies and rivalries, it would be so. 

At all events, society had undergone many changes with the coming of applied science and the progress of the machine. Of great significance was the changed position and outlook of the working class, which we must now take space to consider.

B. Social Reform as an Issue The Coming of Social Reform 

We have already seen that the idea that everyone should be free to carry on his business as he chose and that there should be no intervention from the State on the one hand or combinations of workers on the other in other words, the idea of laissez-faire- had gradually been modified in the nineteenth century. The time had passed when the 

British manufacturer or mine-owner could force women and children to work as long as he pleased and under conditions that were harmful to their health. Thus, we have the factory and mine acts, passed during the thirties and forties of the nineteenth century.

The State intervened to limit the working day for women and children in the textile mills and coal mines, and safeguards were provided for the health of all workers. During the sixties and seventies these measures were extended to almost all mills and factories. In 1901 the minimum age for child workers in factories was placed at twelve; in 1900 the minimum age for those working underground had been fixed at thirteen.

Protective legislation of this sort came later on the Continent. It had its beginnings in 

Great Britain. It was also in Great Britain that trade-unionism first developed, seeking to advance the interests of the workers by a system of collective bargaining; though the movement had been too much hedged about by legal restrictions to be very successful. 

Yet trade-unionism had given the workers a feeling of class unity, a vivid realization of their common interests; and the winning of the suffrage (political democracy) seemed to open up a new era of promise.

The Shift to a New Phase 

In the period we are now considering most of the working class had come to enjoy a power they had never known before. In most countries, with universal suffrage, had come the ballot. Thus they were now able to make their influence felt. They were also able through socialist agitation, which, under

Marx, had become well organized, to put their case squarely before public opinion. At the same time it came to be realized more and more that merely to cut down the hours of labor or to protect the worker from the dangers of his employment were not enough. 

The specter of poverty always hung over the worker, since his wage was insufficient to tide him over periods of illness or unemployment or to provide for his old age. Thus social reform as an issue came to shift to a broader problem, that of safeguarding the workers against poverty.

It was Germany, not Great Britain, who first put into operation a system of State insurance for the working class. 

c. Germany's Policy of Social Reform 

Bismarck's Policy and Its Motives 

It was Bismarck who planned a new experiment in social reform. Primarily his object was political. The socialists in Germany had gained in numbers and increased their representation in the Reichstag. Bismarck had tried repressive measures, but still this element grew. So he thought that by bringing direct relief to the workers he could draw them away from socialism. "Give the workingman the right to work as long as he is healthy," Bismarck urged in 1884; "assure him care when he is sick and maintenance when he is old,

Do not fear the sacrifice involved or cry out at 'state socialism.'... If the State will show a little more Christian solicitude for the workingman, then the socialists will sing their siren song in vain, and the workingmen will cease to throng to their banner as soon as they see that the government and legislative bodies are earnestly concerned for their welfare." 

But Bismarck had also a broader interest in view. He felt that the State "should discharge, besides the negative duty of protecting existing rights, the positive duty of promoting the welfare of all its members, and especially those who are weak." The working class was a minority and could not itself force consideration of its interests, but Bismarck felt that it was a matter of social justice to promote its welfare. Moreover, there was the very practical motive that a contented and efficient working class would redound to the interest of the manufacturer himself and make for a happier and more efficient Germany. 

Bismarck's Social Legislation

Bismarck introduced his program in 1883, and several laws were passed in succeeding years which put it into operation. The scheme included insurance against accident, insurance against illness or invalidity (disablement from injury), old-age and survivors' pensions, and insurance for salaried employees, as well as compulsory treatment for tuberculosis in State sanatoriums.

Under the accident insurance law, the sum paid the worker during the time when he was laid off was derived from funds provided by the employers. In the case of sickness insurance, the support paid the worker during his illness came partly from his own contributions, partly from his employer. This was likewise true of invalidity, old-age and survivors' pensions, except that the State also contributed to the pensions. The old-age pension was paid to a worker who had completed his seventieth year. The sum he received was about two thirds of the amount he had received when he had employment.

Survivors' pensions were due the widow and children of the deceased worker. These insurance measures were all compulsory. There was also compulsory insurance for salaried As a means of destroying socialism, Bismarck's policy failed, but as a method of saving the workers from destitution, it proved immensely successful. There was little real poverty in the German Empire, and certainly no workingmen in Europe were more contented and more efficient than the German. Progress of Trade-Unionism 

The granting of the ballot to most of the workingmen by the Reform Bill of 1867 was a great boon to that class. They were now an important element among the voters, and parties could not ignore them. Gladstone, on becoming Premier in 1870, found himself steadily pressed to give the trade unions legal standing, and under his leadership Parliament took this important step in the following year. But an amendment, passed soon afterward, made it still illegal to employ certain methods of intimidation.

It was therefore left for Disraeli to grant the unions complete satisfaction. The objectionable act was repealed in 1875; thus the unions were free to adopt any measure short of the actual destruction of property to win their ends.

Trade-unionism broadened to include an increasingly large proportion of the working class, and strikes were often effective in securing better conditions. But the movement received a blow when, in 1901, it was decreed by the House of Lords, acting in its capacity as the highest court of justice, that a trade union might be held responsible for damages during a strike. In virtue of this decision trade unions were continually being sued. When men went out on a strike, the union was even held responsible for breach of contract. Tradeunionism was paralyzed for several years. 

The lesson learned by the workers from this affair was that they must exert a greater influence in politics.

Rise of the Labour Party 

In 1893 the Independent Labour Party had been formed, but it later merged with a larger group to form the Labour Party, or, as the British often simply term it, "Labour." (The name, as you will notice, is always spelled with a "u," since the word "labor," in England, is spelled "labour.") In the general election of 1905 the Labour Party sometimes profited by fusing with the Liberals, and it succeeded in electing twenty-nine members to the Commons a number increased to forty in 1910. The importance of the "Lib- 

Lab Alliance," as it was called, soon became evident. The Trade-Disputes Act in 1906 

exempted trade unions from suits for damages when its members engaged in a strike. Shortly afterward, when the House of Lords ruled in another suit that unions must not pay members of Parliament (naturally a workman could not serve in Parliament for nothing), the Labour Party secured the passage of a bill by which, for the first time, members of Parliament were to receive salaries. We shall presently note the influence of the working class in securing insurance legislation.

It is important, therefore, to remember that the workers had not only the trade unions to push their interests but a political party as well. They had an economic weapon and a political weapon, and the political weapon was for the time being more important. We must now go back a little and see how the older parties, made up of members of

E. Social Reform in Great Britain The Conservatives and Social Reform 

It will be remembered that Disraeli had advocated for his party the championship of the interests of the workers. It was Disraeli who had granted to the trade unions the position they had wanted. Thanks to him, though actually he did little, Conservative interest in social reform became a tradition; and though many of the party were rather indifferent, the addition to its membership of a former radical 

Liberal, Joseph Chamberlain, gave Disraeli's policy a chance for further achievement.

Chamberlain was a member of the middle class, a wealthy manufacturer of Birmingham.

As reform mayor of that city, he had shown an unfailing sympathy for the masses. His chief failing was that he sometimes threw himself into an issue so heartily, as, for instance, "tariff reform,' "I that he would end by letting other questions slide. He was, however, a very forceful personality, an original and constructive thinker, and a powerful debater. 

When the Conservatives recovered power after the elections of 1895, Chamberlain, as a member of the Salisbury ministry, declared that, in spite of Gladstone's prediction to the

Interest in the peasants was natural enough to a party that derived most of its strength from the landed elements; and we have mentioned its solution of the question of agrarian reform in Ireland. But the Conservatives were evidently seeking the support of the town worker as well. Addressing the

Commons as early as 1892, Chamberlain had urged a pension system for industrial workers. "I ask you to pledge yourselves," he said, "to the great principle that it is the duty of the State to provide for the veterans of industry just as it provides for the veterans of the army and the navy." Undoubtedly, too, the party was much influenced by public opinion. An exhaustive survey of London's working conditions, a work which had been financed by a philanthropist, Charles Booth, had called the attention of the public to the hardships of the working class. It was revealed that upwards of thirty per cent of Londoners were in a state of dire poverty.

The revival of social reform was marked by the enactment of a Workmen's Compensation 

Law. Though Gladstone had admitted the principle that a workman who had suffered an accident in the course of his work was entitled to compensation, it was difficult sometimes to prove that the case was not the workman's fault. As the law was then interpreted, the workman had to prove he had not been negligent. By the new law, passed in 1897 under Chamberlain's inspiration, the burden of proof was placed upon the employer. other words, the injured workman was assumed to be innocent unless a case of negligence could actually be proved against him. 

Unfortunately, compensation was provided only for some of the more dangerous trades.

But the fact that most of the rich manufacturers were members of the party that passed In

this measure speaks much for the influence of Chamberlain. Later a commission was appointed by the Commons to study and report on the general problem of the aged worker; and this report became the basis of the action that was taken later. (One section of public opinion in the matter is illustrated by the cartoon on page 228.)

Yet this policy of social reform had hardly more than been initiated when Chamberlain came to believe that the tariff question was much more vital. The Conservatives also, including Chamberlain, had allowed their country to be drawn into an aggressive policy in South Africa. Imperialism, for the moment, interrupted this hopeful trend toward social reform.

The Liberals Take up the Problem 

It was the Liberals who revived the movement when they won the general election of 

1905. The Conservatives had been badly defeated, partly because Chamberlain had come to advocate a protective tariff and the country evidently preferred to cling to free trade; partly because the war in South Africa, the Boer War, had resulted in increased taxes; and partly because the Liberals had loudly clamored for social reform and consequently had been able to fuse with Labour in the elections. The new Liberal ministry, which took office in 1906, immediately made plans to relieve the hardships of the working class. 

And again a forceful personality assumed leadership, not the Premier, but the Chan cellor of the Exchequer, David Lloyd George. 

Lloyd George was a Welsh lawyer, very liberal in his views, and a keen and witty speaker. In his younger days he had been something of an idealist, and soon after his election to the House of Commons he had made himself very unpopular by his vehement opposition to the Boer War. At one time he narrowly escaped being killed by an infuriated audience whom he had addressed on the subject. But his jovial good nature, his ready wit, and his undoubted ability enabled him to live down the disapproval he had incurred, and he became one of the chiefs of the Liberal Party. He was at bottom a very shrewd politician, and he learned, in course of time, British Combine FIGURE 146. DAVID LLOYD GEORGE (1863- ) 

Lloyd George was Prime Minister of England from 

1916 to 1922. What reforms did he sponsor? What rôle has he played in foreign affairs? Do you recognize the figure on the right? the art of compromise. He was also energetic and very ambitious. Since, moreover, he had risen from humble beginnings, he was able to understand and to sympathize with the hardships of the masses.

First Measures of the Liberals 

The vast problem of relief was seriously attacked. A new Workmen's Compensation 

Law, passed in 1906, extended the benefits of Chamberlain's measure to almost all manual workers. An injured workman should receive half his week's wages, up to a maximum of five dollars, provided his injury laid him off as much as a week. The same year, incidentally, the miners were voted an eighthour day, though the act was not to become operative till 1909. Already the influence of Labour had become apparent. Another problem to receive attention was child welfare. By laws passed in 1906 and 1908, free meals were to be furnished needy children in

the elementary schools, recreation grounds provided, and measures taken for the safeguarding of children from bad habits and for the correction of juvenile crime. 

In 1908 came the very important experiment, old-age pensions. So important had this issue become that very few candidates in the elections of 1905 had failed to endorse this project. Opposition to the project when it came before Parliament was not strong. 

Most persons had come to believe that insurance legislation, whether a good thing or not, was desired by the public. The chief argument against these pensions was that they might encourage persons to lean on society instead of doing their best to save money for themselves hardly a sound judgment considering the smallness of the pensions as well as of the wages received by the great majority of workers. A member of the Labour Party, speaking for the bill, declared: "Here in a country rich beyond description there are people poverty-stricken beyond description. 

There can be no earthly excuse for the condition of things which exists in the country today. If it is necessary to have a strong army and navy to protect the wealth of the nation, do not let us forget that it is the veterans of industry who have created that wealth." 

Quite apart from the middle-class brains which lay behind British prosperity, the labor of the industrial workers certainly had contributed powerfully to that end. At all events, the Old-Age Pension Bill was easily passed.

By this bill of 1908, workers, men or women, on attaining the age of seventy, became entitled to a pension; and the smaller the wage, the higher the pension. The maximum pension, $1.25 a week, was given to the worker whose income was no more than $105 a year. 

The pension was not supposed to give the recipient full support, for clearly he would still be compelled to save for his old age; but, unlike the case of Germany, the State was to bear the whole expense. 

Security in old age was something from which all workers could benefit. But there was also need of relief for those still able to work. Especially was this true in the case of "sweated" labor. We are told that "sweating" was a term originally used by journeymen tailors of those of their number who worked at home out of hours. It came to be employed to characterize trades where long hours and very low pay were universal, and where often unsanitary conditions were likewise present. These were the trades in which machinery was not used, and where the workers were employed either in small and crowded shops or at home. Hence the employers were not bound by the regulations of the factory laws. Moreover, the character of the work was such that persons could always be easily found to do it. Hence this labor was very cheap, and those who were so engaged had nothing to do but submit to the conditions. Those trades included tailoring, dressmaking, lacemaking, and box-making, in all of which the labor was performed by hand. 

The sweating system was first investigated by a parliamentary committee at the time when the Conservatives governed, but nothing much was done till the Liberals came into power. power. Just before the elections of 1905, some dressmakers had attracted the attention of the public by overworking their girls because certain fashionable ladies had to have their gowns in a hurry. Some of the newspapers made a stir over the treatment of the poor seamstresses. After a new investigation by the government a bill was passed, in 1909, which provided for a minimum wage in certain sweated trades, and under the provisions of this act (the Trade Boards Act) 250,000 workers immediately benefited, of whom fully two thirds were women. Provision was also made for its extension to other trades, and eventually as many as three million workers were brought under the reform. In the meantime, in 1912, a minimum wage for miners was granted after a very formidable strike, the largest, in fact, that had ever been witnessed in England. 

Another serious question involving the working class as a whole was that of unemployment. It is noticeable that in the building trade there is always some unemployment, since masons, carpenters, and plasterers seldom have steady work. Aside from this casual unemployment, there were occasional hard times when a good many thousands were

SOCIAL 

231 

PROBLEMS  

turned out of their jobs, simply because business had slackened. The first remedy attempted was in 1909 in the so-called Labour 

Exchanges Bill. Eighty labor exchanges, what we would generally speak of as employment bureaus, were opened in the country at large, where employers could look for labor and workers could apply for a job. It was not, of course, a complete solution of the problem, since often there were not enough jobs available, and in any case a worker could not always afford to pay his fare to the nearest labor exchange. It furnished some relief; but the evil of unemployment still continued. 

The National Insurance Act 

The problem was again attacked in 1911. 

The so-called National Insurance Act provided insurance against both unemployment and illness. As to the former, a sum was to be paid the insured workman from the beginning of the second week of unemployment up to a maximum of fifteen weeks. The bill applied, however, only to workers in a few trades, where a certain amount of unemployment was chronic. It was thus in the beginning only an experiment; but we shall notice that after the 

First World War it was extended to practically all manual workers.

The other feature of the National Insurance Act concerned the matter of illness. Every manual worker was entitled under this act to a certain amount in event of illness for a period of twenty-six weeks, and then a smaller figure for "invalidity," if he were still disabled, up to the time when he should be eligible for an old-age pension. The scheme also provided for free medical attendance during illness, and maternity benefits for women workers and even for the wives of insured men. 

Insurance against both accident and illness was compulsory, and the funds for paying the premiums were contributed partly by the employer, partly by the employee, and partly by the State.

Impressions of These Measures 

In general, the British program of social insurance covered more ground than that of the German, since it was made to include insurance against unemployment. It was also more generously financed by the State. The 

Labour Party was not wholly satisfied, however. While they welcomed social insurance as an undoubted step forward, they felt that the workers should not be expected to contribute anything at all. tribute anything at all. Perhaps some of the discontent among the workingmen resulted from the fact that, while wages had been generally increasing for some time, they had not kept pace with the rising cost of living.

During a period of relative prosperity the workers had not profited proportionately to their employers.

But, though there was disagreement over certain features of these acts, there was really remarkably little opposition. Those Conservatives who had some reasonable doubts on the subject pointed out that such measures were partial to a single class, the working class, which benefited from the taxes of all classes; that clerks and many small merchants also needed financial aid; and that it was much too easy for a party enjoying power to expend more and more money on the workers as a means of getting their votes. It is probably true that the Liberals regarded this policy as likely to strengthen their hold upon the workers, but it is also certainly true that the class that was singled out for these benefits was the one that ordinarily earned too little to protect themselves against the risk of destitution.

F. Social Progress in Other Countries Trade-Unionism 

Trade-unionism was never so vigorous a force on the Continent as in England. Even in a great industrial country like Germany it was a much less effective weapon of the workers than their political organization, the 

Social Democratic Party. Yet there was hardly any country where trade unions did not exist; and in France and Italy, in particular, they were responsible for a number of strikes.

In France the working class was small in number, as compared with either Germany or Great Britain. Large-scale industry was nothing like so common as in other countries,

Sometimes they had apprentices working under them for a wage, but such people were too scattered to form unions. 

Yet trade unions had long been in existence. The French Revolution had banned them, as we have noticed, but after 1815 they sprang up here and there as secret organizations. Napoleon III allowed them to carry on quite openly, though he did not give them legal recognition. Under a democratic régime, the Third Republic, the cause of the working class had much more chance of public support; and in 1884 trade unions were given legal recognition. In 1895 a general federation of trade unions was formed. 

Somewhat later, in Italy, trade unions received legal recognition, and here, as in

France, a general federation of labor was founded.

Social Reform 

Bismarck's great innovation, social insurance, was copied in nearly every country of Europe, though such measures did not as a rule go so far as those in Germany. Generally such reform was due to the influence of socialist parties, who, because of the bloc system, possessed considerable weight. It should be noted, too, that most of the socialists were moderates, who expected to reach socialism by easy stages. 

Outside of Europe, two British dominions,

Australia and New Zealand, were conspicuous for their activity along the lines of social reform, and New Zealand actually went farther than Great Britain herself. In New 

Zealand, where the railways were owned and operated by the government, freight rates were reduced automatically as soon as profits had attained a certain figure, and special passenger rates were given to workers, while children in the elementary grades were Meanwhile, with the increased political carried free. One reason for the low rates

was to induce people in the crowded districts in the towns to move into the country, where sheep-raising is an important industry. (The picture on page 232 shows a flock of sheep on 

Australia's excellent grazing ground.)

New Zealand also enacted insurance measures, such as invalidity insurance and old-age pensions, before the mother country had done so, and her work was somewhat of a model for Lloyd George's legislation. The general principle of wage regulation was long in force in Australia and later adopted also in New Zealand. The New Zealand government includes a labor department which undertakes to find work for people where possible. 

Peasants are normally less aggressive than the working class, but this movement of social progress did not altogether exclude them from consideration.

The Problem of the Peasants benefit from the advance of democracy in Europe. A curious exception was the case of Great Britain, where comparatively little was done for the relief of this class, and the explanation lies in the fact that agriculture was there a dying industry. The general assumption of the government was that the nation would buy most of its foodstuffs abroad. 

When Chamberlain tried to procure a tariff on wheat, he was decisively defeated at the polls.

In France, which was chiefly agricultural, a great deal was done for the peasants. Not only were they given the advantage of a tariff on their products and liberal means provided for lending them capital, but agricultural societies were allowed by the same law which had legalized trade unions. Such organizations enabled the peasants to engage in collective buying, market their produce on better terms, and keep up with the latest im- It was natural that the peasants should provements in agricultural machinery. WEIGHING BUTTER ON A DANISH FARM 

Denmark in peace time marketed her dairy and other agricultural products in Great Britain and on the continent. was predominantly the land of the peasant proprietor. It was the peasants and small shopkeepers, who, living on small incomes and constituting the bulk of the population, made France conservative at heart. In few countries were people so nearly on the same economic level.

In Italy the number of peasants was even larger in proportion to the total population than in France, but Italy was both a younger and a poorer state, and such measures as the government enacted in the interest of the peasants were quite inadequate to relieve their poverty. Those peasants who owned their land were comparatively few. Most of them were tenant sharecroppers, dividing their expenses and profits with their landlords, or rural workers on large estates at a pitifully low wage. It was because of poverty that so many of this class emigrated to the 

New World. The greatest need of the Italian peasant was to become a free proprietor. 

A large proportion of the German peasants, on the other hand, were free proprietors, though East Prussia was still predominantly a land of large estates; and so great was the influence of the landlord class, the Junkers, that they obtained the financial aid of the 

Prussian government. Some land, however, was bought for the farm laborers in this district; and in Germany, as in France, agriculture was amply protected by a tariff. 

Probably the most progressive peasants in the world were to be found in Denmark, where dairying was the leading industry. (Weighing butter on a dairy farm in Denmark is shown on this page.) To begin with, more than nine tenths of them were free proprietors, and though few of the Danish people could be said to be wealthy, the great mass of the population was comfortably off. Democracy was successful because it rested on something approaching economic equality.

The chief clue to the prosperity of Denmark lay in the vigorous spirit of enterprise which her peasantry displayed. The great majority of peasants belonged to co-operative societies which enabled their members to obtain loans, to share in whatever facilities were needed to aid production, to market their produce under the most favorable conditions, and to follow a severely uniform standard of quality. Through organization they worked and planned together; and they bought and sold as a group.

It was because of their collective skill and respect for standards that these peasants were able to win such striking success in marketing their products; and the butter, eggs, milk, cheese, hams, and bacon, produced by Denmark, were in greatest demand in the markets of England and Germany. Each member of a co-operative was, of course, an independent producer, but by collective effort he was assured a reasonable profit at a minimum of expense. 

Here in Denmark the peasants solved their own problem.

G. Changing Position of Women The Woman's Revolution 

Another important social change in this period was the changing position of women.

SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

235 

If you compare the woman of today, who is free to enter business or a profession, and in most civilized countries can cast a vote, with the pampered or browbeaten woman of

Luther's day, you can realize what a transformation has occurred. In the period we are considering much of this change took place, though complete emancipation, such as we now know in English-speaking countries, did not come till after the First World War. 

Looking back over many centuries, we can see that a revolution has taken place.

A Man's World 

In the old days a woman's normal sphere was the home, as it is, in fact, today; but there was then no chance of escape from its dull monotony. A woman's chief duty was to rear a family, and if she belonged to the lower classes, she might also have to work in the fields or perhaps do some spinning at home for the family support. She was completely under the domination of her husband, or, if unmarried, of her father. Those who did not serve men were intended to amuse them. Such was the rôle of the fashionable ladies. Even their education, if they were given any at all, was intended simply to captivate some man. little music and dancing, the etiquette of the ballroom, perhaps a smattering of a foreign language, and some little skill with the needle these were about all that was necessary for even a young noblewoman to know. "Women," said a leading gentleman of the eighteenth century, "are only children of a larger growth. A man of sense only trifles with them, plays with them, humors and flatters them, as he does with a lively, forward child." In France of that period young women of the upper classes who did not marry were usually relegated to a convent. 

It was remarkable under such conditions that a woman was ever able to achieve any distinction. Yet in some countries they were not, strangely enough, excluded from thrones; for the cases of Elizabeth of England and 

Catherine of Russia will be recalled. These women did actually rule men, and showed themselves by no means inferior beings. 

France some women were able to hold salons, as we have noticed, and acquired a certain In distinction in the literary world. 

But they did not, for all that, effect a change in the traditional attitude toward women as a class. 

The law allowed a man to beat his wife; her property was his; there were few countries where a woman could be freed by divorce from a cruel husband. She was excluded not only from every public office, but from all professions except teaching, and from business. She was deemed an inferior being who must serve the purposes of men.

Opening the Way for Women 

But perhaps the literary ladies of the salons won sufficient respect to gain for their sex some sympathy at least. During the time of the Enlightenment there were men, who, finding flaws in the social order, thought that women were not given a square deal. "In all countries of the world," said one of the philosophers, "the lot of women is to submit to tyranny." Another philosopher, Condorcet, went so far as to advocate equal rights for women; and during the French Revolution a young girl drew up, quite vainly, a “Declaration of the Rights of Women" as an accompaniment of the Declaration of the Rights of Man. These are perhaps the earliest evidences of feminism, or the movement to obtain equal rights for women, though in actual fact there was hardly a "movement" as yet. A few years later, an Englishwoman, Mary Wollstonecraft, championed the rights of her sex in a vigorous tract, entitled The Vindication of the Rights of Woman. She contended that nothing but their inferior education prevented women from showing their intellectual capacity, and she argued for equal rights, both political and economic, with those of men. 

But most of her contemporaries treated this tirade only with contempt. Walpole sneeringly dubbed her "a hyena in petticoats."

But the nastiest slur on her sex was that of Napoleon, who expressed himself on "the weakness of women's brains and the unsteadiness of their ideas," their "need of a kind indulgence and easy charity," and he believed that religion should be stressed in their education, though they might also be taught a little' geography and history, as well as some needlework.

Was woman never to be taken seriously?

The French Revolution was a man's revolution, for women did not benefit as a class. 

More important for her future was the Industrial Revolution, for that made her a wageearner; and were it not for the hardships she endured, one might feel that she was free. In any case it was the first step toward economic freedom.

Rise of Feminism 

But it was still a man's world, and the position of women was not appreciably changed till after the middle of the nineteenth century. 

Perhaps the courageous career of the English nurse, Florence Nightingale, who founded the first base hospital in the Crimean War, had something to do with a growing respect for women. At the time of the Second Reform 

Bill, John Stuart Mill, a British writer, urged that the ballot be given to women. proposal was received with merriment and defeated by a large majority. Yet in 1869 The women were allowed to vote for members of municipal councils; and even though, themselves, excluded from Parliament, women in England took an active interest in politics, and each of the great parties had its organization of women. The fact that the cause was making considerable progress was shown by the 

Woman's Property Act of 1882, which for the first time allowed a woman the possession of her own property; and similar action was taken in other countries. Even the divorce laws were relaxed; and in France the right of a girl to marry without her parents' consent was finally obtained. Gradually, as the century wore on, women were admitted to the professions in most countries, and it was not unusual any longer for a woman to conduct a business. It goes without saying that educational opportunities were provided, and that women were now able to pit their intellects against men's. 

But man's last stronghold was in politics. 

He might admit woman to the professions; he

SOCIAL PROBLEMS 

237 

might take her into his employ, usually, it must be admitted, at a lower wage; he might let her try to compete with him in business if she chose; but he was loath to grant her political equality. Aside from two of our states in America, the first country to give the suffrage to women was New Zealand, in 1893. 

In 1907, woman suffrage was granted in Finland; in 1908, in Norway. In other countries there were organizations of women battling unceasingly to that end. The organization in England was popularly known as the "Suffragettes," and they labored in every way to bring their cause before the public. Not satisfied with processions and other forms of propaganda, they attempted to mob members of the House of Commons, broke windows, and defaced churches. One woman gave her life, throwing herself in front of a horse at one of the races. Many of these disturbers were, of course, jailed, but when they started a hunger strike, refusing to eat, the authorities were so afraid that they would become martyrs and thus add to the strength of their cause that they often let them go.

This violent phase of the movement was interrupted by the First World War, and then, as we shall see later, the women earned the ballot in another way. in another way. But at least we can say that woman suffrage had become an issue in certain countries. (What the general public thought of this campaign is indicated in the cartoon on this page.)

H. Other Social Changes Gradual Change and Then a Quickening 

The social life of the period after 1870 was a matter of steady evolution. It was an increasingly practical age. No one knew what inventions might suddenly take place that would alter one's way of living. People had to adapt themselves constantly to change. It was much more difficult to live a secluded life in 1870 than it had been in 1830. Railroads and trolleys brought the world almost to one's doors. It was likewise more difficult for class distinctions to persist, and this became more apparent as time went on; for just as the barriers had fallen in western Europe between the upper and middle classes, so, as time went on, FIGURE 151. they became lower between the middle class and the workers.

Yet it must always be understood that the mass of the people change their tastes and manners very slowly. It often takes courage to try a new thing, and few people seem to be able to stand ridicule. Habits, indeed, are extraordinarily tenacious. Even to this day the French are slow to adopt some of the modern conveniences. The English also feel an immense respect for the things which gave their grandfathers prestige in the community. 

The very fact that the self-made merchant still longs for a country mansion shows that tradition has its weight. Few people are independent of convention. So the social changes of the period were very gradual; and it was only toward the end of the nineteenth century that the speeding-up of life became noticeable. 

That was the time, more than ever, that wealth held the key to social position; and even kings hobnobbed with millionaires. 

Manners and Diversions

The manners and interests of people changed slowly during the first twenty years of this period. The theater and opera developed higher standards; more attention was given to the promotion of education both higher and lower; and there was perhaps a finer idealism in general than there had been in the time of Louis Philippe and Palmerston. 

Gladstone, with all his proverbial stiffness, had a profound feeling of respect for the public service; and the corrupting influence of the great corporations was only just beginning to push nations into scrambles for colonies. The extension of the suffrage to more and more of the masses led to a feeling of greater interest in society as a whole. The middle class had 

The middle class had become used to the position they had acquired, and for a time at least were less selfish and less foolish.

But that vein of idealism we mentioned seemed to strengthen the old barriers for women. They were still regarded as a class that must not soil itself by contact with the sordid things of life. Modesty was deemed a woman's most sterling virtue. It was not until the nineties that women seemed to acquire more social freedom. They began then to ride bicycles, as well as to play tennis (both, of course, in long skirts), and some of them also rode horseback (though always, of course, side-saddle). Even in walking their ankles were now revealed to the horror, no doubt, of their grandmothers. After the beginning of the new century, many of them threw themselves into the suffrage movement, and acted sometimes in a quite unladylike manner. the whole, the woman on the Continent, before the stress of a world war, was much less independent than her sister in England; yet the very existence of a movement for equal rights showed that women were less disposed to remain the sheltered and idealized creatures that man had ordained. On

All this had some bearing on the home. In the seventies domestic life and the marriage tie had been looked upon as possessing particular sanctity. The Anglican Church was, of course, opposed to divorce, and Victoria went so far as never to allow even the innocent party to a divorce to attend her court. That draggy and hymn-like song, Home, Sweet Home, had an immediate and immense popularity. But the increasing interest of women in public affairs meant for many a welcome relief from the absorbing details of domestic life; and by the turn of the century many families had established themselves in apartments, where the duties of housekeeping were likely to be less exacting. Similarly, dining at restaurants became an attraction for the fashionable set, a practice which may have been borrowed from life on the Continent. 

The growth of cities and the steady improvement in methods of communication brought people much closer together. Clubs were on the increase among the upper and middle classes; while for the poorer people in Protestant lands the chapel or the tavern (called in England the public house) furnished means of association, just as in France the sidewalk cafés performed the same service. Cheap excursions on the railroads gave all classes a chance to travel a little. Bicycles increased in popularity until the countryside was covered with them. In England games of cricket and football soon ceased to be confined to schools and colleges, and the matches of professional teams drew thousands of eager spec-

tators. In fashionable circles tennis supplanted the once popular game of croquet, but horse-racing still remained a favorite pastime of the upper classes. The playing of bridge, introduced in the late nineties, became a permanent institution — especially in the upper circles. circles. Social life was already displaying much greater variety. The coming of electric signs in the great cities seemed to make the nights more glamorous. And naturally dress was affected by this new and more active spirit.

Costume 

Women's costume continued to vary from time to time. When the crinoline disappeared, skirts no longer were prized for their bulk, but merely flared at the bottom, and usually projected into a train, sometimes three yards long. The principal eccentricity was the bustle, which lasted in popularity from the seventies to the nineties. Generally speaking, dress, while no less expensive at this time, was much simpler; and silk was used strictly for lining. For a while in the nineties the wearing of balloon sleeves was the proper thing, and ladies got into jackets with much difficulty. Another uncomfortable fashion (a little later) was the hobble skirt, a skirt so tight at the knee that women sometimes fell in trying to mount a curb or step. But the woman of the early years of the twentieth century was probably more attractive to the eye, even if less comfortable, than the woman 

SUMMARY of Important Concepts of today. Her dress followed the natural curve of her figure and fell to the ankle; her hair was arranged in a high pompadour, and crowned with a large "picture" hat, which, in the case of a woman of means, was often trimmed with ostrich feathers. Sometimes a feather boa encircled the neck. It is to be noted, however, that the coming of readymade clothes made for a general uniformity of design.

Men's costume had long ceased to present variety or interest. The frock coat and silk hat remained the badge of the gentleman; but at least as early as the beginning of the twentieth century these embellishments came to be reserved more and more for formal occasions. Lounge suits and either derbies or soft hats (or straw in summer) came more and more to supplant the frock coat and top hat for everyday wear. With the coming of cheap, readymade clothes, the distinction between classes became even less apparent. In the meantime, men on bicycles wore short breeches, fastened by a buckle below the knee, and loose, belted jackets. For sport the wearing of shorts came into vogue in the late eighties. While the dress suit had long held sway for formal evening dress, the tailless dinner jacket made its appearance at the turn of the century for certain less formal occasions. 

Yet neither of these evening costumes gave any chance at all for variety or even color. 

Only the military uniforms retained the gorgeous hues of an earlier age.

CHAPTER XI International Rivalry in the New Age: 

THE REVIVAL OF IMPERIALISM 

What caused the great nineteenth-century revival of interest in colonial expansion? 

What were the areas in which rivalry for imperial supremacy developed? 

What were the results of clashing imperial interests?

ANOTHER SIDE OF THE HISTORY of this com plex period, the Machine Age, was the extension of European interests into Asia and Africa and the rivalries and conflicts of the great powers over these openings for enrichment. It was the second period of modern imperialism, the first being, you will remember, the expansion of Europe which followed the Great Explorations. In general, the weaker and more backward peoples of the world were helpless to defend themselves, though they did, of course, benefit in certain ways from the influence of a higher civilization. But nothing more clearly demonstrated the dangers that lay in the sentiment of patriotism-overriding overriding the weak and risking conflicts with the strong. as the natives are usually unable to resist the pressure. 

When there is complete political control, the region becomes a colony. Sometimes the native state which has been subdued is allowed an appearance of self-government, its ruler being permitted to keep his throne and to receive a certain homage from his people, but actually having little to do with the governing. This type of colony is known as a protectorate, and is not quite so offensive to native pride as outright annexation. Sometimes, too, a native state is subjected to little interference in the operation of its government, but is compelled to grant to the citizens of a given power certain exclusive economic rights, such as the privilege of building railroads or developing mines. Then we speak of a. Revival of Interest in Imperialism the region where such concessions lie as a 

What Imperialism Is sphere of interest.

We have mentioned imperialism, you may Imperialism as a Tradition remember, as a type of nationalism. It has as its object the political and economic control over regions occupied by relatively backward peoples. So far as we deal with European imperialism, it applies, as a rule, to regions in other continents, such as Asia and

Africa, where there were great natural resources to be tapped. This statement implies that the motives behind imperialism are largely economic, and so they frequently are, though we shall note that political motives sometimes loom as more important. In any case it is necessary for the power pursuing an imperialistic policy to obtain political control over that region whose resources it aims to monopolize, not, as a rule, a difficult matter, You will remember that modern imperialism developed out of the voyages of discovery in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Vast colonial empires came into being, and many struggles were waged for some of the choicest sources of wealth. The British Empire, as we have noticed, passed all others in respect to size as well as importance, and even Napoleon, ardent imperialist that he was, found himself quite unable to match his rival, "perfidious

Albion," as he called her. During much the greater part of the nineteenth century public interest in imperialism noticeably slackened, since nationalism and democracy in Europe were then claiming that continent's attention, and statesmen seemed preoccupied with prob-

RIVALRY IN THE NEW AGE 

lems nearer home.

It was much more due to accident than to any deliberate planning that France acquired Algeria in the thirties, and even the opening of China was the result rather of the difficulties of a trading company than of any deliberate policy of the British government. The British, during this period, seemed to show their contempt for colonies by utilizing Australia as a place for dumping their convicts!

And yet, about the middle of the nineteenth century, there were portents of an imperialistic revival. Napoleon III, who always strove to follow the example of his famous uncle, was very evidently an imperialist, as was evidenced by his interest in the Suez Canal as well as his Mexican expedition. Moreover, thanks to the Industrial Revolution, the industries of Europe were turning out commodities in ever-increasing volume, and business now clamored for new fields of opportunity. Finally, the great revival of science in the nineteenth century led to an exceptionally keen interest in exploration, and explorers from various countries flocked to Africa to force their way into its dark, unopened interior.

The exploits of these explorers had much to do with rousing public interest in distant lands. When the explorer, Henry M. Stanley, went in search of his fellow-explorer, David Livingstone, who was lost somewhere in the jungles of South Africa, the public interest became intense; and the success of 

Stanley's mission became the leading topic of the day. The age-old spirit of adventure seemed now to be kindled anew. Close on the heels of explorers came the missionaries, and, following them, the merchants. The way was undoubtedly paved for a great revival of imperialism. Let us now examine the motives which impelled national governments to embark on such a movement. 

Motives of Imperialism 

The motives were of two sorts, economic and political. They were economic in so far as there were people in various countries seeking new fields of investment, great manufacturing concerns looking for raw materials or new markets, and national governments Oil hoping for new sources of food supply that would render the nations in their charge more self-sufficient. In general, it was only small groups who really profited from such adventures. Yet the popularity of bicycles, and later automobiles, later automobiles, inevitably produced a great demand for rubber to make tires; and in this respect the public also gained. was another commodity in great demand, and here again certain remote countries could meet the need. But colonies soon proved to be expensive, for there were natives to be subdued, and often governments shouldered the great expense of making them profitable fields of investment. In the end it was the taxpayer who carried most of the burden; and scholars seem to agree that most colonies do not pay.

It was, however, the political and sentimental motives that chiefly accounted for the public interest. Patriotic people like the 

Germans wanted colonies so that emigrants would have a place to go and yet remain Germans. Colonies would enable Germany to conserve her man power instead of seeing it steadily dribble to other countries. Moreover, Germany and Italy were young nations which felt it to be necessary to their prestige to construct great colonial empires after the example of their older rivals. Each nation wanted to spread over more of the globe as a means of demonstrating its greatness. Then, too, each nation longed to bring its peculiar brand of civilization to backward peoples. 

Imperialism was represented as a civilizing mission. As with nationalism in general, vanity or self-interest was the motive force behind this new imperialism. 

Now how have imperial powers treated their colonies? Let us survey from this standpoint the leading world powers; and then perhaps we can decide whether they deserved to be the guardians of backward peoples. 

B. How the Leading World Powers Treated Their Colonies 

Great Britain

Great Britain acquired most of her enormous empire before the period we are now considering. By 1875 she had possessions in

every corner of the world, and today the British Empire covers at least a quarter of the world and contains a quarter of its population. Generally speaking, the empire was composed of two types of colonies: dominions and crown colonies.

The dominions were not, properly speaking, colonies at all. They were entirely selfgoverning; for all intents and purposes independent. A governor-general represented the Crown, to emphasize the allegiance to the imperial bond, but his position was hardly more than ceremonial. The dominions in 

1914 were Canada, Newfoundland (which later ceased to be a dominion), Australia, New 

Zealand, and the Union of South Africa.

Most colonies where the native population was predominant were commonly known as crown colonies, and were treated in various ways. Some, like those in the West Indies, had limited self-government; others, mainly in the tropics, were managed by chartered companies, which took the full responsibility of governing them, until, as in most cases, they were directly taken over by the government. 

There were also numerous protectorates. 

Egypt, as we shall see, was virtually in that class, though it was not regarded as a permanent possession.

British India was the chief example of a colony in the hands of a chartered company until the government found it necessary to take it over. The East India Company had abused its powerful position by swindling the

Under him, and often exercising a good deal of discretionary power, was the viceroy. But not all of India was under his jurisdiction. About a third was composed of various protectorates, some of them very rich, but subject to the control of British "advisers." The British government kept a permanent army in India, consisting of native soldiers (known as "Sepoys") under British commanders.

India is a country, between one third and one half the size of Europe, with an immense population, which numbers nearly 350,000,- 000. The mass of the people still live in the country and are very poor and ignorant. 

These people can hardly be called a nationality. There are over two hundred languages alone; and religiously and socially the population is hopelessly divided. There are some 70,000,000 Mohammedans, 11,000,- 000 Buddhists, perhaps 5,000,000 Christians, as well as several hundred thousands belonging to lesser sects. ing to lesser sects. But as many as 200,000,000 profess a religion known as Hinduism, which had its origins in India and is centuries old. 

These religious differences make for mutual dislike, and Mohammedans and Hindus cor-

Why does England need an army in India? How does it happen that some of the troops are natives? dially detest one another. There is also among these natives a caste system, according to which an individual belongs to a certain grade or lot in life and cannot possibly rise above it. There are literally hundreds of these castes, the origins of many of which are still unknown; and there are also people so low as to belong to no caste at all. The feeling between these castes is much too strong to admit of unity. The highest caste of all, which, of course, looks down on all the others, is a group known as the Brahmins. They are intellectuals, proud of their ancient Hindu civilization, but interested in the spiritual and philosophical rather than in the practical things of life. Most Orientals, though the 

Japanese are an exception, have little or no conception of the art of government. It was because of this fact, and still more because of the inner divisions along religious and social lines, that British rule in India seemed amply justified. And though little was done for the natives as compared with the profits that passed into British hands, yet the fact of holding down such an enormous population was a prodigious feat.

British imperialism, like the imperialism of other countries, has its bad and its good side. 

The pioneers who came to North America in the early days had little sympathy for the Indians and unmercifully despoiled them. A thoughtless disregard for native feelings in British India led to a serious rising in 1857, known as the Sepoy Rebellion, which was ruthlessly suppressed. Yet, in general, though the Englishman may not grasp the native viewpoint, he tries to do him justice, and, on the whole, British imperialism has been a civilizing force. It has brought law and order to many lands, and its sea power has done much to suppress the slave trade and to exterminate piracy. Moreover, outside of the dominions, who are able to do as they please, the British Empire was just as free to the commerce of foreign countries as to that of the mother country itself, though naturally most of the trade was with the latter. 

What holds this vast empire together?

In

particular, what keeps these full-grown children, the dominions, still tied to Mother 

Britannia's apron strings? Before the First

World War there were periodic conferences in London, attended by representatives of the dominions for the purpose of consultation with British ministers. Chamberlain, who sponsored this experiment, was anxious to convert the empire into an economic unit with tariffs against the rest of the world, but with very low tariffs between the mother country and the dominions. The project failed, however, since the people at home did not want to give up free trade. In any case, commerce serves as a unifying bond; and the empire is also a favorite field of investment for British capital. 

Great Britain feels great pride in the dominions, and the dominions feel a warm attachment to the mother country. The strength of the empire lies not so much in political organization as in common commercial interests and a common loyalty to the Crown. 

In other words, the ties are economic and sentimental. But we are thinking, rather, of the dominions than of the crown colonies.

With the latter, the chief link has been an efficient civil service, the quality of which, especially in India, has probably no equal today. France

France had lost most of her colonies in the Seven Years' War; and the creation of a new empire, almost eleven times the size of the mother country, was one of the greatest achievements of the Third Republic. The government of this empire has been largely a matter of experiment, and there is none of that uniformity that one finds in the government of the French Republic itself. Some of the colonies were given representation in the French parliament, but, except for a very limited amount of self-government in two of them, all to this day are autocratically governed. Algeria came to have a peculiar position, for, while treated as a colony in some respects, it is also governed as part of France itself, being divided into departments just like France. Very often the colonies have been the victims of indifference, for in spite of a certain pride in their colonial empire, Frenchmen do not let their attention wander very far from home. Those colonies which have benefited most owe this fact, as a rule, to the governors they have had.

In commercial matters France has been ungenerous to her colonies; for the products which they send to the mother country pay a duty. The growers of beet sugar in France itself do not want the competition of cane sugar from the colonies; and the colonies are thus restricted in their market, particularly as tariffs tend to limit their trade with foreign countries. This deliberate sacrifice of colonial interests to those of the mother country reminds one of mercantilism. The treatment of the French Congo, ruthlessly exploited for the benefit of a few companies, affords another example of the greed which often underlies imperialism. Yet Frenchmen have a knack of getting along with backward races. and are likely to understand them rather better than the British.

Two Newcomers in the Colonial Field - Italy and Germany

Italy and Germany entered the colonial scramble late, and were therefore forced to put up with what was left. Italy started her empire in the region of the Red Sea, and her colonies were almost worthless and much too hot to tempt the Italian emigrant. But she tried to make the best of a bad situation, and succeeded at great expense in giving these colonies something of a future.

Germany had somewhat the same experience.

The colonies she acquired, whether in Africa or in the Far East, were not profitable. 

Those which possessed resources were uninhabitable by white men; those which were fairly habitable were almost worthless. Most of them were left for chartered companies to exploit, and the natives, as a rule, fared badly. 

After a time the government pursued a more enlightened policy, and much was done to interest the German public in colonial development.

Powers Whose Imperial Expansion Merely In volved the Extension of the Frontiers- 

Austria and Russia

Austria and Russia were world powers in the sense that they extended their power or

influence into undeveloped countries, but, unlike the other powers we have mentioned, their expansion was merely an extension of their frontiers. Austria, bordering the Balkans, came to look upon this peninsula as a market easily available for her products and her capital; and her efforts to play a leading rôle there will be noted later. 

Russia had early expanded into the trans- Caspian region and Siberia, and soon she cherished the ambition to obtain additional outlets on the sea, as, for example, on the 

Pacific, or the Persian Gulf. Russia also wished to loom as a great power; and largely 

Asiatic, she felt herself predestined to assume a commanding position in Asia. But her record of achievement was not distinguished.

Although Siberia is a land of considerable promise, she had little capital to expend, and she did little for the natives themselves beyond keeping them in order. Her general policy was, rather, to retard the development of the Orient, hoping thereby to keep it weak and easier to handle.

We must now give our attention to the chief areas of exploitation which attracted these five great world powers. c. Asia as an Area of Exploitation 

China and Its Importance

The old Chinese Empire was largely fashioned by physical geography. Ranges of mountains, some of them very high, almost completely enclosed it on three sides, the fourth side being the Pacific. The greater part of this empire was, however, very poor and sparsely populated. High plateaus and deserts covered most of it. The only productive portions were China proper and some of the eastern outlying regions, such as Manchuria. 

China proper is a country of great resources. 

Her soil is very fertile, and, though the rice grown is chiefly for needs at home, much of the land is devoted to the raising of tea and cotton. There are also extensive beds of coal and iron.

Ever since 1644, the Chinese Empire had been ruled by princes of a foreign race known as Manchus, a very unpopular dynasty, which made the Chinese people wear the pigtail as a sign of their subjection. Unlike the rest of the empire, which was very loosely controlled, China proper, or China of the Eighteen Provinces, as it was often called, was directly managed by the central government at Peking. Yet even here government was very lax and inefficient. The Emperor, the "son of Heaven," as he was called, was treated somewhat as a god, who never stooped to concern himself with the worldly affairs of his realm. His principal duty, in fact, was to pray to Heaven for his subjects. Various councils acted in his name, and the whole machinery of government was in the hands of a civil service, admission to which depended upon a knowledge of Chinese classics, such as philosophy and music. These mandarins, as they were called, seldom showed any fitness to govern, and were notoriously corrupt. The amount that was raised in taxes was generally as much as the collectors could extort from a patient and long-suffering population. Up to a certain point people seemed to be willing to be fleeced, and as the central government was weak, the mandarins made the most of their opportunities.

The population of the Chinese Empire was believed to number four hundred million souls, though no census has ever been taken. 

Most of this vast horde, about ninety-seven per cent, was concentrated, however, in the 

Eighteen Provinces, especially those along the Pacific and in the valley of the Yangtze- Kiang. The masses were hard-working, and, as a rule, very peaceably inclined, but superstitious, like most Orientals, and densely ignorant. Ancestor worship was the leading feature of their religion, a custom which probably arose out of the strong family feeling which had always characterized the Chinese. 

They also believed implicitly in evil spirits. 

If one's hat blew off, it was the work of an evil spirit. If one tripped and fell, the cause was the same. The Chinese invented fireworks in order to light up the darkness as a protection against evil spirits. Of course, the great majority of the Chinese had little or no notion of the comforts or decencies of life, and were, in fact, miserably poor. Their condition is suggested in the picture on page 249. 

Famines and floods were frequent, and the

congestion of the population added greatly to the number of dead when such calamities occurred. But the sleepy Chinese government knew little of how to improve the lot of the people, and in any case preferred to let things drift.

The Opening of China 

For a long time practically the only port open to Western commerce was that of Canton; and even there trade suffered from burdensome restrictions, as well as from the systematic grafting of the provincial mandarins. 

Knowing no other culture but her own, China regarded the rest of the world as distinctly inferior to herself, and spoke of foreigners in general as "barbarians."

The central government, therefore, did not want any trade with the West, and persistently repulsed all efforts at an understanding. Unfortunately, Unfortunately, however, its authority was very weak, and the provincial mandarins saw a chance of lining their own pockets by allowing some trade to go on, provided it paid them a heavy toll. 

Moreover, they liked to smoke opium, which was the commodity chiefly imported by foreign merchants. Though there were many causes of friction, and though the pressure of Western business interests would certainly, sooner or later, have forced the Chinese to submission, it was an energetic attempt of the imperial government to bar opium that provoked the crisis which led to the opening of China.

By Great Britain, who enjoyed most of the trade with China, began the struggle known as the Opium War in 1840. As China was easily humbled, Great Britain seized the opportunity to put trade on a better footing. the Treaty of Nanking (1842), five Chinese ports were opened to British commerce, and the amount of the tariff was fixed. Later, China conceded that a Britisher who was charged with any offense might be tried under

Soon other powers obtained by treaty the same political and economic advantages as Great Britain; and foreigners were allowed to enjoy what was known as a concession in the treaty ports; that is, quarters occupied by foreigners who were permitted to govern themselves on payment of rent to the Chinese authorities. By the Treaty of Nanking, Great 

Britain had also secured (for the better protection of her trade) the island of Hongkong, and later, for purposes of defense, she acquired the tip of the peninsula on the adjacent mainland.

Except for a slight foothold at Macao, held by the Portuguese since 1537, this was the first encroachment on the mainland of 

China proper.

It was a new experience for China to have to let in the hated "barbarians" from the

West, and as the central government was usually too weak to compel the provincial mandarins to respect the treaties, there was nothing for the Western powers to do but resort to force again. Hence, a second war with 

China was fought from 1857 to 1860, in which both France and Great Britain were engaged. 

This time a foreign army approached the sacred city of Peking; and when the Chinese tried their favorite trick of dragging out the negotiations, one of the Emperor's summer palaces was burned by British orders. After this experience new treaties were signed with. 

China. More ports were opened, as well as the Yangtze-Kiang as far as Hankow. Missionaries also were allowed a wider field for their activities. One of the greatest gains was the establishment of permanent legations at
