It is clear that China was helpless against the physical might of the West. Now and then missionaries were murdered (sometimes for exceeding their legal rights), and always China was forced to pay indemnities and sometimes to open further ports. Already, too, the greed of Western imperialism was becoming apparent. Taking advantage of internal disorder, as well as the second war with China, Russia, in 1860, extorted the province of Maritime Manchuria, which gave her a solid footing on the Pacific. Later, France forced a protectorate over a part of Indo-China, and in 1885, after a brief war, compelled China to recognize this conquest. 

The following year, Great Britain wantonly seized Burma. None of these regions had any real ties with China beyond the payment of occasional tribute; but would 

Western powers remain content with just lopping off these outlying regions of the empire? Such seizures might well be portents of danger to China proper. Moreover, France had secured some special economic rights close to the border of her new colony, Indo-China.

But before the Western powers were able to bore any farther into China, another power appeared on the scene as a competitor for the rich spoils of imperialism. 

The Opening and Transformation of Japan 

The Japanese were an island people, inhabiting a land which is mountainous and not very fertile. Earthquakes, plagues, and wars had for centuries served to keep down population. Japan's civilization was largely a borrowing from China; but while the Chinese paid honor to their scholars, the Japanese glorified the warrior. Up to the middle of the nineteenth century this island people knew little of the West, for before that time only the Dutch had traded with Japan, and they had been confined to one small island. The 

Japanese, like the Chinese, did not want any closer relations with the West. (Their life before Western civilization touched the Japanese can be seen in paintings like the one reproduced on page 252.)

But in the nineteenth century it was hard for any people to preserve its isolation. It so happened that American whalers were often wrecked on the Japanese coast, and if captured they were imprisoned and sometimes tortured. To stop this sort of thing, as well as to open commercial relations, if possible, with Japan, the United States sent Commodore Perry with a fleet and a message to the Japanese ruler (the Mikado), as well as many presents. The Japanese were terrified when they saw these modern warships; but they longed to know more of the wonderful things which the Western world had produced. After leaving them for a year to think things over, Perry returned in 1854, and a commercial treaty was signed. Other nations soon followed this country's example. Thus Japan was opened to Western influence. 

The immediate effect on Japan of this contact with the West was overwhelming. The 

Japanese are an alert and adaptable people, and they made up their minds to learn the ways of the West and to make themselves a strong and progressive nation. Accordingly they sent missions both to Europe and to the United States in order to study Western ways; and in an incredibly short time they not only did away with the feudal privileges of the upper classes but remodeled both the government and the army. The country passed through a deep transformation — one might say a revolution. Though retaining the essential features of her own civilization, Japan, unlike China, welcomed at once the practical knowledge that was obtainable from the West. (What evidences that Japan quickly adopted Western ways can you find in the picture on page 253?)

Evolution of Japanese Imperialism 

But Japan, as she grew in power and selfconfidence, was not content with her islands. 

Indeed, a population of over sixty million, cooped up in this narrow space, could scarcely subsist without importing much of its food from the mainland. Besides, as time went on, Japan became more and more industrialized, and the need of China both as a market and

China, it was natural enough that Japan, who was next door, should speedily become a competitor. Furthermore, Japan was near enough to the continent to be threatened by any strong power that managed to get possession of Korea. Korea was to Japan as Belgium was to Great Britain: a first line of defense.

To control and possess this neighboring state, then in a sort of vassalage to the Chinese Emperor, was a matter of life and death. 

Thus, the motives behind Japanese expansion to the continent were partly economic and partly political. But they were not wholly defensive. Japan was eager to exploit the natural resources of the mainland, and she developed in the course of time an ambition to become the dominant power in the Far East. Thus, unlike England, she proposed to become a continental power. 

The first important goal of Japanese imperialism was Korea. The Koreans did not like the Japanese and relied on China to pro-

With the definite withdrawal of China from Korea, the first obstacle in the path of Japanese imperialism had been removed.

But there was still Russia; and Russia was the power that the Japanese really feared.

In order to steal a march on her, Japan had exacted from China the lease of the Liaotung

Up to 1897, no power had staked anything off in China, if we except some special privileges which France had gained in the south. 

But in that year, two German missionaries lost their lives in the province of Shantung, a province so rich in resources, and so important because of its position near Peking, that one might almost imagine that these missionaries had courted death. Immediately the German Emperor talked belligerently of the "yellow peril." A fleet was hurried to the 

Pacific, and China was forced to lease to 

Germany a port on the bay of Kiaochow for ninety-nine years. Germany also secured the right to build railroads in the province of tung Peninsula. France, also in the plot, leased a port; and Great Britain, not to be left out, did likewise. Soon afterward all these powers entered into agreements by which each staked off for itself a sphere of interest, acquiring a virtual monopoly of the natural resources therein. The principle of the open door- that is, commercial equality for all and special advantages for none seemed to be challenged. Western capital poured into

China; and various foreign companies got concessions to build railroads.

Chinese nationalism was at last aroused against the "barbarian" despoilers. After six weeks of suspense, during which the foreign legations were closely besieged, an international army entered Peking, and, as usual, China was forced to pay heavy indemnities as well as to suffer various other humiliations. Thus, instead of winning deliverance, the Chinese felt their chains made even tighter. A weak Oriental state had apparently no right to protect its interests. tionalism was not for the semi-civilized. Na- But in some ways China was materially aided by Western imperialism. Just as the lessons of her calamities had led the imperial government to try to reform her institutions, so the people themselves began to feel the enlightened influence of the West. Many barbarous customs disappeared, while medical science and modern sanitation brought benefits to millions. It would be a long time before the great mass of the population could be raised to a higher level, but now that a beginning had been made, progress was likely to be steady. Thus, with Western capital and 

Western bullying had come a taste of Western civilization. In 1912, the imperial Manchu dynasty was overthrown, and China became a republic. It was then that the Chinese dared to cut their pigtails. But unhappily they proved incapable of developing a unified state; and the country has been in periodic disorder ever since.

And now let us move farther west and consider some other native states. 

The Middle East 

Some of the great continent of Asia lay outside the field of international strife. Siberia and the trans-Caspian region were already Russia's, and no one disputed Great Britain's right to India or France's right to the bulk of Indo-China. Siam managed to keep her in-

INTERNATIONAL 

255 

RIVALRY IN THE NEW AGE 

dependence because she served as a convenient buffer between the British in India and the French in Indo-China. But the 

Middle East, comprising chiefly Afghanistan and Persia, was once a bone of contention, since during the second half of the nineteenth century the British had feared a Russian attack on India. It was not till 1907 that 

Russia and Great Britain came to an amicable agreement and that that fear was apparently dispelled.

But Persia still remained an object of attraction. Because of its geographical position this land was readily open to Russian penetration, and at one time Russia had hoped to obtain access to the Indian Ocean, where a "port on a hot sea" might be secured. The British had, in the meantime, developed interests on the Persian Gulf, and were later attracted to 

Persia by its immense supplies of oil. To both powers Persia was heavily indebted, since the rulers, known as shahs, had steadily mortgaged the resources of their kingdom in order to maintain themselves in luxury. Persia was thus an easy prey for imperialism. 

Up to 1907, Russia was the dominant power in Persia, and her policy was to keep Persia weak and undeveloped. In 1907, Russia and 

Great Britain reached an agreement (already mentioned), and for the next few years they worked together in the exploitation of Persia. 

When the Persians tried to free themselves from their bondage to these two great powers, Russia, with British approval, intervened, and in 1912, Persia became little more than a vassal state of her powerful northern neighbor.

It was only in the south and adjoining India that British sway was maintained. 

Finally, we come to the Near East, in which many powers were interested, as we shall see. 

The Near East 

The Near East comprised the Asiatic dominions of the Ottoman Empire as well as the Balkan Peninsula in Europe, popularly known as "the Balkans." Most of the Ottoman

Empire was now in Asia, but much of this desert country was very loosely controlled by the sultans. Up to 1878, Turkey also held the heart of the Balkan Peninsula, but the new Christian states, such as Serbia and Rumania, were thenceforth bound to play an important part in the history of this region. 

The Balkan Peninsula, unless we include Rumania, was not economically valuable, but its geographical position made it very important. Russia, for example, wished to control the Bosporus and the Dardanelles Straits in order to be sure of access to the Mediterranean; and Germany, as we shall see, eventually tried to enter Asia at Constantinople. 

Austria-Hungary longed for a port on the 

Aegean. Asiatic Turkey had mineral wealth and oil; and Mesopotamia, the part watered by the two great rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates, might easily be developed into cotton land. But, except for a few French and 

British railways running a short distance inland from the Mediterranean, little had been done to open this vast and promising region. 

In the meantime, we must jump to another continent, which before the present period had been least developed of all. The opening and partition of Africa were among the greatest achievements of modern imperialism. 

D.

Africa as a Field of Exploitation 

The Case of the Congo 

Africa was opened, as we have noticed, by explorers. The basin of the Congo River, chiefly valuable for its rubber, was one of the prizes most sought, and Leopold, King of the Belgians, was the one to lead in the scramble. 

At a conference of several powers at Berlin in 1885, the bulk of the Congo Basin was recognized as the Congo Free State, with Leopold himself as sovereign; but the principle of the open door was solemnly affirmed, and measures were taken to prevent the innocent natives from being oppressed. Unfortunately no regard was shown for any of these guarantees. The resources of the state became a monopoly of the King of the Belgians; the rubber was exploited to the point of exhaustion; and the natives were brutally treated. So great was the scandal of the 

Congo that the region ultimately became a Belgian colony, and conditions henceforth improved. But the experience had shown that the powers as a collective body lacked the force to protect their interests.

The General Scramble 

Meanwhile, the scramble for territory in Africa had proceeded. In 1881, France extended a protectorate over Tunis, and in 1885, she acquired the island of Madagascar, as well as French Equatorial Africa, a portion of the Congo Basin near the mouth of that river. 

Great Britain, in 1882, occupied Egypt under circumstances later to be noted (see page 257), and she extended her possessions on both the western and eastern coasts. Germany and 

Italy also entered the field at about the same time. Bismarck's lack of interest was overcome by public pressure, and he acquired in turn German Southwest Africa, German East

Africa, and Togo and Kamerun on the Guinea Coast (as well as some islands in the Pacific). 

Italy got a foothold on the Red Sea, which became the colony of Eritrea, and later she secured Benadir (Italian Somaliland) on the Indian Ocean and Tripoli (since called Libya) on the Mediterranean.

There was comparatively little rivalry for these prizes, since the continent seemed to be large enough for all. As in China, agreements were made by which the powers staked off their various spheres of interest. There was also little resistance from the natives, since most of the people in Africa were savage races, lacking in organization, and having only the most primitive weapons.

There was, however, one exception to this rule. Abyssinia or Ethiopia was a state with traditions and a people that was higher in civilization than the Negroes of the tropical belt or the wild tribesmen of the desert. When 

Italy undertook to scale the heights of Ethiopia, she met with disastrous defeat in the battle of Adowa (1896) and was forced to withdraw to her sandy, inhospitable footing on the Red Sea.

The Shadow of Coming Trouble 

But there were still other stakes in Africa to be sought. The sultanate of Morocco, in the northwestern corner of Africa, was important for its position at the entrance of the Mediterranean, as well as for its good grazing land and certain minerals, such as iron ore. 

For these reasons, and because of its nearness to Algeria, the power chiefly interested was 

France. Near the southern end of the continent were two republics settled by Boers, as they were called. These Boers were Dutch who had originally dwelt at the Cape of Good Hope, but had tired of British rule, and had trekked into the interior. These states would become important if ever their diamonds and gold were discovered. Thus imperialism had still some things to win.

As long as Africa seemed large enough for each to have its share, there had been no serious friction between the powers. But as the field narrowed and the prizes became fewer and possibly more valuable, rivalry was sure to develop. Moreover, watered by the 

Upper Nile and particularly adapted for raising cotton was a region, known as the Sudan, in which the two powers most concerned had not come to any agreement as to the limits of their spheres of interest. It was the rivalry for this territory that nearly produced a war. It is now time to relate the story of clashes between the powers for some of the choice stakes of imperialism. 

E. The Clash of Interests 

As imperialism led naturally to keener rivalries and even came to include a vigorous Asiatic power, the danger of war proportionately increased. Indeed, one of these clashes was actually to lead to war, as we shall see. 

Moreover, there was always the chance that the powers might in the end become so involved that a war in some locality would engulf them all.

FRANCE VERSUS GREAT BRITAIN- EGYPT AND THE UPPER NILE AS STAKES 

An Old Feud Revived

Anglo-French rivalry was nothing new, for Great Britain and France had repeatedly fought over colonies and commerce. In this period of revived imperialism, they were again the leading colonial powers, and perhaps it was only natural that they should quarrel. 

We shall not take space to relate all these squabbles, which were many and sometimes bitter. But we shall give our attention to the

stake of principal importance namely, Egypt. But France was passing through a Egypt.

The Case of Egypt 

Egypt was a land of great economic value. 

It was excellent cotton country, for the river Nile overflowed annually to deposit rich soil along its banks and thus give this land a wonderful fertility. More than that, Egypt 

More than that, Egypt commanded the short route to the East. If a canal should be cut through the narrow isthmus of Suez, most of Europe's commerce with the East would pass through it instead of taking the long route round the Cape of Good Hope. Great Britain, as the leading commercial power, was bound to be interested in Egypt.

But France had cherished designs on Egypt first. Napoleon, you may remember, had at one time tried to appropriate it for France; and French interest continued undiminished in the nineteenth century. We have mentioned the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869. 

Though the capital for this enterprise had been furnished by many persons, French, British, and Egyptians, France had taken the leading rôle in the affair.

Egypt belonged by right to the Sultan of Turkey, but it was ruled by a prince called the khedive, who simply paid annual tribute to the Sultan. The khedives, like many rulers of backward states, managed to live in elegant style on borrowed money, and the one who ruled at the time the canal was dug had borrowed so much from European bankers that he finally found that he could no longer pay the interest especially as his affairs were badly handled. Hence, in 1876, France and 

Great Britain formed a partnership to take over the Egyptian finances in order that the bondholders might get their interest. But in 

1881 a young Egyptian, Arabi Pasha, told his people that foreign powers were trying to put their country in bondage. The result was a fierce revolt, in the course of which a number of Europeans lost their lives.

This was clearly the time for France and Great Britain to intervene if they wanted to protect the interests of people who had invested in Egyptian bonds, as well as to safeguard the lives and property of foreigners in Al- cabinet crisis, one of her frequent changes of ministries, and consequently held back. So 

Great Britain acted alone. She sent a naval force which bombarded Egyptian ports and landed an army which soon put down the rebellion. Then she decided to stay in Egypt, to "restore order," as she explained. though she promised to leave as soon as this task was accomplished, she never kept her promise, and established what was practically a protectorate over Egypt. She did, however, allow the canal to be opened to the trade of the world, and meanwhile stationed a British force to protect it. Great Britain did much for Egypt, not only in keeping order, but in promoting its agricultural prosperity. 

The Fashoda Crisis 

France was bitter when she found that Egypt had slipped through her fingers, and her relations with Great Britain became very prickly. The two powers had many disputes over adjusting their claims in Africa, and it looked as if this friction might ultimately end in war. When, in 1885, as the result of a native uprising, Egypt lost her southern province, known as the Egyptian Sudan,

France thought that she might step in, take over this region, and extend French influence in an unbroken line from Senegal on the 

Atlantic to French Somaliland on the Red

Sea. This plan, as a matter of fact, clashed with a British plan of extending British influence all the way from Cairo to the Cape of 

Good Hope. The point of intersection was the region of the Upper Nile. 

The thrilling story of the race for the Upper Nile is too long to relate here in any detail, but the British were much aroused when a brilliant French officer, Captain Marchand, with a force principally of natives, hacked his way through tropical jungles and in September, 1898, reached the village of Fashoda on the Nile. Great Britain, meanwhile, had sent a large force to recover the Sudan, and the native revolt had been crushed; but the 

British commander, Kitchener, was much surprised when he suddenly came upon Marchand at Fashoda. Each officer raised his flag over the town, but they were sensible

IN THE NEW AGE INTERNATIONAL RIVALRY 

enough to avoid coming to blows, leaving the question for the home governments to decide. 

Public opinion was much inflamed on both sides. After an acute crisis, however, France backed down and recalled Marchand, chiefly because she decided that the question was not worth a war. The boundary was then fixed between the British and French spheres, with the British in control of the Upper Nile. 

RUSSIA VERSUS JAPAN-MANCHURIA AND KOREA AS STAKES 

The Advance of Russia in the Far East 

You will remember that the powers had pounced upon China and had carved out spheres of interest. The Russian sphere was north of the Great Wall, which long ago had been built to protect China from invaders. 

During the Boxer Rebellion, Russia had sent an army into Manchuria; and after the trouble was over, she seemed in no hurry to withdraw. 

The Trans-Siberian Railroad, which completed in 1902, showed that she meant to make the most of her strong position on the 

Pacific. With Dalny, a commercial port, and

Port Arthur, a naval base, she had at last secured outlets on a "hot sea"; and a railway through Manchuria linked them with the Trans-Siberian line. Manchuria itself was fairly rich country, and, regardless of China, Russia seemed to be treating it as her own. 

Next she began to edge into Korea, gaining the right to cut timber on the frontier and also negotiating for a port.

One can imagine the fears of Japan as she saw the Great Bear moving ever nearer to her shores and threatening to exclude her from the mainland. Two imperialisms were now about to collide.

The Anglo-Japanese Alliance 

But Japan was wary, for she knew that 

Russia had friends. Fortunately for her,

Great Britain was an old enemy of Russia. 

Their rivalry, as we know, had run through all the history of the Near and Middle East, and Great Britain did not like to see Russia in a position where she could force her will upon China. So, in 1902, Japan formed an alliance with Great Britain, and it was agreed that, if either were attacked by two powers, the other would come to its aid. Japan felt now quite sure that France would not venture to give any aid to Russia in the event of war, and she was not afraid of meeting Russia alone.

The Russo-Japanese War- Japan Becomes Su preme in the Western Pacific

Having finally decided on war, Japan launched an attack on Russia early in February, 1904, while the latter's fleet was still icebound in the Russian port of Vladivostok.

Japanese troops occupied Korea and then pressed into Manchuria. While it is true that Russia's army was larger than that of Japan, it was not so well commanded, and it was forced to travel thousands of miles to reach the theater of war. Japan had the advantage of nearness to the spot and in both organizing skill and fighting spirit she quite outclassed her enemy. In the end she was able to defeat the Russian fleets, clear all of southern Manchuria, and take Port Arthur.

But these efforts had quite exhausted her, and she was glad when Russia, seriously threatened by revolution at home, decided to end the The treaty of peace was signed in the town of Portsmouth, in New Hampshire, under the guiding hand of President Theodore 

war.

The war was thus closed in 1905 by the Treaty of Portsmouth. Japan secured the lease of the Liaotung Peninsula, as well as the southern half of the island of Sakhalin; and 

Russia withdrew entirely from southern Manchuria, which was henceforth regarded as a Japanese sphere of interest. Russia also yielded to Japan "paramount influence” in Korea. The second stone in the path of Japanese imperialism had been removed. amine the cartoon on page 259 to see how a British paper regarded this struggle.) (Ex- Though Japan repeatedly promised to respect the independence of Korea, she soon established a protectorate over that country, and in 1910 annexed it. Now at last she had gained a solid footing on the continent. Save for the sphere in northern Manchuria, Russian imperialism had quite receded to the frozen land of Siberia. land of Siberia. Japan was now the sentinel

of the western Pacific- 

able to warn off other powers and to play a decisive part in the Far East.

GERMANY VERSUS GREAT BRITAIN- SOUTH AFRICA AS A STAKE The Triple and Dual Alliances 

While Japan was the great military power of the East, Germany was the great military power of the West. Bismarck had made her unquestionably the strongest power in Europe; for, aside from her excellent army, he had formed the Triple Alliance - Germany, Aus tria, and Italy -in 1882, and also maintained cordial relations with Russia. Even with 

Great Britain, who usually held aloof from the Continent, he kept on friendly terms. France, who was supposed to be Germany's natural enemy, was quite isolated and friendless, as 

Bismarck had intended. 

But in 1890, Germany "dropped her pilot."

The new Emperor was not the sort of person to get along with so forceful a personality as 

Bismarck, and the old chancellor was driven into retirement. In 1892 France succeeded in making a defensive alliance with Russia - the so-called Dual Alliance. One wonders if this would have happened if the Iron Chancellor had still been at the helm.

Yet, though France's isolation was ended, the Triple Alliance was the stronger of the two combinations. Germany was certainly strong enough for defense, and, if she pursued a cautious policy and confined her interests to Europe, she had nothing to fear for the future. 

Unhappily for her, German imperialism was entering upon a new and ambitious stage.

A New Note in German Imperialism 

William II, who succeeded his father as 

German Emperor, in 1888, was a man of some shrewdness but very impetuous and flighty. He had none of Bismarck's caution, and he was ambitious to make the greatness of Germany felt throughout the world. was not that he thirsted for war, but he was conscious of Germany's power, and he meant that that power should be feared. In 1900, he launched a naval program which made Germany second only to Great Britain on the It dirty Va 10.

Such talk aroused the fears of the Mistress of the Seas. Great Britain was already jealous of Germany's great commercial advance, and now she wondered if Germany meant to challenge her long supremacy on the sea.

There was also evidence that the Kaiser, as William II was usually called, had great hopes for German imperialism.

To this young sovereign the colonial empire which Bismarck had amassed seemed a very sorry spoil. There was nothing that any 

German could be proud of. William must find for Germany a "place in the sun," as one of his chancellors put it. Yet as he looked at the world of his day, the prospect was anything but promising. The Monroe Doctrine was a barrier to German expansion in America. 

It was something, of course, to get a foothold

And William came to realize, too, that the older powers, those which already rejoiced in great empires, were not content to rest with what they had. Imperialism reared its head on every side. So where was the Kaiser to find his "place in the sun"?

The Race for South Africa 

The first opening seemed to present itself in South Africa. The Boer republics, long on very bad terms with the British, were disposed to look to the Kaiser as their patron. He sent to the president of the Transvaal, one of the republics, numerous decorations and many words of encouragement. Now, the Transvaal was perhaps the choicest region in all Africa- not only because of its climate, but because of its gold and diamond mines. 

Unfortunately for Germany, the British also had cast their eyes on lands so marvelously rich. Many British adventurers had swarmed into these states, and the Boers did not like it, since they were afraid that they might lose their dominant position. When, in 1895, a certain Doctor Jameson made an unauthorized raid into the Transvaal, the Boers captured his force. The British government, which was innocent in the matter, was much embarrassed; but the Kaiser was simply furious. Although his advisers succeeded in dissuading him from declaring a protectorate over the Boers, he sent President Kruger of the

Transvaal a telegram of congratulation for having successfully repelled the invaders. 

British public opinion was at once aroused, and though the Kaiser was a grandson of Queen 

Victoria, he was always disliked after that.

Such a challenge, without naval power to back it, was just a stupid exhibition of bad temper. 

Thus the Kaiser did not get the Boer republics. Friction between Great Britain and the 

Boers finally reached a climax in the Boer 

War (1899-1902), and after breaking a stubborn resistance, Great Britain annexed the republics. Then, wisely enough, she made them into a dominion, the Union of South Africa, which has ever since been governed by the Boers themselves. 

GERMANY VERSUS FRANCE-MOROCCO AS A STAKE, AND THE RISE OF THE TRIPLE ENTENTE The Entente Cordiale and the Case of Morocco 

Germany had lost one chance, and her jealousy of Great Britain greatly increased. 

When Great Britain, weary of isolation and mindful of her recent rivalry with France, tried to make a friend of Germany, the Kaiser would have none of it. Only if Great Britain would submit to Germany's terms would he welcome any advances. He had, however, committed a very serious blunder, for Great Britain, rebuffed by Germany, now turned to France.

Both these powers had come to feel that 

Germany was a very dangerous neighbor; and, forgetting their old grudges, they entered into an agreement, known as the Entente Cordiale,

Germany: "Ouch! I thought it was paper and it seems to be stone." How did Germany stub her toe in 1911? How long did this friendly understanding between France and Great Britain continue? in 1904. Although it was by no means an alliance, it cemented a close friendship, and it settled all their outstanding differences. (See the cartoon above.) France accepted

Great Britain's position in Egypt, and Great Britain allowed France a free hand in Morocco. 

When France proceeded to put through certain police measures in order to protect her interests, it did not require much shrewdness to see that Morocco was going to become a 

French protectorate. 

Germany did not like these developments at all. She knew that France had satisfied not only Great Britain but Spain and Italy, while she herself was apparently being ignored. If 

France expected to pluck a prize like this, she should be willing to give Germany some "compensation." Since France's ally, Russia, was then embroiled in the Far East, Germany decided to force the issue. As a challenge to

French motives, she let it be known that she regarded Morocco as an independent state, and then with a great flourish demanded that the future of Morocco be submitted to an international conference. In this way she believed that France would be checked and that the Entente Cordiale would be exposed as of little importance.

France was loath to submit to bullying, but the friendly pressure of President Theodore 

Roosevelt, who led her to believe that she would win her case in the end, finally persuaded her to yield; and the Conference of 

Algeciras was the result. France secured the right to police a restricted area in Morocco, and her position there was strengthened because it now rested on an international treaty. 

Moreover, the crisis had drawn France and Great Britain closer together, their military staffs even discussing projects of common defense. Hence it appeared that Germany had really lost by all this rumpus. 

The Formation of the Triple Entente 

In the same year as the conclusion of the 

Moroccan crisis, 1906, Sir Edward Grey, who cherished an intense distrust of Germany, became British foreign secretary. Just as his predecessor had made a friend of France, so Grey proposed to end the long feud with Russia; and he did so by a treaty or convention, as it was called in 1907. This 

Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, which adjusted differences in Asia, marked the beginning of cordial relations between the two powers. This combination, France, Great

Britain, and Russia, came to be known as the 

Triple Entente. Only France and Russia were allies, but the three powers were likely to stand together against Germany.

It looked, indeed, as if German imperialism were blocked. Without regard for Germany's own desires, her rivals were getting all the choice pickings. There remained, however, the Near East, where Austria also had interests. We must, accordingly, give our attention to the Eastern Question, which, as you will remember, was the question of what should become of the Ottoman Empire. It is well here to pause a moment and study the map (see page 263), noting not only the Balkan states but the two great neighboring powers, Austria and Russia, as well as the British position in Egypt (page 261).

AUSTRIA VERSUS RUSSIA-THE BALKANS AS A STAKE 

The Balkan Upheaval of the Seventies The Balkans had been comparatively quiet for nearly twenty years following the Crimean

War. The Rumanian people had won their national unity in 1861; but this change had been due chiefly to the skillful diplomacy of Napoleon III, not to any recourse to armed revolt. Yet the rise of nationalities with their own ambitions and interests was likely to make the Eastern Question more complicated than ever. The "great powers" were not the only ones interested in the future of the Balkans. 

The rickety Ottoman Empire was still largely peopled by Christians who had cause for discontent, and in 1875 the oppressed peasants of Bosnia rose in revolt. The peninsula was so inflammable that a blaze in one quarter soon ignited all the rest. Serbia and 

Montenegro joined the revolt; the Bulgars also rose; and Rumania was ready to jump in at small notice. The "great powers" tried to straighten out the difficulties, but in vain; and finally Russia decided to act alone. So in 1877 she declared war against Turkey.

Great Britain, then under the premiership of Disraeli, nearly came to blows with Russia, but the crisis was surmounted. In any case, when Russia brought the war to a victorious close and extorted a peace that would have left her in virtual control of the Balkan Peninsula, the other powers decided to force a revision of the settlement.

The result was the Treaty of Berlin, the product of an international congress at Berlin in 1878. Russia slightly extended her boundaries, but, on the whole, profited little from the war, and naturally felt humiliated. Meanwhile, Serbia, Montenegro, and Rumania gained recognition of independence, and the Bulgars got self-government. By a supplementary treaty Great Britain obtained the right to occupy Cyprus.

The Development of Austro-Russian Rivalry 

Austria was the chief gainer by the Treaty of Berlin. She had exacted Russia's consent to her seizure of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the price of her neutrality in the recent war, Clash of Interests in the Balkans Miles

As a result of the Balkan Wars, Turkey was all but driven out of Europe. Not only were the Balkan states jealous of each other, but the imperial interests of Austria and Germany clashed with those of Russia. and by the Treaty of Berlin she gained the right to govern them indefinitely. Taking advantage of her position, she acquired a dominant influence in the Balkans. She was the readiest market for supplying the industrial needs of the Balkan States, and close political ties naturally followed. Serbia was little more than an Austrian dependency, and Rumania, in 1883, secretly entered the Triple Alliance. 

But Russia was not to be robbed of her accustomed influence in the Balkans if she could help it. Toward the end of the nineteenth century she came into friendly relations with Bulgaria; and in 1903 a palace revolution in Serbia led to the accession of a new king who favored Russia. It would seem that the balance was now being restored between the rivals. Russia's eye was, of course, on 

Constantinople. What she wanted was the exclusive right to send her battleships through the Straits into the Mediterranean. Then in case of war she could sally forth and attack

IN THE NEW AGE INTERNATIONAL RIVALRY 

an enemy's fleet in the Mediterranean, while her own fleets were safe in the Black Sea from all attack. In 1908 she secretly proposed to 

Austria that the latter should annex Bosnia and Herzegovina, while she herself should force 

Turkey to give her the use of the Straits.

The Bosnian Crisis 

Unfortunately for Russia, Austria annexed the provinces in question without waiting for her rival to overcome British objections to the project regarding the Straits. Austria was obviously breaking the Treaty of Berlin, since the provinces still nominally belonged to Turkey. Yet the only power which threatened to fight was Serbia, who, though not a party to the treaty, had long cherished the hope of possessing Bosnia herself, as that land was peopled by Serbs. In 1909, war between 

Austria and Serbia appeared to be imminent. 

But Russia, after her recent war with Japan, was in no position to assist her little friend, and when Germany threw her influence on the side of Austria, there was nothing for Russia to do but accept a diplomatic defeat. 

Secretly, however, she passed the word to 

Serbia and Bulgaria' that Austria's day of reckoning would come. The Bosnian crisis (1908–1909) greatly increased the tension between the two great rivals for supremacy in the Balkans. 2 A lull seemed to follow the Bosnian crisis but not for long. In 1911 Italy forced war upon Turkey and seized Tripoli; and, more serious than this, Germany and France locked horns again in Morocco. Believing that

France was about to extend a protectorate over that kingdom, Germany suddenly sent a gunboat to the Moroccan port of Agadir, as a means of telling France that if she did not agree to hand over one of her colonies, she (Germany) would wage war. It was then that Great Britain suddenly took a hand. 

Fearing that Germany would force war upon

France, she made it clear that she would not hesitate to fight if she felt her vital interests to be affected. Germany promptly withdrew

Bulgaria had taken advantage of the Bosnian crisis to proclaim her independence in 1908. 

2 She also acquired the Dodecanese Islands in the eastern 

Mediterranean. The war closed in 1912. her gunboat and received from France a small slice of her Congo colony, in return for which she acknowledged a French protectorate over 

Morocco (1912). But she deeply resented

British interference. Once again her prestige had received a blow.

The Balkan Wars 

Then, in 1912, Russia made a significant counter-move against Austria. She encouraged the Balkan States (except Rumania) to form a league that should fight either Austria or Turkey. As a matter of fact, the Balkan 

States were only too anxious to extend their frontiers at the expense of Turkey. So in 

1912 the Balkan League, composed of Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, and Greece, pounced upon Turkey. To the surprise of the "great powers," who had not been able to stop them, the League was wholly victorious; but when it came to the question of dividing the spoils, its members quarreled violently. Taking advantage of the situation, Austria, who looked upon the League as a Russian instrument and wanted to see it dissolved, incited Bulgaria to attack Serbia. Thus began the 

Second Balkan War. This time Serbia, Rumania, Greece, and even Turkey were ranged against Bulgaria, who naturally got the worst of it. By the Treaty of Bucharest (1913), which finally ended this Balkan upheaval, all the Balkan States (with the exception, of course, of Turkey) made territorial gains, though Bulgaria got much less than she had expected, and she had had to cede a strip of land to Rumania. If you will examine the map (page 263), you will see that very little of Turkey remained in Europe. Would the "Sick Man" be able much longer to hold the Straits?

On the whole, though the Balkan League had collapsed, Russia had gained in power and prestige, for Serbia had been strengthened, and Austria's friends, Turkey and Bulgaria, had been humbled. Both Austria and Germany were fully determined that the situation which the Balkan Wars had created should not continue. Thus the struggle for supremacy in the Balkans was certain to breed more trouble. 

In the meantime, German imperialism had been active.

GERMANY'S "PLACE IN THE SUN" 

Hamburg to the Persian Gulf 

Germany had at last found her "place in the sun." The German plan was to get the concession for a railroad from Constantinople to Baghdad and the Persian Gulf. Germany would then be linked by rail to a port that faced India, and might open up a new route to the East. But the chief object of this plan was to exploit the country traversed by the railroad. With the aid of German science this land could be made a profitable field for the investment of German capital. Perhaps, indeed, Germany could get the colony she wanted without the need of challenging 

British sea power. And perhaps, in course of time, all this vast area from Hamburg to the Persian Gulf might become a great economic unit, able to supply the German people with all the food and raw materials they needed, though such a plan required Austrian 

Thus again we supremacy in the Balkans. can see the importance of the Eastern Question. (It is shown graphically in the cartoon on this page.)

Carrying Out the Project 

For some time Germany had enjoyed a great influence with the Turks, and the Sultan himself had displayed an interest in railway development. In 1898, the Kaiser had made a spectacular trip to the Holy Land, and had announced himself the defender of the 

Mohammedan world. The following year

Germany obtained Turkey's approval of the railroad project, and in 1903, the contract was definitely made with a German company. 

It would be far too long a story to relate all the difficulties Germany encountered. The construction proceeded slowly because the

SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

1. The economic expansion resulting from the Industrial Revolution created a need for markets, sources of raw materials, and places to invest surplus capital. a. Although imperial expansion brought profits to relatively few people, the masses generally supported the movement for patriotic and other reasons. b. Great Britain possessed a great empire, but joined in the scramble for territories (to be exploited). c. The areas chiefly affected by the new imperialism were China in the Far East, the countries of the 

Middle and Near East, and Africa.

IN THE NEW AGE INTERNATIONAL RIVALRY 

2. Imperial rivalry quickly led to serious clashes of interest: Great Britain vs. France in northern Africa;

Japan vs. Russia in Korea and Manchuria; Germany vs. Great Britain in South Africa; Germany vs. 

France in Morocco; and Russia vs. Austria in the Balkans. 

3. The aggressive imperialism of Germany alarmed France and Great Britain and led to an understanding between them. (Entente Cordiale.) a. Generally speaking, Germany was balked in Morocco. b. The understanding of Great Britain with France was extended also to include Russia, the ally of France. (Triple Entente.) Great Britain feared German imperialism more than Russian.

DIVISION FOUR The World in Upheaval 

Preview 

RIVALRY FOR COLONIES and spheres of interest, a frenzied race in armaments, and the longing of one nation (Serbia) to achieve its nationalist unity are among the major causes of the First World War. After a hard, four-year struggle the British blockade and the force of numbers compelled Germany to sue for peace. 

The First World War took a terrible toll of life and property, and caused people to cry out that such a tragedy must never happen again. 

This wish for a better world found expression in movements for democratic government, legislation to provide greater security for the masses, and, above all, the creation of an association of nations to prevent war. These gains, however, were offset by a peace settlement which left Germany humiliated, and which raised many troublesome political and economic questions. One answer to such questions was a movement in Italy and Germany known as fascism.

The Russian people were attempting, meanwhile, to create a new social order. The inefficiency of the Czar's régime had resulted in colossal losses during the war and finally in revolution. Soon the communists got hold of this movement and established a dictatorship. But they experienced many difficulties in trying to carry into effect a socialist program on a large scale, and success was only partial.

In Germany a republican government was established following the war. Never popular, because of its acceptance of the harsh peace dictated by the Allies, the republic was further weakened by the discontent and despair which followed the economic depression. Under such circumstances the National Socialist (Nazi) Party, which promised everything to everybody, rapidly gained in strength. Finally, its leader, Hitler, became Chancellor, in 1933, and established a new society based upon force. Germany then proceeded to set aside the restraints imposed by the Versailles Treaty and became the strongest military power in Europe. 

In Italy Mussolini had already established the model of such a dictatorship, embracing the whole political, economic, and cultural life of the people in other words, a fascist or totalitarian state. And here also was a spirit of reckless nationalism. By their militant diplomacy and rash acts of aggression Germany, Italy, and Japan repeatedly endangered the peace. The League of Nations proved powerless to restrain them, and the great democracies were content to pursue a policy of "appeasement" rather than run the risk of war.

The destruction of Czechoslovakia by Germany finally roused France and Great Britain to take some action. But their weak policy had cost them the co-operation of Russia, and Stalin, the Russian dictator, meanwhile reached an understanding with Hitler. When 

Hitler, in the fall of 1939, moved against Poland, France and Great Britain, though unable to save that country, promptly declared war against Germany.

During the first year of the war Germany was able to crush all opposition on the Continent, and gradually established her rule from Norway to Greece. Great Britain, though subjected to merciless air attacks, and seriously threatened by Germany's submarine warfare, continued the struggle, aided directly by the dominions (except Eire) and indirectly by the United States, which made itself an "arsenal of democracy." When Russia and Germany came to blows in the summer of 1941 the conflict became probably as murderous as the 

First World War. A few months later Japan treacherously attacked the United States, and that country finally engaged in open war with the Axis powers. With fighting raging in the 

Far East, northern Africa, the plains of Russia, and on the high seas, the struggle had become a Second World War.

CHAPTER XII The First World War: 

Its Causes, Course, and Results 

What were the underlying causes of the First World War? 

How did a quarrel between Austria and Serbia come to involve all of the great powers and many of the smaller ones?

What was the character and course of the struggle? 

What were the results of the First World War? 

We have said a great deal about nationalism and noted how very dangerous a force it was. In spite of the forward march of civilization the spread of democracy, of popular education, of social reform, and of the many benefits of applied science -the pressure of fear and hatred led the civilized nations of the West to risk a war that cost millions of lives, destroyed many of the fruits of this long and patient upbuilding, and brought about untold misery throughout the world. So terrific a struggle as this, involving as it did a large part of the world, was bound to have important and far-reaching effects. It was the greatest upheaval in Europe since the French Revolution, and in view of some of its results might itself be called a revolution. While we may not call it inevitable, for the folly of a few people was the determining factor in the end, yet Europe had long been headed for this disaster.

A. The Underlying Causes of the First World War The causes of the First World War may be boiled down to three: militarism, imperialism, and irredentism. We have already explained 

We have already explained imperialism and irredentism.2 Militarism means the arming for war whether war was to be avoided or desired. We must now see how it works.

Pages 242 ff. 2 Page 210. 

MILITARISM Militarism for Defense 

When the German Empire was founded as the result of superior military power, France, in self-defense, established a large standing army. Yet in spite of strenuous efforts she could not keep the pace which Germany had set, for the latter possessed a greater and fastergrowing population. Only when France secured Russia as an ally was there anything to balance the strength of the Triple Alliance.

In the twentieth century all the "great powers" with the exception of Great Britain had huge standing armies; for all with the exception of 

Great Britain had instituted conscription. 

Practically every able-bodied man spent at least two years in military service after which he passed into what was known as the reserve. 

By this method there was not only in each of the states a standing army, but a very much larger group that could be called upon in an emergency.

The results of the Balkan Wars led Germany and Austria to increase their standing armies. 

Then France and Russia responded by lengthening the term of active military service. One can see that there was a sort of race of military armaments in the years just prior to the First 

World War. 

There was a race of naval armaments as well. Great Britain had long felt that it was absolutely essential to have a navy equal in size to any two navies on the Continent. 

When she adopted the "two-power standard,"

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 269 

as it was called, she had in mind the Dual Alliance, since she was then on rather bad terms with both these powers (France and Russia). In case of war she must be able to command the seas because it was only by the seas that she could get sufficient food for her population.

But Germany also wanted a strong navy, not so much to assure an abundant food supply as to defend her colonial empire and her commerce in the face of a possible war with Great Britain. So in 1900 she spent a tremendous sum on naval armaments, designed, as she said, to defend her "against the strongest naval power." At one stroke she became the second naval power in the world. Were 

The British were greatly alarmed. they about to lose their cherished supremacy of the seas? The result was a strenuous race to keep the lead. When Germany built more battleships, Great Britain did likewise. Germany, of course, never caught up with her rival, but Great Britain appeared to be much afraid that she would. Several times the 

British Liberals, who preferred to pour money into social insurance, tried to get the Germans to agree to a "naval holiday," as it was called'; but Germany demanded conditions that 

Great Britain would not accept. So, you see, there was a race in naval armaments parallel with the increase of standing armies. (The charts on page 270 show the expenditures for war, and the size of armies and navies in several countries of Europe.)

Militarism for Its Own Sake 

Now all such measures were, strictly speaking, for defense. None of these governments really wanted war; but each distrusted and feared the other side and, accordingly, wanted to be prepared. Moreover, outside of governments, were certain elements which seemed really to want war. There were members of the general staff in certain countries, especially Germany and Austria, who longed for a chance to test their country's military strength.

Moltke himself had once declared that wars were sometimes needed to preserve the purity of the race.

These army officers constantly exerted an influence on the civil governments, doing their best to arouse fear and distrust. It

Militarism and Public Opinion 

But could not something be done to stop this frenzied race in armaments? In 1899, an international conference met at The Hague to consider a Russian proposal of a general reduction of armaments, but unhappily none of the governments seemed to take the idea seriously, and nothing was done. The German deputies to the conference had frankly stated that, far from feeling that a large army was a crushing burden, the German people bore their taxes for that purpose as a patriotic duty. Since 

Germany came to believe that the Triple Entente was trying to encircle her and threaten her with strangulation, it is interesting to notice how blind she was to the chance of getting relief.

It may have been a sense of insecurity, a feeling that perhaps her policy was under suspicion, that led so many Germans to boast of their strength - as if, indeed, they were

Any visitor to Germany was impressed with the presence everywhere of soldiers. There is no doubt that German militarism was very largely an inheritance from Prussia, whose traditions had always been military to the core. The Junkers were an essentially military class, still feudal in their attitude toward war. Commissioned officers acted as if they were privileged, and woe to a mere civilian who got in their way! A uniform was held in the greatest respect, and the Kaiser seldom deigned to wear anything else. 

Even the members of the Bundesrath always met in uniform. It was this conspicuous parading of the paraphernalia of war that made Germany's rivals think that she was "spoiling for a fight."

But somehow the general public seemed to feel that armies and navies of prodigious size were unavoidable. If the army of one's country was too large, it was simply the fault of one's neighbor who was still more heavily armed. The press often magnified these dan gers. In any case the frenzied race in armaments had a thoroughly disquieting effect, and served to increase the fears it was supposed to allay. allay. Europe was divided into two great armed camps, which, because of a series of clashes, already discussed, were becoming a prey to mutual suspicion and fear. Every power, one might say, kept its gun loaded and even had its finger on the trigger. 

And, unhappily, the same powers were steadily pushing their interests beyond their borders.

IMPERIALISM The Menace of German Imperialism 

We have already devoted a chapter to imperialism, surveyed its essential character, and observed its dangers. There is no doubt that

German imperialism was a most disturbing factor in international relations. It was a movement with tremendous power behind it, and the world was forced to make room for it. 

The older nations, steadily pushing their own imperialist projects, were staggered by the thought of this bold intruder, boasting of its strength, and rattling its sword. 

We can hardly blame Germany, to be sure, for aspiring to become a leading world power. Her selfrespect demanded that she count for as much as

But unfortunately for herself and the peace of the world, she pursued tactless methods to get the fair consideration that she deserved. Her diplomats were too ready to bluff and bluster, too quick to threaten force before discussion had commenced. She had all the sensitiveness of a young nation, conscious of its strength and immensely proud of its greatness, but which feels that the world at large does not appreciate these facts. 

Because of a growing distrust of German militarism, as well as a growing dislike of her bullying methods, France and Great Britain had drawn together in self-defense. They, too, had imperial interests which had to be considered, and they did not see any reason to be generous. 

Moreover, British opinion was as anxious over Germany's rapid commercial and naval advance as German opinion was jealous of Great Britain's enormous empire. For all these reasons German imperialism was balked to some extent, though the Baghdad railway scheme promised to succeed, unless accidents occurred.

Balkans, where Russia's ambitions threatened 

Austria and Germany alike.

The Menace of Russian Imperialism 

Russian imperialism was not of the swashbuckling type, like German imperialism, and yet it was just as dangerous in its way. Russia was able quietly to weaken Turkey by secretly encouraging the ambitions of the Balkan States and then to use them as cat's-paws in her struggle to dominate the Near East. If Serbia should feel that Russia would support her against Austria, then she might seek to draw both herself and Russia into war. Since small states are apt to think that the bigger ones will, in the end, do most of the fighting, Russia's policy was reckless, to say the least.

Yet fundamentally Russia's policy was defensive. She felt that she must be sure of having access to the Mediterranean, for if the Straits were closed, she could not ship wheat from her southern ports to foreign markets. 

These grain-growing regions of the south would then be the victims of depression and doomed to slow decay. Now if Austria and 

Germany should succeed in controlling the

Balkans, Turkey, already the tool of German imperialism, might at any time close the Straits. Clearly Russia was faced with a critical problem. Yet Germany, for her part, could not safely allow Russia to dominate the Balkans, since the long road to Baghdad and the 

Persian Gulf would thus be cut. Germany's problem was not so much a matter of life and death as Russia's, but her interest was none the less clear. It was a clash of two imperialisms, with its intersecting point, Constantinople.

Thus this city of the Caesars had become the principal stake in the struggle for supremacy in the Balkans.

Before the First World War, Austria-Hungary was a conglomeration of discontented minorities ruled by Austrians and Hungarians. Perhaps no man or group of men could have been wise enough to reconcile the racial antagonisms characteristic of the Dual Monarchy. In any event, the Hapsburgs made little effort to conciliate the nationalities they ruled. 

Serbia as the Storm Center of Europe 

Yet the actual point of tension was farther west. Russia had come to look upon Serbia as the outpost of her power in the Balkans, a barrier against the dreaded onrush of Austro-German power. And Serbia, for reasons we shall now note, was a constant danger to Austria- Hungary. We have, in short, a commingling of imperialism and irredentism. 

IRREDENTISM 

Irredentism as a Factor in Europe Irredentism was one of the thorniest factors in international politics. France never ceased to pine for Alsace-Lorraine, which was mainly French in feeling. In Germany there was a group who talked of Pan-Germanism the dream of gaining for Germany all the Germans who happened to live outside the empire. Italy also hoped to get the Italians who lived in Austria, and that is why she was never really loyal to the Triple Alliance. Above all, Serbia wanted to acquire the Serbs of Austria- Hungary, and circumstances led her into employing dangerous methods to that end. Before going on with this story, let us first cast a glance at Austria-Hungary. (See map on this page.) 

Austria-Hungary an Offense to Nationalism 

You will remember how the Dual Monarchy arose, this partnership of two bitter enemies the Germans and the Magyars. Both in Austria and in Hungary there were other nationalities, held in subjection to German-Magyar rule. The best excuse for the Dual Monarchy was that it constituted an economic unit. 

Austria was industrial and Hungary agricultural, and the 53,000,000 people of this strange empire were fairly prosperous because of the economic interests they had in common. But politically this state was obsolete. It had been built up through the centuries in various ways, sometimes by marriage treaties between the

For Serbia, an advance to the Adriatic was naturally of greatest importance, for then she could export her pigs without difficulty. The chance to expand across Bosnia was definitely closed when Austria annexed this territory, though Serbia was so incensed that she nearly brought on a war, as we have noted. Unsupported by Russia, she was forced not only to back down, but to sign a treaty with Austria, promising henceforth to behave as a friendly neighbor. Of course, this promise meant little, for Serbia, as you will recall, had been secretly encouraged by Russia to believe that satisfaction would be ultimately obtained. 

The Importance of the Balkan Wars 

During the First Balkan War a unique opportunity seemed to have arrived for getting this coveted outlet. One of Serbia's armies marched across the mountainous country peopled by the Albanians and reached the Adriatic. But Austria at once refused to allow 

Serbia to win release. She insisted that the 

Albanians, in conformity with the principle of nationality, should have a state of their own. 

For Austria, of all powers, to support nationalism seems to us ridiculous, but politics often leads to strange maneuvers, and Austria needed some excuse for her action. She mobilized part of her army; then Russia, unwilling to see the 

Serbs browbeaten, did likewise; and a very serious crisis was the result. Fortunately, however, the Triple Entente was not disposed to risk a war on Serbia's behalf. So the state of

Austro-Serbian Feud 

Serbia disliked Austria for two reasons. In the first place, neighboring peoples are more than likely to dislike each other, and Serbia was anxious to free the Serbs of Austria-Hungary, as we have said. It was a case of irredentism. In the second place, Serbia was a landlocked power, and nearly all her trade had to flow through Austria-Hungary. This placed her in a position of almost economic vassalage to the Dual Monarchy. An outstanding result of the Balkan Wars was the territorial expansion of Serbia. Austria, it is true, had kept her from acquiring a seaboard, but she had doubled in size and doubled in population. And she might also be said to have doubled in ambition. She had

The Ideal of a Great Serbia as a Menace to Austria For some time there had been serious unrest in Bosnia, where Austro-Hungarian rule had never been popular. Both here and in the neighboring provinces of the Dual Monarchy the Serbs were restless; and even their kinsmen, the Croats, alike in looks and language but differing in religion, were thoroughly discontented with their treatment at the hands of Hungary. The Serbs, in particular, looked to 

Serbia for help. As a matter of fact, Serbian secret societies were busily engaged in Bosnia, encouraging the Serbs of that province to get ready for the moment of liberation. Serbia's dream that all Serbs, or perhaps one might say all Serbs and kindred peoples, should be united under the scepter of the King of Serbia was an example of the most intense irredentism.

Naturally Austro-Serbian relations were much strained, and throughout 1913 the two were quarreling and barely kept from coming to blows. Yet there was a statesmanlike way in which Austria might well hope to parry the danger which was threatening her. Force was not the way, for Austria was not yet sure of Germany's support. But what of conciliation?

The Archduke Francis Ferdinand, nephew and heir of the aged Francis Joseph, was credited with the plan of giving the southern Slavs (Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs) a kingdom of their own on a par with Austria and Hungary. It would mean turning the Dual 

Monarchy into a triple one.

Such a policy, of course, would be ruinous to Serbian ambition. If the Slavs of Austria- 

Hungary were satisfied, they might not want to come to Mother Serbia after all. The 

Archduke was therefore an obstacle to Serbia's B. The Sarajevo Crisis and the 

Outbreak of the First World War The Sarajevo Tragedy 

On June 28, 1914, the Archduke Francis Ferdinand, with his wife, the Duchess of Hohenberg, made an official visit to Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. This day happened to be 

Serbia's national holiday, and the Archduke was warned that Bosnia was not a very safe place for him to visit at such a time. In fact, Serbia herself had sent an informal warning to that effect. But Francis Ferdinand was a fearless man and he would make no change in his plans. (In the picture on page 276 you can see him as he looked that day.)

Sarajevo is a quaint old town, where minarets peep from behind lovely cypress trees, and give it a sort of Oriental appearance. Through it passes a placid little stream spanned by oldfashioned bridges over which the peasants bring their produce to market. No town could seem more peaceful, more unlikely to stage a tragedy. Yet a bomb was thrown at the car containing the visitors, as it passed along one of the streets, and barely missed its target. 

The imperial pair rode on, however, and were accorded a formal welcome by the mayor in the town hall, after which they took their departure in the Archduke's car. The comment was made later that insufficient guards had been provided for the occasion. The streets of Sarajevo are very narrow, and at this time they were full of holiday crowds. As the car rounded a corner, it was forced to slow up, whereupon some shots were heard, and the car stopped. The Archduke and his wife had been murdered! The assassin was a Bosnian, a member of a secret society, known as the "Black Hand," with headquarters in Belgrade, the capital of Serbia, and the pistol which he had used had been provided by an official of the Serbian government. 

Was Serbia therefore to blame? Although the plot was not concocted by the Serbian government, and it had nothing actually to do with its execution, we know now, though we did not know it then, that the government had

The world was greatly shocked by this tragic It was remembered that many Serbians, three of her princes, in fact, had met a violent end, and many felt that such people could hardly be regarded as really civilized. 

A wave of genuine sympathy went out to Austria. At the same time many feared that the bitter Austro-Serbian feud had brought on a crisis that would be difficult to surmount. 

Might not this tragedy prove to be the spark that would light a general conflagration?

As far as Austria was concerned, the assassination meant war. She was determined to end the Serb menace once and for all. After assuring herself that Germany would come to her aid in case Russia should side with Serbia, and after certain other difficulties had been disposed of, she issued an ultimatum (July 23), which Serbia was required to accept within forty-eight hours. The ultimatum was so sweeping in its demands that Austria was sure that Serbia would not yield, and there is no doubt but that she expected and wanted war. 

Serbia, though she accepted most of the demands, would not humble herself completely. 

In consequence Austria broke off all relations, and on July 28 declared war. 

Outbreak of the War

Austria could hardly have taken the steps she did if Germany had not loyally stood behind her. Indeed Germany had encouraged her to act: "Now or never," had said the Kaiser, possibly meaning that at some future time 

Germany could not promise this timely aid. (The Kaiser is shown on page 271 as he appeared at this time, and his troops as they paraded frequently.) paraded frequently.) With Russia still un-

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 277 

prepared for a great European conflict, and with Great Britain on the verge of a civil war over the Irish Question, the moment for striking a blow was well chosen, though a general war was, of course, not desired. At all events, Germany blocked all efforts of other powers to get an impartial judgment of the quarrel; and when war actually broke out between Austria and Serbia, the crisis became considerably more acute.

Unable to induce Austria to yield an inch, Russia, assured of France's backing, began to mobilize her army. At about the same time 

Germany began to fear that Great Britain, in the event of war, might possibly side with the Dual Alliance after all; so she began to press 

Austria to make concessions. But Austria, feeling sure that she could count on Germany in any event, would not yield; and anyway such efforts were too late. The alarm caused by Russia's mobilizing her huge army (for Russia, under the influence of her military chiefs, soon passed to general mobilization) roused the military element in Germany to insist upon a showdown. Though the Kaiser and his chancellor certainly did not want war, they let themselves be stampeded. The fact that the Czar pledged his word of honor that

Russia's action was purely defensive made no difference. The fact that Germany might have mobilized her own army and still have sought peace was not considered. On July 31, Germany sent an ultimatum, demanding that

Russia issue an order for demobilization within twelve hours. Since Russia ignored the demand, Germany declared war against Russia,

August 1, 1914. 

None of the nations had wanted a general war, but Russia would not permit Serbia to be crushed lest she lose her strong position in the Balkans. Better war than a repetition of the experience of 1909! Germany, on the other hand, would not let the Austro-Serbian squabble be settled without war, lest she seem to give way to the pressure of her rivals. Unfortunately, the powers were so inextricably tangled up with one another through their system of alliances that war between Germany and Russia was certain to mean a general war. 

c. The Widening of the War The Great Powers Drawn In 

Germany forced war upon France, August 3, on the assumption that France was bound to side with Russia. Great Britain wavered for a day or two, since she was not legally bound to join her friends. But when she learned that

Germany proposed to strike at France through Belgium, she sent an ultimatum to Berlin, demanding that Germany respect Belgium's neutrality, or the British ambassador would leave within twenty-four hours. As a matter of fact, when the ambassador duly presented his ultimatum, a German army had already entered Belgium. The German Chancellor bewailed the fact that "two kindred nations" like Germany and England should come to blows over what he called "a scrap of paper" 

(the Belgian Neutrality Treaty of 1839). But 

Great Britain, unlike Germany, felt bound to respect her treaty obligations, and besides she could not afford to see a great military power encamped so close to her shores. It is true that she had promised France that she would protect her shipping in the Channel, but it took the invasion of Belgium to persuade Parliament and the British public of the necessity of war.

So Great Britain entered the war on 

August 4.

Japan came into the war in the same month (August) in virtue of her alliance with Great

Britain, and with an eye, of course, on Shantung. Her coming into the war meant that 

Asia too was involved in this great struggle. 

Italy, however, hesitated. Since she felt that Germany and Austria were not fighting a defensive war, and since the Triple Alliance was solely defensive, she felt under no obligation to join them. Besides, Italy had more to gain by changing sides and joining the Triple Entente. She had always looked upon Austria as the power most to be feared, for Austria held not only the Brenner Pass but the Tyrol, the southern portion of which sloped down into Italy. Besides, in this portion of the Tyrol, as well as across the Adriatic, were thousands of Italians who wanted to be redeemed. 

It was another case of irredentism. So after bargaining with the Entente Powers, who promised her what she wanted in event of victory, Italy entered the war as their ally in 

May, 1915.

We shall give separate attention to the intervention of the United States. Now what of the other powers that were drawn in?

Greece, after long hesitation, followed suit in 1917. Portugal entered the war by virtue of an old alliance with Great Britain. All these powers entered from motives of self-interest. Several other powers outside of Europe also entered, after the 

United States had urged all neutral powers to stand beside her when she herself entered the war. 

The "Central Powers" consisted of Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, and Turkey. The "Allies" consisted of Russia, France, Great

Britain, Japan, Italy, the United States, and numerous smaller powers. Altogether there were twenty-seven belligerents, including two in South America. It was truly a world war. 

The United States Drawn In 

The war had been raging for more than two years and a half before the United States entered. In fact, both the President, Woodrow

Wilson, and the American people as a whole would have preferred to stay out of it. But this does not mean that America had no interest whatever in the war. American bankers lent money to the Allies, and with this money the Allies bought munitions in America. It was for some people a very profitable war.

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 

But there was danger in such contacts. 

Germany, whose trade with America was largely interrupted by the British navy, deeply resented the fact that her enemies could supply their needs as they pleased. She could not, of course, protest, since Americans were willing to sell to any country, and some indeed did sell cotton to Holland and other countries to be shipped to Germany - until the British broke up this traffic. 

But Germany tried to stop this flow of munitions to the Allies by using her submarines to blow up vessels that she thought were carrying them. Moreover, by the use of this weapon she tried to cut off the British Isles from the outside world, hoping in this way to starve Great Britain into submission. As such warfare, however, resulted in the loss of American lives and property, the American government was forced to protest with vigor. Indeed, the patience of the American public under stress of these offenses was truly remarkable. (The German warning concerning the Lusitania is reproduced on page 281.)

The position of a neutral power during a conflict as desperate as this one was bound to be precarious. Great Britain, following her own interpretation, declared contraband many of the products Americans were trying to send to Germany; and by "contraband" we mean things intended for military purposes and therefore not supposed to be carried by the ships of neutral powers. Wilson, it is true, protested strongly to both countries against infractions of our neutrality, but he could not but feel that the loss of American lives was far more serious than loss of profits. Moreover, German agents tried to blow up American munition plants; and they even made an effort to get Mexico to attack us. When Wilson could not persuade Germany definitely to restrict the use of her submarines, he came to the reluctant conclusion that war was unavoidable. When he asked Congress for a declaration of war, he spoke of German methods as a "war against humanity." There was no hesitation in Congress about support-

The United States entered the war in April, 1917. But Wilson had made the mistake of not preparing early enough for such an emergency, and it was more than a year before America was ready to put much strength into the struggle. Let us now resume the story of the war itself.

D. The Character and Course of the War General Character of the War The First World War was the greatest test of human skill and human endurance that had ever occurred. The governments of the fighting powers concentrated all their resources on winning the struggle - even to inspiring their citizens with an intense hatred of the enemy.

Food and munitions were, of course, the first essentials. (The special types of war machinery that figured in this conflict are shown on page 282.) Governments controlled agriculture, industry, and transportation for the purpose of making sure of sufficient supplies. There was also a strict censorship in every country in order to prevent any expression of discontent. Non-combatants performed what services they could, and no previous struggle had been so truly a peoples' war. 

Never before, too, had science played such an important part in war. The field telephone, wireless telegraphy, and the airplane for scouting are only a few examples. 

Science also made war much more horrible, for never had artillery fire covered so long a range, while submarines and suffocating gases contributed to the agonies endured. 

It was largely an artillery war. Parallel lines of trenches faced each other, and gains could be made only with the greatest effort and at a terrific loss of life. There was little of that freedom of movement which Napoleon's armies had shown. It was like a prolonged siege most of the time. 

There was some naval warfare, but few great naval battles, for the principal German fleet was bottled up. Submarines (like the

Comparison of the Belligerents 

The Central Powers had certain distinct advantages over their enemies. 

There was much more unity among them, for what the 

German general staff decided was seldom if ever questioned by Germany's allies. Since 

Germany was much the strongest power of the four, military policy was determined in Berlin. The Central Powers had also certain geographical advantages. Germany could march troops to the aid of her allies whenever necessary. The Allies, on the other hand, were more or less cut off from one another.
