across the Channel, and France could easily get in touch with Italy, but Turkish control of the Straits and German sea power in the Baltic made communications with Russia especially difficult. Co-operation was hard to secure among the Allies, and between France and Great Britain there was often disagreement as to policy. Finally, we know that Germany had the best-organized army, and for a long time surpassed her enemies in the quantity and quality of its equipment. 

The Allies had, of course, superior sea power, which meant that Germany's oversea commerce would be destroyed, and that her food supply was bound in the end to fail. 

The Allies had also greater man-power to draw on, and greater material resources, which would make a great difference if the war was of some duration. Time, in other words, was on their side if they could only hold their own in the beginning. 

On the other hand, Germany, in order to win, must score early, while she held the decided advantage.

Germany's Plan for Winning the War - The 

Battle of the Marne

Germany hoped to win the war by striking a decisive blow in the first campaign. Her plan was to crush France before Russia could bring her immense army into action; for it was expected that Russia would need at least six weeks to complete her mobilization. Then with France eliminated, Germany and Austria could dispose of Russia at their leisure. this was to take place before Great Britain could put an army of any importance in the field. All

This plan was carried out, and a huge German army swept through Belgium into France. German atrocities were invented by the Allies as a means of inciting hatred of the enemy, it is undoubtedly true that there was plenty of wanton destruction both in Belgium and in northern France. In any case the occupation of Belgium came to be looked upon as a peculiarly outrageous act: Germany, a great power, had crushed a little, defenseless nation, whose neutrality she herself was pledged to respect. Hence, the Allies felt they were dealing with a peculiarly ruthless power, and were resolved to pursue the war to the bitter end. 

Germany Victorious in the East

In the east Germany was much more successful than in the west. An old veteran, General von Hindenburg, was chosen to defend the eastern frontier, and though the credit for German victories perhaps should be given to two of his staff, Hindenburg became later chief of staff and a German national hero. The Russians, poorly commanded, and compelled to fight among marshes and woods, were disastrously defeated in the battle of Tannenberg. Though Russia did succeed in worsting the Austrians for a time, Germany was able finally to turn her out of Poland and even to extend her lines beyond. The chief cause of Russia's collapse was the depletion of her military stores, since she had never been prepared for a great war. Her allies sought to help her by forcing the Dardanelles, but their expedition failed. In the spring of 1915, Russia was decisively defeated in the battle of the Dunajec, and her power as a belligerent amounted to little after that. In the spring of 

1918, she definitely withdrew from the war. 

Other Fronts 

In the meantime, Serbia was crushed by a superior Austrian army, and when later 

Rumania came in, she too was quickly overwhelmed by Germany and Austria, aided somewhat by Bulgaria. On the Italian front neither Austria nor Italy was able to snatch a decisive victory. 

Only from operations outside of Europe did the Allies seem to gather any encouragement. Japan had easily captured Kiaochow and the German islands of the Pacific; indeed, all the German colonies were conquered, since

the mother country, of course, could not reach them. Meanwhile, the United States was still neutral, though the Ailies were able to get from her a steady flow of munitions. 

The Deadlock 

The next years of the war (1916-1917) were a costly deadlock. Germany had tried a smashing attack at France in the battle of

Verdun, but she failed, in the end, to break through. Her submarines were active, and 

Great Britain at one time feared that her supplies of food might be cut off. Italy sustained defeat at the hands of Austria in the battle of Caporetto, but she managed with French and British help to make a stand farther south at the river Piave. All the nations were weary of the war, and discouragement was general. It was to raise morale in France that a staunch and fiery patriot, Georges Clemenceau, was chosen premier; and in Great Britain 

Lloyd George headed an all-party government. 

In the spring of 1917, the Allies were encouraged by the entry of the United States into the war, though it would be long before she could send an army to Europe. Looking forward to eventual victory, President Wilson issued in January, 1918, his famous Fourteen

Points an outline of his proposed terms of peace.

As time went on, strikes had become common among the workers, though Ludendorff had managed to suppress them and some of the workers had been punished by being forced into the army - not a very sensible action, for it spread discontent to the front. Anyway the Germans had apparently reached the limit of their endurance. 

It was now that Ludendorff intervened. 

When he came to the conclusion that Germany had lost the war, he urged his government to sue for peace at once. He had lost some of his confidence in the spirit of his troops, and he was afraid that a crushing defeat was now inevitable unless the war could be suddenly stopped. No German relished the thought of an invasion, and German morale had certainly cracked. There was in Germany none of the heroic spirit which the French had shown in 1871 when the odds were so heavily against them. The government was also afraid of a revolution like that of Russia, one of the communist variety. So Ludendorff's advice was heeded, and Germany begged for an armistice, as a forerunner of peace. 

The Armistice

Wilson was the one whom Germany addressed, but he insisted that he would not treat until her government truly represented the people. Even after a ministry had been appointed that commanded a majority in the Reichstag, Wilson still took the position that the government was autocratic; and it was evident that he was aiming at the Kaiser. 

When the public saw that the Kaiser was the sole obstacle to peace, revolution settled the question, for the Kaiser was forced to abdicate the throne. In the meantime Wilson informed both the French and British governments regarding the status of the negotiations, and except in two particulars it was agreed that the 

Fourteen Points should become the basis of the peace. 

Great Britain reserved her own interpretation of the pronouncement regarding "freedom of the seas," and she stipulated that an indemnity must be imposed on Germany to cover all damages to civilians. 

Germany was in no mood to bear reverses. 

She had suffered for two years from shortage of provisions, and from 1916 on it had been necessary to ration food to the entire population. The winter of 1916-1917 was popularly called the "turnip winter," for there was hardly any other vegetable to be had, and 11.

Before we consider the terms of peace it may be well to mention the results of this terrible conflict. 

E. Results of the War

Some of the results were immediately felt. 

These results included the hardships that immediately followed, and the destruction of life and property which the war had brought about. It also led to immediate territorial changes the liberation of numerous nationalities or fragments of nationalities; and in 

1 For this provision, however, Foch was not responsible. some of the defeated countries, as well as Russia, there were great internal upheavals. 

In fact, the war itself was in a sense a revolution, for it seemed to turn Europe upside down.

LOSSES AND DESTRUCTION Loss of Life 

The cost of the war was truly appalling. 

The number of fighting men who lost their lives totaled over ten million, and the number of non-combatants who died as the result of the war was still greater. Millions, indeed, perished from epidemics, such as typhus fever in the east and influenza in the west; and the loss of life was very heavy in Germany as a result of the blockade. The French army and navy recorded a loss of about 1,360,000 men; the German, over 1,750,000, though this loss. was much less than that of the French, if we think of it in proportion to the total population. It is worthy of note that nearly a million Armenians are said to have been massacred by the Turks.

Loss of Property 

Property losses were likewise staggering.

The countries which had suffered the most, in

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 

proportion to size or population, were Rumania, Serbia, Belgium, and the lands which came to form the republic of Poland. But parts of France were terribly devastated, too. 

The occupied regions had been the chief industrial part of France; and the Germans had systematically damaged its mines and wrecked its factories. Much fertile land and extensive forest areas had also been ruined by artillery fire. Including the money expended on fighting the war itself, a leading authority computes the total cost of the war at over $300,000,000,000. (The pictogram on page 

287 shows these costs strikingly.) 

Suffering in Central Europe

Germany and Austria did not suffer from the actual ravages of war as did some of the Allied countries, but they nonetheless suffered terribly from privations. Germany had need of raw materials to run her factories, but the blockade made it difficult to procure them, and in any case she lacked the money to pay for them. There was widespread unemployment. There was insufficient food. thing Germany could spare had gone to the army, and her stocks had given out. Every- Austria, if anything, suffered more than Germany. She had lost all her non-German territories, and with tariff walls raised on every side she could not possibly feed herself. 

In 1919, a British journalist found that eightythree per cent of the children of Vienna were suffering from rickets as a result of undernourishment. There was also great suffering from cold, for during the winter months there was little fuel to be had. The years following the war were for Vienna simply a long-drawnout agony. And in central Europe as a whole epidemics were very prevalent, since the human body had been weakened by underfeeding.

Economic Disorganization 

Much suffering in Europe came to be due to the rapid rise in the cost of living. In most countries new money was issued without the proper security - the process known as inflation. 

You will doubtless remember the story of the "assignats" during the French Revolution.

Manufacturers and merchants could, with difficulty, adjust their prices to the general trend, but wages fell behind. The workers, and more especially the salaried people, were sometimes reduced to desperate straits. Still worse was the condition of those who lived on their savings a class which included many elderly people. In some countries, especially 

Germany, there was at times an orgy of spending, since no one knew what his money would be worth on the morrow, and one might as well spend it before it was worthless. 

In all countries, too, there were thousands of demobilized soldiers who had to find their way back into employment, and in central Europe, where business was particularly slack, many of them joined the swelling ranks of the unemployed. There was only a comparatively small group of merchants and manufacturers who, charging high prices for things because they were scarce, really profited during these and the instability of exchange, foreign trade years. Moreover, because of tariff barriers was rendered difficult, and that, in turn, greatly hampered industrial recovery.

In Great Britain alone economic conditions were bright just after the war, for British goods were needed on the Continent. But as soon as the Continent began to recover a little, the British experienced a slump; and from 1921 on, Great Britain suffered a continuous depression. steady, there was a large and ever-increasing While wages, it is true, stayed fairly group of permanently unemployed. In 1924, Great Britain was forced to come to what is popularly known as "the dole," the worker insurance, not for a limited number of weeks, enjoying the benefits of his unemployment but for as long as he was out of a job. In 1932, twenty per cent of the working class was without employment.

In France the greatest losses were sustained by those who lived on government bonds; for the government was forced to devalue the currency, and those who had lent a franc that was worth nineteen cents were credited with only four cents instead. The government, though gaining at the expense of its creditors, nevertheless had taken upon itself a tremendous debt; for it had to restore the devastated regions and compensate the people who

THE FIRST AND RESULTS 289 WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, had lived there. This is why France was most insistent on making Germany pay for the havoc she had wrought. The question of "reparations" was destined to be the thorniest problem for the peacemakers to settle.

No doubt the widespread demoralization, due to physical ills and economic hardships, explains the political unrest which followed the war.

An unrestrained nationalism led to a number of petty wars. Moreover, a species of socialism known as communism threatened to upset Europe. Proceeding from Russia, where we shall see in a later chapter that it was first established, communism for a time engulfed Hungary and threatened Austria, Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states. In some of these countries it was largely the result of despair.

Yet there was a bright side of the picture. 

THE TRIUMPH OF POLITICAL AND Increased Importance of the Peasantry and the Work ing Class

In all countries the influence of the peasants and the working class was certainly greater than it had ever been before. In the new 

Baltic states and in Rumania and Czechoslovakia most of the large estates of the nobility were broken up, and hundreds of thousands of peasants became landed proprietors. They also usually controlled the government in some of these countries. Austria and Germany were for a time governed in the interest of the working class, and social reform was attempted on a large scale. Italy was for a while a prey to working-class domination, amounting almost, in fact, to anarchy - a situation that ultimately led to a violent reaction and the establishment of a middle-class dictatorship. 

Russia, like central Europe, was the victim of revolution, and passed from a régime of democracy to an unusual form of working-class dictatorship. In England the Labour Party

Democracy made great gains as a result of the war. In some countries, such as England, it was felt that the many sacrifices borne by the ordinary citizen justified the widest possible extension of the suffrage. All men who had not come under the previous parliamentary reform bills were in 1918 given the ballot, and all women of thirty or over likewise received it. This discrimination against women was removed some years later in 1928. most of the states created or remade by revolution, universal suffrage was adopted. In

Monarchy is not always out of harmony with democracy, as the case of Great Britain proves; but in some of the countries on the 

Continent the monarch had enjoyed a considerable power. Many of these thrones quickly crashed as a result of the war. Monarchy was brought to an end in Germany, Austria, Russia, Turkey, and for a time in 

Greece. Later Spain followed suit. Monarchy in the countries which had sustained the most crushing defeats had been thoroughly discredited, and the change to a republican form of government was only natural. 

It is classing the Liberals, who were badly beaten in the elections of 1918, and twice, with the aid of the Liberals, obtaining the government, though it did not succeed as yet in forming a majority in the House of Commons. easy to see from these cases that everywhere the working class or the peasantry, or both, gained greatly in political influence. At last it would seem that equality of opportunity, which is the essence of social democracy, was coming to be realized. The fact that these gains did not, in general, prove to be lasting was due to circumstances to be noticed later. 

It is also worthy of note that an International Labor Office was provided by the peace settlement, and under its direction international congresses were held annually. These meetings set a standard for the working class, recommending certain reforms to all countries, such as the eight-hour day and equal pay for men and women. The result was to create a public opinion more favorable to reform.

Such action at the congress proved the importance nations attached to the labor question. 

Advance of Feminism 

It is noticeable, too, that nearer to equality with men. women came

In most states

AND RESULTS COURSE, COURSE, created or remade as a result of the war women received the suffrage, at least for a time. Their economic position had also improved, for hundreds of thousands of women had been employed in munition factories or in other forms of war work, and after the war many of them stayed in industry. It was because of this valuable service on the part of British women that the vote had been accorded to so many of their number in the Reform Bill of 1918. In Russia women eventually acquired complete equality with men, being entitled to the same wages that men received for the same work.

It is noticeable also that women enjoyed a freer style of dress than they had had before the war. In factories they had often worn trousers during the war; and after its close they commonly donned trousers at least for sport. 

For general wear their clothes tended to be looser and more comfortable. Women at last had taken the position that their dress and general conduct were their own affair, no longer to be subjected to any man-made traditions and taboos.

Revolution Follows War The Making of a New 

Germany

In many countries both political and social changes were the result of revolution following the war.

After the collapse of the Dual Monarchy, Austria became a republic, and for a while was ruled by a party of moderate socialists. Hungary, like Russia, went through a period of greater turmoil, but with these exceptions no country was more shaken than Germany.

The old German imperial régime was doomed by defeat, though the Kaiser hoped for a time to save his position; and early in 

November a chancellor was chosen who possessed the confidence of the Reichstag. In the meantime revolution broke out on the coast.

The rank and file of the navy refused to obey an order to put to sea when their officers had decided on a desperate last-minute sally, and fearing capital punishment for their mutiny, the insurgents turned their movement into a real revolution. At Kiel and other ports, soldiers' and sailors' councils were formed, very much like the workers' councils in Russia, as we shall see. There is little doubt that communism had already spread to Germany from Russia; and for a time there was a soldiers' and workers' council at Berlin.

But the largest party in the Reichstag, the 

Social Democratic Party, had meanwhile taken over the government. The Kaiser was compelled to abdicate, and he quickly fled to Holland. His conduct was far from dignified or brave, but his going doubtless eased the situation. On November 9, the republic was proclaimed, and a provisional government was formed.

But the early days of the republic were trying in the extreme. The continuation of the blockade with resultant hardships, the bitter suspense while the Allies were settling Germany's fate, and the activities of a group of rabid communists rabid communists — all these things made the position of the government difficult. It managed, however, to put down the communists, and the feeling of most of the public was that radical revolution should be avoided, else the war might be renewed and the peace be made more severe. Said one of the leaders: "I saw the Bolshevist folly staring us in the face face the Bolshevist¹ tyranny, the substitute for the tyranny of the czars. No, no, Germany should not have that on top of all her other miseries." In March, 1919, the blockade was finally lifted, and when the treaty of peace was finally signed, the republic, in spite of the harsh peace terms, was able to face the future with some hope. Two efforts of the royalists to overthrow the government signally failed. 

In the meantime, the government had done the wise thing of putting Germany in the hands of her people. In February, 1919, a constituent assembly, elected by universal suffrage, met at Weimar, a town in Saxony, to organize the republic. The constitution which it made was thoroughly democratica contrast to that of the old imperial régime. There was a declaration of rights, and women were declared to have rights and duties equal to those of men. The Reichstag became the supreme legislative body, to which the ministry (headed by the chancellor) was responsible, though the

Reichsrath, the new name for the Bundesrath, had the right to reject a bill which the other

body had put before it; and the Reichstag must then muster a two-thirds majority to quash this veto. 

There was also a president, elected, like the Reichstag, by the people, but his position was unimportant unless he should decide that the nation was facing a crisis. Then, with the chancellor's approval, he might take extraordinary measures to restore order. One might feel that an unscrupulous president might manage to become a dictator and overthrow the republic if he so desired. But what the republican statesmen feared was a communist revolution. The president must be free to deal with a danger of that sort if ever it arose. 

It was a new thing for the Germans to try a democratic régime. It remained to be seen whether it would last. But the prospect seemed very hopeful.

Social Reform in Post-War Europe 

Most of the leaders of the German Republic in its early days were socialists, though socialists of the moderate type, who concentrated their efforts on social reform. It was the first time that men who called themselves socialists were able to hold a professorship at a German university or to obtain high public office. 

Workers were given an eight-hour day, and efforts were made to settle labor disputes by compulsory arbitration, as was done in 

New Zealand. Unemployment insurance was adopted in 1927.

In Great Britain the system of unemployment insurance was made more liberal. By a law of 1920, the benefits were applied to nearly all manual workers. In 1924, the period of receiving help was no longer limited, as had previously been the case. This policy of the "dole" was necessitated by the immense number of unemployed workers during the depression which had begun in 1921. In Great 

Britain, and also in France, the minimum wage was greatly extended. France, in 1928, adopted a program of social insurance almost as far-reaching as that of Germany and Great Britain.

Side by side with the progress of liberty and equality was the triumph of nationalism. 

¹ The principal exceptions were farm hands and domestic servants, since unemployment is not supposed to be common in these classes.

THE INCREASED IMPORTANCE OF NATIONALISM Gains of the Victor Powers 

Nationalism gained, of course, when the

Allies successfully promoted their national interests. France recovered Alsace-Lorraine as the result of the war. Italy gained a stronger national frontier by getting part of the Tyrol, which brought her across the mountains, and she also acquired territory across the Adriatic. 

Both France and Great Britain secured the right to manage certain of the colonies which had formerly belonged to Germany. They were supposed to govern these colonies, however, in the interest of the natives, as we shall explain in the next chapter. 

Some gains of the victorious nations were perhaps not so permanent. Great Britain was more than ever mistress of the seas, now that the German navy had been seized, but Germany, as we shall see, later built a new navy. 

In the United States industry expanded as a result of the war, but most of the money lent to the Allied nations was never repaid, and eventually a serious depression greatly reduced the national income. Finally, although 

France became, thanks to her army and alliances, the strongest power in Europe, that strength was destined to shrink, as time went on.

The Liberation of Nationalities in Subjection 

Nationalism gained greatly when nationalities in subjection gained freedom or the right to unite with their brethren in some independent state. New nations arose from the wreck of the Russian Empire - Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Poland also came back on the map again, and the Czechs and Slovaks joined to form the independent state of Czechoslovakia. The liberation of the Irish has been mentioned already.

Then there were also successful cases of irredentism. Rumania gained the Rumans who had lived outside of her borders in Russia and Austria-Hungary. Serbia took in all the southern Slavs of the latter state, and became known as Jugoslavia (Jugoslavs meaning southern Slavs). Meanwhile, Greece got most of the Greeks who had lived in the Otto-

RESULTS THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND 

man Empire. Finally Denmark won some 

Danes who had formerly been in Prussia, and France recovered the people of Alsace-Lorraine. 

Most of the people in Europe seemed now to be able to live under a government of their choice. 

Economic Nationalism 

Economic distress seemed to inspire, not a spirit of co-operation, but a more intense nationalism. All the new nations seemed determined to develop their own industries, and limit by tariffs their trade with one another. 

In the world in general tariff walls rose higher than ever, and even the United States, while she expected her late friends to pay their debts and knew that these must be paid mostly in goods, raised her tariffs so high that it was almost impossible to do this. In 1932, Great 

Britain herself, under the lead of the Conservatives, finally adopted a protective tariff, thus ending more than eighty years of free trade. 

Not since the days of mercantilism has economic nationalism been carried to such a height. 

Meanwhile, nationalism had also gained in strength outside of Europe.

Nationalism Outside of Europe 

The war profoundly affected the British Empire. Since the dominions had contributed loyally to the defense of the mother country, the common bond of sentiment seemed to have been strengthened by the war. On the other hand, the dominions, like most of the world, had been swept by an intense spirit of nationalism. While still remaining Britishers and loyal to the Crown, the people of the dominions were also staunch Canadians, or Australians, or whatever the case might be; and they now asserted the right to share in the shaping of imperial policy. Canada was even allowed the privilege of having her own minister at Washington; and later Ireland secured the same right. By the Statute of Westminster in 1931 the dominions were placed on a complete plane of equality with the mother country. Here was a case of dual nationalism empire spirit and dominion spirit. Whether the British Empire was somewhat weaker as a result of the war was hard to say. 

Nationalism also stirred the Hindus and Egyptians, and forced Great Britain to make important concessions to both these peoples. 

In India, she granted in 1935 a large measure of self-government, though not dominion status, as the Hindus vigorously demanded. 

The agitation was largely inspired by a spiritually minded native named Gandhi, who, disapproving of violence, urged the boycott as a means of putting pressure on the 

British. To Egypt, Great Britain granted independence in 1936, reserving, however, for the present, the right of guarding the Suez Canal. 

Arab nationalism proved, in the meantime, a restless force in the Near East, making endless trouble for both the British and the French. 

The First World War had shaken the world to its foundations and Europe has been a victim of instability ever since. 

GENERAL INSTABILITY IN EUROPE Economic Instability 

Economically Europe never regained the prosperity enjoyed before the war. There was something that seemed like recovery between 1924 and 1929, but it depended almost entirely on American capital, the withdrawal of which, as well as other reasons, produced a widespread slump, often spoken of as the "Great Depression." This was very discouraging to Europeans, and economic distress was a factor that partly explained the rise of dictatorships in several countries.

Political Instability 

Political unrest was also a legacy of the war. 

In many countries democracy was unable to hold its own, and in time it gave way to a new form of autocracy, known as fascism. Dictatorships sprang up eventually in Italy, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Rumania, Turkey, Bulgaria, Jugoslavia, and Spain, in addition to the one in Russia, set up during the war itself. Germany, her pride humbled by defeat, wanted above all else to re-establish herself as a powerful military nation. It is true that internationalism gained a slight impetus from the war, but in the end it proved too weak to preserve peace in the face of a nationalism strengthened by adverse conditions. You will understand these evil results of the war much more fully after reading the next two chapters.

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 293 SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

1. Military rivalry, imperialism, and nationalism were important underlying causes of the First World War. 

2. The prevailing system of alliances was largely responsible for the fact that conflict between Austria and Serbia quickly involved most of the great powers and many lesser ones. 

3. For three and a half years the war was a deadlock. a. Germany's headlong attack on Paris and the Channel ports was checked and trench warfare began. b. The Central Powers were victorious on the Eastern front and in the Balkans, and to a degree in Italy. c. Great Britain remained mistress of the seas, and aided by Japan conquered Germany's colonial empire. d. The neutral nations suffered at the hands of both sides, though Germany's attacks were more serious since they involved loss of lives (submarine warfare). GAINING Skill You

A. Where to Get Information. Look in your homes for books, magazines, and newspapers dating back to the First World War. Perhaps your father or uncle was a soldier during this war and kept a diary. will also find it possible to interview veterans and to have them tell you about their experiences.

THE FIRST WORLD WAR: ITS CAUSES, COURSE, AND RESULTS 

Perhaps you have seen movies dealing with phases of the First World War. Sergeant York is an example. 

Also there are pictures made up of "shots" from news reels issued during that struggle. 

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. From your reading and discussion, reach an agreement as to the underlying causes of the First World War. In themes, floor talks, cartoons, and so on, try to make clear exactly what these causes are and how they lead to war. Then see if you can suggest ways for re- moving the underlying causes of war. Perhaps you can present your conclusions in an assembly program. 

Plan an exhibit to illustrate fighting on land, sea, and in the air during the First World War. Include in the exhibit charts and graphs to show the extent to which each power took part as well as the costs of the war.

Make comparisons between armaments and the costs of armaments in 1914 and in 1939. 

C. How to Evaluate Information. Try to determine the comparative war guilt of the great powers and 

Serbia. Note exactly what each country did that contributed to the outbreak of war. 

In each case, try to decide whether the particular country was justified or not justified in taking the step? What are your general conclusions?

Try to find books containing songs sung by American soldiers during the First World War. What do these songs reveal as to the attitude of the soldiers toward the war? 

Try to find history textbooks published in the years after 1914. Read these carefully to learn what they include about the war. Can you discover any changes in conclusions and emphasis? Can you explain the reasons for changes you discover?

CHAPTER XIII The Victor Powers Try to Make a New Order 

Why was it difficult to arrange a just peace in 1919? 

What were the important terms of the peace settlement? 

How did the Congress of Paris seek to prevent future wars? 

What problems were raised by the peace treaties?

THE MAKING OF PEACE after the close of the First World War presented a great opportu nity. Here was a chance to settle all discordant issues which had troubled the peace of Europe for half a century or more. Here was a chance to make a new world — a world in which nationalities should have the government of their choice; in which backward peoples should have a real chance of selfdevelopment without being exploited; and in which all mankind should be freed from the dread of war and from the crushing weight of armaments. Was it not possible for statesmen to remove the outstanding causes of war?

And seeing that, even if justice were intended for all, there was still the danger that nations would quarrel, was it not possible to force such nations to bow to some stern arm of the law that would keep them from taking up arms against one another? In other words, could not civilized nations resolve to banish war? As we look back upon this needless waste of life in the First World War and then consider the world today, we may wonder why the people of 1919 did not see their own advantage better than they did. Let us follow the work of the peacemakers, and see what they did, and why they fell short of a thorough job.

A. Getting Ready for the Peace Two Statements of War Aims 

There had been some discussion of peace, as the result of Wilson's efforts in 1916, but neither side was ready to consider a compromise, and so the war went on. On January 

5, 1918, Lloyd George, under pressure from the

Labour Party, advocated the liberation of various subject nationalities and even demanded an international organization designed to lessen the danger of war in the future. 

Three days later, largely in response to Russian inquiry, Wilson announced his Fourteen 

Points. Without examining these point by point, we may say that they demanded the liberation of certain subject nationalities, such as Alsace-Lorrainers, Greeks, Italians, and 

Poles (also promised access to the sea); home rule for the various nationalities in Austria- Hungary; a general reduction of armaments; removal, as far as practicable, of tariff walls; the freedom of the seas; security for the natives of backward regions; and an international league to enforce peace.

A Compromise Peace? 

Both the British and American pronouncements were intended to assure the enemies that defeat would not carry with it annihilation. Both had tacitly accepted the existing organization of the German Empire, the attachment of Austria to Hungary, and the continuance of the Turks in Europe. The Fourteen Points in particular seemed to stand for what Wilson had termed an "equitable peace." 

If, with the British reservations, they had been reasonably interpreted, the result would have been a very fair compromise.

Meanwhile, all sorts of people gathered for the great assemblage at Paris where the treaties were to be made; for every little nationality suffering from oppression seemed to believe that there was its chance to obtain redress. In December, Wilson made a tour of

FIGURE 188 

Keystone

Georges Eugène Benjamin Clemenceau (18411929), while implacable when he defended his principles, was wise enough to treat his associates with tact and consideration. His judgments were clear and decisive in contrast with the more vague ideas of Lloyd George. He prided himself upon seeing matters of state realistically rather than idealistically. 

What was his attitude toward small nations? 

England, France, and Italy, and was everywhere greeted with loud acclaim. Somehow, without knowing why, the people of Europe seemed to believe that this American idealist would really establish a new world with peace and justice for all.

But would these people be willing to make the sacrifices needed for such an end? The victorious nations had suffered so long an agony that they meant to wreak vengeance on their enemies now that they were beaten; and, above all, they meant to be paid for their heavy losses. In a campaign for re-election in 

December, 1918, Lloyd George had actually made his fight on the slogan, "Hang the Kaiser and make Germany pay for the war." orator had declared that Germany should be squeezed like an orange until one could "hear the pips squeak." Similarly, in France the One uppermost thought was to make the enemy pay for the colossal losses sustained. This obviously did not promise a compromise peace. 

B. The Congress of Paris at Work Opening and Character of the Congress 

The Peace Conference, more properly called the Congress of Paris (since it was much more than a conference), opened on January 18, 1919. Though its task may well remind us of that of the Congress of Vienna, which made a new map of Europe after the Napoleonic wars, there was much more disposition to be just than had been true of that earlier congress. 

Some of the delegations brought over experts who tried to aid the Congress in fixing the best possible boundaries; and, in contrast to the empty show which had characterized the Congress of Vienna, this congress gave its entire attention to its work. There were undoubtedly able men in the Congress of Paris, though they were not as independent as they might have wished; for each was ever the servant of public opinion. France, Italy, and 

Great Britain being democratic countries, their leaders at the Congress had to defer to the popular will, else they all might have been ousted before their work had been fully accomplished. Wilson, it is true, had lost his hold on the American Congress in 1918, and the American Constitution does not provide for a change of executive in accordance with the shifts of public opinion. Yet he seems to have believed that his work would win the approval of the American people. 

The Congress was made up of the victor powers. The defeated powers were not given representation; nor was Russia, since she had long since left her allies in the lurch, and was now, in fact, a prey to revolution and civil war. 

The Congress was, in a sense, a body to pass judgment on the defeated. Such a procedure was natural enough, though it helps to explain the rather one-sided character of its work. 

Organization of the Congress 

The Congress consisted of the representatives of twenty-seven nations. While the number of votes allotted to each was supposed to depend on its relative importance, the

THE VICTOR 

297 

POWERS TRY TO MAKE A NEW ORDER 

one. "great powers" received five and the smallest powers, like Cuba, Siam, and Liberia, only But the Congress as a whole was far too big to settle the difficult problems before it, and the five "great powers," France, Great Britain,

Italy, Japan, and the United States, assumed the right to make all the really important decisions. Eventually, however, since Japan's interest was only in the Far East, the deciding group narrowed down to four; and after a rupture between Italy and the Congress, it fell to three: the President of the United States and the Premiers of Great Britain and France.

So the major features of the peace were the work of three men: Wilson, Lloyd George, and

Clemenceau. 

Of all the persons at the Congress none probably worked harder than Wilson, for his reputation as a disinterested statesman caused him to be interviewed by any number of people seeking favors from the Congress. Though he showed the strain that he was under in various ways, he usually managed to keep his temper, and partly because he was not a European, he took a broader view than any of his colleagues. 

The United States had, after all, no axe to grind, and was not threatened by any aggression. Lloyd George was sometimes witty, sometimes explosive, sometimes rather shifty, and often, like Wilson, rather badly informed. 

Clemenceau, always wearing his gray gloves, sat in his chair, saying little, but taking the measure, as it were, of his two associates, and deciding how far he could bend them to his will. Unlike Lloyd George and Wilson, he always knew exactly what he wanted, and earnestly pushed to that end. He was easily the most skillful of the three. 

Problems and Difficulties

But decision was often difficult. It was decided that Germany should pay reparations for the damage she had wrought, but as no figure was high enough to satisfy public opinion at this time, and as Lloyd George and 

Clemenceau knew that to fix a moderate sum would insure their defeat at the polls, and, in consequence, the upsetting of the Congress, the amount to be exacted was not determined. 

This shelving of the problem was probably the greatest blunder of the Congress; for the Germans could not know what to expect (and such doubt was very discouraging), and the whole vexing question was doomed to drag on for many years without solution.

More pressing, no doubt, was the question of providing security against another disturbance of the peace, or, at least, if wars must continue, adequate defense against the aggressor. Wilson's own solution was a league of nations to enforce peace, and out of deference to him this problem was put first on the docket of the Congress. This decision was doubtless unfortunate, since the working out of this intricate institution delayed the drafting of the treaties of peace and thus prolonged suspense for the defeated powers. But

Wilson felt that he had to make sure of his league, and he insisted that it should form a part of the treaty of peace to be imposed upon Germany.

France, Great Britain, and Italy had really little faith in Wilson's device. Great Britain felt that her need was already met by the confiscation of the German navy. France wanted the left bank of the Rhine to be free of forts and German soldiers and preferably under

French military control; and Italy wanted a frontier that would bring her over the mountains to the Austrian side. tains to the Austrian side. Japan was in no danger, but she wanted the German leasehold in China transferred to her, as had been promised. Wilson did not approve of some of these things, though he was willing to make concessions in order to make sure of getting the establishment of his league; and the handing over to Italy of 230,000 Tyrolese (descendants of the sturdy mountaineers who had once defied Napoleon) was certainly not to the credit of the great idealist. Wilson also expressed annoyance because a number of secret treaties had been made by the Allies during the war, dividing the spoils in advance, though he had probably known of some of them, and they did not, in the end, greatly affect the decisions of the Congress.

Some of the extreme claims, however, caused a good deal of quarreling. France put in a bid for the Rhine frontier and wanted also the Saar Basin, once a portion of Lorraine, chiefly valuable for its coal, but inhabited by some 600,000 Germans. Once, when Wilson

POWERS TRY TO MAKE A NEW ORDER THE VICTOR 

objected, Clemenceau called him "pro-German" and left the meeting. At one time

Wilson himself was so discouraged that he threatened to go home. In the end it was agreed that the left bank of the Rhine-in other words, the Rhineland- should be unfortified. France was also promised the joint assistance of Great Britain and the United States if she were again attacked, though it turned out that Wilson was promising more than he was able to fulfill. Meanwhile, the

Saar Basin was placed for fifteen years under an international commission responsible to the League of Nations, and was then to vote on the question of its future. By this agreement the coal mines were temporarily made over to France.

If some of the claims of France nearly ruptured the inner council of the Congress, those of Italy actually did so for a time. Not content with the terms she had been offered when she entered the war, Italy put in a demand for Fiume, a town, mostly inhabited by Italians, near the head of the Adriatic. This port was needed, however, by the Hungarians and Slavs in the interior. Wilson, who had consented to the transfer to Italy of lands peopled by 300,000 Slavs, objected to adding Fiume to the spoils, and when Italy remained stubborn, he published his views. Angered at what they regarded as an appeal to the Italian people over the heads of their government, the Italian delegation left Paris. It was a sort of strike against the Congress. Though in time the 

Italians returned, no final decision was reached before the Congress itself adjourned. Many Many years afterward that is, in 1924Italy acquired Fiume, as she was powerful enough then to enforce her will.

Of course, all the numerous questions security and reparations, as well as the drawing of national frontiers to fit the principle of nationality were taken up in connection with the making of the peace treaties, and we must now consider these settlements in some detail. 

c. The Peace Treaties 

There were four powers which had fought the Allied nations, but at the time of the peace there were five instead of four to deal with. The explanation is that the old Dual 

Monarchy had broken into two independent states, Austria and Hungary. Thus there were five defeated nations with whom the victors would have to deal.

THE SETTLEMENT WITH GERMANY THE TREATY OF VERSAILLES The Signing of the Treaty 

The German treaty was finally finished early in May, 1919, and a German deputation was summoned to Versailles to receive it. 

The ceremony was held in the palace of Versailles, where Germany, in 1871, had enjoyed her moment of humiliating France. The deputation did not relish the experience, as they plainly showed, but they were helpless in the matter.

Then the German government was allowed to make any comments it wished in formal notes, and of course they protested strongly that the treaty was not in accord with the 

Fourteen Points. So great, in fact, was the storm of indignation across the Rhine that 

Lloyd George got excited and urged that it might be necessary to make concessions. But 

Wilson was greatly annoyed that the Germans had dared to say that the treaty did not live up to the Fourteen Points, to which he declared that it absolutely adhered. Consequently, Germany got but little satisfaction in the end. 

Finally, on June 28, 1919, two German officials came to Versailles and there signed the treaty. As they left the palace, they were stoned by a French mob.

The Terms of the Treaty 

The treaty was based on two main ideas: a stern and relentless justice, as the victors interpreted it, and the need of protecting Europe against any possible future revival of German ambition. Reparations came under both heads, since the Germans were supposed to repair the damage they had done, and at the same time by so doing, that is, by giving up so much of their wealth, they would weaken themselves as a nation.

She was forced to give up the lands inhabited by subject nationalities - Alsace-Lorraine to France, and parts of Prussia to Poland; while in certain regions where nationalities were mixed, the people themselves were to vote their destination. In some of these plebiscite areas the vote was against Germany, and in that way Danes and Belgians were transferred to Denmark and Belgium respectively. In other areas the vote was in favor of Germany, but the case of Upper Silesia, chiefly valued for its coal, caused much squabbling, and this territory was later divided between Germany and

The little Saar Basin was also detached from Germany, as we have noted; likewise, the port of Memel, which eventually went to Lithuania. Besides these losses of territory in Europe, Germany was to give up all her colonies and her leasehold and sphere of interest in China.

Other demands showed very clearly the spirit of avenging justice. Germany was to pay an indefinite sum in reparations as well as to support an Allied army of occupation; she was to pronounce herself guilty of the war; and she was to hand over for punishment a list of officers who were alleged to have committed atrocities during the war. At the head of the list was the Kaiser, but, as, at that time, he was safe in Holland, nothing could be done.2 

The rest of the "war criminals" were eventually left to the mercy of a German court; and there they got plenty of mercy, as you might imagine.

The military clauses of the treaty were intended to prevent Germany from becoming again a great military power. Universal military service was abolished. The German army was limited to one hundred thousand men, including not more than four thousand officers; and lest a steady stream of recruits

The navy was reduced in size even more than the army. No submarines or military aircraft were allowed, and there was even a limit set to the manufacture of munitions. Moreover, the left bank of the Rhine was not to be fortified or used for military purposes, and the Allies were privileged to occupy this zone as well as three bridgeheads on the right bank for a period of fifteen years. This last provision was intended as a guaranty that Germany should observe the military provisions of the treaty. Finally, in order to prevent future expansion, she was forbidden to incorporate Austria, though its people, being 

German, might come to desire it.

Some Reflections on the Treaty The Treaty of Versailles stripped Germany of 25,000 square miles of territory and 6,000,- 000 people in Europe, as well as all her colonies with a population of about 12,000,000. 

While defeat always involves humiliation, some of the sacrifices imposed were particularly resented. The projection of the Polish Corridor to the Baltic, though obviously just to the Poles, split Germany in two, and to this the German people could never be reconciled. 

The limitations which had been set upon their armaments seemed to the Germans equally unfair, unless the victors promptly reduced their own armaments as well, in compliance with the Fourteen Points. Compulsion to assume responsibility for the war was a blow to German pride; and the loss of the colonies, on the explicit ground that they had not been governed properly, was looked upon as an insult. 

The indefinite sum to be paid as reparations was much resented, since it was naturally believed that the conquerors were simply bent on bleeding their victim. Finally, exclusion from the League of Nations amounted to saying that the German people were not as yet fit to be trusted.

Perhaps we shall agree that some of the provisions of the treaty were needlessly offensive, and, in consequence, unwise. Perhaps

THE VICTOR POWERS TRY 

301 

TO MAKE A NEW ORDER 

the peacemakers took too little account of human nature. Yet one should also realize that Germany had been so anxious to end the war that she had been willing to be disarmed, and that she had thus lost the opportunity to bargain for better terms. A country that admits defeat to that extent has hardly reason to expect the victorious enemy to spare its feelings. After all, Germany was not permanently crippled, and the military occupation of the Rhineland was intended to be only temporary. 

There was no certainty at all that the Treaty of Versailles would not be broken sooner or later. In view of the fact that Germany was able to revive and that hatred growing out of the Treaty of Versailles contributed to produce another war, some people have expressed the belief that the victors were either too harsh or else too merciful. A generous treaty, they say, might well have enlisted Germany's hearty support in behalf of peace. On the other hand, a sterner treaty might have made it quite impossible for Germany ever to endanger peace. It is a question that one might ponder. 

In some ways the treaty with Germany served as a model for the other treaties. The armies of all the other defeated states were reduced, and, with the exception of Turkey, these countries were required to pay indemnities. (Germany's attitude toward the treaty is clearly shown in the cartoon on this page.)

The Treaty of St. Germain 

The reckoning with Austria came next.

She would have liked to form a tariff union with her neighbors and in that way feel more sure of her food supply, or better still to become a part of the German Republic. But

Italy would not allow a tariff union, which might possibly lead to a revival of the Dual

The Treaty of Neuilly 

She

The reckoning with Bulgaria was the Treaty of Neuilly, signed November 27, 1919. lost some small districts to Jugoslavia and Greece, and those ceded to Greece deprived her of her seacoast on the Ægean, gained in the Balkan Wars. In other respects the treaty followed the lines of the one with Germany. 

The Treaty of Trianon 

The settlement with Hungary was delayed somewhat by the fact that she had fallen into disorder. Hungary feared that the victors meant to deprive her of certain districts peopled by Magyars, and when, in desperation she set up a communist régime, she speedily got into trouble with her neighbors. In the absence of an Allied force to maintain order, a Rumanian army marched on Budapest, pillaging right and left, and the communist régime collapsed. After a reactionary régime had been established, Hungary declared herself a kingdom under a regent, and presumably hoped to restore the House of Hapsburg.

The Treaty of Trianon, signed June 4, 1920, deprived Hungary of her subject nationalities and even of some lands that were mainly inhabited by Magyars. In other respects the treaty, like that of Neuilly, followed the lines of the Treaty of Versailles.

Hungary was not in such plight as Austria, for she was largely agricultural and was thus in no danger of starvation. But she lost her access to the sea, as did Austria, and she fell, like Austria, to the status of a third-rate power. 

Considering the fact that Hungary with Austria had long kept little Serbia from reaching the sea and that Hungary had oppressed her subject nationalities, one might feel that her fate was a piece of historic justice. But it was certainly unnecessary to hand over so many of her people to other states. (The four statues in a public square in Budapest that are shown on page 304 symbolized Hungary's mourning for the provinces she has lost.)

D. New Nations and Enlarged 

Old Ones

How Certain Great Powers Gained 

France, as we have noted, gained only 

Alsace-Lorraine, though, like her neighbor, Great Britain, she profited in other ways.

Italy gained territory to the north and east, acquiring the southern Tyrol and the Adriatic shore around to Fiume, as well as some islands off the coast. Russia was not a gainer by the war, and she lost heavily as the result of revolution, as we shall see.

How Some Smaller Nations Became Larger 

Five smaller nations enlarged by the war were Denmark, Belgium, Serbia (which we must now call Jugoslavia), Rumania, and 

Greece. Denmark and Belgium made slight accessions of territory at the expense of Germany. Jugoslavia included Serbia, Montenegro, and most of the former Austro-Hungarian lands inhabited by southern Slavs in other words, Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs.

New Nations 

Poland was the leading "new nation." She had been promised "independence and access to the sea" by the Fourteen Points, and she was made out of territories taken from Germany, Austria, and Russia. She got back most of the lands she had lost in the "partitions," and acquired a slice of Silesia which

TO MAKE A NEW ORDER THE VICTOR POWERS TRY 

she had never ruled before. So greedy did she become that she tried to expand to the east beyond the boundary given her by the Congress and this was one of the causes of war with Russia (1919-1920). While not quite so large as she had been before the partition of 1772, she was sixth among the European powers in population, which totaled, in 1919, about 23,000,000. Several of these millions, however, were non-Polish, and eight per cent of her population was Jewish - a larger proportion than was true of any other European country. (Some of these Polish Jews are shown on page 305.)

Czechoslovakia emerged out of the wreck of Austria-Hungary and had a population of nearly 14,000,000 at the time of its founding. 

The two principal nationalities were the Czechs and Slovaks the former, mostly industrial, and the latter, agricultural. Czechs and Slovaks were not always happy together, any more than were Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, but, in general, Czechoslovakia was well governed.

Other new nations were those formed at the expense of Russia, and were to be found lining the Baltic. Aside from Poland, part of which was formed out of Russia, these new nations were Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.

All were cases of liberated nationalities. Finland, as you will remember, had enjoyed a certain amount of home rule under the Russian Empire but, like the others, took advantage of the Russian Revolution to become independent. Memel, which had formerly belonged to Germany, was seized by Lithuania while the Allies were undecided what to do with it. As it was her only possible port, no serious objection was raised. 

The Baltic nations were fairly good friends except for Poland and Lithuania, who both wanted to possess the town of Vilna. In population it was largely Polish, but the surrounding area was Lithuanian. The League of

Nations, to whom the dispute was finally referred, assigned the city to Lithuania, but in 1921, a Polish freebooter seized it, and the 

Poles were so delighted that the government took it over.

Lithuania, being much the weaker power, did not dare to fight. It was another case of "might making right."

Meanwhile, the Kingdom of the Hedjaz, lying along the Red Sea, was formed out of the Ottoman Empire. This Arab state had been helped to independence by the British. 

The Treatment of Nationalist Minorities 

To a large extent the boundaries of nations were drawn on the principle of nationality, but we have already noted some exceptions. 

One of the most serious cases was that of a large block of Magyars given to Rumania because they happened to be surrounded by Rumanians. There were also submerged nationalities in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Jugoslavia, and Greece. What was to be done with these people? Was there not danger that the alien power that came to rule them would seek to repress their nationalism? Would the

Magyars, handed to Rumania, be allowed to enjoy the free use of their language?

The United States became the sponsor of a plan for the protection of nationalist minorities. Special treaties, which most of the Danubian and Balkan states were required to sign, guaranteed that nationalist minorities should enjoy the free use of their language, religious freedom, and equal civil rights. Such a safeguard was certainly needed by the Jews, of whom there were large numbers in Rumania and Poland, and who had often been victims of persecution. Some states, like Rumania, objected to this guaranty as an encroachment on their rights as sovereign powers, but their protests were overruled. 

The enforcement of these rights of nationalist minorities was the task of the League of Nations, and it is obvious that the success of the new experiment must depend on the strength of the League. We must now get better acquainted with this institution. 

E. The League of Nations 

Origins of the League of Nations The idea of a league of nations to enforce peace was not new. You will remember the part played by the Concert of Europe after the Napoleonic wars. That body, unhappily, had thought chiefly of putting down revolutions as the greatest danger to the peace, and its policy came to be meddlesome and despotic. Na-

tions did, however, learn to co-operate in many matters not connected with the problem of international peace. A Universal Postal Union, for example, founded in 1864, fixed rates for foreign postage. Similarly, nations banded together to prevent the spread of epidemics, to preserve certain wild animals and birds, and, in fact, to do many things by collective effort that otherwise could not be done with much success. We might also bear in mind the Red 

Cross, founded chiefly by an humanitarian Swiss, Henri Dunant, a non-official organization, which, though national in character, has an international committee sitting permanently at Geneva. Nations were subject to rules they had made to govern their relations, namely, international law; but there never had been machinery to enforce it, and so the world was still, in the last analysis, in a state of anarchy. The Hague Conference of 

1899 had provided for an international court of arbitration, but no power was bound to bring a dispute before it unless it chose. 

But the horrors of the First World War led many to feel that some means must be found of averting war for all time. Many hopeful people had called the First World War a "war against war."

We have noticed that both Lloyd George and Wilson had expressed themselves in favor of a league of nations to enforce peace, and when the Congress of Paris opened, Wilson made it the central feature of his program. The Covenant of the League of 

Nations, which was, in a sense, its constitution, was incorporated in the Treaty of Versailles, as he had wished. Unfortunately Germany herself was not included in the membership; nor were the other defeated powers; nor was Russia. 

Machinery of the League

The League consisted of four organs: an assembly, a council, a court, and a secretariat. 

The assembly was composed of representatives of all the member states on terms of perfect equality; all had an equal vote. 

It was a place where any danger to the peace was aired, and it controlled all expenditures by the League. It also appointed the non-permanent members of the council and shared with the council the right of appointing members of the international court. 

The council was composed of representatives of the "great powers" - that is, of those who cared to be members and also four others who occupied temporary seats. This was the body which tried to settle international disputes; and, meeting oftener than the assembly, it was really the most important organ of the League.

The secretariat was the business end of the League, kept the records, and supplied information when demanded.

The international court decided on the merits of questions referred to it by the council. If the council wanted to know which of two quarreling nations was in the right, it might ask the court to rule on the matter in question. 

Value of the League

The League did not by any means exclude the possibility of war, but it was hoped that through its handling of a crisis it might lessen the chances of war. Member states were to present any of their differences or disputes before the council of the League and not go to war until three months after the council had given its decision. This would enable two quarreling nations to cool off a bit. Moreover, if either of the two insisted on going to war despite the decision of the council, all the members of the League were supposed to join forces against the culprit. That might mean cutting off all trade relations or at least putting a ban on materials used, for war (what was known as "economic sanctions"), and it might mean using force ("military sanctions").

The council was the one to decide what the member states should do. It was then left to those states to decide whether they would stand by the League and carry out its instructions. We may also note that any member state, not waiting for the council to act, might bring before it a case which seemed likely to bring on a war. Thus Great Britain brought before the League the quarrel between Poland and Lithuania.

The chief value of such a body lay in its power to lessen the likelihood of war; and many small disputes were adjusted by its action. When Jugoslavia quarreled with Albania, the mere threat of a boycott was

POWERS TRY TO MAKE A NEW ORDER THE VICTOR 

enough to give Jugoslavia pause. A dispute between Germany and Poland over the possession of Upper Silesia was settled by the League. It was also to act as the protector of certain regions, such as the free city of Danzig, which could hardly stand alone; and it was to serve as the supervisor for mandated regions.

Finally, it was to prove a valuable medium for procuring co-operation between nations in a number of things, such as checking the traffic in opium, reaching agreement on labor problems, combating epidemics, and so on. 

One of its greatest services was to rescue bankrupt Austria and put her on her feet. 

The Defects of the League The League had, unfortunately, certain obvious limitations. A unanimous vote was the general rule for decisions by the council, and that meant that one nation could block the wishes of the rest and thus prevent action in a crisis. Then, secondly, the exemption of "regional understandings" from the jurisdiction of the League, while intended originally to safeguard the Monroe Doctrine, opened the way for any power to claim the exclusive privilege of watching over the peace of a certain region; and such a claim, as we shall see, was made by Japan. Clearly a hands-off policy would simply mean to abide by the wishes of Japan, thus limiting the reach of the League. It might be questioned whether any power should enjoy a privileged position in the League. The United States was not a member, but suppose she was should she have a moral right of guardianship, apart from the rest of the League? 

A third weakness of the League, a moral rather than a practical defect, was the fact that it was bound to uphold the existing frontiers of nations. Each nation was pledged to guarantee the territorial integrity of member states. The boundaries drawn by the Congress of Paris were far from perfect, and yet they were supposed to be treated as sacred. 

Should the German Tyrolese wish on grounds of nationality to join Austria, the League would have to support Italy's claim to keep these people because they lay within her boundaries. 

Finally, the League had no means at its command for enforcing its decisions. France, who saw this weakness, urged the organization of an international army to execute the League's decisions, but most of the other states were unwilling to provide an effective military weapon that might be used against themselves.

So if the council should recommend a certain procedure, it could not be sure that the member states would carry it out. The League had to depend, in fact, on the good faith of its members, and that was all. 

Efforts to Strengthen the League

Yet it was possible that the League might develop into something better. In 1924 it was proposed that its members should agree to the device of compulsory arbitration in the event of a dispute in which any of them should be engaged. The members should also pledge themselves to combine against an aggressor. 

But unfortunately, Great Britain was unwilling to assume further obligations. She guessed that existing frontiers would create dissension, and she did not wish to be drawn into wars to uphold them. Indeed, as long as certain powers resented their losses and certain other powers regarded the map they had drawn as almost sacred, there was little chance of that spirit of fellowship necessary to the effectiveness of the League. Germany, being excluded for several years, regarded the League merely as an instrument of the victor powers.

The Question of Backward Peoples 

Upon the strength of the League depended not only the fate of nationalist minorities, but also the welfare of certain areas taken under the League's general protection. Early in the peace negotiations it was decided that Germany should forfeit her colonies, and that

Turkey should lose most of her Asiatic lands. 

The inhabitants of these regions were not, in most cases, able to take care of themselves.

They had not reached a stage of civilization that would justify independence. What, then, should be done with them?

Imperialism had sometimes promoted the welfare of backward peoples but, unfortunately, responsibility rested solely on the power which had them in charge. At the Congress of Paris a new principle was adopted, namely, that the welfare of the peoples themselves was of prime

THE VICTOR POWERS TRY 

309 

TO MAKE A NEW CRDER 

concern. As the result of a project of General 

Smuts, the Premier of South Africa, Wilson made himself the sponsor of the so-called mandatory system.

By agreement between themselves, France and Great Britain distributed among certain powers both the Asiatic lands taken from Turkey and the former German colonies; and the power having any of these regions in charge was accountable to the League of Nations, which supervised its work. The responsibility assumed by such a power was termed a "mandate." In the case of the former Turkish dominions the native government was still allowed to function, but with the "advice" (which, of course, had to be obeyed) of the mandatory power. In the case of the other regions the mandatory power directly governed the natives, but with due regard for their customs, and with the obligation to debar traffic in liquor, firearms, and slaves. The principle of the open door must also be respected, and that, of course, meant that the mandatory power could not grab all the economic advantages for itself. 

Every year the mandatory power must submit a report of its stewardship to the League of Nations.

France and Great Britain divided among themselves the former Turkish lands peopled mostly by Arabs; and the former German colonies were distributed among France, Belgium, Japan, and Great Britain or one of her dominions. Italy, for some reason, was not included among the mandatory powers. 

The system has seemed to work fairly well; and in a few cases the people under a mandate have been regarded as deserving independence. 

In 1932, Great Britain relinquished her mandate over the Arab Kingdom of Iraq, though on condition that she might occupy the country in case of need; and in 1936, France promised to free Syria and the Lebanon as soon as certain formalities had been fulfilled. But after the League of Nations ceased to exert an important influence in world affairs (as we shall note in a later chapter), the success of the whole system was put in peril. 

Estimate of the Work of the Congress of Paris 

Some of the work of the Congress of Paris was good. It created the League of Nations, which was at least a step in the direction of permanent peace.

It achieved the liberation of certain nationalities, like Poles and Czechs, who had long sought their freedom. It offered some protection to nationalist minorities and to certain backward peoples; though logically the Allies should have taken upon themselves the obligation to protect their own nationalist minorities and to extend the mandate system to the colonies they already had. 

They should also have carried out the recommendation in the Fourteen Points regarding a general reduction of armaments. They should certainly have seen to it that the new nations should not raise tariff walls against one another, for if nationalism had been in that way restrained, much of the misery of central Europe after the war could have been avoided. 

Perhaps the gravest mistake of the Congress was its handling of the question of reparations, but for that we should probably blame public opinion, as we have said. 

The most hopeful experiment of the Congress of Paris was the League of Nations. Perhaps we should not criticize the Congress for not making the League a much stronger body, for the nations were not yet ready to place their interests under a collective supreme power, as Texas or Illinois yield in authority to our federal government. Nationalism, in other words, was still much too strong for internationalism. But it is hard to resist the feeling that Germany and Russia should have been invited to become members from the outset. One of the greatest blows to the League was, of course, the attitude of the United States.

F. The United States "Goes Home" Reaction Against Europe 

When Wilson returned from Paris with the Treaty of Versailles, he found that the majority of the people had turned against him. 

It was not so much because Americans felt that Germany had been treated badly. It was, rather, that they did not approve of the League of Nations, which they did not fully understand, but which, in Wilson's opinion, was the greatest constructive achievement of the peace.

What was the life-preserver? Was the oarsman willing to transport a passenger so dressed? What happened? How do we feel today about the failure of the United States to enter the League of Nations in 1919? Why? because of geography, very insular in feeling. 

To a large extent we are sufficient to ourselves, and we do not like to be bothered by problems arising three thousand miles away. We could not, of course, hold completely aloof from the rest of the world, and we found that a great war could reach us even across a great expanse of ocean. But now that the war was over, we seemed to feel that everything was settled, and that the past, as far as possible, should be buried. In short, American public opinion had begun to tire of the Old World. 

Perhaps if Wilson had been at home instead of at Paris while the treaties were being made, he might have talked to the American people about the righteousness of his cause, and his idealism might have impressed a people that is readily moved to champion great causes. 

But as it was, the revolt against his leadership had gone too far. (The cartoon on this page emphasizes the attitude of the country as a whole.)

The result was that the Senate would not accept the League of Nations in its existing form. It insisted upon certain reservations which tended to free the United States from certain provisions of the Covenant. Probably these reservations would not have seriously mattered, and they might have been only temporary, but Wilson felt that the moral strength of the League would be impaired if they were accepted; and so he quite refused to compromise. Instead, he proposed to take his case to the people. Public opinion, after he had enlightened it, should decide. Unfortunately, he was stricken with paralysis while engaged in a speaking tour; and thenceforth he had to live the life of an invalid, unable to do a thing for the cause for which he had staked so much. In the elections of 1920, the Republicans were overwhelmingly victorious, and this victory showed the strength of the opposition to Wilson's policy. 

Wilson had, as a matter of fact, incurred a good deal of criticism because he had not consulted more of the able political minds in this country; he even had failed to pay much attention to the American delegation at the Congress. As a matter of political tactics, it would have been wise to consult some of the leaders of the Senate, which would eventually be called upon to ratify the treaty. The Republican Party was resentful, and the Republicans, as it happened, controlled both houses of Congress.

Yet we must not attribute this rising tide of criticism entirely to Wilson's mistakes or to the maneuvers of his political opponents. CHAPTER XIV The Russian Revolution and the Rise of 

Communism

What were the underlying causes of the Russian Revolution of March, 1917?

How was the popular revolutionary movement transformed into a communist dictatorship?

THE RUSSIAN REVOLUTION was perhaps the greatest upheaval that resulted from the First World War, though it had certainly been on its way for a long time. Soon after the revolution broke out, it changed its character, becoming a violent class movement under the guidance of a dictator. Thus emerged a communist régime - a kind of socialism in operation, made for the masses but not by them. In any case it created a new Russia, just as autocratic as the old, but resting on an entirely different foundation.

A. The Origins and Background of the Russian Revolution

Autocracy and Its Enemies that Russia was very backward, and the masses, chiefly peasants, were ignorant and poor. Yet, backward as Russia was, and almost sealed against outside influence, some enlightenment managed to filter in from the West. A few of the more liberal nobles vainly urged the czars to grant a constitution. to grant a constitution. Meanwhile, a radical group, known as "nihilists," hoped by systematic terror to frighten autocracy into submission. Plotting in secret, they assassinated many of the police, and even, on one occasion, a czar himself, Alexander II. It was this czar, as a matter of fact, who had shown a reforming spirit, his greatest achievement being the emancipation of the serfs (1861). It was unfortunate, however, that the peasants, freed from serfdom, had been allowed so little land of their own to till, for their poverty increased. 

Moreover, so much of their harvest was taken in taxes that they had barely enough food to sustain themselves.

Autocracy and the Industrial Revolution 

Autocracy in Russia still lingered on after it practically ceased to exist in most of Europe. 

Ruling by divine right, the czar was supposed to be all-powerful and accountable to God alone. To the superstitious peasant the "little father," as he was called, was looked upon almost as a god himself. Actually the czars Though possessed of enormous resources, were generally men of small ability, and it was Russia was chiefly a land of nobles and peasusually not their ministers, but a group of ants, and agriculture was still the great source court nobles, who influenced them most. of livelihood for her people. There emerged, as you might guess, a small but wealthy middle class, as well as a large working class, in the Russian cities.

As the government took but little interest in bettering conditions, some of the workers, restless under oppression, turned to socialism, as some of the nihilists had done. In 1897 was formed the Social Democratic Party, with socialism as its creed. Just as the new middle class was inclined to democratic views, the workers of the towns became the followers of Marx. Later on, socialism made some appeal even to the peasants.
