The Czar also appointed an able minister, Peter Stolypin, who carried out a policy of ruthless repression. So many people were done to death that the hangman's rope was called "Stolypin's necktie."

Stolypin and Reform 

Stolypin, nevertheless, was an able states- He tried to relieve the peasants by enman. acting laws that enabled them to become free proprietors, instead of remaining subjected to collective ownership, as had long been the practice. He also saw to it that millions of acres of crown lands were sold to the peasants on easy terms, and he enabled the more enterprising peasants to adopt more modern methods of farming. Stolypin believed that if he could develop among the peasants a strong minority that was prosperous and contented, he would find the strongest ally for autocracy. 

Even steps were taken for the establishment of an elaborate system of public education. The 

Old Régime in Russia seemed at last to be reforming.

But, unfortunately for Stolypin (and perhaps for Russia), he was too honest a man to be popular with a corrupt and reactionary court, and in 1911 he was assassinated by a police spy. His loss was as serious for absolutism in Russia as the fall of Turgot had been for the absolute monarchy in France.

Meanwhile, the revolutionary movement seemed to have died out. It took another disastrous war to revive it.

B. The Failure of Autocracy in the First World War 

Humiliation and Degradation

The First World War was Russia's undoing. 

As in the Crimean War and the Russo-Japanese War, autocracy proved unequal to the test. 

But this struggle, so much more difficult than any Russia previously had waged, did more than bring discredit to the czarist régime. It brought it to final ruin. for the ordeal. Her railways were unequal to the transportation of large armies, and even at best her munition plants could not turn out artillery in sufficient quantity. The government was hopelessly incompetent, and the minister of war was even suspected of graft. 

The result was an appalling scarcity of almost everything needed shells, cannon, rifles, even uniforms and boots. Hence, disaster followed disaster, and most of the western provinces fell into the hands of the invader. 

Under pressure the Czar dismissed his incapable minister of war, but little was done to better the situation.

The Czar's government merited the disgust of every Russian. 

Nicholas himself, though an exemplary husband and father, was hopelessly incapable as a ruler. He was a man of small mind and weak will, completely under the domination of his wife, the stately and beautiful Alexandra. Of a strong and unyielding nature, the Czarina thought only of the welfare of her son, the little Czarevitch, whose future power as czar must not be weakened. She hated the war because she was afraid that Russia would be defeated and that autocracy would suffer. She hated it also because she distrusted Russia's allies, France and Great Britain, fearing that democratic principles would spread to Russia. Above all, she was greatly worried over the health of her little son, who suffered from an incurable disease. Someone told her, however, of the utterances of a Russian seer: that he could cure the little Czarevitch and that his own fate was entwined with that of the dynasty. 

This man, one of the foulest creatures that ever dishonored history, was a huge Russian peasant, Gregory Rasputin (whose picture appears on page 317). He had managed through his cunning and a sort of hypnotic influence to make many people believe that he was a man of great piety; and he was known as "the holy man.' He also, it seems, practiced the art of healing, presumably by means of his mental powers. But he was at the same time an uncouth and filthy creature, and his character was base and vile. Yet he had managed to gain an entry into Petrograd¹ society and had

There was plenty of enthusiasm as Russia entered the war. All parties and all classes rallied to the national defense under the leadership of the Czar. The socialist parties declared that the defeat of Russia in this war would be a "defeat in the struggle for freedom." "The Russian people," declared the president of the Duma, "have not shown such a wave of patriotism since 1812."

Alexandra, who was notoriously superstitious, employed him to treat her son whenever his sufferings became acute, and it was said that Rasputin had pulled him through a crisis. 

Unfortunately this scoundrel used his influence with the Czarina to meddle in politics. 

He made and unmade ministers; he even tried to interfere in the conduct of the war. 

It was commonly believed that he was secretly working for a separate peace with Germany.

The Gathering Storm 

Even hidebound conservatives resented the fact that this filthy adventurer ruled Russia. 

As one of the court nobles remarked later, "If the revolution had not broken out from the bottom, it would have broken out from the top." Whenever the Duma met, there was an uproar. Its members railed against the ministers, who were thought to be tools of Rasputin, and begged the Czar to grant representative government. But the Czarina would never let the Czar give way. "Be firm," she told him; "be master." And, of course, she would not believe a single word against her favorite. There seemed no way of getting rid of this wretch except by murder. 

On the night of December 30, 1916, a prominent nobleman lured him to his apartment, and there he was done to death, and his body cast into the Neva.

The Czarina, of course, was furious, but she had no redress. She came to rely mainly on the minister of the interior, a little wildeyed man, who claimed that he communed with the spirit of Rasputin. The Czar, himself, was usually at army headquarters, and the government, meanwhile, drifted before the storm, plainly headed for destruction. In February, 1917, Alexander Kerensky, a socialist leader in the Duma, openly prophesied revolution. "Its lightnings," he said, "already illuminate the horizon." At the same time there were serious strikes in Petrograd, involving by the first week of March nearly 200,000 people. 

On March 8, however, without any apparent concern, the Czar left for his suburban palace. 

It was on that very day that the Revolution began.

c. The Outbreak and Early Course of the Revolution-From Democracy to Communism

Outbreak of the Revolution and Establishment of the Provisional Government 

Petrograd was primed for revolution; but the immediate cause was hunger. There was a food shortage in the capital, owing to a partial breakdown of the means of transportation, partly attributable to the severity of the weather. On March 8, there was some looting of bakeries, and the disorders grew worse with each succeeding day. The police were powerless to restore order, and the garrison refused to interfere. A soviet, or council of workers' deputies, was established; mobs thronged the streets and occupied the Fortress of Saints Peter and Paul, the Russian Bastille; and the red flag waved from the Czar's residence, the Winter Palace.

All this time the Duma had been trying to persuade the Czar to return to Petrograd, but he would not heed its warning. Finally, on 

March 12, it definitely joined the Revolution.

It set up a provisional government and sent two messengers to the Czar to request his ab dication. Believing resistance useless, Nicho las complied; and an effort was made to get his brother to take the throne, but without success. Thus Russia became a republic. 

As for the Czar and his family, they were confined in one of his palaces. 

Meanwhile, the Revolution was hurrying on its fateful course - faster even than the 

French Revolution; for Russia, utterly exhausted by the war, had much less stability than Bourbon France of the eighteenth century.

The Collapse of Russia 

It is not surprising that the Provisional Government proved unequal to its difficult responsibility. Composed mostly of moderate liberals (members of the nobility and middle class), it aimed to establish a democratic Russia, while it also hoped to continue the war till victory had been won. victory had been won. Meanwhile, it promised a constituent assembly, to be elected by the people. Unfortunately, the masses had no interest in a constitution, and yearned for more tangible things. The peasants wanted land; the army wanted to go home; the workmen wanted large increases of pay. Soon the 

Petrograd Soviet quite eclipsed the Provisional 

Government by appealing more directly to the masses.

On the model of this first soviet, to which deputies of soldiers had been added, soviets were formed in all the towns of Russia. One is reminded of the famous Jacobin Club, which had so much to do with the downward course of the French Revolution. But this

system was even wider, for there were peasant soviets in the various villages; and before long a congress of soviets came into being. This strange machinery of mass representation was far more important than the twelve men who composed the Provisional Government. 

A general collapse was practically inevitable. 

Few any longer recognized any duties. The army was drawn into politics through representation in the soviets, and refused to obey orders. Most of the rank and file, conscripted peasants, thought only of going home to seize land; and thus the military front was caving in. In the meantime the peasants refused to hand over the grain which the government required, and began to seize the lands of the nobility. At the same time, workmen in the factories insisted upon choosing their own superintendents, struck for higher wages and shorter hours, and did little or no work. was far more pleasant just to sit and talk politics! Thus the towns were short of food and the country was short of manufactured products. The economic life of a great empire had gone to pieces. It

Establishment of a Communist Régime 

The Bolsheviks were a seceding faction of the Social Democratic Party, who instead of expecting the gradual evolution of a socialist régime, as the majority of the party anticipated, wanted to establish one immediately and by violence. Before the war most of the Bolsheviks had been in exile, but they scurried back to Russia when they heard of the Revolution. 

Their leader was a very remarkable man, Nikolai Lenin (whose portrait is shown here).

When the Revolution broke out, the German government gave him passage across Germany, and he made his appearance in Petrograd during the latter part of March. 

Lenin this was the opportunity of a lifetime. 

He was For

Lenin was a man of great force. not a magnetic speaker, but he knew how to win the devotion of his followers, who regarded him as one inspired. He had undoubtedly a natural talent for organization and a tenacity

THE AND THE RISE OF COMMUNISM RUSSIAN REVOLUTION 

that never knew defeat. A devoted follower of Marx, he made up his mind to destroy the existing Russia and to substitute a socialist régime. The war and revolution had given him his opportunity. Lenin's great chance lay in the fact that the Russian people wanted peace, whereas the Provisional Government was loyally determined to continue the war. 

He was not immediately successful in getting control of the soviets, but he worked to destroy the fighting spirit of the army and he never ceased to attack the Provisional Government. 

Fortunately for him, the Provisional Government steadily lost ground. Its leading member, Kerensky, a man of more enthusiasm than wisdom, tried to fire the Russian army with a new determination to beat the Germans, but after some brief success, the army was driven back in rout. "All In the confusion that followed, the Bolsheviks rapidly gained the upper hand. power to the soviets!" was their watchword.

They promised the people to end the war, and thousands of the moderate socialists began to rally to their lead. In October, they gained control of the Petrograd Soviet; and on November 7, they finally overthrew the Provisional Government. Such was what is sometimes called the November Revolution. The first revolution had brought autocracy to an end. 

This second revolution went much deeper. 

The Class War and the Red Terror - the End of the Revolution as a Popular Movement 

One of the results of the November Revolution was a separate peace with Germany. It was not an honorable peace, for Russia could not talk to Germany as an equal when her army had gone to pieces. But Lenin was bent on peace at any price, for he wanted to give the people what they wanted and to be free to commence the reconstruction of Russia. By the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 3, 1918, Russia surrendered her Baltic provinces to Germany, ceded certain southern districts to Turkey, relinquished the Ukraine (which was placed under German protection) and agreed to pay Germany an indemnity of a billion dollars. She lost at least seventy million people, as well as most of her outlets to the sea, and laid herself open to German exploitation. 

It was a terrific price that Lenin had paid for peace. But he may have expected Germany's ultimate defeat, and in any case he was mainly interested in strengthening his position at home. For that purpose he must have peace. "He is no socialist," he declared, "who will not sacrifice his fatherland to the triumph of the social revolution."

It is useless to blame Lenin for not being a patriot. He did not think of the world as divided into nations, but, rather, into classes. 

His one end and aim was to wage, not national war, but class war, till Russia should belong to the working class. And he hoped that the class war would spread to other countries till in all the world the workers would be supreme. 

But we must remember that the working class was hardly fifteen per cent of the population, for most of the people were peasants. 

Moreover, the Bolsheviks numbered only a minority among the workers. Probably not more than three per cent of the adult population belonged to that party. So Lenin had to pursue extraordinary methods in order to consolidate his power. consolidate his power. On one side, however, his policy was conciliatory. He tried to please the peasants by decreeing that all land was the property of the peasants. For the factory workers he enacted the eight-hour day, equal pay for all workers regardless of skill, and workers' control of industries.

Those who were not willing to follow his lead he subdued by force. One of the first acts of the new government was to forbid all public meetings. Also a strict censorship was established, none but Bolshevik papers being permitted. But there was still the assembly which had been called before the Bolsheviks came into power the Constituent Assembly. 

Lenin did not venture to prevent its election; indeed, he seemed to hope by violence to control it. Nevertheless, the great majority of delegates were found to belong to a moderate socialist party.

When these representatives of the people gathered in the capital, they found themselves in an atmosphere of hostility. Some of the more moderate deputies were arrested and two of them were afterward murdered. The assembly hall itself was closely picketed by "Red 

Guards." Soon after the assembly met, on

Lenin meant that the Russian movement. masses should follow his lead, whether they wanted to or not. In order to prevent any organized opposition, he launched a reign of terror. Doubtless this was his only chance of success; for the Ukraine had fallen away, foreign powers were intervening, and civil war was raging. By force he had risen to power, and by force he meant to keep it. 

The Russian Terror bears some resemblance to the French Terror of 1793. A revolutionary tribunal, called the "Cheka," was established to deal with cases of opposition. Its members had power to punish without trial; and many thousands were slain on mere suspicion, or because they belonged to the hated aristocracy or middle class. Hostile peasants fared little better, and even moderate socialists were treated as enemies. Sometimes "mass terror" was instituted, thousands being shot down at one time. To suppress insurrection, a new force, the "Red Army," was available, and it did its work most thoroughly. It was the Red 

Army that furnished the power on which this new despotism rested.

Among the victims of the Red Terror were the members of the imperial family, who had been brought from western Siberia, where they had been confined during the winter, to a town in southeastern Russia. On the night of 

July 16, 1918, they were commanded to descend to the cellar of the building in which they were housed, and were there summarily shot.

One will never know the number of victims of the Terror, and it is sometimes hard to distinguish between the murders planned by the Cheka and those which were the result of the general disorder, for Russia was still in a state of anarchy. But Lenin was getting a stronger grip on Russia with every month, and by systematic terror he prevented opposition from developing in the heart of the country. 

For meeting attacks from outside the Red

Thus Lenin was doing well with the class war. war. Meanwhile, he had begun the organization of the new Russia. It is to this that we must now turn.

D. The Communist Dictatorship 

The Bolsheviks had adopted as their party label the name "Communists," and by this name we shall henceforth call them. A dictatorship was necessitated by the fact that they were a minority and also by the fact that only a despotic government could lift Russia out of anarchy and defend her successfully against foreign interference. Then, too, a workers' dictatorship was for these communists a matter of principle. Let us now study this dictatorship both in its internal policy and in its relations with the rest of Europe. 

INTERNAL ASPECTS OF THE COMMUNIST RÉGIME What Communism Means 

Com- Someone has called communism "socialism in a hurry." Socialism, as conceived by most of its champions, is grounded on a democratic basis, and is expected to come gradually, preferably by peaceful evolution. munism implies the immediate establishment of socialism by force and the dictatorship of the working class even though it be still in a minority. But the difference is one of method rather than of principle. Both of them have as their object a socialist régime. 

Communism, however, as worked out in Russia, seemed to stand for more than this. It seemed to signify four things. In the first place it meant a social revolution, whereby the working class, formerly at the bottom of the social scale, should rise immediately to the top. Other classes eventually should be merged in this class or become outcasts. Or, to put the matter differently, Russia should eventually develop a classless society, all being workers and all having practically the same

THE RUSSIAN REVOLUTION AND THE RISE OF COMMUNISM 

pay, or at all events "pay according to one's needs." The old socialist slogan had been, "From him according to his talents; to him according to his needs." It was not presumed that needs would vary greatly in a socialist community, for if workers' children should be cared for by the State, as some of the communists now hoped, then the size of a worker's family would scarcely affect his needs. In any case, much socialist theory had yet to be worked out in practice. Secondly, communism meant a religious revolution (which is also in a sense social), replacing the Orthodox religion by the creed of socialism. People should cease to believe in God, but should believe without any question that socialism was best for all. The Hereafter did not count; one should consider only the comforts of this temporal world, and unite with others to raise the material well-being of the masses. 

Communism meant, thirdly, an economic revolution, whereby private capital should cease; interest, rent, and employment of hired labor should be abolished; and everyone should become a paid employee of the State, the workers' state. This would be essentially socialism and would be the first attempt in history to realize it on a large scale. Finally, it meant a political revolution in the sense that instead of parliaments representing people according to their numbers there should be councils and assemblies representative of industries or professions. If all such sweeping changes should be achieved, Russia would have passed through a social, religious, economic, and political transformation the like of which the world had never seen. publics. The existence of these various republics was a concession to the principle of nationality, as the Ukrainians had one of their own, and so did various Asiatic peoples. On the other hand, the term "Russian" did not appear in the name of the state for the reason that it was hoped to include all other nations. 

A world state of the working class was the ultimate aim.

Representation, as we have pointed out, was vocational. Every factory or trade or profession chose members of the local or town soviet; and the town and village soviets, the latter made up of peasants, chose representatives to larger bodies above them. Without going into details, there was an ascending scale of soviets till we reach a small legislative body, known as the "Presidium," and another, a sort of ministry, known as the "Council of Peoples' Commissars," of which Lenin himself was chief. This system with certain variations applied both to the member states and to the union as a whole. Until 1936, the peasants were given smaller representation than the workers, since as yet the mass of the peasants were neither communists nor wage-earners, and this was supposed to be a "dictatorship of the working class." The seat of the new autocracy, which someone has called “czarism in overalls," was Moscow.

But none of this machinery meant that the workers really ruled. Though Lenin's ideal was the "dictatorship of the working class,' the working class did not, in point of fact, rule Russia. It was the party machine that ruled, or, perhaps more accurately, its chief.

Of much greater importance than this machinery of government was the Communist Organization of Communism and the First Attempt Party, the only political party allowed to to Operate It 

The first requisite for putting communism into operation was the reorganization of the state. In July, 1918, a constitution was made for Russia proper; that is, the country occupied by Russians as distinguished from certain other nationalities. Later, in 1923, after the civil war was over, a constitution was made for the entire country, the state thus formed being known as the Union of Socialist Soviet Re- I Lenin believed that in time the State itself could be dispensed with. It would "wither away," as he expressed it. exist in Russia. This party was composed of persons whose "communism" was thoroughly assured. Every confessed communist (and it was hardly safe to admit being anything else) was not a member of the party, but only those whose records showed them to be zealous workers for the cause. 

There was a very severe test for party loyalty, and every year members were struck from the list for being lukewarm or supposedly disloyal. But to become a member of the party was considered a great honor.

It gave such a person a chance

THE RUSSIAN REVOLUTION AND THE RISE OF COMMUNISM 

323 to hold an important office in the state and to be looked upon as a missionary and guardian of the faith.

The party had its grip on all Russian life and thought. It had its elective assembly and also its inner council, the Political Bureau, consisting of nine men, who formed a sort of working cabinet for the dictator. It was in this select body that Russian policies were shaped, and the various government organs were forced to obey it. In order the better to insure loyalty among the masses, the party had its little groups, known as "cells," in every shop, village, and regiment. At the same time, all suspects were summarily dealt with by the Cheka (later replaced by a similar body, known by its initials as the "Ogpu"), which kept the Russian people more or less in a state of fear. Meanwhile no ideas were permitted to enter from the West, for the censorship was strict and very effective. No one, except for an official purpose, was permitted to leave Russia. Every means was employed to make the Russian people sincere and convinced communists. Propaganda was systematic and ceaseless.

The economic organization of the state was, for a time, as strongly centralized as the political. Lenin soon ceased to allow the workers to run everything to suit themselves or the peasants to sell their produce as they wished. 

More and more the government itself took over the industries, and operated them as far as possible itself. At the same time it began to exercise a strict control over the peasants, exacting the surplus of their products, and distributing it among the industrial population in exchange for goods at a fixed rate of exchange. Some of the larger industries, such as railways, oil, and textiles, were organized under central boards of control; while over the whole system was placed the Supreme Council of Public Economy. It was this body that handled Russia's foreign trade, the one commercial link with the outside world. 

Such a policy of State ownership or control was the more necessary because Russia was still engaged in civil war, and she must be sure of having sufficient food and clothing, adequate railway service, and oil and coal for transportation purposes. But in any case

Lenin wanted the workers' government to run the nation's economic life.

The combined political and economic systems of government required a huge corps of officials, altogether much larger than the machinery of the Old Régime which they had replaced. Probably in some cases men had passed from one régime to the other; and Lenin once declared that of every hundred Bolsheviks there was "one true Bolshevik, thirty-nine adventurers, and sixty fools." Most of the true Bolsheviks, being workmen, had, of course, no executive experience, and sometimes no moral principle. moral principle. But standards were doubtless raised by the practice of treating graft or corruption as capital offenses. This period, sometimes spoken of as "war communism," was, however, a trying ordeal for the Russian people. The small stock of food left to citizens after the army had been fed had to be rationed, and as the manual worker got the lion's share, there was little or none left for the middle class. But the workers themselves were often surly and quarrelsome. The fact that they called one another "comrade" did not make them more polite in the struggle for food. Often they found relief for their emotions by persecuting those people, now outcasts, who had once been comfortably off.

Class hatred was at its height during this period.

Hundreds of thousands deserted to the country to get food, and many of those who stayed behind were clumsy and slack in their work. The factories, therefore, went at a slow pace and production greatly declined. Lenin's chief difficulty, however, was with the peasants, who refused to give up their grain. But none of these measures met with much success, and Lenin's extension of the class war to the villages had a disastrous effect. The peasants refused to raise sufficient crops, since they made up their minds that they would not produce a surplus, and the result was the terrible famine of 1921 in which three million perished. Moreover, the workers themselves, on whose loyalty Lenin depended, were sullen and discontented. There were frequent strikes and riots; and in 1921 a mutiny in the 

Baltic fleet seemed to suggest that even the armed forces could no longer be relied upon.

For these reasons Lenin decided that he had carried his policy farther than had been wise, so, in 1921, he adopted what was known as the "New Economic Policy," popularly known as the "Nep." While the government retained its grip on the major industries, some of the plants were now turned back to their original owners, or were leased to persons who wished to run them for profit, though the government reserved the right to tax heavily these "Nepmen," as they were called, if they enriched themselves unduly. It was a compromise with capital. Lenin also made concessions to the peasants, who were allowed to sell their grain on condition of paying a fixed tax in kind. All this meant that capitalism was tolerated once more. For Lenin had feared that his government would end in failure unless production were increased and misery relieved. Some of his followers did not agree with him, however, and many thousands were struck from the party rolls for their opposition.

This was, of course, not communism in full. 

But Lenin seemed to believe that the State would eventually outstrip private industry by showing a greater efficiency. In the meantime, the principal object was attained: production increased. But Lenin himself was breaking under the strain of his hard labors, and he died in January, 1924, at the age of fifty-three.

The Return to Pure Communism Who was to take the place of the great leader? After a good deal of maneuvering for the honor, the acknowledged leadership passed to one of Lenin's co-workers, Joseph Stalin. 

As with Lenin and most revolutionaries, this was not his original name, but one that he had adopted, and it fittingly meant "steel." 

Stalin was a native of the Caucasus, with a long and checkered career as a revolutionist.

He was not the man of learning that Lenin had been, but he possessed a cold and calculating mind and an indomitable will. Though he preferred to remain in the background (his only position was an office in the Communist

Under Stalin there was gradually a return to pure communism. Conditions had become improved during the Nep, and it was felt that the government could now safely go back to its former policy. Most of the thousands of 

Nepmen were therefore taxed out of existence, and the government gradually appropriated all industries again. In 1928, Stalin launched the famous "Five-Year Plan," by which it was intended that production should be more than doubled. Immense plants were constructed; dams and power-houses multiplied; and industry expanded with a speed never heretofore experienced in any land. Russia was to be 

Russia was to be made into an industrial country able to satisfy all her needs. In the meantime, agriculture must be made to increase its store. Accordingly, Stalin turned on the peasants, and forced them to work their lands under government supervision in return for a moderate profit fixed by the government. Yet Stalin won in the end; and some of the peasants became reconciled to the scheme by the chance afforded them of using agricultural machinery. In the meantime, the Five-Year 

Plan, as far as volume of goods was concerned, was a huge success. (The pictogram on page

But to carry out this work of increased production the present was deliberately sacrificed to the future. An immense amount of food and goods were exported to foreign countries in return for machinery and other things that would make possible more and more factories. 

This meant that the Russian people themselves had barely enough to keep going. "We must give up butter and turn it into bricks," said a Russian official. "We deny ourselves meats in order to convert them into machines." Food

Housing conditions, too, were very bad, since the towns were overcrowded by the rapid inflow of workers to man the factories. Some people lived in cellars; others slept in bunks one above the other; and sanitary conveniences were primitive. Such hardships were bearable only because the Russian people were accustomed to great privations. Even so, many of them wondered whether the dictatorship of the working class was really worth the price.

Social Changes 

Yet some things were given them by way of compensation. Much leisure time was secured by fixing the working week at five days and the working day at seven hours (six, indeed, for miners). Then there were plenty of cheap amusements theaters, movies, libraries, clubs, and excursions on the railways. 

The young men and young women were encouraged to take part in sports. And there were occasional attacks on persons suspected of trying to make personal profit, for the class war must go on to sustain the enthusiasm of the people. In place of the old religion, with its clergy and images and ceremonies, good communists embraced the ideals of the Revolution. 

Lenin's tomb, shown on page 328, was a shrine which everyone might visit and there see the departed leader, so effectively embalmed that he seemed only to be sleeping. Family life was not so strong as it had been, for the woman was a worker as well as the man, and sometimes children were looked after in nurseries run by the State. But women enjoyed equality with men - equality in rights and duties. 

Just as the old religion was dying, so the old idea of right and wrong was changed to some extent. Murder was dealt with mildly as a rule, but to plot against the government or even to swindle it brought death. Meanwhile, low as the standard of living undoubtedly was, every ablebodied person was sure of

One of the greatest achievements of the Communist Régime was the reduction of illiteracy. Hundreds of thousands of peasants were taught to read, and there were also schools in which people were given the elements of vocational training. One felt that once again, as in the time of Peter the Great, a despotic government was forcing Russia to catch up with the material achievements of the West.

A Mysterious One-Man Dictatorship 

Finally, thanks to a second five-year plan, which took more note of the actual needs of the people, general conditions somewhat improved. In 1935, the rationing system was suspended, and there were even a few luxuries for the people who could afford them. In 1936, on the ground that a classless society had finally been attained, Stalin granted a new constitution, allowing the people to vote directly for a national legislative body, and for the first time giving the peasants a voice in proportion to their numbers. Even freedom 

Authenticated News of speech, press, and assembly was guaranteed. 

Did this, then, mean that Russia was becoming democratic, or, in communist language, a "dictatorship of the proletariat"? No, there were indications that the Communist Party had not relaxed its grip in the slightest degree. would be a mistake to suppose that Russia was under a dictatorship of the proletariat. More and more had power come to be concentrated in the hands of one man the dictator, Stalin. It

There was even a growing departure from communist ideals. More and more, wages came to vary, with both classes and individuals. 

Special rewards were given to those who displayed conspicuous merit, and those in high positions received relatively high salaries and even some special privileges, such as the exclusive right to patronize certain stores or to eat in the better restaurants. The peasants were also remunerated according to the amount and the quality of the output, but, considered as a whole, they were allowed to profit so little from their toil that their exploitation was almost as great as it had been in czarist days. All this was in violation of

THE RUSSIAN REVOLUTION AND THE RISE OF COMMUNISM 329 

Lenin's principle that workers as far as possible should be on the same economic level. 

Other indications of a reaction were the scrapping of the chain system of soviets by the constitution of 1936 and public allusions to the "honor and glory of the fatherland" - a displacing of the class spirit by the familiar creed of nationalism. It is no wonder, perhaps, that Stalin punished with death most of the leading followers of Lenin. To the West, Communist Russia has been a puzzle difficult to solve.

Can we imagine, perhaps, that Stalin was trying to make Russia stronger, at the expense of a better life for the Russian masses? Perhaps a clue may be found in the story of Russia's relations with the rest of Europe. This story brings us back to the time of Lenin, when Communist Russia was forced to face a thoroughly unfriendly world. 

EXTERNAL ASPECTS OF THE COMMUNIST RÉGIME Communist Russia on the Defensive 

Europe as a whole did not like the Communist Régime. Accustomed to capitalism, the countries outside of Russia naturally hated and feared communism. What if the working class of the West should imbibe these doctrines and also resort to revolution! Then, too,

Russia's allies in the First World War blamed the Communist Régime for what they regarded as a betrayal of the common cause. Some of their citizens, too, had great difficulty in leaving Russia, and a few of them had been murdered during the anarchy that prevailed. 

France was also indignant because the Soviet government had repudiated foreign debts, for 

Russia owed France $3,000,000,000.

When the representatives of the Allied powers met in Paris in 1918, they were forced to give some attention to the Russian problem. 

France tried to persuade the other powers to adopt a policy of outright intervention on a large scale, but neither British nor American opinion was in favor of another war. 

As a matter of fact, small international armies had been landed at Archangel and Vladivostok during the war in order to keep a check on the Bolsheviks, who were suspected of being the WURF.

Europe Makes Peace with Communist Russia 

Fear of communist propaganda made outside powers hesitate to come to terms with Russia. But after the inauguration of the 

Nep, and as danger from Russian policy seemed to subside, they began to consider the benefits that might be derived from trading with Russia. Great Britain set the example by making a commercial treaty with Russia in 1921, and, the following year, Germany formally recognized the Soviet government. Soon afterward most of the other powers followed her example. Stalin, for his part, anxious to purchase machinery in the West, let it be known that Russia was content with establishing socialism at home instead of clinging to Lenin's ideal of a world revolution. When in 1934, Russia was actually admitted to membership in the League of Nations, she might feel that her days as an outcast were long since past.

Russia Once More an Important Factor in European

In 1935, Russia entered into a defensive alliance with France. There are people who believe that the constitution of 1936 was merely a gesture to make it appear that Russia was even becoming a democracy. As late as March, 1939, Russia was still disposed to unite with France and Great Britain against the common German menace.

CHAPTER XV The Rise of Fascism and the Making of Another Great War 

What are the characteristics of fascism? What conditions led to fascism in Italy and in Germany?

How did the imperialistic policies of Germany, Italy, and Japan threaten world peace? Why did these acts of aggression go unchallenged?

PERHAPS MORE DANGEROUS to the world even than communism was a philosophy or movement known as fascism. Though resting on a capitalistic basis, it involved, like communism, a dictatorship that gripped the whole political, economic, and cultural life of the nation concerned; and unlike communism (in theory), it was characterized by an intense and aggressive nationalism. To grapple with 

To grapple with this force the democracies of Europe seemed for a long time unfitted. Their instrument, the League of Nations, which was supposed to safeguard peace, was allowed to languish into impotence. Little by little, the new order, established at Paris in 1919, was whittled away by the aggressions of three autocratic powers, Japan, Italy, and Germany. not until they were driven to desperation that the democratic powers, France and Great Britain, took up the challenge. The result was another great war.

A. What Fascism Means An Answer to Democracy 

Fascism was bred, as we shall see, of the conviction that democracy was essentially inefficient and lacking in vigor. Thus fascism

Thus fascism stood first of all for autocratic government. 

But as dictatorships were nothing unusual in history, this hardly expresses the peculiar meaning of fascism. As a matter of fact, there was little new in this curious type of régime, but it embraced a combination of certain ideas,

The Essentials of Fascism 

The There appeared to be three essential characteristics of fascism. In the first place, fascism stood for a dictatorship that was organized through a party. The dictator was the leader of that party, the only political party legally allowed; and that party expressed all the fascist ideals as well as taught them to the nation. the nation. Obviously the tendency was to produce a people who thought alike. individual counted for nothing beside the State and must subject himself completely to its will as determined by the dictator. 

Such a state was known as a totalitarian state, since the total population must stand together in devotion to the same ideals. In the second place, fascism stood for strict regulation of the entire economic life of the nation. Unlike communism, private enterprise lay at the basis of the system, but it was subject to government dictation. Thus the government might fix prices, restrict output, limit or even prohibit imports, as well as control the banks and other agencies of credit. It also supervised the relations of capital and labor. Thirdly, fascism stood for an intense nationalism. It sought conquests for glory. It aimed at economic self-sufficiency, since this made for strength in war. It was thus allied with militarism and opposed in principle to peace. "Fascism," said Mussolini, "... believes neither in the possibility nor in the utility of perpetual peace... cowardice in the face of sacrifice. War alone brings up to its highest tension all human energy and puts the stamp

OF FASCISM THE RISE 

of nobility upon the peoples who have the courage to meet it.”

B. The Rise of Fascism in Italy 

After-War Conditions in Italy Origins of Fascism Fascism in Italy was the result of after-war conditions. There was economic distress following the war, and consequent disorders; and there was a general feeling that Italy had been cheated of her share in the spoils of war. 

The economic distress was much the same as in other countries. There was a large army to get back into regular employment, and since business was disorganized by the war, there were a lot more men than jobs. 

About four hundred thousand men were without employment. Moreover, prices had gone up, partly because the production of goods to meet ordinary needs had been sacrificed to the making of arms and hence there was a general scarcity of everything; and partly because money was worth less than before the war, owing to inflation. It was even believed that "big business" deliberately kept up prices in order to swell its profits. Moreover, many soldiers, after army discipline was over, had a feeling that they did not want to settle down to a normal existence.

Especially restless were the workers. There were constant strikes (as many as two thousand in 1920); and in many places workers seized the factories and tried to run them. The disorders even reached the countryside, where ill-paid farm laborers seized land from their employers. There was also a sharp revulsion against the war, which the workers felt was responsible for their woes, and ex-service men were frequently insulted. Sometimes a railway union stopped a train because a veteran got on board. Italy was almost in a state of anarchy and seemed to be headed for communism.

If the government had been capable, something might have been done to remove the causes of this disorder; or if the government had been strong, it might have suppressed it. 

But aside from the weakness of the ministries which followed one another during this period, Italians had little confidence in their government. They seemed unable to realize that their parliament was supposed to represent them and to reflect their wishes. Most

Italians took no interest at all in politics which was the reason unscrupulous men had so often come into power. 

But the government not only was defied by riotous workmen; it was bitterly criticized by many of the middle class. There was a feeling among this class that Italy's allies in the war had cheated her of her just share of the spoils. 

She had failed to get additions to her colonial empire; failed to share in the spoliation of 

Turkey; failed to get all that she coveted on the Adriatic. Therefore the politicians must be to blame, and something should be done about it. The government was pressed on both sides - harassed from below and ridiculed from above. It was likely to go to pieces between the two.

The Rise of Fascism 

Such were the causes of the unrest which led to fascism. Fascism drew some of its strength from those elements who were determined that if the government could not enforce law and order, private individuals should do so; if the government could not do anything to make Italy respected, then somebody must be found who would. Various bands, or fasci (to use the Italian word), were formed among private citizens, who talked a good deal of patriotic duty and the need of restoring unity. They got a lot of comfort out of a raid made on Fiume by the Italian poet, Gabriele d'Annunzio, and hailed him as a second Garibaldi. They also took the law into their own hands, attacking workers' organizations and meting out wholesale violence to communists. Was there truth in their proud boast that they had rescued Italy from anarchy? No, for by 1921 the worst disorders were over. The workmen, who could not, of course, run the factories, had given them up; and the danger from communism had passed. But the restless fascist bands had made an impression, and that was the fact which brought their leader into the limelight. 

Benito Mussolini (whose picture appears on page 335) was the son of a poor blacksmith.

He was, in fact, largely self-educated. After a time he became a journalist and showed a gift for writing. By temperament and principles he was something of a radical socialist, but he was much too restless a person to believe in neutrality for Italy when the First World War broke out. He advocated Italy's entering the war, and by becoming a militant patriot, he had to break with his socialist friends. Yet he lost little by his action, for he served in the army and had the distinction of being wounded. 

Mussolini was not impulsive, like many

Italians; he was calculating and determined. 

His big black eyes, deep-set in his forehead, seemed to burn like live coals when he made a decision. His great vitality gave one the impression, as a reporter has expressed it, of "an electric shock." He was an effective speaker, though his vanity often made him rather ridiculous. Endowed with a real genius for organization, he was also shrewd and unscrupulous in his methods. Above all, he was at this time a man of consuming ambition. 

Mussolini welded the fascist bands together and headed a partya party the Fascist Party.

Though he had failed on a former occasion, he managed, in 1921, to win a seat in parliament, and by that time he believed himself strong enough to denounce the existing government for its cowardice. Breaking completely with socialism, he declared for private enterprise, and he stressed the importance of maintaining order and of insisting upon respect for Italy abroad. Such were the main points he offered the public in his platform.

The Coup d'Etat 

But Mussolini, at the head of a minority in parliament, could not expect to head the government; and in fact, he refused a seat in

FIGURE 210 

In Hyde Park the British tradition of free speech enables any man to voice his ideas, speak against the government, or urge reforms. A force of two thousand Fascists, clad in those black shirts which already had made them famous, marched on Rome. Mussolini followed by train, and found the King ready to receive him. As the army was apparently favorable to the Fascists, Victor Emmanuel had not the courage to do otherwise. At all events, he made Mussolini Premier, and since the parliament as a whole was not Fascist, this was clearly a coup d'état. Democracy had surrendered to a dictator.

With the power of the Blackshirts behind him, Mussolini now proceeded to dominate parliament as well as to choose a ministry subservient to himself. He forced the passage of an electoral law which would give the party polling the most votes three fifths of the seats in the popular chamber. Since public opinion seemed, after all, to approve the coup d'état, the elections of 1924 gave the Fascists the control they wanted. Mussolini thus consolidated his power. 

Political Organization of the Dictatorship

The organization of the dictatorship occupied the next few years. It was ruled that every law had to receive the approval of the Premier in advance, and frequently the government, which really meant Mussolini, itself enacted laws. After a time the system of election to the Chamber of Deputies was changed, the government being given the right of nomination, and the Senate meanwhile lapsed into subservience. The country became more centralized than ever, not the slightest degree of self-government being permitted. But the real power in the state was, of course, Mussolini himself, who presided over the body which really decided what the parliament was to do. This was the Grand 

Council of the Fascist Party. 

So the strength of the fascist dictatorship lay not in the organs of government, but in

the Fascist Party, which was the only party permitted in the state and came to number nearly two million men. This party held the nation in its grip; and part of it was made up of the Blackshirts, a sort of special police who stood ready to repress the slightest opposition. 

Many persons were sentenced to terms of imprisonment and some were brutally murdered, though the stock method of dealing with most offenders was to make them drink a quantity of castor oil. In order to control public opinion, a strict censorship was established. "Fascism," said Mussolini, "tolerates no difference of opinion."

Economic Organization of the Dictatorship 

Mussolini made it clear that he believed in private enterprise, and he gave his favor as a rule to "big business." But while he did not intend that the State should operate industry, as in Russia, he insisted that the State should control the entire economic life of the people. 

Not ownership but regulation was his policy. 

Every merchant must have a license, and so also must every member of the professional 

Wages and prices, working and living conditions everything must be regulated by the State. was less corruption; less waste of money. 

The railroads were better run. Public buildings were kept cleaner. No longer did the country swarm with beggars. Fascism also made for unity in certain ways. Mussolini was able to work out a peace with the Papacy, in 1929, whereby the Church was allowed complete control over a certain section of Rome and received a generous indemnity for the loss of its temporal power, and in return recognized the King of Italy. Fascism roused a fervent patriotism, and Mussolini's achievements in foreign affairs gave Italy a prestige she had never had before. He was successful in getting Fiume and in persuading France and Great Britain to make some slight additions to Italy's colonies in Africa. In 1924 he made Albania practically an Italian sphere of interest. He also made a business of and on more than one occasion he showed his trying to Italianize the Germans of the Tyrol, contempt for the League of Nations. 

this promoted national feeling and strengthened the dictatorship.

It is clear enough that Il Duce (the leader) a twentieth-century thought of himself as

Caesar and desired to make of Italy a second Rome. He was thus a frank imperialist, as was soon to be shown by his war with Ethiopia. on the Mediterranean. But whether Italy was strong enough to play such a grandiose rôle remained to be seen.

For the better ordering of the economic life, Italy, like Rome, must rule a great empire and to prevent "labor troubles," there were formed two parallel groups of federations, one of employers, one of workmen, which kept in touch with the government on economic questions and adjusted all labor disputes. 

There was even a labor code, which fixed certain rights for the working class, such as one day of rest a week and the enjoyment of social insurance. An eight-hour day was not guaranteed, since the working day was supposed to depend on business conditions in the country. The wage scale, always low, steadily declined.

What did fascism achieve? What services did it render in return for taking away a people's liberties?

Achievements of Italian Fascism 

It is undoubtedly true that this dictatorship was a much more efficient government than anything that had preceded it. There There 

The Weakness of Italian Fascism 

Was Italy really happy under a dictatorship? 

One could not say; for there was no chance for anyone to voice criticism of any sort.

Everyone's feelings or interests were subordinated to the interest of the State, as Mussolini determined it. Hundreds of thousands of liberals preferred to seek happiness in exile than to submit to the will of one man; and the 

King, who was nothing but a puppet, might have wished that he could do likewise. 

Moreover, Italy under a vain and blustering autocrat was a constant danger to the peace. 

Much of an autocrat's power lies in his ability to rouse his people to feel hatred of the outside world. This was also to be true of 

Hitler.

OF FASCISM THE RISE c. The Rise of Fascism in Germany 

Germany accepted fascism ten years after it had established itself in Italy. Here, too, discontent and wounded vanity furnished the inspiration.

THE CAUSES OF REACTION IN GERMANY AND THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A NEW GERMANY 

The Weakness of the Republic The democratic régime which had been established in 1919 was not strong enough or popular enough to last. This was due partly to the character of this new régime, and partly to the trials which it was obliged to undergo. 

Let us detail the various causes of the reaction. 

In the first place, Germans came to dislike the republic for its failure to "talk back" to the Allies, and for the moderation of its statesmen, especially Stresemann, who tried to work out an understanding with these powers. They smarted under the many humiliations they had received, and felt that they would never really regain their self-respect till they were strong enough or bold enough to defy the powers which had made the Treaty of Versailles. It was a case of offended nationalism which burned to express itself. Under a liberal régime this brandishing of the sword was hardly to be expected. 

In the second place, most Germans had passed through a period of terrible suffering, and even as the years wore on, their standard of living was still rather low. The inflation of the currency had beggared many millions. 

The lower middle class, composed of professional people and shopkeepers, had lost all their savings and were hardly able to do much more than live. The peasants also were injured because the price of the grain they raised had failed to keep pace with the prices of things they had to buy; and though wages had gone up during a short period of industrial revival, they had slumped again later, and the evil of unemployment became more serious than ever. 

Before the end of 1932, there were as many as six million unemployed. 

Germans became discouraged, and began to wonder if there was not something wrong with the kind of government they had set up. 

Though the republic could scarcely have done otherwise, they blamed it for paying anything to the Allies as "reparations."

Actually the sums paid in reparations were not so great as the sums spent on the building of new homes for the poor, the creation of amusement parks, and an elaborate system of unemployment insurance which the republic had provided for its workers. But the German people preferred to believe that reparations were responsible for their woes, and one party, the National Socialists, openly expressed this view. When the reparations scheme finally collapsed, the democratic régime had given way to a temporary dictatorship. Thus it would seem that the stronger the government was, the more likely it would be to defy Germany's "oppressors.”

In the third place, the Great Depression, which swept over the world in the late nineteen-twenties, resulted in new hardships for the German people, and made them unwilling to help the government in its predicament. 

The Chancellor, Bruening, tried to cut down government expenses, but the Reichstag blocked his efforts. Few seemed to show the patience or the sense of patriotic duty that might enable the government to grapple with the crisis.

In the fourth place, all the ministries which had governed under the republic depended on coalitions or party groupings for a majority in the Reichstag, and this tended to make them timid. If they showed unusual courage, some party whose support was, perhaps, essential, might drift away. They had never dared to be firm with the royalist elements - not even when two of the leading statesmen were murdered by royalist fanatics. 

There were a number of armed bands, or private armies, which carried out their own ideas of justice, and yet were tolerated by the government. 

In the fifth place, the constitution had given the President (with the Chancellor's consent) extraordinary powers during an emergency, and no one had seemed to realize that such authority might be abused. In 1925, the veteran, Marshal von Hindenburg, a royalist by conviction, was elected President, and when in 1932, he disapproved of Chancellor Bruen-

The President was thus for the time being a dictator, keeping ministers in power by his own authority alone. Parliamentary government had been indefinitely suspended. 

The Rise of Hitler and National Socialism 

Meanwhile, we must consider the sixth cause of the reaction: the rise of Hitler and the National Socialists, who had long been agitating against the republic and attracting more and more followers to a military leadership.

Adolf Hitler (shown on this page at the height of his power) was of peasant extraction, a native of Austria, born in 1889. He had not, as a rule, applied himself at school, caring for little but painting. Apparently, however, he lacked the talent that would have qualified him for admission to an academy of art, and this was one of his keenest disappoint- After the death of his parents, he ments.

Acme moved to Vienna, where he worked at odd jobs, doing almost anything he could to make a living. These were certainly days of bitterness for young Adolf, for he felt himself superior to his fellow workers; and though experience gave him acquaintance with the masses, he refused to share their interests and secretly despised them. It was here that he learned to hate the working class, as well as the Jews, and even the city of Vienna itself. 

Finally, in 1912, he moved to Munich, where he managed to support himself chiefly as a house painter. When the war broke out, he was enrolled in the German army as a dispatch-bearer, and was noted for his prompt obedience to orders. Unlike most of his fellows, he got a real thrill out of the war, which seemed to him a kind of romantic dream. He was wounded and gassed, and received the iron cross, though he never was able to rise higher than a corporal. He was a good subordinate, but somehow not believed to possess the qualities of leadership required of an officer.

At the close of the war Hitler entered politics. He was not very sure of himself and was still rather shy and "stand-offish"; but

He knew how to appeal to the emotions and could readily put an audience into a frenzy.

Though he occasionally read a little, he never deeply studied any subject, and he harped on certain ideas such as the wickedness of the Jews and the need of a greater patriotism to rescue the beloved fatherland from the "tyranny" of the Allies. He told his compatriots that the republic had failed to defend the national honor. He even asserted that 

Germany had never really been beaten, but that the socialists who set up the republic had simply "stabbed her in the back."

All this, of course, appealed mightily to a people who liked to believe that they had not been defeated in battle, after all, and that therefore they might still hold up their heads with pride. In 1919 Hitler joined with others in organizing the National Socialist Party or "Nazis," for short. The emblem of the party was the swastika (), and most of its members wore brown shirts, reminding one of the Blackshirts of Italy. The party was ultra-nationalist, but could hardly be called socialist in any true sense of the term, notwithstanding some of its attacks on "big business." 

Indeed, the party was partly financed by a few industrial magnates who hoped to use it to push their own interests. Hitler was very lavish in his promises during these days, and he made a point of appealing to the unemployed (many of them, old soldiers), and especially to the lower middle class, for whom nothing had been done in the way of relief. They did not realize in those days that Hitler could break a promise as easily as he made it. 

A little too confident at first, Hitler, in 1923, seconded an effort of General Ludendorff to overthrow the republic, but the affair ended in failure, and he had to suffer a two months' imprisonment as a result. 

It was then that he began to write of his aspirations in a book called, Mein Kampf (My Battle).

By 1924, the Nazis had gained sufficient support to poll a large vote in the elections of that year. In 1928, the party lost ground, for

Germany was then in the midst of an industrial revival, and there was somewhat less discontent. But in 1930, after the Great Depression had set in, they polled more than six million votes; and two years later Hitler nearly defeated Hindenburg for the presidency. 

Bruening actually offered him a place in the cabinet, as did Hindenburg later, but Hitler preferred to wait until he could force his way into power on his own terms. No one could have any doubt as to what that victory would mean, for Hitler had sounded the warning that if ever he should come into power, "heads would roll in the sand."

Hitler Reaches His Goal 

After Hindenburg had made the mistake of breaking with Schleicher, there seemed no alternative but Hitler, and the President appointed him chancellor on January 30, 1933.

For the time being he had the support of the Junkers' party, to whom he had given some seats in the cabinet, and his problem was now to maneuver in such a way as to make himself dictator.

Yet, notwithstanding his alliance with the Junkers' party, it was still a matter of some doubt whether Hitler would have control of the new Reichstag, for which elections were soon to be held. It is true that the Nazis declared that they would remain in power anyway, but it was important to be able to show that the German people approved their rule.

Luckily for them, on the eve of the election, the building where the Reichstag met was burned, and it was only too easy to blame this act on the communists, and to appeal to the German people that the only way to stave off revolution was to give their votes to Hitler. Probably the whole truth about this fire will never be known, but it is now generally believed that some of the Nazis themselves burned the building. "A sign from Heaven," Hitler called this lucky break, and he proceeded to make the most of it. 

Since none of the opposition parties had been allowed to electioneer, no one could answer the charge that the communists were plotting revolution; and Hitler and his friends won the election. True, the margin of victory was very small, but it was enough to accomplish

Thus the Weimar constitution was a thing of the past, and a bloodless revolution had been accomplished. When Hitler removed the members of the Junkers' party from his cabinet, his supremacy was complete. The Nazis felt that a new Germany was born. Now what was to be the nature of this new régime?

CHARACTER AND ORGANIZATION OF THE NEW GERMANY The Work of Destruction 

Once in power, Hitler turned upon the socialists and communists, abolished their organizations, and clapped many thousands of them into prison. He next broke up the trade unions and confiscated their funds. He also commenced a policy of boycott and organized violence against the Jews. (The type of propaganda used is shown on this page.) They were deprived of their rights as citizens, debarred from the professions, and discriminated against in every way. 

How many Jews were murdered by the Storm 

Troopers of the Nazi Party we shall probably never know. Many thousands emigrated, including the most famous of living scientists, Albert Einstein. That, however, is what the Nazis wanted. They wished Germany to be a land only of people of the Aryan race.' 

But communists and Social Democrats fared almost as badly as Jews, and even moderate liberals found it wise to keep very quiet. 

All the rights which the constitution had granted to the people were at an end. Anyone was in danger of being haled before a court and condemned to either imprisonment or death. There was no longer freedom of opinion or freedom of assembly. A censorship was established, as strict as that of Italy or Russia. Also the secret police, known as the "Gestapo," spread its agents throughout the country ready to pounce on any person who seemed dissatisfied. The terror even struck down some of the Nazis themselves, as well as certain others in politics who happened to be suspect. 

Hitler's closest friend, Roehm, whom he regarded as a possible rival, as well as the former chancellor, Schleicher, were among the number, possibly a thousand, murdered by official order during the summer of 1934. Hitler's own nature was callous and vengeful, and most of his closest associates were men who can perhaps best be described as "gangsters."

The Work of Construction and Consolidation 

In the meantime, Hitler was reorganizing the government. Each of the states which had formed the German confederation was placed under an official who took his orders from the central government; and the federal chamber, the Reichsrath, was abolished. 

Germany was centralized as never before in her history. The Reichstag was still elected, but no longer did it have the slightest control

GERMAN VOTER From the London Daily Express

Is it a fair representation of the attitude of the German people toward the Hitler régime? over the government. Only one party was permitted, the National Socialist Party, and as Hitler was its leader (Der Fuehrer), the Reichstag, composed of Nazis, naturally let him have his way. The party was really the backbone of the State. To the State the individual owed obedience and devotion.

Members of the party were to be found in every department of the government and in every industry, forming "cells," as in Soviet Russia, and keeping watch on the behavior of the people. The only uncertain factor was the army, which was not quite so devoted to Corporal Hitler as he would like; but in the end even the army bowed to his will. 

The nation's economic life was organized in a manner similar to the political. That is, unity under the government was insured. Just as in Italy, employers and workmen were brought together in common organizations, which were supposed to regulate their common interests and settle all their disputes under the guiding hand of the State. In order to grapple with the depression, which became worse rather than better, the finance minister was given dictatorial powers. He could regulate the amount that any industry produced and fix prices. Yet the great industrialists were still behind Hitler, for they felt that with trade as bad as it was, only strong leadership could save Germany from collapse.

A class that suffered considerably were the workers. It is true that unemployment was much reduced, for jobs were found by forcing workers to take less pay and make room for more of their number on the working staffs, and the making of armaments again drew hundreds of thousands back into employment.

Besides, a lot of jobs were deliberately created at government expense, such as membership in the Storm Troopers, the uniformed police of the Nazi Party. But the level of wages fell, and the standard of living among the workers tended to decline. Someone had to carry the cost of the armaments Germany was building, and someone had to pay for the decline in trade, which was largely due to her strained relations with other powers.

The workers were the ones who chiefly bore the brunt of these conditions, though other classes also felt the pinch. 

And what was all this sacrifice for? Hitler believed that Germany must force the world to give her what she wanted. A militaristic 

Germany once more threatened the peace.

OF FASCISM THE RISE D. The Unstable Peace 

The peace of the world was not insured by the peace settlements made by the Congress of Paris. It was not insured by the Covenant of the League of Nations. What was the trouble? Let us look at the problem.

THE PROBLEM OF PEACE OR SECURITY The Fundamental Trouble 

If you look at the world as a political entity that is, as a huge something made up of sixty or more states you must realize that all these states are independent. There is no authority above them to say that they shall do this or not do that. The world has no supreme ruler. It is in anarchy - international anarchy.

It is a very different matter, of course, within a state. There is no anarchy within a civilized state. If a revolt should occur in 

Wales, threatening life and property, the British government would promptly put it down. If the local police were not strong enough to quell disorder, the army would do the job. Even in democratic countries one must obey the law.

But there is no body to enforce international law. Therefore one nation is always free to attack another. Is it not surprising that civilization has reached the stage where peace and order reign within a state and yet in the world at large there is anarchy?

Some say that wars are, after all, inevitable because people by their very natures like to fight. It is human nature, so they say. 

We get angry with our neighbor and so we attack him. Or perhaps he has something we want, and we fight him in order to seize it. 

But if we do, we get into trouble with the police. The law protects us all from the violence of our neighbors. We may be impelled to fight, but we know that we must pay for it if we do. Granted then that humanity is pugnacious, this does not mean that citizens fight one another. The law prevents their fighting, or punishes them if they do.

But unfortunately in the world at large that force we call nationalism is unwilling to be held in check, and the idea of world unity has never proved workable in practice. 

Thus, when nations want to fight, there is no power standing above them, no international police, let us say, to hold them back. Should there be such a power? there be such a power? Should some superstate, with representation from all the civilized countries, supply that need? Should such a state, or some such body as the League of Nations, have the right to say that the United States had wronged Mexico in some dispute and should yield to Mexico as a means of preventing war, and that if she did not do so, an army would be employed to enforce justice? 

We shall not answer that question. Some would say yes; some would say no. But the fact of the matter is that nations through the centuries have grown up to independence, and the citizens of every nation feel that no outside power should tell them what they should or should not do. If a nation feels outraged, and of course, it may be altogether wrong, it feels that it has a right to take such steps as it sees fit. That is why we have these huge armies, navies, and air fleets. Yet obviously no nation, especially in a temper, is fit to be a judge of its own case. All this would seem to show that for the sake of humanity at large some means should be found for putting a curb on nationalism. If Yet much of the constant friction between nations could be avoided if they were willing and able to remove the causes of war. there were nothing especial to fight about, nations might live at peace, for war is such a hardship that few nations, of their own free will, would wage it. Was there, then, no way to assure a nation that its reasonable demands would be granted? If Russia could be quite sure that she might always send her merchantmen through the Straits, she would not, perhaps, be tempted to seize Constantinople. Could not one hope that disputes might be settled, in a real spirit of justice, by collective decisions of the powers? Could not the peace of the world be made the business of all? But here again one must realize that only when the powers were really in earnest would an aggressive nation be made to feel that it could not break a treaty or resort to force without force without offending against them all.

Hence it was only through some strong-willed

international organization that law and peace in the world could be enforced. It was here that the League of Nations seemed to fulfill a real need.

The Declining Prestige of the League of Nations 

Unfortunately, the League of Nations never managed to obtain the confidence of the world at large, and even disappointed the hopes of those who wanted it to amount to something. 

It had a bad start when it was dominated in the beginning by the great victor powers, The defeated powers, it is true, were later admitted, but, in the meantime, much of its moral strength had been lost by futile efforts to make it stronger. Though the League had managed to settle some minor disputes, the real test of its worth must be its competence to settle a quarrel in which a "great power" was involved. And the League had been practically ignored when Mussolini, in 1922, had quarreled with Greece and won his case. 

Viewing the League as affording too little security for herself, France had built up a system of alliances, designed to safeguard the peace against Germany, on the one hand (in case Germany became strong again), and

Russia, on the other. This system included 

Poland, Rumania, Czechoslovakia, Jugoslavia (the last three being known as the "Little Entente"), and, for a time also,

Belgium. But such a policy hardly afforded security for Germany, who, unless the League would work, was practically defenseless. And here we must go back a little.

The Invasion of the Ruhr and the Pacts of Locarno 

You will remember that the powers had left the reparations question in a muddle. Germany made some reparation payments, but never as much as demanded, and the total, of course, had never been decided upon.

One matter that seriously complicated the situation was the fact that the Allies owed an immense war debt to the United States, and reparations from Germany were intended largely to balance this huge bill. After a time, however, Great Britain came to believe that Germany should be treated rather more lightly. She wanted Germany to recover because normally that nation was one of her best customers. France, on the other hand, thought of her own huge debt and her wasted lands, and refused to relent a particle. It was the friction that developed between these two that partly encouraged Germany to default. Besides, the new republic did not feel particularly strong, and dared not increase taxes just to send money out of the country. 

Finally, in despair, since Germany continued to default, France, with Belgium's cooperation, invaded the Ruhr (1923), which is the heart of Germany's mining region in the west. Germany's reply to this action was to command all the miners to quit their jobs rather than work the mines for the French, and, in order to support them in the meantime, she issued paper money in enormous quantities. 

This, of course, was wild inflation, and soon her money was rendered practically worthless. 

People who lived on their investments lost everything they had, and people with salaries or wages were reduced to the greatest distress, since prices were so high they could not meet their needs. In the meantime, France, for her part, collected little or nothing in the way of reparations, though she did force the powers to give the question more serious attention; and when Germany's finances were finally put in order, the latter was able to and did pay further installments until, with the coming of the Great Depression, she again defaulted. 

The invasion of the Ruhr had, however, an important bearing on the peace of Europe. 

Though the invading army withdrew, Germany felt that she must never be subjected to such acts again. As a result, her foreign minister, Gustav Stresemann, proposed some treaties that would protect France and Germany from each other. Such were the Pacts or Treaties of Locarno of 1925. France, 

Great Britain, Germany, and Italy guaranteed the frontier which divided Germany on the one hand and France and Belgium on the other. Should either France or Germany attack the other, Great Britain and Italy were pledged to assist the one attacked. This meant that Germany renounced any hope of recovering Alsace-Lorraine, and it also meant that France was no longer free to invade Germany. But the Pacts of Locarno seemed to be evidence that the League of Nations was felt to be unequal to dealing with a difficult problem of security. Here a group of powers, acting outside the League, took steps to prevent war. This was nothing more than a return to the old diplomacy, though with a worthy goal in view. Yet the old diplomacy had never been successful in preserving peace when new conditions tempted a power to aggression.
