The Emergence of New Dangers 

In any case we must remember that the war left hatreds which made the maintenance of peace unusually difficult. Germany longed to revenge herself for defeat. France hated and feared her as a power that could never be trusted. Imperialism received a fresh impetus, because three powers, Japan, Germany, and

Italy, claimed that they were cramped and must obtain additional land and raw materials. 

Wounded vanity and ambition were paving the way for new wars. Let us examine the attitude of these powers in some detail. 

E. Japan Moves Again Japan Yields to Temptation and Grabs Manchuria 

Japan was the restless power of the Orient. 

She had taken advantage of the First World 

War to try to force a protectorate on China, and though she had not been able to bring this about, she had made important economic

gains. As a result of the First World War she had come into possession of three German groups of islands in the Pacific. Though she did restore to China in 1922 the former German leasehold in Shantung, she received some compensation. Now Japan, like other countries, suffered from disturbed business conditions after the war, and many of her manufacturers held the opinion that the acquisition of lands possessed of great natural resources' would help her back to prosperity. Such territory could be found only in China. 

Relations with China were never very friendly. When China resented the conduct of her powerful neighbor, she usually resorted to a boycott of Japanese goods; and as China, next to the United States, was Japan's principal customer, these boycotts cost Japan considerable business. It was well known, however, that China was loosely governed, and a prey to constant disorder. She was certainly not in a position to repel an attack.

And Japan did not need to look far. land that seemed best suited to meet her needs was Manchuria, the southern part of which had long been a field for Japanese investment. Manchuria had a population of something like thirty million, but there was plenty of room for more, and it was rich both in timber and in mineral wealth. Other powers, however, had interests in Manchuria and might not take very kindly to Japan's appropriation of this region. It was fortunate for 

Japan that in 1931 the world was in the pangs of the Great Depression, and that the powers were not in a position to risk a war. Again we have a case of Japan using a European crisis to her own advantage.

For this new revival of Japanese imperialism a group of militant patriots in the army and navy were principally responsible. Though 

Japan had a parliamentary system and, since 1925, universal manhood suffrage, the principle of ministerial responsibility had never been well established, and the ministers of war and marine (both representing the armed forces) had direct access to the Emperor, who might let them do as they pleased quite regardless of the civil government. In the end Japan advanced even beyond Manchukuo, till she stood on the very threshold of China proper. Russia, her only formidable rival in the East, had stepped out of northern Manchuria in order to avoid war, and seemed to restrict her interest to Outer Mongolia, most of which is desert, yet important as flanking Siberia on the south. In 1934, Japan made the startling announcement that she considered herself responsible for the maintenance of peace in the Far East, and significantly referred to those "regional understandings," like the Monroe Doctrine, which, according to the Covenant of the League, were outside its jurisdiction. Evidently she considered herself the guardian of the Far East. She felt that she should be free to do with China as she chose free to close the door to any other foreign interests and to appropriate the rich resources of China for herself. This, however, is a questionable form of "guardianship" and altogether different from the Monroe Doctrine.

So, in July, 1937, while Europe was being harassed by Germany and Italy, Japan picked a quarrel with China, and began an "undeclared war." The Chinese were powerless to resist the swarms of well-trained Japanese troops; and all their great cities were, one after another, taken by storm and thoroughly looted. By 1939 Japan had conquered much of China, though the war still dragged on, for the Chinese established bases in the mountains of western China and made continuous raids on the Japanese forces, refusing to admit defeat. For the Chinese people the invasion had been a terrible experience. Their cities had been bombarded from the air; and literally millions of civilians had been killed by Japanese shells or had died of want or exposure, as they fled from their burning homes. Despite a stubborn resistance, it seemed doubtful whether Chinese independence would survive. 

There was evidence also that Japan intended that none of the other powers trading with China should any longer retain their privileges. There was, in other words, to be an end of the "open door." Whether these powers would submit to being excluded would probably depend on the outcome of the great European war which broke out in 1939. 

Even more important than Japan as a menace to the peace was Germany. 

F. Germany Defies Europe Germany Causes Trouble Again 

Germany's policy of conciliation ended with Bruening, and even before the coming of the

Nazis she began to tug at the restraints placed upon her by the Treaty of Versailles. Chancellor Bruening, whose position at home was far from strong, tried to gain popularity by attempting to effect a tariff union with Austria. 

There was no doubt that Austria needed such an arrangement, for, as it was, tariff walls surrounded her on all sides. It would also have helped Germany to obtain the Austrian market, and therefore might be considered as one of Bruening's methods of combating the depression.

Unfortunately, such a step might pave the way for the annexation of Austria to Germany, which, you will remember, had been forbidden by the Treaty of Versailles. France feared this move, since she believed that it would lead to political union, and she had enough influence to thwart it. The result was most unfortunate for Germany, since bitterness over this failure led to political unrest, the Nazis gaining in strength, and in consequence foreign bankers were loath to risk any further loans to German industry. The effect was, therefore, to intensify the depression. 

The End of Reparations - The "Tearing-up" of the 

The "Tearing-up" of the

Treaty of Versailles Begins 

Yet Bruening was successful in one thing. 

He was able, in 1932, to bring about a conference of the powers at Lausanne to reconsider the problem of reparations, and though no final decision was reached at this meeting, it was generally felt that the reparations question was now dead. The depression had made it impossible for Germany to continue her annual payments, and as the Allies were no longer paying any part of their huge debt to the United States (for the same reason), it looked as if these relics of the war were gone forever. For Germany this meant a glad release from one of the fetters of the Treaty of Versailles.

The Problem of Military Equality - Germany 

Under Hitler Breaks with the League

But Germany was still restless. Bruening was followed by two reactionary chancellors, 1 This amounted to over $11,000,000,000. 

Finland was the only nation which did not, sooner or later, default. who determined to get rid of more of the 

Treaty of Versailles. What Germany most wanted was the right to have an army as large, in proportion to population, as that of any of the other "great powers." She chafed under the restriction of the treaty, limiting her to one hundred thousand men. 

The very fact that the Allies had not reduced their armaments, despite the pledge in the Fourteen Points, seemed to give her a strong case.

The question was discussed at a disarmament conference at Geneva in 1932-33.

Anxious to show a spirit of conciliation, the powers were willing to grant Germany's reasonable demand for military equality. But there were many points to be settled in connection with a general reduction of armaments, and the conference dragged on for over a year without reaching any solution. Unhappily, after Hitler's accession to power in January, 1933, it became increasingly clear that any agreement was out of the question. France, distrusting the Nazis, who had been trying to undermine Austrian independence, insisted that a general reduction of armaments should be carried out very gradually, while the German army should remain at its present figure. Finally, in October, Germany abruptly withdrew from the conference and also from the League of Nations.

Hitler Defies Europe and Flouts the Treaty of Versailles

It is more than doubtful if Hitler really wanted co-operation. The Nazis had always championed violent patriotism, and Hitler's fierce denunciations of the Treaty of Versailles had been part of his stock in trade and had helped him come into power. He had voiced his intention of bringing all Germans into 

Germany -the old idea of Pan-Germanism, according to which Germany should possess herself of Austria, Danzig, Memel, part of Czechoslovakia, and portions of other states containing German populations. He also wanted the colonies which Germany had lost by the Treaty of Versailles, and in his book he had even proposed eastward expan-

It was because of the threatening attitude of Germany that Russia had joined the League of Nations in 1934, and some of the powers concluded so-called "non-aggression" pacts agreements not to fight one another for a period of years. Thus they could better avoid picking quarrels over minor matters while Germany was threatening the peace. Hitler's first open breach of the Treaty of Versailles came in March, 1935, and was the outcome of his failure to secure military equality. Reminding the powers that the question of reducing armaments had hung fire for sixteen years, he announced that Germany would immediately rearm. She should have a large army, as well as a navy and air force, and all the necessary equipment. In other words, she would no longer abide by the restrictions of the treaty. The powers were much disturbed, though as a matter of fact the army had been secretly growing larger for some time and no one was really surprised at this public announcement. In order to make his action the more impressive, Hitler asked the German people to endorse it in a plebiscite, which they did by a huge majority. But outside Germany everyone disapproved. The council of the League formally denounced this action; those powers who were guarantors of "Locarno" renewed their pledges to maintain it; and France and Russia signed a defensive alliance for five years. That was as far as anyone was willing to go, for no one wanted war though many felt that Hitler would bring on war sooner or later. 

And then came a chance for him to rattle his saber again.

Mussolini Grabs Territory in Africa war.

Mussolini felt that he had not done enough to make the world realize that Italy was a "great power." It annoyed him to think that 

France was the leading power of Europe and it rankled in his heart that Italy had not benefited from the distribution of colonies after the Moreover, the depression had caused hardship in Italy, as it had elsewhere, and he realized the need of satisfying the national vanity, as a means of diverting his compatriots from thinking too much of their own troubles. 

A border quarrel with the African state of Ethiopia gave Italy the chance to add a colony to her empire, and perhaps to dream of even greater conquests. Whether Ethiopia was a valuable country no one knew. The Italians liked to think that it contained great mineral wealth. They also liked to regard it as suitable land for colonization, for Italy was overcrowded. Apparently, however, Ethiopia was almost uninhabitable for white men. Much of this country was either too high or too low, and in general very unhealthful. 

But Italy had long been casting a hungry eye on Ethiopia; and she was eager, too, to avenge the humiliating defeat which the Ethiopians had inflicted on her in 1896.

On the part of Italy, it was a clear case of aggression. Whether or not Ethiopia had really been to blame for the border incident, her emperor was willing to refer it to the League of Nations, of which Ethiopia herself was then a member. But Mussolini refused to leave the question to the League. The council of the League merely floundered, much as it had floundered in the case of Japan. Great 

Britain, it is true, was much disturbed, for she was afraid that Italy, once she possessed Ethiopia, might threaten the security of Egypt and the Suez Canal, but France, always keeping an eye on Germany, did not want to antagonize Italy. In January, 1935, France had gone so far as to give Italy a portion of the French Somaliland; and it was believed that she had intimated that Italy might do as she pleased with Ethiopia. If true, it was a shabby deal. for it was obviously contrary to the principles

In other words, her back would be safe if she chose to seize Austria or Czechoslovakia. In another way, too, Hitler's action was most significant. From a moral standpoint this action was much more serious than that which he had taken in 1935. The Treaty of Versailles, though he had once promised to respect it, had at least been forced upon Germany. But the reoccupation of the Rhineland was a breach, not only of "Versailles," but of "Locarno"; and Locarno was a treaty which Germany had been chiefly instrumental in bringing about and had signed of her own free will. 

Furthermore, less than a year ago, Hitler had publicly proclaimed his loyalty to "Locarno." 

Who could now trust Germany's word?

As a matter of fact, Hitler, throughout his career, showed an absence of any sense of right and wrong, whenever Germany's own interests or power was concerned. Yet the British still deluded themselves into believing that he was a person with whom they could reason. 

When he now offered a non-aggression pact to last for twenty-five years, Great Britain felt that it deserved some consideration, but he hedged and finally ignored her when she insisted upon certain guaranties. France, for her part, thoroughly distrusted his offer, partly on the score that he had not included Russia, whom he had publicly denounced. He would have nothing whatever to do with "Jewish bolshevism"! So the months slipped by and nothing at all was done. Sensing the weakness of his enemies, Hitler repudiated the statement Germany had made that she was responsible for the First World War. This was tearing up

another clause of the Treaty of Versailles. 

Whatever the justification, it was done in a spirit of defiance.

But would not a policy of aggression, if carried out persistently, lead inevitably to war? 

G. Little by Little, Germany Forces 

Europe into War 

Germany as a Menace to the Peace

There were fundamental reasons for distrusting Nazi Germany. Everyone knew that her policy was shaped by a dreamer, who, as a despot, held his people in an iron grip. If he decided upon war or acted in a manner so as to provoke war, they would have to fight. His book revealed that he was a man who would stop at nothing to accomplish the aims for 

Germany he had in view. He even threw out the hint that Germans aspired to world domination. Economic conditions also pointed the way to war. In the matter of food and natural resources, such as oil, iron, and rubber, Germany was far from self-sufficient. German chemists had found ways of making synthetic products to take the place of wool and rubber, but such substitutes were far from satisfactory, and there were some things that could not be supplied by miracles of science. Having suspended payment of interest on foreign loans, Germany's credit was bad, but even if she could meet her needs by trade with foreign countries she ought, in Hitler's opinion, to become completely self-sufficient. Then, indeed, she could wage a victorious war! Moreover, the making of armaments kept millions of Germans employed; and what were these armaments for? War might give Germany the hope of expansion, of material prosperity through her conquests, and also of proving to the world the superiority of the German people. 

It was this violent patriotism, combined as it was with militarism, and guided by a fanatic, that made for general distrust and rendered 

Germany the greatest menace to the peace.

Every German youth was taught that the grandest of all virtues was courage in battle. 

There was no greater glory on earth than the sacrifice of one's life on the field of battle. 

Through pulpit, press, school, radio, and movie the population of Germany was incited to feel an intense desire to make Germany the greatest power on earth-if necessary by force. Perhaps Hitler's greatest talent was that of knowing how to twist the popular mind in other words, talent for propaganda. The people were herded like sheep behind their leader, who was believed to be inspired, and, as one of his henchmen declared, "always right." It goes without saying that no one on pain of imprisonment or death could question the "Fuehrer's" wisdom. Whether there were many Germans who did so in their hearts one could not say. To the outside world it seemed as if a nation of nearly seventy millions was behind their chosen leader for any adventure that he willed.

The Impending Danger to Austria-Hitler and 

Mussolini Become Friends

The ease with which Germany occupied the 

Rhineland led many to ask the question: 

Where would Hitler strike next? Some believed that it would be Danzig or Memel, in which cities groups affiliated to the Nazis had shown considerable strength; others, however, believed that it would be Czechoslovakia, where there was a German population of about three millions. There was a chance, of course, that it might, instead, be Austria, with its population of almost seven millions; but heretofore Italy had blocked the way to the fulfillment of this design.

Austria had been a prey to internal troubles for some time. The conservative parties, strong in the country districts and fervently Catholic, had long disliked the socialists in Vienna, the Austrian capital. Ever since 1920 the conservatives had been in control of the national government, and, in 1934, on the plea that the socialists were plotting an insurrection, they had overthrown the socialist government in Vienna. For this bloody affray the peasant statesman, Dollfuss, who had made himself dictator, was chiefly responsible. But the very same year Dollfuss himself had fallen a victim to a Nazi attempt on the government an attempt which was finally suppressed. 

The conservatives' policy had had the approval of Mussolini, who, when the Nazis made this attempt to cement Austro-German union, had sent troops to the Austrian frontier as a warn-

OF FASCISM THE RISE 

ing to Hitler. Schuschnigg, who had succeeded the murdered Dollfuss, had been shocked at the brutality of the Nazis, and was anxious to maintain Austrian independence. 

In this he counted heavily on Italy's support. Undoubtedly Mussolini's chief concern was the fear that Germany might try to annex the large German population in the southern 

Tyrol, not to mention the port of Trieste which

Germany would probably want if she acquired Austria, for it would thereby make her a 

Mediterranean power. No wonder Mussolini looked upon Austria as a buffer against his formidable rival, Hitler. 

But in 1936, some circumstances resulted, strangely enough, in converting these two rivals into close political friends. In that year a civil war broke out in Spain. It began as a conservative revolt against the new Spanish republic, which had come into being in 1931. 

The insurgents, who were fascist, apparently represented a minority of the Spanish people, but they received timely aid from Germany and Italy, both of whom, Italy more than Germany, took a direct hand in the conflict. Russia sent munitions to the "loyalist" government since it contained a communist element, but was willing to cease doing so if all powers agreed to adopt a strictly "hands-off" policy.

Unhappily an attempt on the part of France (backed by Great Britain) to make non-intervention effective broke down because of the insincerity of Italy and Germany. Their object was probably to threaten the security of France, while Mussolini, in particular, thought to gain new laurels for Italy. Thanks to this assistance, and in spite of one disastrous Italian defeat, the insurgents steadily gained at the expense of the government, and finally, if we may look ahead a little, brought the war to a successful close in 1939. It had been a terrible conflict, taking, it was said, a toll of five hundred thousand lives as well as involving a terrific destruction of property. 

Because of fascist intervention, the Spanish lost their chance of social reform in what was probably the most backward country of Europe. But the chief importance of the war from the standpoint of Europe was the cementing of friendly relations between the two great fascist powers.

This cordial co-operation was commonly spoken of as the "Rome-Berlin Axis." 

It was a lucky thing for Hitler that Mussolini had got himself so deeply involved in the Spanish war; for while he was sure that the British and French would meekly close their eyes, he remembered that Mussolini had once barred his way to Austria. And the Axis, as we shall see, sealed the doom of more than Austria.

The End of Austria 

Reasonably sure now of Mussolini, Hitler was ready to deal with Austria. In 1937, in order to make sure of the loyalty of the army, he ousted its chief of staff, and vested in himself the supreme command. In February, 1938, he summoned Schuschnigg to a conference and insisted that Austrian Nazis be permitted to engage in propaganda and that a Nazi be appointed minister of the interior, since this official had general charge of the police and might use the weight of his office to protect his party. Perceiving now that

Austrian independence was at stake, Schuschnigg tried his last resource. He announced that there would be a plebiscite to enable the Austrian people to vote on the question of annexation to Germany. It was a rather clever move, for if the plebiscite were held, he was convinced that the Austrian people would vote against union; and if the plebiscite were called off at Hitler's command, it would show that Hitler dared not leave the question to the people's choice.

It was soon evident that Hitler did not dare to risk the plebiscite. On March 11, he curtly demanded the suspension of the plebiscite, as well as Schuschnigg's resignation; and the army prepared to move. Schuschnigg, his spirit broken, promptly complied; but there was no saving of Austria. On the 13th, a 

German army entered Vienna, heralding Hitler's own arrival on the following day triumphant return to the city he had once hated. On the 15th, annexation was proclaimed. Thus Austria, once a great European power, had ceased to exist. She was treated as a conquered land. Nazis were imported to fill all important positions; 

German police patrolled Vienna; and all who were thought to be enemies of Hitler were quickly dispatched to concentration camps.

OF FASCISM 

Nearly a month later, after methods of force and trickery had done their work, Hitler held a plebiscite, himself, on the question of union, and the decision was overwhelmingly in his favor. It could hardly have been otherwise. 

In the meantime, the Jews had been outlawed, and thousands of them treated with great indignity. The Jewish population of 

Vienna was said to be three hundred thousand, and among them were men of distinction who had done much to make Vienna a center of art and science. As in Germany, huge bonfires were lighted of books that were supposed to be contrary to Nazi ideals. While much was done for the material good of the Austrians, their culture was now to be molded in the 

Nazi pattern. 

What Next? 

What next? was now the universal thought.

Hitler had reason to gloat over his triumph. 

The union of Austria with Germany had meant one more pillar of the Treaty of Versailles demolished. Germany increased her population to over seventy-three millions. The new acquisition also gave her a commanding position on the Danube, and with Hungary on her side, it looked as if she might decide to resume her old push to the East. The Little Entente could hardly expect to stop her; and neither France nor Great 

Britain had lifted a hand to rescue Austria. 

Even Italy had cause to be disturbed, for she had lost her precious buffer. But after the seizure of Austria, Hitler paid a formal visit to Mussolini; and an understanding was reached. 

Germany promised to respect the existing frontier - which was supposed to mean that 

Italy need not fear to lose the southern Tyrol.¹

In return, it is believed that Germany was assured a free hand against Czechoslovakia.

The Position of Czechoslovakia 

It turned out, as many feared, that Czechoslovakia was next. She was, of course, greatly imperiled by this much enlarged Germany, for, as one can see on the map, she was encircled on three sides. To be sure, Hitler had 

¹ In 1939, by agreement with Italy, the quarter of a million Germans in the southern Tyrol were forced to migrate to 

Germany. 

said that he would not harm Czechoslovakia, but he had said much the same thing many times in respect to Austria, and no confidence whatever could be put in any of his promises. 

We may recall that Czechoslovakia had a German population of about three millions. 

She also possessed other nationalities, Ruthenians, Poles, and Magyars. The Czechs and 

Slovaks, for whom the state had originally been created, numbered only ten millions out of a total population of about sixteen millions. One may wonder why this hodge-podge of a state had ever been erected. But the Congress of 

Paris had felt that the districts inhabited by Germans, being devoted chiefly to mining and manufacturing, were needed by the rest of the lands included, which were mainly agricultural. It was felt that Czechoslovakia would not thrive unless her economic life were wellrounded. rounded. Moreover, these German districts were needed to give her a strong mountain frontier to protect her against Germany; and the Czechs were thus enabled to skirt these mountains with an exceptionally strong line of fortifications. Finally, it was realized that the 

German element had shared the same government with the Czechs for many centuries. 

Together they had belonged to Austria-Hungary, but never to the German Empire. 

Now Czechoslovakia was a democratic state, and she had treated her nationalist minorities rather better than any of the other states which had the same problem. It is true that the German element had some just grievances and that the Czechoslovakian government had been much too slow to redress them; but these Germans were a difficult people to handle, and Czechoslovakia felt that to give them the self-government which they wanted might endanger the security of the state. After the union of Austria with Germany, this element received direct encouragement from Germany, and the Czechs naturally suspected them of being disloyal. Just as in the case of Austria, Hitler's method was to weaken a state from within before he attacked it from without.

Aside from her fortifications and a large and well-equipped army, Czechoslovakia's strength lay chiefly in her foreign alignments. France. had been her ally since 1924, and three French

OF FASCISM THE RISE 

premiers had given public assurance that she would stand behind her pledge. Russia, too, was pledged, since 1936, to come to Czechoslovakia's assistance in case of attack, as soon as the French had done so. Great Britain was not bound by any alliance with the Czechs, but she, like France and the United States, had shared in making this state, and she was also bound by the Covenant of the League of Nations to do her part in defending it against aggression. We are told that Czechoslovakia might have come to terms with Germany, as Poland had done, perhaps receiving temporary safety, but she preferred to trust to her friends. She could not believe that the great democracies of the West would let her down.

The Position of the Friends of Czechoslovakia Unfortunately, France had long been torn with bitter internal strife over labor and financial questions, and had let her armaments dwindle till Germany had an immense military advantage. She had also no assurance that Great Britain would come to her aid if she were drawn into war with Germany over Czechoslovakia, and she seemed to have some doubt as to the value of her Russian ally especially after Stalin had put to death a number of his generals. Finally, her leading politicians had for a long time been men of poor caliber, some of them corrupt, some of them seeking only to advance their political fortunes, and a few actually conspiring against the republic. Never was France so sorely in need of a leader. She needed a man of patriotism and force, like Clemenceau. 

Great Britain, as we have noticed, had long played an indecisive part in world affairs. 

She had made no serious effort to save China, though her interests in the Far East were very extensive. She had failed also to check Mussolini, though her interests in the Mediterranean seemed to be threatened at both ends Egypt and Spain. She had even allowed her merchantmen, bearing food to the Spanish loyalists, to be sunk by the Spanish insurgents.

These experiences, it is true, had induced her to strengthen her Eastern naval base, Singapore, and to increase somewhat the strength of her navy and air force, though, on the other hand, she had given up to Ireland the use of its naval bases, allowed by the treaty of 1921. 

Generally speaking, Great Britain's policy, as you can see, had been timid and ineffective.

Worse still, like France, she was painfully unprepared for a sudden war especially as she had insufficient defense against bombardment from the air. The British, who had always supposed that a strong navy was sufficient to afford protection, were now slow in adjusting themselves to a new situation, and so, like the French, had fallen far behind Germany in the strength of their air forces. It is clear that, just like France, Great Britain had been cursed with sorry leaders, who for many years had been drawn from the Conservative Party. 

The leader of the Conservatives, Neville 

Chamberlain, who had been Premier since. early in 1937, was the son of Joseph Chamberlain, whom we recall as a prominent statesman before the First World War. A wealthy business man, he belonged to a class that had a deadly fear of communism, and looked upon the fascist powers as really much less dangerous than Russia. Being old with some of the stubbornness of old age - he clung to the feeling that he could safely make concessions to the fascist powers, and that somehow, perhaps, Germany would get involved in a war with Russia, and that Great Britain would then be safe. Clearly in such a struggle he would not want Russia to win, for a beaten Germany might possibly succumb to communism. What he failed to realize was that Germany was much more dangerous now than Russia, and that democracy might perish in other countries, as was happening in Spain. He had even encouraged Hitler to seize Austria, hoping that the dictator would then be satisfied. 

If, as was now threatened, Germany became, indeed, the dominant power of Europe, the age-old British tradition of the balance of power would be ended, and England herself would be in deadly peril. Yet he spoke of the Czechs as "a people we know nothing about," and seemed quite blind to the fact that Czechoslovakia was one of the strongest defenses of the democracies in Europe. The only excuse for Chamberlain, a vain and narrow man and wholly inexperienced in foreign affairs, was the fact that his country was far from safe against air attack in the event that the

Czechoslovakian question should happen to provoke war. As a matter of fact, Germany, during the summer of 1938, could not afford to risk war, for her fortified line in the west was still unfinished. "The Great Betrayal"

Faithful to his policy of buying peace at any price, Chamberlain let it be known in May, 1938, that he favored the cession of the German districts in Czechoslovakia to Germany.

Yet in that very month, when Hitler moved some forces to the frontier, Czechoslovakia promptly responded by mobilizing part of her army, and Hitler withdrew. At that time 

France upheld her strongly; and though both

France and Great Britain urged her to make sweeping concessions to her German subjects, the fact remains that firmness had won the day. If the anti-fascist powers would only hold their own, it looked as if Germany would have to halt her policy of aggression. Such was the lesson of the "May Crisis." Such

But Chamberlain was not the one to face crises; and he now played a very shifty part. 

He sent a friend to Prague to patch up peace between the factions, but indirectly he gave so much encouragement to the Germans that Hitler came out boldly and declared for the right of the Germans of Czechoslovakia to dispose of themselves as they wished. Again it looked as if a serious crisis impended. France at once took fright and told Chamberlain that she would not respect her pledge to Czechoslovakia in the event of war. The British 

Premier, accordingly, made up his mind, if,

Hitler insisted on having these Germans, to buy peace at Czechoslovakia's expense. Having got in touch with Hitler, he flew to Berchtesgaden, the German dictator's country estate, where he received from Hitler the demand of the German districts in Czechoslovakia - emphasized by a threat of war. Chamberlain having then got the consent of the French 

Premier, Daladier, the two powers informed the Czechoslovakian government that it must yield, though Chamberlain added his assurance that he would try to get an international guaranty for the remainder of the state. 

Czech proposal that arbitration, as provided by "Locarno," be applied, was curtly rejected, and the French foreign minister insisted, on his own authority, that France would not fulfill her pledge of military aid if Czechoslovakia refused to yield. Deserted by her friends, Czechoslovakia felt that she had no choice but to submit. 

But Hitler thought that he could push

Chamberlain farther, and he now demanded the right to march in and seize the prize he wanted, including some districts in which the Czechs were clearly in a majority. Chamberlain began to feel that he had been duped, and the result was that France and Great Britain hastily prepared for war. In London thousands of gas masks were distributed, and trenches were dug in the parks to protect a few of the more fortunate in case of an air attack. 

Interestingly enough, Prague was as calm and plucky as Paris and London were panicky. 

It was a week of dreadful suspense, however, as no one knew whether Hitler would mass his army and commence war. Finally Chamberlain succeeded in getting in touch with Mussolini, who persuaded Hitler to agree to a meeting at Munich to arrange a settlement. Russia was not invited, though she had promised some weeks before that she would stand by the Czechs, if the French did likewise. Neither was Czechoslovakia herself invited, though certainly she was the power which had most at stake. stake. Only Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain, and Daladier were present; and it was they who made the agreement, on September 30, which ended the long dispute. 

By the terms of the Munich Agreement Hit ler might take possession of the German districts, his troops taking four days in the process. In doubtful districts, where no one knew whether Czechs or Germans predominated, plebiscites were to be held; and an international commission was to fix the final frontiers. 

After Poland and Hungary had helped themselves to the districts inhabited respectively by Poles and Magyars, an international guaranty should be given to what was left of Czechoslovakia. That meant, of course, that she was to be defended against all aggressors. 

Returning home from the meeting, Chamberlain declared to jubilant crowds that he had "brought back peace with honor." "I believe," he said, "that it is peace in our time.".

The Mutilation and End of Czechoslovakia 

99 

Yes, it was peace but not "with honor," and possibly not "in our time." No plebiscites were held in the shattered country; no guaranties were given; and the international commission, under threats from Hitler, took away from Czechoslovakia many districts in which Czechs were unquestionably in the majority. The result was worse than the demand which Chamberlain had formerly rejected on threat of war; yet, as far as we know, he did not even protest. Altogether some eight hundred thousand Czechs were handed over to greedy neighbors. But this was not all. 

Six months later, without encountering any resistance, Germany took over all that was left of Czechoslovakia, save a portion that went to Hungary. Even the little nation's available gold reserve, amounting to $92,000,000, was seized and taken to Berlin - an act which may be compared to the robbing of a bank by armed bandits.

The Czechoslovakian affair had been a showdown between the fascist and the democratic powers, and the democratic powers had lost the game. They had virtually handed over to the German dictator a sturdy little democratic country, one of the strongest lines of fortifications in Europe, an excellent air fleet, and a rich industrial region - all this without firing a shot!

The defects of the Munich Agreement had left some misgivings, though France and Great Britain had both followed this settlement by signing non-aggression pacts with Germany, and Chamberlain paid a visit to Mussolini. 

Both powers were greatly worried over the victory of the fascists in Spain, and shouts in the Italian Chamber of Deputies, "Tunisia!

Corsica!" seemed to show that Mussolini expected to frighten France into concessions, as Hitler had already frightened both France and Great Britain. Meanwhile, the Jews in Germany were subjected to fresh outrages; and 

Hitler forced his smaller neighbors to cease all criticism of Germany. He actually warned 

Great Britain that she must not employ as ministers certain men whom he disliked. 

Chamberlain tried to appease him by sponsoring negotiations for a trade agreement with Germany, and, curiously enough, he trusted to Hitler's assurance that he (Hitler) had in Europe no further territorial ambitions and wanted none but Germans in his state. 

The falsity of Hitler's statement was proved by the sudden and ghastly destruction of Czechoslovakia in March, 1939, followed quickly by the seizure of Memel. Soon afterward the Nazi press began to howl that the Germans in Poland were being mistreated. It was the same sort of tactics that had been used against Czechoslovakia, and indicated Poland as the next victim.

But at last France and Great Britain became aroused. In both countries there were people who felt ashamed over their governments' re-

Germany annexed Austria on the ground that the people were Germans; similarly she took the Sudetenland which was a part of Czechoslovakia, a country created by the peace settlements of the First World War. She took Czechoslovakia on another pretext. What was it? On what pretext did she go into

RUSSIA 

Premier made some half-hearted efforts to form an alliance, but it was much too late. 

Hitler, despite his many tirades against "bolshevism," had been secretly trying for many months to make a friend of Stalin, apparently thinking that the grouping of Russia and Germany would frighten the western powers into letting him do with Poland as he pleased.

Stalin, for his part, gave him plenty of encouragement. Besides "getting even" with Chamberlain, he welcomed the thought that the great capitalistic powers might tear one another to pieces in a great war. A sort of bargain was struck. A commercial treaty was signed on August 19, followed four days later by a non-aggression pact. Obviously the western powers had definitely lost their chance of winning Russia, and that nation's vast resources would presumably be available to Hitler. Hitler, for his part, looked for another "Munich." Chamberlain, he felt, would certainly yield again.

But if Hitler had forfeited the faith of the democratic powers when he had seized Czechoslovakia, he risked a more serious crisis when he next pounced upon Poland. For the British had pledged themselves to come to her aid. 

The Outbreak of War 

Hitler had made up his mind to get Danzig and the Polish Corridor; and as Poland, trusting to her allies, refused to be browbeaten, he launched his army against Poland on September 1. Apparently to the surprise of the German dictator, Great Britain and France respected their pledges to Poland, and declared war on Germany, September 3. Fascism had at last plunged Europe, and perhaps the world, into a war, the extent of which no one could foresee.

FASCISM THE RISE OF SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

1. Following the First World War Italy, and later Germany, organized themselves into so-called totalitarian states. The political, economic, and cultural life of each people was closely controlled by a dictator. 

Fanatical nationalism characterized domestic and foreign policy. After 1936 the two dictators acted in close co-operation in matters of foreign policy. a. Economic distress and popular dissatisfaction with the peace settlement and with the “inefficiency” of democratic government help to explain the rise of fascism. Germany systematically set aside the restraints imposed by the Treaty of Versailles and made herself the strongest military power in Europe. 

She annexed Austria, destroyed Czechoslovakia, and partitioned Poland. b. Italy built a military machine which she tested in the conquest of Ethiopia and Albania, and in the 

Spanish civil war. 

2. In the East, Japan embarked on a reckless imperialistic policy which resulted in the establishment of a puppet state, Manchukuo, and in a horrible war to establish economic and political control over China. 

3. Repeated acts of aggression on the part of Germany, Italy, and Japan caused alarm among the democratic powers, and finally led to a Second World War. a. The League of Nations proved powerless to act effectively, partly because of half-hearted support from Great Britain and France. b. Great Britain, fearing Russian communism, at first favored a policy of "making deals" with the dictators. c. France concluded a defensive alliance with Russia, but this alliance was not popular, and did not meet with the approval of the British ruling class. d. Following Munich, Hitler and Stalin found it to their mutual advantage to co-operate. e. France and Great Britain finally realized their desperate plight, concluded an alliance, and offered jointly to guarantee the security of such nations as Poland, Rumania, Greece, Turkey, and so on. f. Hitler nevertheless launched a successful attack against Poland, in which he received a measure of support from Stalin. 

g. France and Great Britain respecting their pledge to Poland, declared war on Germany, and proceeded to bring the same type of economic pressure to bear on Germany that proved successful in the 

First World War.

GAINING Skill

A. Where to Get Information. History grows ever longer and to learn the history of yesterday you must rely on the newspaper, the news reel, and the radio. Who are your favorite news analysts? Why? What are your favorite radio programs treating historical developments of long ago or of today and yesterday? Why?

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. Read the claims made for dictatorship by Hitler and Mussolini. According to them, what are its advantages? Do you agree? What have the dictators achieved for their peoples? What have been the costs?

Refer to the Constitution of the United States and of your state, as well as to Magna Carta, the Petition of Right, the Bill of Rights, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man in order to learn what are the great rights of free people. List these rights and note which of them are enjoyed by citizens living in totalitarian states. Express your conclusions in cartoons, poems, or essays. 

Discuss this question in class, "Why do the citizens of a totalitarian state take their citizenship responsibilities more seriously than do the citizens of a democracy?" 

C. How to Evaluate Information. History has practical value for the citizens of a democracy because it impartially records the wise decisions and mistakes of the past. And a knowledge of the past is essential for wise thinking and intelligent action now and in the future. 

When the Second World War broke out many people asked themselves why. What were the causes of this conflict? Why did the order established by the peace treaties closing the First World War break down? What was wrong with that settlement? If it had not been for fascism, would tensions gradually have been removed? Or is a major war in each generation inevitable? How should the peace settlement following the Second World War differ from that which ended the First World War? 

It is difficult to secure completely accurate news when it is to the interest of some powerful group (perhaps a foreign government) to "slant" it in one way or another. In order to help you evaluate what you read and hear, we suggest that your class study carefully the suggestions for clear thinking made in "An American Answer to Intolerance," published by the Council Against Intolerance, Lincoln Building, New 

York City, 1940.

THE SIGNIFICANCE OF  

is yet to be fully realized. But some of its characteristics were soon revealed. 

General Character of the War The Second World War was as widespread an upheaval as the First World War, and fought with even greater desperation. The emphasis placed on aircraft and mechanical equipment gave this war a unique character. Since Germany possessed an immense superiority in the alr, as well as more numerous and heavier tanks and armored cars, opposition, at least for a time, was quickly crushed. There was not the hard-fought "tug-of-war" which had characterized the First World War. On the other hand, sea power still retained its old importance, and the blockade, whether by battle cruisers or submarines, was a method carried over from the previous war. But unlike all past experiences, sea power was now menaced from the air. 

Because of German tactics, this war was perhaps more terrible for civilians than any war since the seventeenth century. Men, women, and children were killed by air raids; fugitives from the battle front were mowed down by machine guns; and how many millions were victims of organized terror or starved as the result of 

German looting will probably never be known.

Another peculiarity of this struggle was the stress placed by Germany on undermining the unity of a nation she intended to attack — a plan carried out partly by propaganda and partly by bribing people to become traitors. 

Thus a nation had been undermined from within before it had to withstand an armed attack from without, and "insiders" helped the invaders when they arrived. This explains in large measure the fate of Norway, Holland, Belgium, and France, not to mention the bloodless conquest of Rumania.

It is obvious that Germany had no respect for the rights which custom had accorded to other nations. Just as in violating treaties she had broken the laws of peace, so she showed in this struggle an equal contempt for the laws of war. Thus, in order the better to protect them from enemy attack, German tanks were liberally plastered with Red Cross signs. The machine-gunning of civilians was another and more frightful example of a breach of the laws of war which had been agreed upon between nations. Nothing, perhaps, is more striking than the fact that Nazi Germany was a law unto herself.

Much more than the previous struggle, the Second World War was a war of ideals. The 

German aim was to create a "new order," as

Hitler expressed it a Europe in which Germans, as a master people, should dominate all others and exploit them. A German victory would thus mean that all the conquered nations would be autocratically ruled and forced to labor largely in Germany's interest. An aggressive nationalism and imperialism was asserted by all the Axis powers in this war. The powers arrayed against Germany and her allies felt, on the other hand, that they were fighting for the independence of nations, large and small, and for the preservation of individual freedom, as well as democratic govern- Thus fascism and democracy were locked in a bitter struggle for survival. ment.

The German Conquest of Poland The Second World War began on Septem ber 1, as we have noted, and France and Great 

Britain accepted Hitler's challenge on the 3d.

Mussolini, though he had concluded a military alliance with Germany in May, was allowed to remain neutral for the present, since to meet the full force of a French attack while Germany was engaged in Poland might result in Italian defeat and open Germany herself to invasion from the south. In the meantime he could make the Allies uneasy by his threats to come into the war. It was the accustomed "war of nerves," in which the Axis was so adept. 

Poland, despite a spirited resistance, was helpless against the weight of the German attack. Taking full advantage of her superiority in the air, Germany crushed the Poles in less than three weeks' time. Toward the end of the campaign Russian troops entered Poland from the east (presumably after an understanding with Germany), with the result that the stricken country was divided between Germany and Russia. Once more History records a "Partition of Poland."

Meanwhile the civil population was treated with exceptional brutality. Those in the 

Polish Corridor were deported to the center of the country to make way for German settlers, and a large proportion of the fugitives perished from either cold or privation. Hundreds of thousands were also sent to Germany for manual labor. While the mass of the population were deliberately left on the brink of starvation, the Gestapo employed its usual methods of terror. Some evidence exists that the Nazis intended a policy of extermination. cluded also territorial cessions, designed to strengthen Russia's position in the north. 

For a nation of about 3,500,000 to defy a neighbor whose population was about 

170,000,000 was an heroic decision. But the

Finns are a sturdy people, most of them thrifty peasant proprietors, and nowhere in the world was there a more democratic government or a stronger feeling of independence. In the 

Russo-Finnish War, which began on November 30, 1939, both the heroism of the Finns and the weakness of the Russian army were conspicuously displayed, but numbers were decisive in the end, and Finland was at last compelled to yield. By the treaty of peace, signed March 

12, 1940, Russia secured the use of a Baltic port, a strip of land which enabled her to dominate the only Finnish port on the Arctic Ocean, and large slices of territory in the south, which should render her more secure against attack by a dangerous neighbor in alliance with Finland. Swayed by popular opinion, France and Great Britain sided with Finland, and through their influence Russia was expelled from the almost-forgotten League of Nations. But neither of these two powers was in a position to send military aid to the Finns. 

It is probable that Stalin's policy was largely a measure of self-defense against Germany.

He was far too shrewd a statesman to place much faith in Hitler, who had often bitterly attacked "Jewish bolshevism," and had openly revealed his longing to possess some of Russia's rich mineral lands. Apparently in a struggle between dictators the independence of small nations counted for little or nothing.

In the summer of 1940, while Germany's attention was preoccupied in the west, Russia an- Communist Russia Continues Her Own Policy of nexed the Baltic states, and also seized Bessa- Aggression

The Polish lands which Russia took were peopled mostly by Russians, and though her action (like Hungary's treatment of Czechoslovakia in 1938) looked like stabbing a dying neighbor in the back, we should not forget that Poland had seized these lands when Russia was weak. But Stalin had not finished his aggressions. In the fall of 1940 he demanded naval bases from the Baltic states, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Finland.

Only Finland rejected his demands, which inrabia and the northern part of Bukowina from

Rumania. The former (but not the latter) had once belonged to Russia, as may be recalled. 

A Deceptive Calm

Meanwhile, for nearly seven months, the war in the west was a sort of deadlock. There two long fortified lines faced each other, and neither side seemed anxious to begin an offensive. Accustomed to win his victories cheaply,

Hitler begged repeatedly for peace, but this would mean a peace on Germany's terms, and

Keystone

Hitler personifies for civilized men the forces that in all history have sought to gain their ends by destruction, savage force, and brazen flouting of all standards which decent people through the ages have struggled to build up. to this, of course, the Allies would not agree. 

The British government declared, further, that it would make no peace with Hitler, who had broken his word so often. Meanwhile both powers tried to "appease" Mussolini, while

British planes dropped not bombs but propaganda leaflets over Germany. Such efforts obviously could not save Poland!

As a matter of fact, despite the crushing attack upon Poland, Great Britain and France hugged the delusion that, as far as armies were concerned, they could fight a purely defensive war. Such a war would have the advantage of saving countless human lives - an argument that appealed particularly to the French, with their almost stationary population. Far from expecting to meet a German attack, the French felt perfectly safe behind their strongly fortified line (though they had left their defenses weak along the Belgian frontier); and the British pinned their faith on the ability of their navy to prevent Germany from adding to her stock of raw materials, such as oil. It is obvious that without lubricating oils and gasoline the German war machine would become useless. 

Cherishing such hopes, the Chamberlain government turned out armaments in its accustomed leisurely fashion; and in both England and France the rate of airplane production lagged far behind that of Germany. 

This fact was the more serious because Germany's air strength already far exceeded that of France and Great Britain combined. 

France was also painfully short of tanks, as her high command had never expected to meet their old enemy in open combat. Perhaps worse still, the French soldiers lost much of their fighting spirit while marking time for so many months, especially as they read or listened to propaganda from Germany, which told them that the war had been forced upon them by the British, who were ready to betray them. Some think that Hitler deliberately put off launching an offensive in order first to weaken the French morale. 

Fighting Begins in Earnest - Norway Falls to 

Germany and Churchill Succeeds Chamberlain in England 

In April Hitler decided to assume the offensive. It is possible that he was led to it by the efforts of the British to cut the water route, close to the Norwegian shore, by which Germany got her iron from the mines of northern 

Sweden. On April 9, German troops invaded

Denmark and immediately poured into Norway. Denmark, having only a tiny army, made no effort to defend herself, and Norwegian resistance was weak, largely because the Germans had bought the allegiance of a number of 

Norwegian officers in key positions. Great

Britain, already accused of having allowed so many small nations to be crushed, felt forced to send aid to Norway, but her efforts were badly directed, and the Germans quickly overran the country. By so doing they acquired new bases from which eventually to launch an attack on England and Scotland. 

The Norwegian disaster exasperated public feeling in both France and England. Though in France political squabbling had already led to the fall of Daladier, whose place was taken

by Paul Reynaud, it was the failure to save Norway that produced a change of cabinets in England. Striving to the last to keep his power, Chamberlain was finally overthrown on May 10. His successor was Winston Churchill, a brilliant and vigorous statesman, who, as a member of the Conservative Party, had for years warned the government against the growing air strength of Germany and had vainly urged more adequate preparations. It was now his fate to inherit the results of his predecessor's fumbling. Eloquent of speech, and always frank even when things appeared to be blackest, Churchill won and retained the confidence of the British public. "I have nothing to offer," he told Parliament, "but blood, toil, tears, and sweat." a German force driving into France. It seems that the Germans had pierced the weaker line of French fortifications at a point which the 

French chief of staff, General Gamelin, in his moving of troops to the north, had left almost undefended. Greater negligence could hardly be imagined.

Threatened with annihilation, the British then executed one of the most brilliant retreats in history. Covered by the heroic stand of two small Allied units, and with the aid of their own air forces and fleet, the British troops, together with a detachment of the French army, and numbering in all 335,000 men, debarked from Dunkirk and safely reached the English shore. 

Even so, it was a disaster, for all this army's equipment was left behind. Moreover, Hitler

The May Offensive and the Collapse of France 

The conquest of Norway proved only a prelude of worse to come for the Allies. Hitler decided to turn his Blitzkrieg (“lightning war”) on his enemies in earnest. On May 10 a huge army, without warning, invaded Holland and Belgium, with a view of dealing a smashing blow at France. The Allies hurried troops forward to aid the Dutch and the Belgians, but the strength of the German assault proved beyond their powers of resistance. Now, at last, they realized what their negligence had cost them. Bombing planes which dived low to hit their targets, huge tanks in apparently unending numbers, parachute troops which descended behind the lines, and, often aided by traitors, disrupted communications - all this showed the power of Germany's highly mechanized forces, to meet which the Allies' strength was, indeed, sadly insufficient. Dutch resistance was beaten down in five days, and the Germans, in order to spread additional terror, destroyed a fifth of the city of Rotterdam, causing the death of some twenty thousand civilians. The Belgian army held out somewhat longer, but failing to hold its defenses, and undermined by treachery within, it surrendered on May 29. As the French and 

British armies, operating in Belgium, were by now in an advanced position, they were caught in a perilous pocket between the Channel and enemies. With greatly superior numbers the 

Germans threw the full weight of their armored divisions upon France. Reynaud hastily replaced General Gamelin by General Weygand, but the situation was desperate in the extreme. 

Unable to rally, the main French army steadily retreated, and the Germans entered Paris on June 14. The eastern fortified line (the "Maginot Line") had obviously been outflanked. And already, on June 9, Mussolini, now sure of a German victory, had entered the war in order to grab some of the spoils an act which President Roosevelt characterized as a "stab in the back." The resistance of her armies completely broken, France capitulated to Germany on June 17.

The terms of the armistice were severe. 

They enabled Germany to occupy about three fifths of France, including the Channel ports, important for attacks on England. A French army of more than a million and a half men were to remain prisoners till the end of the war. 

In the meantime, support of the German army had to be borne by France - an obligation which amounted to about $8,000,000 a day. So humiliating a defeat was even worse than France had sustained in the Franco- Prussian War. It is also worthy of note that 

France agreed to deliver to Germany all the refugees from German persecution. No men of honor would have consented to buy peace at such a price.

The collapse of France had been due partly

WORLD WAR THE SECOND 

to lack of preparedness, partly to poor generalship, and in some degree to treachery in high places, as well as a failure of the nation as a whole to realize until too late the gravity of the crisis. Moreover, the stream of refugees from 

Belgium and northern France, deliberately machine-gunned by the Germans as they fled, had created indescribable confusion and blocked the efforts of the retreating army to make a stand. Reynaud himself had wanted to continue the war in the French colonies, since a quarter of a million men were there in arms, and the navy was still intact. But most of the governing circles were victims of panic, and Weygand had the curious delusion that a communist revolt was about to break out. It was he who had insisted upon an armistice. 

The Fall of the Third Republic 

After Reynaud's resignation on June 16, a new cabinet was formed in France under a veteran of the last war, Marshal Pétain, and it was under his auspices that the armistice was signed. This change was also preliminary to the destruction of the Third Republic, which was abolished by the French Parliament on July 11. A fascist government was then set up at the little town of Vichy in the unoccupied part of France, with Pétain at its head. 

The collapse of French democracy was almost as great a shock to liberal opinion throughout the world as the military collapse. 

The parliamentary system with its constantly changing cabinets had had disastrous results, but the task of making it better was apparently not even considered. Most of the men who had forced the surrender to Germany were men who favored autocratic rule, and, furthermore, they believed that Germany would speedily win the war and that a fascist type of government might soften Germany's heart whenever the treaty of peace was finally concluded. 

Democracy in France was probably not so strong in the hearts of the people as in England, though we shall have to admit that Frenchmen as a whole were not consulted. 

The new France proceeded to humble itself to Germany in many ways, and measures were even taken against the Jews. It was also characteristic of the Vichy government that it jailed some prominent persons, such as Daladier, Gamelin, and Reynaud, as scapegoats for French defeat, while the men who had failed to arm the country for war were left unscathed. Another Frenchman, General de

Gaulle, who had gone to England to set up a "free France," pledged to continue the war, was tried in his absence and sentenced to death for treason. The fact that this young officer had once pleaded the importance of tanks and airplanes did not make him very popular with his superiors. 

Meanwhile, thoroughly bewildered, the French people awaited the doom of their late ally. 

Great Britain Carries on

But the doom of the British was not so obviously sealed. Hitler had made two big miscalculations. He had underrated the quality of the British people, and he had underrated the quality of their air force, of which Churchill truly said: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." 

Inspired by Churchill's dauntless leadership, the people of England, Scotland, and Wales settled down to endure the worst rather than yield. Air shelters were provided in most of the cities, and patrols kept careful watch for 

German bombers. Anti-aircraft guns and fighter planes gave the enemy a warm reception. If docks or factories were smashed, they were speedily rebuilt; and between raids business went on as usual.

Meanwhile every effort was made to defend the whole coast line against invasion, and a force of 2,000,000 men was put in readiness for action. Women largely replaced men in running the busses and other means of transportation and also in staffing the factories. Most of the national wealth had to be drawn upon to pay the mounting expenses of the war, and labor was conscripted for any service that might be required. Since Churchill had admitted Liberals and Labourites into his Cabinet, the government was now truly representative, and the war was clearly waged as a people's war. The King and Queen, whose palace was partly wrecked, mingled freely with their subjects and were more than ever symbols of national unity. As someone well remarked, "All are equal under the bomb." And not in

their darkest hour did the British seem to doubt had to restrict themselves to raiding after dark. of ultimate victory. 

The "Island Fortress" Holds Its Own 

Perhaps Hitler had made a mistake when he failed to attack the island kingdom after "Dunkirk," before its people had been able to replace the equipment lost or make adequate preparations for defense. The fact that the collapse of 

France had put the British in grave peril was shown by a decision which Churchill made in July. By the terms of the armistice, France, contrary to a solemn pledge to Great Britain, had agreed to place her navy in Germany's charge. Now if this naval strength were added to that already possessed by the Axis powers, Great Britain might thereby lose command of the sea and in consequence suffer invasion. 

Churchill, accordingly, made up his mind to force, in one way or another, the demobilization of the French navy. Warships lying in 

British and Egyptian ports were taken over without much trouble, and some of their crews were anxious to enter the service of "Free France," that is, the France of General de Gaulle. But the admiral of a squadron in the 

Mediterranean refused to accept the British demands, whereupon the British admiral opened fire, and most of the French vessels were damaged or sunk. The Vichy government, by way of protest, severed diplomatic relations with Great Britain. Yet the fact of shedding the blood of a former ally caused the British genuine pain, and was justified only by the gravity of the crisis. It was also characteristic of Churchill's daring that while his country was still threatened by invasion, he sent large quantities of equipment to the army in Egypt in readiness for the time when the British themselves could take the offensive.

Meanwhile Hitler, with his many thousands of planes, hammered away at the British Isles, hoping to destroy factories and airdromes with a view of crippling the British war effort, and hoping also to break the spirit of the people. But in neither of these efforts was he successful. Throughout the fall and winter of 

1940 and the spring of 1941 he talked much of his plans of invading England, but no invasion was seriously attempted, and daylight air raids proved so costly in planes that the Germans 

Meanwhile, the R.A.F. (Royal Air Force) was strong enough to bring the war home to Germany. Not only were French, Belgian, Dutch, and German ports constantly blasted, but railroads, factories, airdromes, and oil refineries in Germany itself were showered with bombs and high explosives. Yet the Germans had the advantage of possessing bases close to England, while the British, to bomb Germany, had to cover a longer range; and though military objectives were generally missed by the German raiders, some towns, such as Coventry, were almost demolished; some of the finest buildings in 

London were destroyed; and the civilian dead numbered twenty thousand by the end of the year 1940. The fortitude of the British under the strain of these attacks, and during the long period of suspense when invasion was expected, was an example to all humanity. People proudly insisted, "We can take it!"

One thing that heartened the British was the feeling that they were not fighting alone. The dominions (with the sole exception of Ireland) came to the aid of the mother country, for truly the empire itself was now at stake. Moreover, munitions could be purchased in America as long as the British kept their accustomed command of the sea, and the American people themselves were beginning to feel that the saving of England was for all democratic peoples a common cause.

Axis Strategy 

The continuous bombardment of England at least forced the British to be on perpetual guard against invasion, and thus to keep most of their fighting forces at home. But the failure of his invasion plans forced Hitler to resort to other alternatives. He must, if possible, by means of the submarine, cut the British lines of supply from the outside world. Since, however, this would entail a long struggle, he hoped first to smash Great Britain's hold on the Mediterranean and sever her famous “life line" with the East. If this were accomplished, the British would have to round the Cape of Good Hope in order to reach the Far 

East; and the oil fields of Iraq and Iran (formerly Persia) would be brought within reach of the Axis. Hitler's plan embraced

two features. Italy should move from Libya against Egypt and the Suez Canal; while Spain should be persuaded, if possible, to attack Gibraltar. Thus it was expected that Great 

Britain would be driven from the Mediterranean. A second plan, soon afterward formed, was to induce Japan to join the Axis and threaten the British holdings in the Far East, such as Australia and New Zealand, with their、 great outpost of defense, the naval base of Singapore. Great Britain should thus be attacked on three fronts: the Far East, the Mediterranean, and the home front.

For a time the situation looked pretty grave for the island kingdom. Mussolini's Italian army penetrated nearly a hundred miles into Egypt, which the dictator fondly hoped to add to his empire. Japan bullied France into al lowing a Japanese force to occupy Indo-China, and on September 27, 1940, she entered the "Triple Alliance" with Germany and Italy.

Japan had, obviously, her own plans of aggression, coveting in particular the rich Dutch East Indies, but her threats were enough to keep a British squadron in the Pacific. In the meantime, Germany herself was busily occupying Rumania, probably mainly to protect the oil fields, on which the Germans heavily depended; and, incidentally, Hitler forced Rumania to cede much of Transylvania to Hungary, as well as the Dobrudja to Bulgaria. 

Yet none of this activity brought the Axis very much nearer a final decision. China, provided with munitions by Russia, Great Britain, and the United States, was still a serious distraction for Japan; the Italian army in Egypt was soon stalled for lack of oil and other necessities; the Italian navy, in turn, was afraid to risk a battle with the British fleet; and 

Spain, for the moment, refused to join the Axis, knowing that England would at once blockade her shores and reduce her people to starvation. 

Hitler hoped then to win over France by promising her lenient terms in the final peace (instead of having to cede some colonies to 

Italy) if she would give him the use of what was left of her navy, as well as air bases in 

Tunis and Morocco.

But the Vichy government, whatever its subservience, would not yield to that extent. 

Apparently it was decided that possession of this fleet, together with a large North African army, would serve as useful clubs to keep German oppression of France within reasonable bounds. On the other hand, the men of Vichy did not want Great Britain to win, and though the British blockade allowed shipments of food for a hungry people whom Germany had looted, the chance that such a government would stay neutral for very long was slim indeed. 

Italy in Distress

While the Axis had so far made but little headway, Mussolini, piqued by the knowledge that Hitler was selling him out to France, decided to pull off a stroke of his own, designed to give him a stronger position in the Mediterranean and to add to his own prestige. Accordingly, on October 28, 1940, he dispatched an ultimatum to Greece, demanding the right to occupy ports on the Mediterranean. It may be gathered that Mussolini blithely expected 

Greece's submission. But without hesitation

Greece promptly rejected this arrogant proposal; and an Italian army moved against her from the direction of Albania. Then most of the world was surprised to learn that the Greeks were not only able to repulse the Italians, but to invade and occupy a large portion of Albania. 

Taking advantage of Italy's plight, Great

Britain assumed the offensive. The British 

Army of the Nile, commanded by General Wavell, made a surprise attack on the Italians, and not only hurled them out of Egypt but captured the Libyan port of Benghasi; while, almost simultaneously, other detachments of the army conquered Italian Somaliland, Eritrea, and Ethiopia. These campaigns resulted in the taking of more than 150,000 Italian prisoners. 

Meanwhile, a British air raid damaged a large portion of the Italian fleet, lying at anchor in the harbor of Taranto; and later the British fleet added to the toll of Italian ships sunk or otherwise put out of action. Italy's continual humiliations showed the glaring inferiority of her air and naval forces, serious deficiency in equipment for her army, and poor fighting qualities on the part of her troops. It was evident to all observers that the Italians did not have their heart in the war, and there was even some expectation that they would pull out.
