But this, Germany herself must prevent at all costs. 

An air bombardment of Malta, to be sure, proved ineffective. Nor did the addition of Bulgaria to the Axis (which already included 

Hungary and Rumania) succeed in scaring the Greeks, who went on, as before, whipping the Italians. Finally, in desperation, Germany took over Italy itself, subjecting the country to a military occupation. It was hard to see how 

Mussolini, kept in power now by German troops, could ever again become a national hero.

Yet, as far as the fascist cause as a whole was concerned, Germany was able to restore the balance. 

Germany Gains the Balkans and Threatens British 

Power in the Mediterranean

It was evident that, when Germany occupied Bulgaria, she was planning to intervene in the Near East and end the war between Italy and 

Greece. Moreover, if she could dominate the Balkans, she would be in a position to threaten the British hold on Egypt, as well as make a dash for the oil fields in Iraq. Whether the Turks and the British fleet could effectually bar the way remained to be seen. For the present, the British felt forced to send a detachment of the Army of the Nile, totaling 75,000 men, to aid the Greeks.

Meanwhile, in order to accomplish her purpose, Germany needed the use of the railway line which traversed Jugoslavia, and she was able to bully that country into joining the Axis. 

But the Serbs, who formed a part of its population, were a race of stubborn fighters, and suddenly, led by the army, they rose against their rulers, and, setting up a new government, repudiated the bargain with the Axis. This meant that Germany would have to fight Jugoslavia, as well as Greece and her British auxiliaries, for the mastery of the Balkans. 

But Germany had an enormous army gathered for this offensive; and on April 6 she commenced her drive. Jugoslavia, lacking the time to complete the mobilization of her army, and lacking the equipment to meet the onrush of German tanks, crumbled quickly. 

Greeks and British put up a stubborn resistance, but by the end of April Greece was forced to yield, while the bulk of the Brit- The ish army successfully effected its withdrawal. 

Unfortunately for the British, the strain on their fleet, both in aiding this withdrawal and in smashing an Italian squadron, sent presumably as a decoy, enabled Germany, with Vichy's connivance, to smuggle an immense number of tanks into Libya, while large reinforcements came by air. Germany was thus able to join 

Italy in a new drive against Egypt. Wavell, who had weakened his forces to send aid to Greece, was compelled to fall back from Benghasi, though he managed to hold a position well inside the Egyptian frontier, as well as the port of Tobruk, which threatened the 

Axis flank. Repeated German attempts to capture Tobruk met with failure. 

Throughout May and June war raged about the eastern Mediterranean without decisive result. A revolt in Iraq, engineered by German agents, threatened the British with the loss of their oil fields, but they promptly sent reinforcements, and the revolt was put down. 

Then the Germans took Crete, but the British countered by an advance into Syria. With the aid of a “Free French” force, partly recruited from deserters from the Vichy troops, they completed the conquest of the country by the middle of July. Meanwhile, German operations in the Near East were suspended by an unexpected change in German strategy.

End of a "Marriage of Convenience” 

Germany

Attacks and Invades Russia 

Germany's reasons for attacking her great neighbor on the east are still, as we tell the story, a matter of conjecture. It may be that she needed more oil for her war machine and more foodstuffs for the coming winter than she was getting by her trade agreements with Russia. It has also been suggested quite plausibly that she could not wisely attack the British Isles as long as Russian military power remained intact and indeed was growing stronger, for Russia might suddenly become an enemy. Possibly, too, Hitler wanted to show the world that he could succeed where Napoleon had failed; and, in any case, he must have wanted to include Russia in his "new European order." The official reasons for the assault put the blame, as in all cases, on "the other fellow," but no one outside of Germany

was likely to be impressed—particularly as Stalin had been trying to conciliate Hitler in a number of ways, almost up to the time of the actual breach. At all events, Hitler decided perhaps rather suddenly - to break with his old associate, Stalin, and German armies marched into Russia on June 22. Hungary, Rumania, and Finland also joined in the affray. Contrary to previous practice, Germany accompanied her invasion by a declaration of war. 

Expecting a quick victory, the Nazis found, instead, that they confronted a tough problem. 

Though at first they were able to push the Russians back over a front almost two thousand miles long, Russian resistance soon stiffened, and after two months' fighting, the Germans were still unable to reach any of their three objectives, Leningrad, Moscow, or Kiev. Contrary to previous experience, the German losses were very heavy. The Russians fought desperately, even civilians harassing the invaders, and when they retreated, they destroyed everything, leaving only the "scorched earth,” as

Stalin put it. Great Britain, in the meantime, made a close alliance with Russia, and the United States promised prompt material aid. 

In the west the R.A.F. subjected German cities to a continuous and devastating bombardment. 

By the middle of August, Hitler decided to concentrate mainly on a push into the Ukraine, agriculturally the richest part of Russia and the seat of most of her mineral wealth and industrial power; while beyond lay the oil fields of the Caucasus and Iran. In September the Germans succeeded in crossing the Dnieper, thus conquering a large portion of the Ukraine.

But Russia's military power, in spite of heavy losses, was far from crushed, and there was a long road to be traversed before the coming of the Russian winter. In order the better to guard their oil-fields British and Russian troops occupied Iran. One wondered if the outcome of the war itself might not largely hinge on the fate of Russia's oil.

Danger Clouds 

The slow progress of the German drive into Russia induced Hitler to press Japan to make a 

I Kiev finally fell on September 18. diversion in the Far East. Either an attack on 

Russia from the other side or an advance on Singapore and the Dutch East Indies would serve his purpose. Japan responded readily, and in July she occupied bases in southern 

Indo-China, preparatory to seizing Thailand, which would bring her within striking distance of Singapore. As this advance threatened both Great Britain and the United States (still protector of the Philippines), a serious crisis impended. True, week after week passed without an actual outbreak of war, and both Japan and the United States played for time by an interchange of views on the Far East. But stoppage of Japan's importation of war materials and the fact that the United States would not agree to the Japanese claim to dominate China meant that peace was at best precarious. 

In the meantime, in order to pull off a sensational stroke to balance the failure of his Blitzkrieg in Russia, Hitler persuaded the Vichy government to consent at last to "military collaboration." As this was interpreted to mean a promise to hand over French bases in Africa to Germany, Great Britain and the United States were much alarmed. Casablanca in Morocco and Dakar in West Africa might be used as submarine bases for attacks on British shipping, and Dakar commanded the shortest route from Africa to Brazil a distance of somewhat over eighteen hundred miles. There was already ample evidence of 

German plots in South America. In July an attempt was made to overthrow the Bolivian government but fortunately failed. Yet the danger to the United States in the event that Germany should win the war was evident enough.

The growing complications induced Prime 

Minister Churchill and President Roosevelt to hold some conferences on a British warship in the Atlantic during August. And here we must take space to go back and discuss the previous relations of the United States with the 

Second World War. 

The United States and the War As the war grew in scope and fury, it became increasingly evident that it would be difficult for the United States to remain complacently on the side-lines. That turning-away from

THE SECOND 

375 

WORLD 

WAR

Europe which had characterized American policy after the close of the First World War, seemed, in general, to satisfy the American people, and when fascism arose to threaten the peace of the world, the prevalent idea in Washington was to take special precautions to avoid involvement. Thus the government barred the selling of munitions to the Spanish Republic and even a proposal to fortify the island of Guam in the Pacific was rejected by Congress out of fear of offending Japan. American industry actually supplied Japan with most of her war materials, though loans were made to 

China with whom American opinion sympathized. Except for friendly relations with the Latin-American countries, American policy was, in general, one of aloofness. In 1937, In 1937, the United States limited her rights under international law by prohibiting the sale of arms or the loan of money to any belligerent. It was argued (partly, no doubt, in recollection of the First World War) that this was a wise means of avoiding any involvement in Europe's quarrels. 

With the outbreak of the Second World War, however, this so-called "Neutrality Law" was shown to be one-sided in its effects, since Germany did not need to buy American munitions (even if the blockade had not barred her), whereas France and Great Britain could not possibly win unless they could count on buying arms from American factories. President

Roosevelt saw this clearly, and he was able to persuade Congress in November, 1939, to repeal the embargo on arms, though they were not to be shipped abroad in American vessels and must be paid for on a "cash-and-carry" basis. By the following spring there was sufficient anxiety in America over the course of events in Europe to enable the President to initiate an elaborate program of national defense, including plans for an army numbering perhaps four million. The United States also drew closer to the Latin-American republics in the task of hemisphere defense, and in August, 1940, she traded fifty somewhat antique destroyers for a ninety-nine-year lease of eight British bases in the Western Hemisphere. 

Roosevelt's triumphant re-election in November seemed to show that the American people were not opposed to a strong policy, though there was little sentiment in favor of a formal entrance into the war. The great majority of 

Americans detested Hitler and were even becoming convinced that British resistance was really vital to America's safety, but the formula generally adopted was "all-out aid to Britain short of war." 

While material aid to Great

Britain was approved of as a means of keeping the war "on the other side," the American public assumed that only the British and their foreign friends would do the actual fighting for the common cause. There 

To the British the supreme value of the

United States lay, of course, in the production of armaments, but it soon became apparent that they could not possibly pay for all the airplanes and other equipment that they needed. Hence, on the plea that the defense of the British Empire and the preservation of its sea power was vital to American security, President Roosevelt persuaded Congress to pass the so-called Lend-Lease Bill, February, 1941, whereby billions were voted to finance

British resistance to the Axis powers. was still, however, ground for considerable anxiety in the destruction of British shipping; for German raiders and submarines were sinking transports faster than British shipyards could replace them. Was there not danger that this German counter-blockade would eventually force Great Britain to surrender? render? As the British navy shouldered the stupendous task of blockading Europe, protecting the Mediterranean route to the Far East, and defending the Pacific area against possible

Japanese aggression, few warships could be spared for the high seas. The obvious solution of the problem was for the American navy to convoy British shipping. Unfortunately, perhaps, the fear that such a policy would inevitably provoke German attack was so strong in both houses of Congress that the President was unwilling to take the risk of such a course. 

The most that he would do was to send American war vessels to patrol the Atlantic as far as 

Iceland for the purpose of warning British merchantmen of the proximity of submarines. 

The decision to occupy Greenland and Iceland was meanwhile justified on the ground that they might otherwise be utilized by Germany as stepping-stones for attack on America itself.

"When is a War not a War?"

The relation of the United States to the war was, in fact, becoming increasingly contradictory. On the one hand, American opinion, in general, wanted Great Britain to win, was anxious to give her all the material assistance that she needed, and did not object to the use of patrols, though that service clearly made the United States the active ally of Great Britain on the high seas. Furthermore, responsible officials from the President down had spoken in such scathing terms of Hitler and Mussolini that the United States could no longer be regarded as a neutral power. More than that, after those August mid-ocean interviews, the President had joined the British Prime Minister in a pronouncement which plainly pledged the 

United States to the destruction of "Hitlerism."

On the other hand, American opinion, generally speaking, was still unconvinced that it was necessary or right for the United States to enter the war as a full-fledged belligerent. Roosevelt assured the American public that his conferences with Churchill had brought the nation no nearer to war. One might reasonably ask: what is "war"? Even after an American destroyer was attacked by a German submarine, even after the government adopted the policy of convoys and orders were issued to "shoot at sight," the theory still prevailed that the United States was not at war. 

At all events, the American contribution to the struggle with fascism was still in 1941 considerably short of what seemed necessary to win the war - even in 1943. The production of airplanes was still far below the number planned, and, owing partly to strikes, there was sometimes an actual decline. In August, 1941, the production of tanks had only just got under way, and the construction of the heaviest tanks had not begun. Indeed, the stream of guns, planes, and tanks from this "arsenal of democracy," as the President called America, was (to quote a distinguished commentator) "hardly more than a trickle." American ships, such as tankers, were lent to the British wherever possible, but there were still not enough ships.

There were many facts to explain this situation. No doubt, at best, a country accustomed to peace finds it difficult to pass quickly to a war footing. Plants had to be expanded, models of planes and guns devised and studied, labor satisfied if possible. There was the further complication that the American army itself needed equipment. Moreover, while the outcome of the struggle itself might well depend on the number of ships to carry food and armaments to England, it should be realized that shipbuilding in America had never been anything but a minor industry, and to gear it to meet an emergency was anything but easy. 

Unhappily, too, many of the big industrialists were loath to curtail their ordinary profits to enable their plants to turn out implements of war.

The report of a Senate committee, published in January, 1942, revealed a scandalous lack of effort to meet the emergency, and, what was worse, some profiteering. Some of the largest producers of automobiles had actually been making more profit during nine months of 1941 than during the whole of 1940. "Staggering" profits had also been made at the expense of the government in naval construction. 

The report also disclosed a shortage of such materials as aluminum, indispensable for making planes. Quite obviously the Administration's handling of war production was persistently and grossly inefficient; and the nation was soon to pay for its airplane shortage when the war clouds finally broke in the Far East. 

In any case, the background of all this slackness must be realized. On the part of the public at large there was a great deal of confused thinking — perhaps sometimes wishful thinking. Was the United States really in as great a peril as the government and most of the press seemed to believe? The fact that freedom of expression prevailed (as would not be the case if the nation were technically at war) enabled a small but powerful group of "isolationists" to exert considerable influence in balking the national effort. In general, public opinion seemed to support the President's policy but flinched before the risk of a "shooting war." What the President himself really wanted he did not say, though on August 21 he emphasized the point that if Hitler won the mastery of the Old World he would next attack America. What, then, was behind this warning? Some critics of the government's record held that only if the United

The government tackled its problems with grim determination, and, in general, Congress lent its co-operation. Steps were taken to speed the making of munitions, the building of ships, and the raising by conscription of an army to total eventually 7,000,000. Those who could not fight were ready to serve in any capacity, and all faced the necessity of carrying a heavy financial burden. It was estimated that half the national income would be expended. So far as one could tell, the American people were fully alive to the gravity of the crisis. 

Germany Sustains Defeats 

The entrance of Japan into the war was a significant Axis triumph. Yet, even before the outbreak of war in the Pacific, Germany's hope of a decisive victory was rudely shattered.

While Allied naval power insured the suprem- I Chiefly because of the farming interests, which wanted a higher price for wheat, the Senate refused to allow complete price control to be vested in a single director. But, in general, the country seemed reasonably united and determined to subserve everything to the winning of the war. acy of the Atlantic, Germany's military machine was being strained to the breaking-point. 

In October Hitler had made a determined effort to take Moscow, partly in order to use it for winter quarters, and partly as a means of encouraging Japan to come into the war. But sub-zero weather, with the coming of winter, not only impaired the efficacy of his airplanes and tanks, but brought terrific sufferings to the German army, which was not properly clad for a winter campaign. Moreover, the Russians had drawn reinforcements from Siberia, and with the aid of American supplies, they held the enemy at bay within about forty miles of Moscow. At the end of November a definite turning-point had come, and soon the German army was in retreat along the whole of the long line from the Arctic to the Crimea. Not only had Moscow been saved, but, under the superb leadership of Stalin, the valiant Russians began a strong counter-offensive. Meanwhile a British force invaded Libya, and though unhappily at the cost of sending aid to Singapore, it gave promise of clearing the Axis out of Africa.

Meanwhile it was noticeable that the subjugated nations were more and more restless under German domination which to them had been terrific exploitation. Sabotage by the 

Czechs and the Norwegians continually harassed their oppressors, leading, of course, to a renewed wave of executions by the Gestapo. In occupied France hundreds of hostages were taken and scores of them shot. In Jugoslavia it was estimated that over 350,000 persons had been executed since the beginning of the German invasion. Yet still Serb resistance was unbroken. A guerrilla army of 80,000 harassed the German army with comparative impunity, and a reward of $1,000,000 was offered for the capture of the guerrilla leader. immense German army had to be spared from more active service simply for holding down the conquered.

An The War in the Far East It was only in the Far East that the news was less encouraging. In the Philippines the 

American and Filipino forces were compelled to yield in the end to superior forces, since for a time Japan held undisputed mastery of the sea and air. More serious was the danger of losing 

Singapore, which not only protected the Malay Peninsula, with its immense wealth in tin and rubber, and the Burma Road by which the Chinese received munitions, but also served as an outpost for the Dutch East Indies, rich in oil, tin, and rubber; while these, in turn, were the buttress for Australia. The British (especially the Australians) fought stubbornly to hold this great naval base, and meanwhile Dutch planes took a heavy toll of troop-laden Japanese transports. But the Japanese capture of

Yet, for the Allies, a hopeful portent was the establishment of complete co-operation between the United States, the British Empire, SUMMARY of Important Concepts 

Russia, and China. The war was to be waged on all fronts according to a carefully unified plan, Churchill even crossing the Atlantic in order to further such a movement. It should be added also that nearly all the Latin-American countries threw their weight, in different degrees of co-operation, on the side of the United States. More than ever now it was a world war. 

Looking Toward a Distant Goal

There was a long road ahead - "a long, hard war," as President Roosevelt put it. But even before the American participation he and Churchill, during their midsummer conference, had drawn up the bases of a new and better world. "The Atlantic Charter," as these were called, may be summarized as follows: (1) Disavowal of any territorial aggrandizement on the part of Great Britain and the 

United States; (2) territorial changes only in accordance with the wishes of the people concerned; (3) the right of all peoples to the government of their choice; (4) access on equal terms for all nations to the world's trade and any raw materials needed; (5) freedom of travel on the sea; (6) freedom from want and fear; (7) international collaboration in the interest of social justice; and (8) the disarmament of all aggressive nations. Beside the myth of a superior nation, the exploitation of the weak, the repression of the individual, and the barbaric cruelties of the political police, all of which were clearly implied in an Axis victory, these eight points shone forth as a beacon light in the darkness.

1. The underlying cause of the Second World War was Germany's determination to impose a "new order" on Europe. 

2. In the first year of fighting Germany inflicted crushing defeats on the allies of Great Britain. a. Germany used propaganda to good advantage. b. She had a greatly superior air force and had carried the mechanization of the army much farther than the democracies. c. Nevertheless, Germany, even when aided by Italy and other allies, was unable to destroy British seapower and to beat down British resistance.

3. Russia avoided war with Germany until the latter country attacked her in June, 1941. a. Meanwhile Russia had improved her frontiers and strengthened her forces. b. When war broke out, Germany encountered a fierce resistance and found it impossible to gain a quick victory. 

4. Japan, allied with the Axis, sought to reorganize eastern Asia in her own interest. 

5. The United States took positive action to insure the defeat of the Axis powers. a. The democracies were provided with materials of war, and precautions were taken to insure safe delivery. b. American rearmament was speeded up and necessary steps were taken to provide for hemisphere defense. c. Roosevelt and Churchill made plans for a post-war peace settlement. d. Japan's dastardly attack on Pearl Harbor led to open war.

3. Why was Germany able to crush Poland? What was the rôle of Russia? How were the Poles treated by the victors? Why? Why did Italy take no direct part in the struggle? 

4. What was Russia's policy toward the Baltic states? Toward Rumania? Why? Why was Russia successful? 1 5. Why was there little fighting on Germany's western front during the early months of the war?

11. How did the Axis powers strike at the British in the Mediterranean and in North Africa? Why? 

Why did the Axis powers seek an alliance with Japan? What were Japan's plans? Why?

19. What conditions for a post-war settlement were outlined by Roosevelt and Churchill in August, 1941? GAINING Skill A. Where to Get Information. The Second World War probably does not seem like "history" to you. 

You have read about it in newspapers and periodicals, have seen it pictured in newsreels and picture magazines, and have heard it described in radio bulletins and interpreted by news analysts. Until the war is over, you will largely continue to rely on these sources for information about the struggle. We recommend especially the weekly releases by the Foreign Policy Association which interpret current international events. See also the Headline Books and the World Affairs Pamphlets by this association.

SECOND WORLD WAR THE 

B. How to Locate and Organize Information. Your library probably will have files of magazines and newspapers for the period since September, 1939. In the case of bound volumes you will be able to use the index to help locate the materials in which you are interested. Articles on given topics may also be located through recent issues of Reader's Guide. In the case of single issues of magazines you will have to use the table of contents; for newspapers you simply will have to depend on the headlines to suggest pertinent materials.

You may want to keep a scrapbook on the war, or even a diary in which you record your impression of day-by-day happenings. Perhaps also you should save magazines and newspapers containing accounts of what is taking place. These materials may seem of little value to you now. But what will be your attitude forty years hence? Or that of your great-grandchildren eighty years from now? Perhaps your family treasures certain souvenirs because they once were the property of an ancestor who lived during the Civil War. Does your attitude toward such souvenirs throw any light on how records of this war will be regarded many years from now?

C. How to Evaluate Information. During the Second World War Americans have had an unparalleled opportunity to read and hear news coming from both sides. That is not to say, of course, that they always have obtained an accurate picture of what happened. The Axis countries have persistently distorted news in order to deceive their own and other peoples. Censorship often makes it impossible to obtain complete information quickly; indeed, such a policy is a wartime necessity. 

As a test of the accuracy of foreign news sources, keep a record of radio or news bulletins the veracity of which you can check. What slanting do you detect? Try to explain why in each case.

BIBLIOGRAPHY 

A. Reading for Information

A metropolitan newspaper, the New York Times, for example, reports foreign and domestic happenings in great detail; news magazines, such as Life, Time, and News Week, digest and interpret the news. 

Many magazines print articles of great value to anyone who wants to get a broader grasp of developments. You should examine recent issues of Reader's Digest, Harper's, Atlantic, The Nation, and so on, and decide for yourself what kind of magazine reading you enjoy. You will find the documents which relate to the entry of this country into the war in the magazine, Current History, for January, 1942. 

Space does not permit us to list all the publications of the Foreign Policy Association, but you may learn about them by writing to 22 East 38th Street, New York City. 

B. Reading for Other Points of View 

Since the American press is free, you will have little difficulty finding conflicting opinions about the war expressed in magazine articles, editorials, letters to the editor, and so on. Choose some topic of current interest and see what is being written about it. Often you will find sharply conflicting points of view graphically expressed in cartoons. What do you conceive to be the advantages of a free press? 

C. Reading for Pleasure

Although war is a grim business, soldiers are not as a rule gloomy. Indeed, one of the ways in which soldiers divert themselves is to make light of their experiences in songs, dramatic skits, and cartoons. If you know a veteran of the First World War, he may be able to show you copies of newspapers published during 1917-1918 by the soldiers themselves. Doubtless you will have little difficulty getting similar materials from men in the service during the present struggle. You will then be able to compare the humor of an earlier period with that of today. CL43
